2:
'It comes to be reckoned only as a great mass of water,' etc. In such passages, it is called 'khandha' in the sense of a mass (rāsi). Indeed, a small amount of water is not called a mass of water (udakakkhandha); only a large amount is so called. Similarly, a small amount of dust is not called a mass of dust (rajakkhandha), a few cows are not called a herd of cows (gavakkhandha), a small force is not called an army (balakkhandha), and a small amount of merit is not called a mass of merit (puññakkhandha). Only a large amount of dust is called a mass of dust; only many cows and so on are called a herd of cows, an army, or a mass of merit.

In such passages as 'the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha),' it is called 'khandha' because of quality (guṇa). In the passage, 'The Blessed One saw a great log of wood (dārukkhandha) being carried along by the current of the river Ganges,' it is called 'khandha' because of designation (paṇṇatti). In such passages as 'Whatever mind, mentation, heart... consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha),' it is called 'khandha' because of usage (ruḷhī).

In this context (of the five aggregates), however, the meaning of 'mass' is intended. For the meaning of 'khandha' is the meaning of a heap, the meaning of a group, the meaning of a collection, the meaning of a mass. Therefore, the aggregates should be understood as having the characteristic of a mass. It is also appropriate to say it has the meaning of a portion (koṭṭhāsa). In the world, when people are asked to pay a debt they have taken, they say, 'We will pay in two portions (two khandhas),' or 'We will pay in three portions (three khandhas).' Thus, it is also appropriate to say, 'The aggregates have the characteristic of a portion.' In this way, in this context, the aggregate of form means a mass of form, a portion of form. The aggregate of feeling means a mass of feeling, a portion of feeling. In this manner, the meaning of the aggregate of perception and so on should be understood.

To this extent, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One showed the aggregate of form by grouping together the entire mass of form, which is divided into eleven instances such as past, future, and present, and which has such divisions as the 25 portions of form and the 96 portions of form, described as 'the four great elements and the derivative form dependent on the four great elements.' He showed the aggregate of feeling by grouping together the entire mass of feeling belonging to the four planes, divided into those same eleven instances as 'pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.' He showed the aggregate of perception by grouping together the entire mass of perception belonging to the four planes, divided into those same eleven instances as 'perception born of eye-contact... perception born of mind-contact.' He showed the aggregate of volitional formations by grouping together the entire mass of volition belonging to the four planes, divided into those same eleven instances as 'volition born of eye-contact... volition born of mind-contact' as the aggregate of volitional formations.
3:
The collection of consciousness belonging to the four planes, classified into these eleven bases—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-element, and mind-consciousness element—is collectively shown as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).

Furthermore, in this exposition of the aggregates, all form (rūpa) produced by the four causes is called the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). The feeling (vedanā) arising together with the eighty-nine types of consciousness, starting with the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere, is called the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Perception (saññā) is called the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). The fifty mental factors (cetasikas) starting with contact (phassa) are called the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). The eighty-nine types of consciousness are called the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Thus, the delimitation of phenomena (dhamma) within the five aggregates should be understood.

## 1. Rūpakkhandhaniddesa

Now, in order to show those aggregates such as the aggregate of form by classifying them in detail, [the Buddha] said, "Among them, what is the aggregate of form?" and so on. In that text, "among them" (tattha) means among those five aggregates. "What" (katamo) is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandha) is the indication of the phenomenon being questioned. Now, wishing to classify that aggregate of form in detail, he said, "Whatever form," and so on. There, the words "whatever" (yaṃ kiñci) express the meaning of including [all] without exception. The word "form" (rūpaṃ) expresses the meaning of excluding the inclusion of other phenomena. Thus, by these two words, the inclusion of form without exception is made.

In that context, for what reason is it called "rūpa"? It is called "rūpa" because of the meaning of being deformed (ruppana). Regarding this meaning, the Blessed One said:

"Monks, for what reason do you say 'rūpa'? Monks, it is called 'rūpa' because it is deformed (ruppati). By what is it deformed? It is deformed by cold, it is deformed by heat, it is deformed by hunger, it is deformed by thirst, it is deformed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. Monks, because it is deformed, it is called 'rūpa'."

In that text, "what" (kiṃ) is a question about the cause, meaning "For what reason is it called 'rūpa'?" or "For what reason is that phenomenon named 'rūpa'?" In the word "ruppatīti," the word "iti" indicates the cause, meaning "Because it is deformed, it is called 'rūpa'." "Ruppati" means it is changed, affected, oppressed, or broken. Thus, by this much text, it is called "rūpa" in the sense of being deformed. It is also appropriate to say it is called "rūpa" because it has the characteristic of being deformed. This is because this form has the characteristic of being deformed.
4:
In the words "it is deformed by cold" and so on, deformation by cold is first evident in the Lokantarika hell. Between every three world-systems (cakkavāḷas), there is one Lokantarika hell, eight thousand yojanas in extent. Below that hell, there is no earth; above, there is no light from the moon, sun, lamps, or gems, and it is always in total darkness. The beings born there have a body (attabhāva) three gāvutas in size. Like bats, they cling to the base of the mountains with long, broad nails and hang upside down. While crawling about, when they come within reach of one another, they think, "We have found food," and in their exertion for that food, they tumble over and fall into the water that supports the world. When the cold wind blows, they break off like ripe madhuka fruits and fall into the water. As soon as they fall into the water, because of the extremely salty (extremely cold) water, their skin, sinews, flesh, and bones break and perish; they dissolve with a "phat-phat" sound like a lump of flour falling into hot oil. Thus, deformation by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. Even in regions such as the Mahisaka country where it is cold with falling snow, this deformation by cold is indeed evident. In those places, beings reach the end of their lives as their bodies crack and break due to the force of the cold.

Deformation by heat is evident in the Great Avīci Hell. There, when they are made to lie down on the glowing iron ground and subjected to the fivefold bonding and so on, beings experience great suffering.

Deformation by hunger is evident in the realm of the petas and during times of famine. In the realm of the petas, for the interval between two or three Buddhas, beings never get to take even a little food with their hands and put it into their mouths. The inside of their bellies is like a hollow tree on fire. In times of famine, there is no limit to the number of people who die without getting even a little sour gruel.

Deformation by thirst is evident among the Kālakañjika asuras and others. Among those asuras, for the interval between two or three Buddhas, beings are unable to get even a drop of water to moisten their hearts or their tongues. Even when they go to a river thinking, "We shall drink water," the river becomes a mere sandy plain. Even when they run into the great ocean, the great ocean becomes a stone surface. Those beings wander about, parched and oppressed by intense suffering.
5:
It is said that a certain Kālakanjika Asura, unable to endure his thirst, descended into the great Ganges River, which was one league deep and wide. Wherever that Asura went, the water vanished and smoke arose, and it was as if he were walking on a heated stone slab. While he wandered here and there hearing the sound of water, the night turned to dawn. Then, in the early morning, thirty monks on their alms round saw him and asked, "Good man, who are you?"

"Venerable sirs, I am a peta," he replied. "What are you searching for?" they asked. "Venerable sirs, I am searching for drinking water," he replied. "This Ganges River is full of water; do you not see it?" they asked. "Venerable sirs, it is not possible for me (it is of no use to me)," he replied. "If so, lie on your back on the bank of the Ganges; we will pour water into your mouth," they said. 

The peta lay on his back on the sandy bank. The monks took out their thirty alms bowls, repeatedly fetched water, and poured it into his mouth. While they were doing this, the time for their alms round drew near. Therefore, they said, "Good man, it is time for our alms round. Have you received at least a satisfying amount of water?"

The peta replied, "Venerable sirs, if even half a handful of water from the thirty bowls poured by the thirty venerable ones has reached my throat, may I never be released from this peta state!" Thus, the transformation (suffering) due to thirst is evident in the realm of petas.

Transformation due to gadflies and so on is evident in places where gadflies, mosquitoes, and such are abundant. Here, *ḍaṃsa* refers to gadflies or mosquitoes of a brownish color. *Makasa* refers to mosquitoes themselves. *Vāta* should be understood by way of internal winds, back winds, and so on. Wind diseases arising in the body destroy the hands, feet, back, etc.; they cause blindness, hunchback, the need to move with a wheeled stool, or convulsions.

*Ātapa* means the heat of the sun. Transformation due to that heat is evident in places like sandy deserts. It is said that a woman in a sandy desert was left behind by a caravan at night. When the sun rose during the day and the sand became hot, being unable to set foot on it, she took the basket from her head and stepped on it. Gradually, as the basket also became hot and she could not stand on it, she spread a cloth over it and stepped on that. When that cloth also became intensely hot, she laid her young son, whom she was carrying in her arms, face down and stepped on the crying child; together with him, she died in that very place due to the intensity of the heat.

*Sarisapa* refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by creeping. Transformation due to their touch should be understood by way of the bites of venomous snakes and so on.
6:
Now, in order to show all matter—comprising twenty-five groups and ninety-six divisions—encompassed by the phrase "whatever material form" (*yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ*) by classifying it into portions such as the past, He said: "past, future, present."

After that, in order to show that same matter by classifying it into the four dyads such as the internal dyad, He said: "whether internal or external," and so on. After that, in order to show all this matter, which is completely encompassed by these eleven phrases, by collecting it into a single mass, He said: "all that matter collectively," and so on.

In that passage, "*tad-ekajjhaṃ*" means that matter collectively. "*Abhisaññūhitvā*" means having well-collected it with wisdom. "*Abhisaṅkhipitvā*" means having summarized it. The meaning is this: all this matter of the aforementioned types, having been made into a group by wisdom in the single nature characterized by being affected (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*), is called the "aggregate of matter" (*rūpakkhandha*). By this, it is shown that all matter is called the aggregate of matter because it enters into the state of a group in the characteristic of being affected. Indeed, there is no so-called aggregate of matter other than matter itself. Just as with matter, so too with feeling and the rest, because they enter into the state of a group in the characteristics of being felt and so on (they are known as the aggregate of feeling, etc.). There are no so-called aggregates of feeling and so on other than feeling and the rest.

Now, wishing to show the matter placed in each category by analyzing it separately, He said: "Therein, what is past matter?" and so on. In that passage, "*tattha*" (therein) is a locative case referring to the matrix (*mātikā*) placed in the eleven categories. This is the meaning: in the matrix established by the method of "past, future, present," etc., what is that which is called "past matter"? By this method, the meaning in all questions should be understood.

The terms "past, ceased," and so on have already been stated in the commentary on the classification of the past triad in the *Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa* (DhsA. 1044). The phrase "the four great elements also" is a demonstration of the nature of the matter called past. Just as here, the meaning should be understood in all places. By this, He shows this: past matter is both the great elements and the derived matter (*upādā-rūpa*) produced depending on the great elements. Future matter... (omitted)... far and near matter (are the same). This is because there is no matter other than the great elements and the matter existing depending on the great elements.

Another method: "encompassed by the past portion" (*atītaṃsena saṅgahitaṃ*) means encompassed only by the past portion, having come to be counted in this very portion. How? "The four great elements and the four (derived matters depending on the four great elements)."
7:
The meaning of "materiality derived from the great elements" (upādāyarūpa) should be understood thus in all terms. The descriptive terms (niddesa) for the future and present also have the meanings already stated below.

This classification of past, future, and present is twofold: according to the Suttanta method (pariyāya) and according to the Abhidhamma description (niddesa). In the Suttanta method, it is defined by existence (bhava). Indeed, materiality produced in past existences starting from rebirth (paṭisandhi)—whether in the immediately preceding life or a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons ago—is all called "past." Materiality to be produced in future existences starting from death (cuti)—whether in the immediately following life or a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons ago—is all called "future." Materiality occurring between death and rebirth is called "present." In the Abhidhamma description, however, it is defined by the moment (khaṇa). There are three moments of materiality: arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga). Materiality that has ceased upon reaching these three moments—whether immediately ceased or ceased a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons ago—is all called "past." Materiality that has not yet reached these three moments—whether not yet reached by a single mind-moment (cittakkhaṇa) or not yet reached in a hundred thousand koṭis of aeons in the future—is all called "future." Materiality currently reaching these three moments is called "present." In this context, although this classification is the Suttanta Classification, it should be understood that past, future, and present materiality are pointed out here according to the Abhidhamma description.

Alternatively, this materiality is called "past" in four ways: by period (addhā), continuity (santati), occasion (samaya), and moment (khaṇa). Likewise for the future and present. By period (addhā), for an individual in a single existence, materiality before rebirth is past, after death is future, and between the two is present. By continuity (santati), materiality produced by a homogeneous temperature (utu) or a homogeneous nutriment (āhāra), even if occurring in succession, is called present. Materiality produced by a heterogeneous temperature or nutriment before that is past, and after that is future. Mind-produced materiality within a single cognitive process (vīthi), a single impulsion (javana), or a single attainment (samāpatti) is present. Materiality before that is past, after that is future. For kamma-produced materiality (kammaja), there is no distinction of past etc. by individual continuity. However, its distinction as past etc. should be understood by way of the temperature-produced, nutriment-produced, and mind-produced materiality that support it. By occasion (samaya), materiality occurring in succession within a single muhutta, morning, evening, night, day, and so on, is called present. Materiality before that is past, after that is future. By way of moment...
8:
...matter included within the triad of moments such as arising is called "present." Matter prior to that is past; after that is future.

Furthermore, matter whose function of the [producing] cause and [supporting] condition has passed is past. Matter whose function of the producing cause (janaka-hetu) is finished but whose function of the supporting condition (upatthambhaka-paccaya) is not yet finished is present. Matter that has not yet reached either function is future. Or, matter occurring at the moment of its own function is present. Matter prior to that is past; after that is future. Among these statements, only the discourse on moments (khana), etc., is the literal sense (nippariyāya); the rest are figurative (sappariyāya). Among these, the literal discourse is intended here. The terms of the exposition of the Internal Dyad (Ajjhatta-duka) also have the meanings already stated below in the exposition of the Internal Triad (Ajjhatta-tika). Terms such as "gross" (oḷārika) have the meanings already stated in the commentary on the Section on Matter (Rūpa-kaṇḍa).

In the exposition of the Inferior Dyad (Hīna-duka), the phrase "of those various beings" (tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ) is the genitive case used for many beings. If the Teacher had taught by naming each individual, saying "of another, and of another," He might have had to teach for a whole day or even for a hundred thousand aeons. Therefore, the Teacher, encompassing all beings without exception with just two words, said "of those various beings." By this much, the indication of every "other" is accomplished. "Despised" (uññāta) means recognized as low-class. "Disregarded" (avaññāta) means known with contempt, not even recognized as "matter." "Rejected" (hīḷita) means cast away or discarded because it is not worth taking; some also say it means "loathed." "Insulted" (paribhūta) means overwhelmed and belittled by speech, as in "What is the use of this matter?" "Disregarded" (acittīkata) means not respected. "Inferior" (hīna) means wretched. "Considered inferior" (hīnamata) means known as inferior, regarded as wretched. "Conventionally inferior" (hīnasammata) means what is conventionally regarded as inferior in the world, or what is regarded as [good] by inferior beings, just as dung is [regarded as good] by dung-eating creatures. "Unpleasant" (aniṭṭha) means unloved and disliked, or not sought after for the sake of acquisition. Even if someone were to seek it, let them seek it; nevertheless, the name of this object is simply "unpleasant." "Unlovely" (akanta) means undesired or lacking in splendor. "Disagreeable" (amanāpa) means not reaching the heart. Such an object is not taken to heart. Alternatively, that which pleases or increases (appāyati) the mind (mana) is "agreeable" (manāpa); that which is not agreeable is "disagreeable" (amanāpa).

Another method: It is "unpleasant" (aniṭṭha) because it is devoid of prosperity. Among kamma-produced matter, that which is produced by unwholesome kamma is definitely unpleasant. It is "unlovely" (akanta) because it is not a cause of happiness. It is "disagreeable" (amanāpa) because it is a cause of suffering. The words "visible forms, sounds," etc., are an indication of its nature. In this term, the five cords of sensual pleasure that are unpleasant by way of being produced by unwholesome kamma are analyzed. There is no such thing as unpleasant matter produced by wholesome kamma; all matter produced by wholesome kamma is pleasant (iṭṭha).

The exposition of the term "superior" (paṇīta) should be understood by the method opposite to what has been said for the term "inferior." In this term, the five cords of sensual pleasure that are pleasant by way of being produced by wholesome kamma are analyzed. Matter produced by wholesome kamma...
9:
In matter produced by wholesome kamma, there is no such thing as an undesirable (aniṭṭha) object; everything is only desirable (iṭṭha). Just as there is the state of being desirable or undesirable in kamma-born matter, so it is in matter produced by temperature (utu) and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that in this dyad (duka), desirable objects and undesirable objects are analyzed separately. This is the uniform explanation of the ancient Teachers in the Commentaries. However, a Vitandavādī (sophist) says: "There is no such thing as desirable and undesirable objects separately distinguished; it is only spoken of according to the preference (ruci) of various individuals."

As it was said: "Great King, I declare that among the five cords of sensual pleasure, the pleasing object is the supreme. Great King, those very same forms are pleasing to some and unpleasing to others. Great King, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches are likewise pleasing to some and unpleasing to others." In this way, some people enjoy and delight in those very same forms and so forth, giving rise to greed for that object. Others, however, become angry and offended, giving rise to hatred for that object. For some, they are desirable (iṭṭha), lovely (kantā), and pleasing (manāpā), while for others, they are undesirable (aniṭṭha), unlovely (akantā), and unpleasing (amanāpā). Some take those objects from the "right side" (favorably) as "desirable, lovely, and pleasing," while others take them from the "left side" (unfavorably) as "undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasing." Therefore, [the Vitandavādī argues] there is no such thing as desirable and undesirable objects separately distinguished. For those living in the border regions, even earthworms are desirable, lovely, and pleasing, whereas for those living in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), they are extremely loathsome. For those in the Middle Country, peacock meat and such are desirable, but for others, they are extremely loathsome.

That Vitandavādī should be asked: "Do you say that there is no such thing as desirable and undesirable objects separately distinguished?" If he answers, "Yes, I say so," then after making him confirm this three times, the question should be asked: "Is Nibbāna desirable or undesirable?" If he is a knowledgeable person, he will answer, "It is desirable." Even if he does not answer, let it be. Nibbāna is indeed exclusively desirable (ekanta-iṭṭha). When the virtues of Nibbāna are being told, does not a certain person get angry and ask, "You speak of the virtues of Nibbāna; are there the five cords of sensual pleasure there, complete with food, drink, flowers, scents, ointments, beds, and clothing?" and when told "No," he says, "Enough of your Nibbāna!" and closes both ears in anger while the virtues of Nibbāna are being told? According to that person's wish, let Nibbāna be called "undesirable" in your doctrine.
10:
However, this should not be taken in that way. This is because that person speaks with a perverted perception (saññā). Due to the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa), the very same object may be desirable to one person and undesirable to another.

Desirable and undesirable objects are indeed separately distinguished. If asked, "By whose standard are they distinguished?", they are distinguished by the standard of the average being (majjhimaka-satta). This distinction is not made according to the standard of extremely powerful persons such as King Mahāsammata, the Universal Monarch Mahāsudassana, or King Dhammāsoka. To such kings, even an object similar to those in the celestial realms may appear unpleasing. Nor is it distinguished according to the standard of extremely poor persons who find it difficult to obtain food and drink. To them, even scraps of broken rice or the juice of putrid meat seem extremely sweet and like ambrosia. However, the distinction is made according to the standard of average persons such as accountants (gaṇaka), high ministers, wealthy merchants, householders, and traders, who obtain desirable and undesirable objects from time to time. Such persons are indeed able to define what is desirable and what is undesirable.

However, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga said: "Desirable and undesirable are defined only by the power of the resultant (vipāka), not by the power of the impulsion (javana). The impulsion, due to the power of perverted perception, may be attached to a desirable object or be repelled by a desirable object; it may be attached to an undesirable object or be repelled by an undesirable object." This [desirable or undesirable nature] is definitely defined only by the power of the resultant. It is not possible to deceive the resultant consciousness. If the object is desirable, a wholesome resultant consciousness (kusala-vipāka) arises. If it is undesirable, an unwholesome resultant consciousness (akusala-vipāka) arises. Even though those with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) may close their eyes or feel displeasure upon seeing the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or noble objects like the Great Stūpa (Mahācetiya), and even though they may plug their ears upon hearing the sound of the Dhamma, their eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness are only wholesome resultants.

Even though dung-eating pigs and the like become joyful upon smelling the scent of dung, thinking "We shall get to eat," their eye-consciousness in seeing the dung, their nose-consciousness in smelling its scent, and their tongue-consciousness in experiencing its taste are only unwholesome resultants. And even if a pig that has been tied up and made to lie on an excellent bed squeals, displeasure (domanassa) arises only in its impulsion (javana) due to perverted perception; its body-consciousness, however, is only a wholesome resultant. Why? Because the object is desirable.

Furthermore, the state of being desirable or undesirable should also be understood by way of the sense-doors. For instance, dung, which is like soft mud and pleasant to the touch, is undesirable at the eye-door and nose-door, but it is desirable at the body-door. For the Universal Monarch...
11:
For one who is struck by the gem-treasure of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) or terrified by a golden spike, those gem-treasures and golden spikes are agreeable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) at the eye-door, but at the body-door, they are disagreeable objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa) because they cause great suffering. Why is this? Because they produce great pain. Thus, it should be understood that the agreeable and the disagreeable are determined solely by the resultant (vipāka).

In the phrase "Or whatever [other form]" (taṃ taṃ vā pana), the method mentioned below should not be considered. This is because the Blessed One does not destroy what is conventionally pleasing (sammuti-manāpa), but He does destroy what is personally pleasing (puggala-manāpa). Therefore, in accordance with that phrase "Or whatever [other form]", the states of being inferior or superior should be understood by way of comparison. Indeed, the form of beings in hell is extremely inferior. Compared to that, the form of Nāgas and Garuḷas among animals is superior. Their form is inferior compared to the form of hungry ghosts (petas), which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of country-folk, which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of village-headmen, which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of district-governors, which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of local kings, which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of a Universal Monarch, which is superior. His too is inferior compared to the form of earth-dwelling deities (bhumma-deva), which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of the deities of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), which is superior. Theirs too is inferior compared to the form of the deities of the Realm of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa), which is superior... and so on... but the form of the Akaniṭṭha Brahmās is the most superior, having reached the summit.

In the exposition of the dyad of the far (dūraduka-niddesa), the forms such as the female faculty (itthindriya) have already been analyzed below (in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa). However, in this dyad, subtle form (sukhuma-rūpa) is called "far" (dūre) because it is difficult to grasp and its characteristics are difficult to penetrate by wisdom. Gross form (oḷārika-rūpa) is called "near" (santike) because it is easy to grasp and its characteristics are easy to penetrate. At the conclusion of the section on the nutriment of solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), it is not yet concluded with "this is called form that is far." Why? Because "far" is of two kinds: far by characteristic and far by location (okāsa). Among these, form that is not yet stated as far by characteristic is intended to be shown as far by location; therefore, the phrase beginning with "Or whatever other [form]" (yaṃ vā panaññampi) is spoken. The same method applies to the exposition of the term "near" (santike). In that context, "not near" (anāsanna) means not close; "not proximate" (anupakaṭṭha) means beyond twelve cubits; "far" (dūre) means at a distance; "not near" (asantike) means not in the vicinity. "This is called form that is far" means that the fifteen kinds of subtle form are far by characteristic, while the ten kinds of gross form are called far by location through the influence of the "whatever" (yevāpanaka) clause. The exposition of the term "near" is quite clear in meaning.
12:
"This is called form that is near"—these ten kinds of gross form are near by characteristic, while the fifteen kinds of subtle form are called near by location through the influence of the "whatever" (yevāpanaka) clause. From what distance is form called "near" by way of location? From what distance is it called "far"? Speaking in ordinary terms, the hearing range (savanūpacāra) is twelve cubits. Form within those twelve cubits is called "near" (santike), and form beyond that is called "far" (dūre). Among them, when subtle form is far, it is far both by characteristic and by location; but when it is near, it is near only by location, not by characteristic. When gross form is near, it is near both by characteristic and by location; but when it is far, it is far only by location, not by characteristic.

In the phrase "Or whatever [other form]" (taṃ taṃ vါ pana), the method mentioned below should not be considered. For the distinction was already made below. Here, however, it does not distinguish the far by characteristic, but only the far by location. Here, the far and the near are shown relatively, depending on one thing or another. Indeed, one's own form is called "near," while the form of another, even if inside one's own womb, is called "far." The form of one inside the womb is near [to themselves], while the form of one standing outside is far. The form of one sleeping on the same couch is near, while the form of one standing on the porch is far. Form inside the precinct is near, while form outside the precinct is far. Form inside the monastery is near, while form outside the monastery is far. Form inside the boundary (sīmā) is near, while form outside the boundary is far. Form inside the village limits is near, while form outside the village limits is far. Form inside the district is near, while form outside the district is far. Form inside the kingdom's borders is near, while form outside the kingdom's borders is far. Form inside the ocean is near, while form outside the ocean is far. Form inside the world-system (cakkavāḷa) is near, while form outside the world-system is far.

## This is the Exposition of the Aggregate of Form.

## 2. Exposition of the Aggregate of Feeling

In the exposition of the aggregate of feeling and so on, I shall omit what is similar to what was said below and explain only what is new. By the words "Whatever feeling" (yā kāci vedanā), all feelings belonging to the four planes are included. The words "pleasant feeling" (sukhā vedanā) and so on, which describe feeling by way of the past etc., according to its nature...
13:
The words beginning with 'pleasant feeling' (sukha vedanā) are spoken to show the nature of feelings indicated by way of the past and so forth. In that context, pleasant feeling is both bodily and mental. Painful feeling (dukkha vedanā) is likewise of two kinds. As for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā), it is said indirectly (pariyāyena) to be 'both bodily and mental' with reference to the sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) of the eye and so forth. Among those feelings, all bodily feelings belong only to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). Likewise, mental painful feeling is also of the sense sphere. Mental pleasant feeling, however, occurs in the three planes. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling occurs in all four planes. The past and other states of that feeling in all its aspects should be understood by way of continuity (santati) and by way of moments (khana) and so forth.

In that context, by way of continuity, feelings included within a single cognitive process (vīthi), a single impulsion (javana), or a single attainment (samāpatti), and those occurring in association with a single kind of object, are present. Those occurring before that are past; those occurring after are future. By way of moments and so forth, a feeling included within the three moments (sub-moments), situated between the preceding and succeeding limits, and currently performing its own function, is present. Those occurring before that are past; those occurring after are future. Among these, it should be understood that this exposition (niddesa) of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is made with reference to the past and other states by way of moments and so forth.

In the exposition of the gross and the subtle (oḷārika-sukhuma-niddesa), the words 'unwholesome feeling' (akusala vedanā) and so forth are spoken to show the state of being gross or subtle by way of kind (jāti). The words 'painful feeling is gross' and so forth are spoken to show it by way of nature (sabhāva). The words 'the feeling of one not in attainment' and so forth are spoken by way of the person (puggala). The words 'with taints' (sāsava) and so forth are spoken to show the state of being gross or subtle by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Among those, unwholesome feelings are gross because they are accompanied by the fever [of defilements] and because they have painful results. Wholesome feelings are subtle because they are without the fever and because they have pleasant results. Indeterminate (abyākata) feelings are subtle because they are without effort and because they are without result. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross because they are with effort and with result. Indeterminate feelings are subtle in the same manner as already stated.

Painful feelings are gross because they are disagreeable and because they are painful. Pleasant feelings are subtle because they are agreeable and because they are easy to endure. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle because they are peaceful and because they are sublime. Both pleasant and painful feelings are gross because they are disturbing and because they are pervading. Indeed, pleasant feeling also disturbs and pervades. Likewise does painful feeling. For when pleasant feeling arises, it arises as if shaking, stirring, moistening, massaging, and overwhelming the entire body, like being sprinkled with a jar of cold water. When painful feeling arises, it arises as if thrusting a red-hot ploughshare into the body, or as if burning the outside of the body with a grass torch. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, however, is subtle in the same manner as already stated. The feeling of one who is not in attainment is gross because it is scattered among various objects...
14:
(The feeling of one not in attainment) is gross. The feeling of one in attainment is subtle because it occurs only in a single object-sign (ekatta-nimitta). Feeling with taints (sāsava) is gross because it is a cause for the arising of taints. The occurrence of taints is indeed definitely gross. Taintless (anāsava) feeling is subtle by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

In that context (of classifying feelings as gross or subtle), a certain person is neither skilled in the Wholesome Triad (Kusala Tika) nor in the Feeling Triad (Vedanā Tika). Thinking, 'I will protect the Wholesome Triad,' he destroys the Feeling Triad; thinking, 'I will protect the Feeling Triad,' he destroys the Wholesome Triad. Another person, thinking, 'I will protect the Triad,' destroys the distinction of planes (bhūmantara). Another does not destroy it. How? It is stated in the Feeling Triad: 'Pleasant and painful feelings are gross; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle.' A certain person rejects that, saying: 'Not all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are subtle. For that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Among those, the wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross, and the indeterminate feeling is subtle. Why? Because it appears thus in the text of the Wholesome Triad.' In this way, although the Wholesome Triad is protected, the Feeling Triad is destroyed.

Regarding the statement in the Wholesome Triad, 'Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feeling is subtle,' a certain person rejects it, saying: 'Not all indeterminate feelings are subtle. For that indeterminate feeling is pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Among those, the pleasant and painful are gross, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant is subtle. Why? Because it appears thus in the text of the Feeling Triad.' In this way, although the Feeling Triad is protected, the Wholesome Triad is destroyed. However, one who explains grossness and subtleness by the characteristic of the Wholesome Triad for wholesome things and so forth, without disregarding the Feeling Triad where the Wholesome Triad occurs, and by the characteristic of the Feeling Triad for pleasant things and so forth, without disregarding the Wholesome Triad where the Feeling Triad occurs, is said not to destroy (the Triads).

Also, regarding the statement in the Wholesome Triad, 'Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feeling is subtle,' a certain person says: 'Even if it is a wholesome supramundane feeling, it is called gross; even if a resultant feeling is associated with at least the two sets of fivefold consciousness, it is called subtle.' Such a person, by making the peaceful and sublime supramundane feeling gross, and by making the rootless, inferior, and dull feeling associated with the two sets of fivefold consciousness subtle, while thinking 'I will protect the Triad,' is said to destroy the distinction of planes. One who explains by associating the wholesome in each plane only with the resultant of that respective plane is said not to destroy it. In this regard, this is the method: sense-sphere wholesome is gross; sense-sphere resultant is subtle.
15:
Wholesome feelings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and the supramundane (lokuttara) are called gross (oḷārika). Resultant feelings of the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane are called subtle (sukhuma). A person who teaches according to this method is said not to destroy the boundaries of the planes.

However, the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷanāga said: "The distinction of gross and subtle should not be drawn in unwholesome (akusala) states, for unwholesome is exclusively gross. Nor should it be drawn in supramundane states, for the supramundane is exclusively subtle." This statement was brought and reported to the Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya, saying, "The Elder has spoken thus."

Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya said: "When the Fully Enlightened One reached the Abhidhamma teaching, there is no place where a method should be given for even one or two words in the Pali text where it was not given; there is no place where a method should be applied where it was not applied. In this Dispensation, some people, wandering around saying 'I am a teacher,' hesitate to draw the distinction of gross and subtle in unwholesome states. But the Fully Enlightened One drew the distinction of gross and subtle even in the supramundane." Having said this, he cited this Sutta: "Therein, venerable sir, that practice which is painful and of slow direct-knowledge is said to be inferior in both ways—because it is painful and because it is slow" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.152). In this Sutta, the four practices are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

Regarding the phrase "taṃ taṃ vā pana," the previous method should not be considered; it should be explained only by the power of that "taṃ taṃ vā pana." Unwholesome feeling is of two kinds: associated with greed (lobha) and associated with hatred (dosa). Among them, the feeling associated with hatred is gross, and the feeling associated with greed is subtle. The feeling associated with hatred is also of two kinds: fixed (niyata) and unfixed (aniyata). Among them, the fixed is gross, and the unfixed is subtle. The fixed is also of two kinds: those lasting for an aeon (kappaṭṭhitika) and those not lasting for an aeon (nokappaṭṭhitika). Among them, the aeon-lasting is gross, and the non-aeon-lasting is subtle. The aeon-lasting is also of two kinds: unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and prompted (sasaṅkhārika), where the unprompted is gross and the prompted is subtle. The feeling associated with greed is also of two kinds: associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-sampayutta) and dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhi-vippayutta). Among them, the associated with wrong view is gross, and the dissociated from wrong view is subtle. The associated with wrong view is also of two kinds: fixed and unfixed, where the fixed is gross and the unfixed is subtle. That fixed is also of two kinds: unprompted and prompted, where the unprompted is gross and the prompted is subtle.

In brief, regarding unwholesome states, that feeling which gives many results (vipāka) is gross, and that which gives few results is subtle. Regarding wholesome (kusala) states, however, the feeling with few results is gross,
16:
and the feeling with many results is subtle. Among the four types of wholesome states, the wholesome feeling of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) is gross, and the wholesome feeling of the fine-material sphere is subtle. That wholesome feeling of the fine-material sphere is also gross compared to the wholesome feeling of the immaterial sphere, which is subtle. That wholesome feeling of the immaterial sphere is also gross compared to the supramundane wholesome feeling, which is subtle. This is the method shown without differentiation among the planes.

To show by differentiation: wholesome feeling of the sense sphere is of three kinds: consisting in giving (dāna-maya), consisting in virtue (sīla-maya), and consisting in mental development (bhāvanā-maya). Among these three, the feeling consisting in giving is gross, and the feeling consisting in virtue is subtle. That feeling consisting in virtue is also gross compared to the feeling consisting in mental development, which is subtle. That feeling consisting in mental development is also of two kinds: two-rooted (duhetuka) and three-rooted (tihetuka). Among them, the two-rooted feeling is gross, and the three-rooted feeling is subtle. The three-rooted feeling is also of two kinds by way of prompted and unprompted: the prompted is gross, and the unprompted is subtle. In the fine-material sphere, the wholesome feeling of the first jhāna is gross, and the wholesome feeling of the second jhāna is subtle ... [etc.] ... the wholesome feeling of the fourth jhāna is subtle. That wholesome feeling of the fourth jhāna is also gross compared to the wholesome feeling of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), which is subtle. The wholesome feeling of the sphere of infinite space is gross ... [etc.] ... the wholesome feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is subtle. That wholesome feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also gross compared to the feeling associated with insight (vipassanā), which is subtle. That feeling associated with insight is also gross compared to the feeling associated with the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), which is subtle. That feeling associated with the path of stream-entry is also gross ... [etc.] ... the feeling associated with the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga) is subtle.

Among the four types of resultants (vipāka), the resultant feeling of the sense sphere is gross, and the resultant feeling of the fine-material sphere is subtle. That resultant feeling of the fine-material sphere is also gross ... [etc.] ... the supramundane resultant feeling is subtle. This is the method shown without differentiation.

To show by differentiation: among the resultant feelings of the sense sphere, there are rootless (ahetuka) resultants and rooted (sahetuka) resultants. Among rooted resultants, there are two-rooted and three-rooted. Among these, the rootless feeling is gross, and the rooted feeling is subtle. That rooted feeling is gross if it is two-rooted, and subtle if it is three-rooted. Among those three-rooted resultant feelings, the prompted is gross, and the unprompted is subtle. The resultant feeling of the first jhāna is gross, and the resultant feeling of the second jhāna is subtle ... [etc.] ... the resultant feeling of the fourth jhāna is subtle. That resultant feeling of the fourth jhāna is also gross compared to the resultant feeling of the sphere of infinite space, which is subtle. That resultant feeling of the sphere of infinite space is also gross ... [etc.] ... the resultant feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle. That resultant feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also gross compared to the feeling of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), which is subtle. That feeling of the fruit of stream-entry is also gross compared to the fruit of once-returning ... [etc.] ... the feeling of the fruit of arahantship (arahatta-phala) is subtle.
17:
Among the three functional feelings, the functional feeling of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kiriya-vedanā) is gross, and the functional feeling of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-kiriya-vedanā) is subtle. That functional feeling of the fine-material sphere is also gross, while the functional feeling of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara-kiriya-vedanā) is subtle. Thus, it should first be understood without differentiation. By way of differentiation, however, in the sense-sphere functional feeling which is divided by way of rootless and so on, the rootless functional feeling (ahetuka-kiriya-vedanā) is gross, and the functional feeling with roots (sahetuka-kiriya-vedanā) is subtle. That functional feeling with roots is also gross if it is two-rooted (duhetuka), and subtle if it is three-rooted (tihetuka). Among those three-rooted functional feelings, the prompted (sasaṅkhārika) feeling is gross, and the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) feeling is subtle. The functional feeling in the first jhāna is gross, and in the second jhāna it is subtle. That second jhāna feeling is also gross, while in the third... [Pe]... in the fourth jhāna it is subtle. That fourth jhāna feeling is also gross, and the functional feeling of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-kiriya-vedanā) is subtle. That feeling of the base of infinite space is also gross, and so on up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-kiriya-vedanā), which is subtle. Whichever feeling is gross is inferior. Whichever feeling is subtle is superior.

In the explanation of the Distant Dyad (dūra-duka-niddesa), unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings because of its dissimilar nature and lack of association. In this manner, distance should be understood in all terms. Indeed, even if three people possessed of unwholesome feelings and three people possessed of painful feelings and so on were sitting on a single couch, their feelings would still be called distant because of their dissimilar nature and lack of association. The same method applies to those possessed of feelings of meditative attainment and so on. Unwholesome feeling, however, is called near to unwholesome feeling because of its similar nature and likeness. In this manner, nearness should be understood in all terms. Indeed, even if among three people possessed of unwholesome feelings and so on, one is in the sense sphere, one is in the fine-material sphere, and one is in the immaterial sphere, their feelings would still be called near because of their similar nature and likeness. The same method applies to those possessed of wholesome feelings and so on.

Regarding the phrase "Taṃ taṃ vā pana" (or whatever such), it should be explained by the power of "Taṃ taṃ vā pana" alone, without looking at the method mentioned below. When explaining, one should not extract the near from the distant, but rather extract the distant from the near. Unwholesome feelings are of two kinds: those accompanied by greed (lobha-sahagata) and those accompanied by hatred (dosa-sahagata). Between these two, a feeling accompanied by greed is called near to a feeling accompanied by greed, and distant from a feeling accompanied by hatred. A feeling accompanied by hatred is called near to a feeling accompanied by hatred, and distant from a feeling accompanied by greed. A feeling accompanied by hatred that is fixed (niyata) is called near to one that is fixed. Likewise for the unfixed (aniyata). All distinctions such as those of the aeon-stayer (kappaṭṭhitika), unprompted, and prompted, and the distinctions such as being associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-sampayutta) among those accompanied by greed and so on, should be understood following the power of the detailed explanation in the section on the Gross Dyad (oḷārika-duka-niddesa).
19:
Perception occurring at the five doors is coarse (obvious) because it can be known just by looking. Indeed, one can know just by looking that a person gazing intently with a lustful mind is 'gazing with a lustful mind,' and one gazing intently with an angry mind is 'gazing with an angry mind.'

In this matter, there is this illustrative story: It is said that two young women were sitting and spinning thread. While two young monks were wandering through the village, one of them, walking in front, looked at one of the women. The other woman asked the one who was looked at, 'Why did this monk look at you?' She replied, 'This monk did not look at me with a corrupted mind; he looked only with the perception of a younger sister.' When those monks, after wandering through the village, were resting in the assembly hall, the other monk asked the one who had looked, 'Did you look at that woman?' When he answered, 'I did,' he was further asked, 'For what purpose did you look?' He replied, 'I looked at her because she resembles my sister.' Thus, it should be understood that perception occurring at the five doors can be known just by looking. That perception has the sensitive matter (pasāda) as its physical basis. However, some teachers explain that it is the perception occurring at the moment of javana. Perception occurring at the mind-door, however, is subtle because even if one is sitting together on the same couch or bench, it can only be known by the words of the person who is thinking or reflecting on something else, after asking, 'What are you thinking or reflecting about?' The rest of the explanation is exactly as stated in the Aggregate of Feeling.

## This is the Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception.

## 4. Exposition of the Aggregate of Formations

In the exposition of the Aggregate of Formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the phrase 'whatever formations' includes all formations belonging to the four planes. The terms such as 'volition born of eye-contact' (cakkhusamphassajā cetanā) are stated to show the nature of formations described by way of the past, etc. The meanings of terms like 'born of eye-contact' are as previously stated. 'Volition' (cetanā) is mentioned as the principal formation at the lowest limit of the arising of consciousness. This is because, at the lowest limit, four formations arise together with eye-consciousness as directly mentioned in the Pāḷi. Among those four, volition is principal because it is prominent in the sense of striving (āyūhana). Therefore, only volition is taken. By taking that volition, the formations associated with it are also taken. In this Aggregate of Formations as well, the first five volitions have the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., as their physical bases. Volition born of mind-contact (manosamphassajā cetanā) may either have the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) or be without a physical basis. All volitions are only those belonging to the four planes. The rest of the explanation is exactly as stated in the Aggregate of Feeling.

## This is the Exposition of the Aggregate of Formations.
21: That kalala (embryo) is clear, exceptionally clear, unturbid, and pure throughout, having a color similar to a drop of clear sesame oil. Regarding this, the ancient commentators have said: "Just as a drop of sesame oil or a drop of clear clarified butter is unturbid, so too is the group of matter called kalala, which is similar in appearance." In this way, through the minute continuity of matter, there are three primary groups of matter: the heart-decad (vatthu-dasaka), the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), and the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka)—which is the female-decad for a woman and the male-decad for a man. Among these three, the heart-decad consists of the heart-base (vatthu-rūpa), the four great elements on which it depends, and the color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and life-faculty that depend on those great elements. The body-decad consists of the body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda), the four great elements on which it depends, and the color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and life-faculty that depend on those great elements. The sex-decad consists of the female sex-faculty (itthibhāva-rūpa) or the male sex-faculty (purisabhāva-rūpa), the four great elements on which it depends, and the color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and life-faculty that depend on those great elements. Thus, for beings born in a womb, at the moment of rebirth-linking, there are at most exactly thirty kamma-born matters, which are called the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). The feeling arising together with the rebirth-linking consciousness is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), the mental formations are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and the rebirth-linking consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Thus, for beings born in a womb, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking. If it is a neuter rebirth-linking, the sex-decad is absent. By way of the two decads, exactly twenty kamma-born matters are called the aggregate of matter. The aggregate of feeling and so on are as previously described. Thus, even for neuter beings born in a womb, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking. In this context, the continuity of matter produced by the three causes—consciousness, temperature, and nutriment—should be discussed. However, without discussing that continuity yet, the "arising of spontaneously born beings" (opapātika-samuggama) is shown. Indeed, for spontaneously born beings with complete sense-bases, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the three decads mentioned above and the four decads of eye, ear, nose, and tongue—making seven primary groups of matter—appear. Among these groups, the eye-decad and others are similar to the body-decad. For a neuter being, there is no sex-decad. Thus, for spontaneously born beings with complete sense-bases, exactly seventy or sixty kamma-born matters are called the aggregate of matter. The aggregate of feeling and so on are as previously described. Thus, for spontaneously born beings, the five aggregates are complete at the moment of rebirth-linking. This is called the "arising of spontaneously born beings." Thus, first, the five aggregates should be understood by way of their arising (samuggama).
22:
Regarding the matrix term 'Pubbāparato' (In terms of before and after), it should be examined: among the five aggregates that arise simultaneously without being before or after for beings residing in the womb, which matter (rūpa) arises first to produce matter, or is it mentality (nāma) that produces it? Matter alone produces matter first; mentality cannot. Why? Because the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) does not have the power to produce matter. These sixteen types of consciousness—the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death consciousness (cuticitta) of an Arahant, the ten sense-consciousnesses (dvipañcavinnāṇa), and the four immaterial resultants (arūpavipāka)—cannot produce matter.

Among those, the rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter due to the weakness of its physical base (vatthu), its instability, the deficiency of conditions, and its status as a newcomer (āgantuka). Among these reasons, the physical base that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness is weak at the moment of arising (uppāda); thus, it cannot produce matter due to the weakness of the base. Just as a man falling from a cliff cannot be a support for another, this rebirth-linking consciousness, being cast by the force of kamma, is unstable like one falling into a chasm; therefore, it cannot produce matter.

Furthermore, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises simultaneously with the physical base, so that physical base cannot serve as a condition by way of pre-nascence (purejāta-paccaya). If it could be a condition, it would produce matter. Only when the physical base can serve as a condition by way of pre-nascence is the continuity of consciousness connected, and then consciousness can produce matter without its factors being deficient. If consciousness could produce matter at the moment of presence (ṭhī) or the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), then the rebirth-linking consciousness would also produce matter. However, consciousness does not produce matter in those two moments. Just as a mushroom bud emerging from the earth emerges only after taking up dust on its head, so consciousness, depending on the pre-nascent physical base, arises only after taking up the eight inseparable matters (avinibbhoga-rūpa) at the moment of arising. Since the physical base cannot serve as a condition by way of pre-nascence at the moment of rebirth-linking, the rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter due to the deficiency of conditions.

Just as a guest who arrives at a place he has never been before cannot say to others, "Come, friends, I will give you food, drink, perfumes, and garlands in the village," because it is not his domain and he is not capable; so too, the rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter because it is like a guest in a new life. Furthermore, because the thirty kamma-born matters (kammaja-rūpa) have already taken the place of mind-produced matters and are established, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not produce matter.

The death consciousness of an Arahant does not produce matter because the roots of the cycle—ignorance and craving—have been extinguished. For that Arahant, the roots of the cycle are extinguished in all types of existence, and since there is no further arising, there is no longer any continuity in a future life.
23:
The rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) cannot produce matter (rūpa) because of the deficiency of causal conditions and because it is like a guest arriving at a new existence. Furthermore, since the exactly thirty types of karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) have already taken their place as the basis for consciousness-produced matter, the rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter.

The death consciousness (cuticitta) of an Arahant cannot produce matter because the roots of the round of rebirths—ignorance and craving—have been extinguished. As for the death consciousness of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the roots of the round will only be extinguished upon reaching the eighth existence, leaving seven existences remaining; therefore, it can still produce matter for up to seven existences. A Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) can produce matter in two existences, and a Non-returner (anāgāmī) in one existence. Because the roots of the round of rebirths for an Arahant have been extinguished in all existences, their death consciousness does not produce matter at all.

In the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses (dvipañcavijñāṇa), because there are no jhāna factors, path factors, or roots (hetu), the mental factors are weak and thus cannot produce matter. The four resultants of the formless sphere (arūpavipāka) also cannot produce matter because there is no fundamental matter to be produced in those formless realms. Not only those, but the other forty-two types of consciousness that arise in the formless realm—namely, 8 wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, 10 unwholesome consciousnesses, 9 functional consciousnesses, 4 formless wholesome consciousnesses, 4 formless functional consciousnesses, 3 path consciousnesses, and 4 fruition consciousnesses—also cannot produce matter because of the absence of matter there. In this way, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not produce matter.

Temperature (utu), however, produces matter first. 'Temperature' refers to the fire element (tejo-dhātu) within the exactly thirty types of karma-born matter that arise at the moment of rebirth-linking. When that fire element reaches its static phase (ṭhī), it produces the eight inseparable material phenomena (avinibbhogarūpa). Temperature ceases slowly, while consciousness ceases quickly. While the temperature-produced matter persists, sixteen mind-moments arise and cease. Among those, the first life-continuum consciousness (bhavanga), which occurs immediately after rebirth-linking, produces the eight inseparable material phenomena even at its arising phase (uppāda). When the time comes for the sound-base (sadda-rūpa) to arise, temperature and consciousness will produce the sound-nonad (saddanavaka-rūpa). 

Nutriment (kabḷīkārāhāra) also produces the eight inseparable material phenomena when it reaches its static phase. The nutriment for a being residing in the mother's womb is obtained from the mother. Thus it is said:

“Whatever rice, drink, or food the mother eats,
By that, the person in the mother's womb is sustained.” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.235)

In this way, the child in the womb is sustained by the essence (ojā) of the food and drink swallowed by the mother. That very essence, upon reaching its static phase, produces the eight inseparable material phenomena. If it is asked, “Since that essence is coarse and the embryonic substance (kalala) is subtle, how can it be established there?”—it is not established at first; it is established only after one or two weeks have passed. Whether it be before or after that period, when the essence of the food and drink swallowed by the mother is established in the child's body, it produces the eight inseparable material phenomena.
24:
For a spontaneously born being (opapātika), if they are born in a place where there is naturally prepared food and snacks, the essence (ojā) that reaches its static phase when they take and swallow those foods produces matter. Some spontaneously born beings are born in a forest devoid of food and drink; when they are extremely hungry, they stir their saliva with their own tongue and swallow it. In that case, too, the essence that reaches its static phase produces matter.

Thus, among the twenty-five groups, two material phenomena—the fire element and nutriment—produce matter. Among mental phenomena, two things—consciousness (citta) and volitional karma (kammacetanā)—produce matter. Among these, matter is weak at the arising phase (uppāda) and the dissolution phase (bhaṅga), and strong only at the static phase (ṭhī); therefore, it produces matter at the static phase. Consciousness is weak at the static phase and the dissolution phase, and strong only at the arising phase; therefore, it produces matter only at the arising phase. Volitional karma becomes a condition only after it has ceased. Karma accumulated even over a hundred thousand times ten million eons in the past becomes a condition now. Karma accumulated now will become a condition even at the end of a hundred thousand times ten million eons in the future. This should be understood in terms of 'sequence' (pubbāpara).

'Delimitation of duration' (addhānapariccheda) refers to how long matter lasts and how long mind lasts. Matter is heavy in transformation and slow to cease. Mind is light in transformation and quick to cease. While matter persists, sixteen mind-moments arise and cease. That matter ceases together with the seventeenth mind-moment. For example, a man thinking, “I will shake down the fruit,” strikes a tree branch with a stick, and the fruits and leaves are detached from their stems at the same moment. Among those fruits and leaves, the fruits, being heavy, fall to the ground first; the leaves, being light, fall later. In the same way, the simultaneous appearance of mind and matter at the moment of rebirth-linking should be understood as the time when the leaves and fruits are detached from the stem at once by the blow of the stick. The arising and ceasing of sixteen mind-moments while matter persists should be understood as the fruits falling to the ground first due to their weight. The cessation of matter together with the seventeenth mind-moment should be understood as the leaves falling to the ground later due to their lightness.

In this regard, although matter is slow to cease and heavy in transformation, and mind is quick to cease and light in transformation, matter cannot occur by abandoning mind, nor can mind occur by abandoning matter. The occurrence of both is of equal proportion. Here is an analogy: One man has short legs, and another has long legs. When the two travel together...
25:
While a long-legged man takes one step, another short-legged man, stepping foot by foot in front, goes sixteen steps. The long-legged man, stretching and pulling his leg across the sixteen steps of the short-legged man, makes only a single step. Thus, one cannot overtake the other, and the travel of both is of the same measure.

This illustration should be understood as perfectly corresponding [to the reality]. The short-legged man is like the immaterial (arūpa), and the long-legged man is like the material (rūpa). Just as the other takes sixteen steps while the long-legged man takes one, sixteen mental states arise and cease while the material phenomenon persists. Just as the long-legged man stretches and pulls his leg across the sixteen steps of the short-legged man to make one step, the material phenomenon ceases together with the seventeenth mental state. Just as the two men travel with the same measure without leaving each other, the immaterial arises with the material and the material with the immaterial with the same measure without leaving each other. Thus, it should be understood by way of 'delimitation of duration' (addhāna-pariccheda).

'Same arising, different ceasing' (ekuppāda-nānā-nirodha) should be explained by excluding the final kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa). Indeed, first is the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta), second is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), third is the life-continuum... and so on, up to the sixteenth life-continuum. In each of these, there are three sub-moments: arising (upāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga). In each of these three sub-moments of each consciousness, thirty kamma-born matters arise. Among them, the kamma-born matter that arose at the arising sub-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases exactly at the arising sub-moment of the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness. That which arose at the presence sub-moment ceases at the presence sub-moment; that which arose at the dissolution sub-moment ceases at the dissolution sub-moment. In this manner, starting from the second life-continuum consciousness, the method should be applied by pairing them with their respective seventeenth consciousness. Thus, there are sixteen triads (16 x 3), making forty-eight. This is called the 'succession of forty-eight kamma-born matters' (aṭṭhacatutālīsa-kammaja-rūpa-paveṇī). This succession of kamma-born matter proceeds continuously like the current of a river, even while eating, drinking, sleeping, or being negligent, day and night. Thus, it should be understood by way of 'ekuppāda-nānā-nirodha'.

'Different arising, same ceasing' (nānupāda-eka-nirodha) should be explained by the final kamma-born matter. To explain this: when there are sixteen consciousnesses remaining at the end of the life-continuum (āyu-saṅkhāra) [near death], two groups—the lower sixteen and the upper sixteen—should be joined together. Indeed, the thirty kamma-born matters that arose at the arising sub-moment of the first consciousness in the lower group cease exactly at the arising sub-moment of the first consciousness in the upper group. That which arose at the presence sub-moment ceases at the presence sub-moment; that which arose at the dissolution sub-moment ceases at the dissolution sub-moment. The same method applies to the second consciousness and so on. The kamma-born matter that arose at the arising sub-moment of the sixteenth consciousness ceases at the arising sub-moment of the death consciousness (cuti-citta). That which arose at the presence sub-moment ceases at the presence sub-moment of the death consciousness; that which arose at the dissolution sub-moment ceases at the dissolution sub-moment of the death consciousness. From the dissolution sub-moment of that death consciousness onwards, the succession of kamma-born matter no longer arises. Only that matter which ceases at the dissolution sub-moment of the death consciousness is called the 'final kamma-born matter' (pacchima-kammaja-rūpa). Since this final kamma-born matter arose at the dissolution sub-moment of the sixteenth consciousness, its moment of arising is different from the consciousness, thus it is 'nānupāda' (different arising); and since it ceases simultaneously with the dissolution sub-moment of the death consciousness, its moment of ceasing is the same as the consciousness, thus it is 'eka-nirodha' (same ceasing).
26:
The matter that arose at the presence sub-moment and the matter that arose at the dissolution sub-moment cease exactly at the dissolution sub-moment of that [same] consciousness. In the lower sixteen, the thirty kamma-born matters that arose at the arising sub-moment of the second consciousness... up to the sixteenth consciousness, cease exactly at the arising sub-moment of the death consciousness (cuti-citta). The matter that arose at the presence sub-moment of that consciousness ceases at the presence sub-moment of the death consciousness; the matter that arose at the dissolution sub-moment ceases at the dissolution sub-moment of the death consciousness. From then on, the succession of kamma-born matter no longer proceeds. If it were to proceed, beings would be indestructible, undecaying, ageless, and immortal.

Here, the statement in the Commentary—following the method such as "it ceases exactly at the arising sub-moment of the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness"—which says "matter that arose at the arising sub-moment of one consciousness ceases at the arising sub-moment of another consciousness," contradicts this Yamaka Pali: "For whom the bodily formation (kāya-saṅkhāra) ceases, does the mental formation (citta-saṅkhāra) cease for him?" "Yes (āmantā)." How so? The bodily formation is the in-breath and out-breath produced by the mind. Mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) arises at the arising sub-moment of a consciousness and persists until sixteen other consciousnesses have arisen and passed. It ceases together with the very last of those sixteen consciousnesses. Thus, it ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness from the one it arose with. It does not cease at the arising sub-moment or presence sub-moment of any consciousness, nor does it arise at the presence sub-moment or dissolution sub-moment. This is the nature of mind-produced matter; because it invariably ceases at the same moment as the mental formation, it is said "āmantā" (Yes).

This rule of timing for mind-produced matter is the same for kamma-born matter and others. Therefore, kamma-born matter that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness from then on. Matter that arises at the presence sub-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases at the arising sub-moment of the eighteenth consciousness. Matter that arises at the dissolution sub-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases at the presence sub-moment of the eighteenth consciousness—this is how the connection should be understood here. After that, only the succession of temperature-produced matter (utusamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) remains. It should then be said, "Take it out and cremate it." Thus, it should be understood by way of 'different arising, same ceasing' (nānupāda-eka-nirodha).

'Same arising, same ceasing' (ekuppāda-eka-nirodha) means: matter has the same arising and same ceasing with matter. The immaterial (arūpa) has the same arising and same ceasing with the immaterial. Thus, it should be understood by way of 'ekuppāda-eka-nirodha'.
27:
The state of 'diversity of arising and diversity of ceasing' (nānup-pāda-nānā-nirodhatā) should be demonstrated through the fourfold continuity of matter (catu-santati-rūpa). This is because, in various parts of this body—bounded by the skin, from the soles of the feet upwards to the tips of the hair, and from the tips of the hair downwards to the soles of the feet—the fourfold continuity of matter exists as a compact mass. Even though it exists in this way, its simultaneous arising (eka-uppāda) and so forth should not be noted (it is not necessary to note it as such).

For example, when observing a column of termites or a column of ants, they seem to be one continuous string, but in reality, they are not one continuous string. Near the head of one ant, there may be the head, belly, or legs of another ant. Near the belly of another, there may be the head, belly, or legs of another. Near the legs of another, there may be the head, belly, or legs of another. In the same way, among the fourfold continuity of matter, at the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of one material group, the arising, presence, or dissolution of another matter also occurs. At the moment of presence (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa) of one matter, the arising, presence, or dissolution of another matter also occurs. At the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-kkhaṇa) of one matter, the arising, presence, or dissolution of another matter also occurs. Thus, in these mental and material phenomena, the state of 'diversity of arising and diversity of ceasing' should be understood.

The terms starting from 'atīta' (past) and ending with 'dūra' (distant) have already appeared directly in the Pali text. The 'paccaya-samuṭṭhāna' (origination by conditions) has also been explained below by the method of "kamma-born, kamma-conditioned, kamma-conditioned-temperature-produced," and so forth. The five aggregates are only produced (parinipphanna); they are not unproduced (aparinipphanna). They are only conditioned (saṅkhata); they are not unconditioned (asaṅkhata). Furthermore, they are indeed produced (nipphanna). This is because, among ultimate realities, Nibbāna alone is called unproduced (aparinipphanna and anipphanna).

If it is asked about the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and concepts of names (nāma-paññatti): the attainment of cessation should not be called mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, produced or unproduced. However, it is 'nipphanna' (produced/accomplished) because it must be attained (accomplished) by the person entering it. Similarly, although name-concepts do not receive distinctions such as mundane and so forth, they are 'nipphanna' because they are produced by the namer; they are not 'anipphanna'. This is because only the person who gives the name can take (assign) the name.

## Kamādi-vinicchaya-kathā

Having thus understood the aggregates through their miscellaneous meanings, once again in those very aggregates—

For the sake of the various benefits of knowledge regarding the aggregates,
By way of order, and then by way of distinction,
By way of being neither less nor more, and likewise by way of analogy,
By way of being seen in a twofold manner, and by the accomplishment of the benefit for one who sees thus,
The method of determination should be well understood by the wise.

In the word 'kamatော' (by way of order), order (kama) has many varieties: order of arising (uppatti-kkama), order of abandoning (pahāna-kkama), order of practice (paṭipatti-kkama), order of planes (bhūmi-kkama), and order of teaching (desanā-kkama). Among these, the order such as "first there is the kalala (embryo), from the kalala comes the abbuda (foam)," and so forth, is called the order of arising (uppatti-kkama). The order such as "the states to be abandoned by vision (stream-entry)..." and so forth, is called the order of abandoning (pahāna-kkama). The order such as "purification of virtue, purification of mind," and so forth, is called the order of practice (paṭipatti-kkama). The order such as "sense sphere, fine-material sphere," and so forth, is called the order of planes (bhūmi-kkama). The order such as "the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts," or "talk on giving, talk on virtue," and so forth, is called the order of teaching (desanā-kkama).
28:
