Among those terms, in this word 'kamato' (by way of order), there are many kinds of order: order of arising (uppattikkama), order of abandoning (pahānakkama), order of practice (paṭipattikkama), order of planes (bhūmikkama), and order of teaching (desanākkama).

Among those orders, the teaching such as "First, there is the kalala (embryonic state); from the kalala, the abbuda (foetal state) arises," etc., is called the order of arising (uppattikkama). "States to be abandoned by vision, states to be abandoned by cultivation," etc., is called the order of abandoning (pahānakkama). "Purification of virtue, purification of mind," etc., is called the order of practice (paṭipattikkama). "Sense sphere, fine-material sphere," etc., is called the order of planes (bhūmikkama). "The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts," or "Talk on giving, talk on virtue," etc., is called the order of teaching (desanākkama). Among these orders, in explaining these five aggregates, the order of arising (uppattikkama) is first of all not suitable. This is because the aggregates do not arise in a sequential order like the kalala and so on. The order of abandoning (pahānakkama) is also not suitable because wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned. The order of practice (paṭipattikkama) is also not suitable because unwholesome states are not to be practiced. The order of planes (bhūmikkama) is also not suitable because aggregates such as feeling are included in all four planes.

However, the order of teaching (desanākkama) is indeed suitable. This is because the Blessed One, desiring to liberate those beings who perceive the five aggregates as a self without distinction by showing the breakdown of the compactness of the mass, and desiring their welfare, first taught the gross aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), which is the object of the sense bases such as the eye, so that they might understand easily. After that, [He taught] feeling (vedanā) which experiences pleasant and unpleasant forms; then perception (saññā) which grasps by way of modes the object of feeling, of which it is said, "one perceives what one feels"; then formations (saṅkhāra) which construct and process by the power of perception; and then consciousness (viññāṇa) which is the support and the chief of those aggregates such as feeling. In this way, first, the method of determination 'by way of order' (kamato) should be understood.

'By way of distinction' (visesato) refers to the distinction between the aggregates (khandha) and the clinging-aggregates (upādānakkhandha). What is the distinction between them? The aggregates are first mentioned without distinction (such as with taints or without taints), while the clinging-aggregates are mentioned with the distinction of being with taints (sāsava) and subject to clinging (upādāniya). The Blessed One taught thus:

"Bhikkhus, I will teach the five aggregates and the five clinging-aggregates; listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever materiality, bhikkhus, whether past, future, or present... or near—this is called the aggregate of materiality. Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever formations... whatever consciousness... or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates. And what, bhikkhus, are the five clinging-aggregates?"

Among these aggregates and clinging-aggregates, in states such as feeling, there are supramundane states which are without taints (anāsava) and mundane states which are with taints (sāsava). However, in materiality, there is no such distinction. Nevertheless, the name 'aggregate' (khandha) is suitable for the aggregates because of the meaning of 'group' (samūha). The name 'clinging-aggregate' (upādānakkhandha) is suitable for the clinging-aggregates because of the meaning of 'group' and because of being associated with taints (āsava). Alternatively, the supramundane states without taints such as feeling are taught only among the aggregates, while the mundane states with taints are taught among the clinging-aggregates. (In the word 'anāsavāva', if 'va' is taken as 'ṭhānappayutta' instead of 'aṭṭhānappayutta', it means "In the teaching of aggregates, only states without taints are taught, not states with taints." If that is the case, in the Pali texts of the aggregate of materiality etc., there are only materiality with taints, and those without taints...)
29:
"Monks, whatever form—whether past, future, or present... or near—that is accompanied by taints (āsavas) and is a basis for clinging: this is called the 'clinging-aggregate of form' (rūpūpādānakkhandha). Whatever feeling... whatever consciousness... or near—that is accompanied by taints and is a basis for clinging: this, monks, is called the 'clinging-aggregate of consciousness' (viññāṇūpādānakkhandha). Monks, these five are called the 'five clinging-aggregates' (pañcupādānakkhandhā)."

Among these aggregates and clinging-aggregates, states such as feeling and so on are both untainted (anāsava, supramundane) and tainted (sāsava, mundane). Form, however, is not like that (it is only tainted). Nevertheless, because its nature as an aggregate is appropriate in the sense of a heap, it is spoken of among the aggregates. Because its nature as a clinging-aggregate is appropriate both in the sense of a heap and in the sense of being tainted, it is spoken of among the clinging-aggregates. But untainted states like feeling and so on are spoken of only among the aggregates, while tainted states are spoken of among the clinging-aggregates. In the term 'clinging-aggregates' (upādānakkhandhā), the meaning should be understood as: the aggregates which are the objects of clinging are the clinging-aggregates. Here, however, all of these are intended as 'aggregates' by taking them together.

In the determination 'by way of being neither less nor more,' why did the Blessed One teach only five aggregates, neither fewer than five nor more? It is because of the inclusion of all conditioned things by way of similarity, because these five are the ultimate extent of the basis for grasping at self and what belongs to self, and because other things are included within them.

For when the many various conditioned things are included by way of similarity, form becomes one aggregate by way of inclusion through the similarity of form. Feeling becomes one aggregate by way of inclusion through the similarity of feeling. This same method applies to perception and so on. Therefore, because of the inclusion of all conditioned things by way of similarity, only five are taught. And these five, form and so on, are the ultimate extent of the basis for grasping at self and what belongs to self. For it has been said: "Monks, when there is form, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, such a view arises: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'" ... "When there is feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view arises: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'" Therefore, because these five are the ultimate extent of the basis for grasping at self and what belongs to self, only five are taught. Even though the other five 'aggregates of Dhamma' (dhammakkhandha) such as virtue (sīla) and so on are taught, they are included right here as they are contained within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Therefore, because other things are included within these five aggregates, only five are taught. Thus should the method of determination 'by way of being neither less nor more' be understood.

In the determination 'by way of similes,' the clinging-aggregate of form is like a hospital for the clinging-aggregate of consciousness, which is like a patient, because it is the dwelling place by way of base, door, and object.
30:
The clinging-aggregate of feeling is like a disease because it oppresses (the being). The clinging-aggregate of perception is like the cause of the disease because, through the power of sensual perception and so on, it gives rise to feelings associated with lust and so on. The clinging-aggregate of mental formations is like the partaking of unsuitable food because it is the source of the disease of feeling. For has it not been said: "They construct the conditioned for the sake of feeling-ness"? Likewise, it is said: "Because of having performed and accumulated unwholesome kamma, the resultant body-consciousness arises accompanied by pain." The clinging-aggregate of consciousness is like the patient because it cannot be liberated from the disease of feeling.

In another way, these five aggregates are like a prison, torture, a crime, a torturer, and a criminal. Furthermore, they are like a bowl, food, curry, a server, and an eater. Thus should the method of determination 'by way of similes' be understood.

In the determination 'by way of how they should be regarded,' it should be understood that there are two ways: in brief and in detail. In brief, the five clinging-aggregates should be regarded as an enemy with a raised sword, as taught in the Āsīvisūpama Sutta; as a burden, by way of the Bhāra Sutta; as a devouring ogre, by way of the Khajjanīya discourse; and as an impermanent, suffering, non-self, conditioned murderer, by way of the Yamaka Sutta.

In detail, among these five aggregates, form should be regarded as a lump of foam, feeling as a water bubble, perception as a mirage, mental formations as a plantain trunk, and consciousness as an illusion. For the Blessed One said:

"Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a water bubble,
Perception is like a mirage, formations like a plantain trunk,
And consciousness is like an illusion: so taught the Kinsman of the Sun."

In that verse, the similarity of form and so on to the lump of foam and so on should be understood thus: Just as a lump of foam is essence-less, so too form is essence-less, being devoid of the essence of permanence, the essence of stability, and the essence of self. And just as it is impossible to take it thinking, "I will make a bowl or a saucer with this," and even if taken, it does not serve that purpose but simply breaks; so too, form cannot be grasped as "permanent" or "stable" or "I" or "mine." Even if grasped, it does not remain so, but is only impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Thus, form is just like a lump of foam.
31:
In that verse, the similarity of form and the other aggregates to a lump of foam and so on should be understood as follows. Just as a lump of foam is without essence, so too form is without essence because it is devoid of the essence of permanence, the essence of stability, and the essence of self. Furthermore, just as one cannot intend to take that lump of foam thinking, 'I will make a bowl or a small cup with this lump of foam,' and even if taken, it cannot fulfill the purpose of a bowl or cup but simply breaks; so too, form cannot be grasped as 'permanent,' 'stable,' 'I,' or 'mine.' Even if grasped, it does not remain in such states as permanence or stability, but is only impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Thus, form is like a lump of foam.

Alternatively, just as a lump of foam is full of large and small holes, joined by many joints, and is the dwelling place of many creatures such as water snakes; so too, form is full of large and small holes and joined by many joints. In this form, eighty families of worms reside. This very body is the maternity ward, the latrine, the hospital, and the cemetery for these worms. These worms do not go elsewhere from this body to give birth and so on. In this way also, it is like a lump of foam. Just as a lump of foam is initially the size of a ripe jujube fruit and gradually becomes the size of a mountain peak; so too, form is initially just the kalala (embryonic) drop and gradually becomes about a fathom in length, or the size of a mountain peak in the case of cattle, buffaloes, and elephants, or the size of many hundreds of leagues in the case of fish and turtles. In this way also, it is like a lump of foam. Just as a lump of foam may break just as it arises, or after moving a little, but certainly breaks upon reaching the ocean; so too, form may break during the kalala stage or the abbuda stage. Even if it does not perish in the interval, those who live for a hundred years certainly perish upon reaching a hundred years, becoming crushed to dust in the mouth of death. In this way also, it is like a lump of foam.

Just as a water bubble is without essence, so too is feeling (vedanā). Just as a water bubble is weak and cannot be grasped—one cannot take it to make a plank or a seat, and it breaks whenever it is grasped—so too, feeling is weak and cannot be grasped; it cannot be grasped as 'permanent' or 'stable.' Even if grasped, it does not remain so. Because it cannot be grasped in this way, feeling is like a water bubble. Furthermore, just as a water bubble arises and vanishes in various raindrops and does not last long, so too, feeling arises and vanishes and does not last long; in the duration of a finger snap, it arises and vanishes a hundred thousand times ten million (a trillion) times. Just as a water bubble arises depending on four causes—the water surface, a raindrop, the moisture of the water, and the air that is trapped—so too, feeling arises depending on four causes: the physical base (vatthu), the object (ārammaṇa), the moisture of defilements (kilesa), and the impact of contact (phassa). In this way also, feeling is like a water bubble.

Perception (saññā) is also like a mirage because it is without essence. It is also similar because it cannot be grasped. Just as one cannot grasp a mirage to drink, bathe, or fill a vessel, so it is. Furthermore, just as a mirage flickers and appears like the movement of waves, so too, perception, with its various types such as the perception of blue, flickers and vibrates for the purpose of experiencing objects like blue. Just as a mirage deceives the multitude, making them say, 'It is like a great pond, like a great river,' so too, perception deceives and deludes, making one say, 'This object is blue, it is beautiful, it is pleasant, it is permanent.' The same method applies to yellow and so on. Because of such various deceptions and delusions, perception is like a mirage. Mental formations (saṅkhāra) are also like a plantain trunk because they are without essence. Likewise...
32:
Just as a mirage deceives many people, making them say, "It looks like a full pond, it looks like a full river," so too perception (saññā) deceives and deludes, making one say, "This object is blue, it is beautiful, it is pleasant, it is permanent." The same method applies to yellow and other colors. Because it deceives in various ways, perception is like a mirage.

Formations (saṅkhāras) are also like the trunk of a banana tree because of their lack of essence (asāra). Likewise, they are similar because they cannot be grasped. Indeed, just as one cannot take anything from a banana tree trunk to use as rafters or crossbeams, and even if taken, it does not serve that purpose, so too formations cannot be grasped as permanent and so on, and even if grasped, they do not exist in that permanent state. Just as a banana tree trunk is a collection of many layers, the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is also a collection of many states. Just as a banana tree trunk has various characteristics (for the color of the outer layer is one thing, and the color of the inner layers is another), so too in the aggregate of formations, the characteristic of contact (phassa) is one thing, and the characteristics of volition (cetanā) and others are another. However, when combined, they are simply called the aggregate of formations. In this way, the aggregate of formations is like the trunk of a banana tree.

Consciousness (viññāṇa) is also like an illusion (māyā) because of its lack of essence. Likewise, they are similar because they cannot be grasped. Just as an illusion is transient and appears quickly, so is consciousness. Indeed, it is even more transient and appears even more quickly than that illusion. By that same single mind, a person appears as if coming, as if going, as if standing, as if sitting. In reality, the mind at the time of coming is one, and the mind at the time of going and so on is another. In this way, consciousness is like an illusion. Just as an illusion deceives many people, making them perceive even a certain object as "This is gold, this is silver, this is a pearl," so too consciousness deceives people, making them perceive through that mind as if there is one who comes, one who goes, one who stands, or one who sits. The mind at the time of coming is one, and the mind at the time of going and so on is another. In this way, consciousness is like an illusion. Specifically, the distinct physical form (rūpa) within one's own continuity, even if it has a beautiful object, should be seen as foul (asubha). Feeling (vedanā) should be seen as suffering (dukkha) because it is not free from the three types of suffering. Perception and formations should be seen as non-self (anattā) because they are not subject to one's will. Consciousness should be seen as impermanent (anicca) because it has the nature of arising and passing away.

Regarding the statement, "Because of the accomplishment of the benefit for one who sees thus," the method of determination should be understood through the accomplishment of the benefit for one who sees in these two ways—briefly and in detail. To explain: firstly, one who sees the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandha) briefly as an enemy with a raised sword and so on is not oppressed by the aggregates. In detail, one who sees form and the others as being like a lump of foam and so on does not see essence in the essenceless aggregates. Specifically, one who sees the physical form within one's own continuity as foul (asubha) understands edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra)...
33:
One who sees (the five aggregates) as foul (asubha) fully understands edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), abandons the perversion (vipallāsa) of seeing beauty in the foul, crosses the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), becomes detached from the yoke of sensuality (kāmayoga), becomes one free from taints (anāsava) regarding the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), breaks the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha), and does not cling with the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna). One who sees feeling (vedanā) as suffering (dukkha) fully understands contact-nutriment (phassāhāra), abandons the perversion of seeing pleasure in suffering, crosses the flood of existence (bhavogha), becomes detached from the yoke of existence (bhavayoga), becomes one free from taints regarding the taint of existence (bhavāsava), breaks the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpādakāyagantha), and does not cling with the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). One who sees perception (saññā) and formations (saṅkhāra) as non-self (anattā) fully understands mental volition-nutriment (manosañcetanāhāra), abandons the perversion of seeing self in non-self, crosses the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), becomes detached from the yoke of views (diṭṭhiyoga), becomes one free from taints regarding the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), breaks the bodily tie of the insistence 'This is the truth' (idamsaccābhinivesakāyagantha), and does not cling with the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). One who sees consciousness (viññāṇa) as impermanent (anicca) fully understands consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇāhāra), abandons the perversion of seeing permanence in the impermanent, crosses the flood of ignorance (avijjogha), becomes detached from the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga), becomes one free from taints regarding the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), breaks the bodily tie of misapprehension of rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsakāyagantha), and does not cling with the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna).

Since seeing the five aggregates as a murderer (vadhaka) and so on has such great benefits,
Therefore, the wise person should view the aggregates as a murderer and so on.

## Description of the Suttanta Classification (Suttanta-bhājanīya-vaṇṇanā)

## 2. Description of the Abhidhamma Classification (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya-vaṇṇanā)

Now, the Abhidhamma classification will be explained. Therein, the exposition (niddesa) of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be understood in the same manner as the detailed method explained below in the Section on Form (Rūpakaṇḍa).

In the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), "single-fold" (ekavidhena) means as a single portion. "Associated with contact" (phassasampayutto) means conjoined with contact. All feelings also belong to the four planes (catubhūmika). In the dyad of "with roots" (sahetuka-duka), feelings with roots belong to the four planes, while feelings without roots (ahetuka) belong only to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). By this method, the feelings mentioned in the sections on the wholesome (kusala-pada) and so on should be understood. Furthermore, this aggregate of feeling is shown as single-fold by way of association with contact, two-fold by way of having roots or being rootless, three-fold by way of nature (jāti), four-fold by way of the difference in planes (bhūmi), and five-fold by way of faculties (indriya). Among those faculties, the pleasure faculty (sukhindriya) and the pain faculty (dukkhindriya) are only sense-sphere states based on the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda-vatthu). The joy faculty (somanassindriya) is either based on the sixth base (the heart-base) or is baseless (in the immaterial planes).
34:
(The faculty of pleasure) occurs in the three planes. The faculty of grief arises depending on the sixth base (the heart-base) and occurs in the sense-sphere. The faculty of equanimity occurs in all four planes, arising depending on the four sensitive bases such as the eye-base, or depending on the sixth base, or without any base (in the immaterial plane). Thus, it is shown in six ways according to the bases. Among those six, the first five feelings arise depending on the five sensitive bases and occur only in the sense-sphere. The sixth feeling occurs in the four planes, whether it has a supporting base or not.

In this context, the feeling born of mind-contact is shown in seven ways. The feeling born of body-contact is shown in eight ways. The feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact, mentioned in the sevenfold classification, is shown in nine ways. The feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact, mentioned in the eightfold classification, is shown in ten ways. Indeed, among these seven classifications, the feeling born of mind-contact is divided into two: feeling born of mind-element-contact and feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact. In the eightfold classification, along with that feeling, the feeling born of body-contact is also divided into two: pleasant and painful. In the ninefold classification, the feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact taught in the sevenfold classification is divided into three by way of wholesome and so on. In the tenfold classification, the feeling born of mind-consciousness-element-contact taught in the eightfold classification is also divided into three by way of wholesome and so on.

In these ten classifications, the wholesome triad is taught solely for the purpose of completing the ten. However, in the sevenfold, eightfold, and ninefold classifications, the method was given where it was appropriate to provide a method. When it comes to the Abhidhamma teaching, there is no place where the Buddha did not provide a method when it was appropriate to do so. This is the first cycle in the dyad-rooted section.

Indeed, when the Buddha analyzed the aggregate of feeling in this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method, He took the triads and included them in the dyads, took the dyads and included them in the triads, and presented them by the method of expanding both triads and dyads. He showed the aggregate of feeling in all ways: by sevenfold, twenty-four-fold, thirty-fold, and manifold classifications. Why? It is because of the inclination of individuals (puggalajjhāsaya) and because of the elegance of the teaching (desanāvilāsa). Among the assembly of deities and Brahmas sitting to listen to the Dhamma, those deities who are able to penetrate the Dhamma when it is taught by taking triads and including them in dyads, He taught them in that way as it was suitable for them. To those who are able to penetrate the Dhamma when taught by other methods, He taught them by those methods. This is what is meant by 'inclination of individuals' (puggalajjhāsaya). The Fully Enlightened One, by the power of His own vast range of omniscience, whether by including triads in dyads, or dyads in triads, or by expanding both, or by the sevenfold method and so on...
35:
...He is able to teach in whatever way He desires. Therefore, teaching through these various modes is the power of the Buddha's omniscience, which is the 'elegance of the teaching' (desanāvilāsa).

Among those cycles, the cycle taught by taking triads and including them in dyads is called the dyad-rooted cycle (duka-mūlaka). The cycle taught by taking dyads and including them in triads is called the triad-rooted cycle (tika-mūlaka). The cycle taught by expanding both triads and dyads is called the both-ways-expanded cycle (ubhatovaḍḍhitaka). The cycle beginning with 'by the sevenfold' at the end is called the multi-method cycle (bahuvidhavāra). These are the four great cycles (mahāvāra) to be known first.

Among those four great cycles, in the dyad-rooted cycle, by taking each dyad available among the dyads and combining it with the nineteen available triads—after excluding the feeling triad (vedanā-ttika), the rapture triad (pīti-ttika), and the visible triad (sanidassana-ttika) which are not available among the triads—there are nine hundred and fifty cycles, such as the cycle of combining the first triad with the second dyad. All these cycles are taught in the Pali text in brief, showing what should be shown in each respective cycle. However, they should be understood in detail without confusion.

In the triad-rooted cycle as well, by taking each triad available among the triads and combining it with the fifty available dyads—such as the root-accompanied dyad (sahetuka-duka), after excluding the first dyad and others which are not available among the dyads—there are nine hundred and fifty cycles, such as the cycle of combining the second dyad with the first triad. These too are all taught in the Pali text in brief, showing what should be shown in each respective cycle. However, they should be understood in detail without confusion.

In the both-ways-expanded cycle, starting from the second dyad in the twofold division and the first triad in the threefold division, nineteen cycles are taught by combining the nineteen available dyads with the nineteen available triads, such as the cycle of combining the first triad with the second dyad. This is the third great cycle called 'both-ways-expanded' (ubhatovaḍḍhitaka) because it is expanded from both sides by way of dyads and triads.

In the sevenfold exposition (sattavidha-niddesa) of the multi-method cycle, nineteen sevenfold cycles are taught by combining the four planes (such as the aggregates and the sense-sphere) with each of the nineteen triads available from the beginning. In the twenty-four-fold exposition (caturvīsati-vidha-niddesa) as well, nineteen cycles are taught by way of those same triads. Similarly, it should be noted in the multi-method cycle. Thus, all the multi-method cycles consist of fifty-eight cycles. This is the explanation of the Pali text by way of defining the cycles first.

Now follows the explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā). Among those expositions such as the sevenfold one, the sevenfold exposition first has an obvious meaning. In the twenty-four-fold exposition, in the passage 'Conditioned by eye-contact, there is a wholesome aggregate of feeling' (cakkhusamphassa-paccayā vedanākkhandho atthi kusalo), the wholesome aggregate of feeling born of eye-contact should be understood by way of the eight types of sense-sphere great wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara mahākusala). In the passage 'there is an unwholesome one' (atthi akusalo), the unwholesome aggregate of feeling should be understood by way of the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. In the passage 'there is an indeterminate one' (atthi abyākato), the indeterminate aggregate of feeling should be understood by way of the twenty-four types of consciousness: the three mind-elements, the three rootless mind-consciousness-elements, the eight great resultant consciousnesses, and the ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses (mind-door adverting, the smile-producing consciousness, and the eight great functional consciousnesses). Among those consciousnesses such as the great wholesome ones, the eight wholesome and twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are obtained by way of impulsion (javana). The functional mind-element is...
36:
Since the section on various kinds (bahuvidhavāra) is only one, all the sections (vāra) amount to fifty-eight. This is the exegesis of the Pali text (Pali-vaṇṇanā) by way of defining the sections in this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method.

Now, the exegesis of the meaning (Attha-vaṇṇanā) will be presented. Among those explanations starting with the sevenfold (sattavidha), the sevenfold explanation has a clear meaning. In the twenty-fourfold explanation (catuvīsatividha-niddesa), the passage 'There is the aggregate of feeling that is wholesome, conditioned by eye-contact' should be understood by way of the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses. The passage 'There is the aggregate of feeling that is unwholesome' should be understood by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. The passage 'There is the aggregate of feeling that is indeterminate (abyākata)' should be understood by way of twenty-four consciousnesses: the three mind-elements (manodhātu), the three rootless mind-consciousness elements (ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātu), the eight great resultants (mahāvipāka), and the ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses (kāmāvacarakiriya).

Among those consciousnesses, the eight wholesome and twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are obtained by way of impulsion (javana). The functional mind-element is obtained by way of adverting (āvajjana). The two resultant mind-elements are obtained by way of receiving (sampaṭicchana); the three resultant mind-consciousness elements by way of investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa); the functional rootless mind-consciousness element by way of determining (voṭṭhabbana); the eight great resultants by way of registration; and the nine functional consciousnesses by way of impulsion. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body doors.

In the mind-door (manodvāra), however, the term 'there is wholesome' is spoken of by way of the wholesome consciousnesses of the four planes. The term 'there is unwholesome' is spoken of by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. The term 'there is indeterminate' is spoken of by way of thirty-four consciousnesses: the eleven sense-sphere resultants, the ten functional consciousnesses, the nine fine-material and immaterial functional consciousnesses, and the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Among these, the wholesome of the four planes and the unwholesome are obtained by way of impulsion. Among the functional consciousnesses, the rootless mind-consciousness element is obtained by way of adverting; the eleven resultant consciousnesses by way of registration; and the functional consciousnesses of the three planes and the fruits of recluseship are obtained only by way of impulsion. Although it is appropriate to explain these consciousnesses by establishing them in any of the sections such as the sevenfold, they are explained by establishing them only in the thirtyfold (tiṃsavidha) section because it is easy to understand when shown there.

Indeed, all these consciousnesses are obtained in the eye-door by three modes: by way of strong dependence (upaniśśaya), by way of transcending (samatikkama), and by way of development (bhāvanā). The same applies to the ear-door and mind-door. However, in the nose, tongue, and body doors, it should be understood that they are obtained only by two modes: by way of transcending and by way of development. How? Here, a monk wandering through the monastery sees a kasiṇa mandala and asks, 'What is this called?'
37:
When he asks and is told, 'It is a kasiṇa mandala,' he asks again, 'What do they do with this?' Then they explain to him: 'By developing this, they produce the jhānas; then, based on the jhāna attainments, they increase insight (vipassanā) and reach Arahantship.' The clansman, endowed with the disposition for deliverance (vivaṭṭūpaniśśaya-ajjhāsaya), does not think, 'This is a heavy task,' but reflects, 'I too should produce this quality; however, this quality cannot be produced by one who lies down and sleeps. It is proper to exert effort and purify virtue (sīla) from the very beginning.' Thus, he purifies his virtue. Then, established in virtue, he cuts off the ten impediments (palibodha), remains content with only the three robes, performs the major and minor duties for his teachers and preceptors, learns the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), performs the kasiṇa preliminary work (kasiṇa-parikamma), produces the attainments (samāpatti), and, based on the jhāna attainments, increases insight and reaches Arahantship. In that process, all feelings occurring during the preliminary work are of the sense-sphere; the feelings in the eight attainments are of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; and the feelings associated with the Path and Fruit are supramundane (lokuttara). In this way, because eye-consciousness is a strong dependence condition (upaniśśaya-paccaya) for the arising of feelings in the four planes, the feelings in the four planes are said to be born conditioned by eye-contact. Thus, they are first obtained 'by way of strong dependence.'

When a visible object comes into range at the eye-door, a clansman established in the knowledge of defining—thinking, 'Lust (rāga) has arisen in me toward a pleasant object, hatred (paṭigha) toward an unpleasant object, delusion (moha) due to the inability to observe the object's nature accurately, conceit (māna) because of my attachment, wrong view (diṭṭhi) because of misapprehension, restlessness (uddhacca) because of distraction, doubt (vicikicchā) because of indecision, and underlying tendency (anusaya) because of the strength of the defilements'—recognizes the arising of his own defilements. Thinking, 'If these defilements of mine increase, they will lead to ruin and misfortune; let me now suppress them,' and further reflecting, 'Defilements cannot be suppressed by one who lies down and sleeps; it is proper to exert effort and purify virtue from the very beginning,' he practices in the same manner as described above and reaches Arahantship. In that process, all feelings during the preliminary work are of the sense-sphere; the feelings in the eight attainments are of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; and the feelings associated with the Path and Fruit are supramundane. In this way, because he has gone transcending the defilements that arose toward the visible object, the feelings in the four planes are said to be born conditioned by eye-contact. Thus, they are obtained 'by way of transcending (samatikkama).'

When a visible object comes into range at the eye-door, another person initiates the knowledge of defining thus: 'On what does this visible form (rūpa) depend?' Knowing that it depends on the great elements (bhūta), he defines the four great elements and derived matter (upādārūpa) as 'matter' (rūpa), and defines the states that take that form as an object as 'mind' (nāma). Then, having defined mind and matter with their causes, he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), investigates conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) through the sequence of insight, and reaches Arahantship. In that process,
38: All preparatory feelings are of the sense sphere; the feelings of the eight attainments are of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; the feelings of the path and fruition are supramundane. Because they arise by contemplating the visible object in this way, this feeling is called 'feeling born of eye-contact'. Thus, they are obtained by the power of meditation (bhāvanā). Another monk hears: 'It is said that by performing the preparatory work for a kasina, producing the attainments, and developing insight with the attainments as the proximate cause, they reach Arahantship.' A noble son endowed with inclination, without considering 'this task is difficult', thinks 'I too should produce this quality', practices in the same way as before, and reaches Arahantship. In that sequence of words, all preparatory feelings are of the sense sphere, the feelings of the eight attainments are of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and the feelings of the path and fruition are supramundane. In this way, because the ear-consciousness is a strong cause for the arising of feelings in the four planes, the feeling in the four planes is called 'feeling born of ear-contact'. Thus, first, they are obtained by the power of strong dependence (upanissaya). When a sound comes into focus at the ear-door, the entire passage should be understood in the same way as stated for the eye-door. Because one goes on having overcome the defilements that arose regarding the sound object in this way, the feeling in the four planes is called 'feeling born of ear-contact'. Thus, they are obtained by the power of overcoming (samatikkama). When a sound comes into focus at the ear-door, a certain monk initiates the knowledge of defining thus: 'On what does this sound depend?' Everything should be understood in the same way as stated for the eye-door. Because it arises by contemplating the sound object in this way, this feeling is called 'feeling born of ear-contact'. Thus, they are obtained by the power of meditation (bhāvanā). When odors and so forth come into focus at the nose-door, tongue-door, and body-door, everything such as 'Lust has arisen in me towards a pleasant object' should be understood in the same way as stated for the eye-door. Because one goes on having overcome the defilements that arose regarding odors and so forth in this way, the feeling in the four planes is called 'feeling born of nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact'. Thus, in these three doors, they are obtained by the power of overcoming (samatikkama). When odors and so forth come into focus at the nose-door and so forth, a certain monk initiates the knowledge of defining thus: 'On what does this odor depend? On what does this taste depend? On what does this tangible object depend?' Everything should be understood in the same way as stated for the eye-door. Thus, by contemplating odors and so forth...
39:
This feeling is said to arise due to the causes of nose-contact (ghānasamphassa), tongue-contact (jivhāsamphassa), and body-contact (kāyasamphassa). In this way, (feelings) are obtained by the power of meditation (bhāvanā).

In the mind-door (manodvāra), however, (feelings) are obtained in three ways. Indeed, a certain person sees birth (jāti) as a danger; he sees aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), and death (maraṇa) as a danger. Having seen them as a danger, he thinks, "It is proper to be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, and death; however, it is not possible for one who is lying down and sleeping to be liberated from birth and so forth; it is proper to make an effort from the very beginning and to purify one's virtue (sīla)." Thinking thus, he practices in the same manner as described for the eye-door and reaches the fruition of arahatship (arahattaphala). In reaching that fruition of arahatship, all preparatory feelings (parikamma-vedanā) are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); feelings of the eight attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti) are of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara); feelings of the path and fruition (magga-phala) are supramundane (lokuttara). In this way, birth, aging, sickness, and death are powerful causes for the arising of feelings in the four planes. Therefore, the feeling in the four planes is called that which arises due to the cause of mind-contact (manosamphassa). In this way, first, (feelings) are obtained by the power of powerful support (upanissaya).

In the mind-door, when a mental object (dhammārammaṇa) comes into focus, the entire explanation should be understood in the same manner as described for the eye-door. In this way, having overcome the defilements (kilesa) that arise regarding mental objects, they proceed; thus, the feeling in the four planes is called that which arises due to the cause of mind-contact. In this way, (feelings) are obtained by the power of overcoming (samatikkama).

In the mind-door, when a mental object comes into focus, a certain person begins the discernment thus: "On what does this mental object depend?" (He discerns:) "It depends on the base-matter (vatthu-rūpa)." "On what does the base-matter depend?" "It depends on the great elements (mahābhūta)." That person discerns the four great elements and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) as "matter" (rūpa); he discerns those states having that mental object as "mind" (nāma). Thereafter, having discerned mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) along with their causes, and applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), he contemplates formations (saṅkhāra) through the sequence of insight (vipaśśanā) and reaches the fruition of arahatship. Therein, all preparatory feelings are of the sense-sphere; feelings of the eight attainments are of the fine-material and immaterial spheres; feelings of the path and fruition are supramundane. In this way, because it arises from contemplating the mental object, this feeling is called that which arises due to the cause of mind-contact. In this way, (feelings) are obtained by the power of meditation. At the end of all the twenty-four cycles (vāra), etc., six types of feelings are mentioned: feeling born of eye-contact ...pe... feeling born of mind-contact. These feelings are stated by the power of association condition (sampayutta-paccaya).

## This is the Description of the Aggregate of Feeling (Vedanākkhandhaniddesa).
40:
The aggregates such as the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) should also be understood in this manner. Indeed, in the description of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha-niddesa), among the triads, the triad of feeling (vedanā-ttika) and the triad of rapture (pīti-ttika) are also obtained; and among the dyads, the dyad of accompanied by pleasure (sukhasahagata-duka) and so on are also obtained. In the description of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha-niddesa), because contact (phassa) is also included in the aggregate of mental formations, it is not stated as 'associated with contact' (phassa-sampayutta), but is stated as 'associated with consciousness' (citta-sampayutta). In this description of the aggregate of mental formations, among the dyads, the dyad of roots (hetu-duka) and so on are also obtained. The triads are just similar to the aggregate of perception. In the description of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha-niddesa), instead of stating 'born of eye-contact' and so on, it is stated as 'eye-consciousness' (cakkhu-viññāṇa) and so on. This is because it is not possible to point out consciousness as being born of mind-contact (manosamphassaja). The remaining arrangement here is just similar to what was stated in the aggregate of perception. Only in the description of these three aggregates are the triads and dyads obtained that are in excess of the description of the aggregate of feeling. The distinction of sections (vāra) should be understood by the power of those excess triads and dyads.

## Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification.

## 3. Explanation of the Questioning Section

Now is the method of the questioning section (pañhāpucchaka). In that questioning section, among the five aggregates, whatever term is obtained and whatever term is not obtained by the method such as 'How many are wholesome? How many are unwholesome? How many are indeterminate?', having questioned all that, in the answer, whatever term is obtained by the method such as 'The aggregate of matter is indeterminate', it should be understood that only that term is extracted. Wherever in the answer the text is laid down by the method such as 'some arise, some do not arise' without making a delimitation as 'one aggregate' or 'two aggregates', it should be understood as the taking of all five aggregates in those respective places. The remaining classification of those respective aggregates into wholesome and so on has already been stated below in the Commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī.

In the triads of objects (ārammaṇa-ttika), however, the four mental aggregates have the sense-sphere as their object for a person who, in relation to the fifty-five sense-sphere states, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, comprehending, or reflecting. They have the sublime (mahaggata) as their object for a person who, in relation to the twenty-seven fine-material and immaterial sphere states, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing the delimitation. They have the immeasurable (appamāṇa) as their object for a person who is reflecting on the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. At the time of reflecting on a concept (paññatti), they have the object called 'not-to-be-designated' (as sense-sphere, sublime, or immeasurable), which is the concept.
41:
Those same four (mental) aggregates have the Path as their object at the time of reflecting on the Path by trainees (sekha) and adepts (asekha). At the time of the Path-consciousness, they have the Path as their associated root by way of the conascent root (sahajāta-hetu). At the time of reflecting on the Path having made it a priority, they have the Path as their predominant object by way of the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). For a person who is developing the Path making energy foremost or making investigation foremost, they have the Path as their conascent-predominant by way of the conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati). However, for a person who is developing the Path making desire-to-act foremost or making consciousness foremost, they have objects that are not to be called 'having the Path as object', 'having the Path as root', or 'having the Path as predominant'.

For a person who, in relation to past aggregates, elements, and bases, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing the grasp through the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), they have past states as their object. For a person who acts in relation to future states, they have future states as their object. For a person who acts in relation to present states, they have present states as their object. For a person who reflects on a concept or Nibbāna, they have objects that are not to be called past, future, or present.

Similarly, for a person who, in relation to one's own aggregates, elements, and bases, is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing the grasp, they have internal states as their object. For a person who proceeds thus in relation to the aggregates, elements, and bases of others, they have external states as their object. Even at the time of reflecting on a concept and Nibbāna, they have only external objects. For a person who proceeds thus in states, sometimes internally and sometimes externally, they have internal-external objects. At the time of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) jhāna, it should be understood that they have objects (the concept of non-existence) that are not to be called internal or external.

Thus, the Blessed One, in explaining this Khandhavibhaṅga by way of the Suttantabhājanīya and so on, showed it by bringing forth three rounds of teaching. Even in those three rounds, the delimitation of states is of only one kind. Indeed, the aggregate of matter is only of the sense-sphere in all methods. The four mental aggregates, however, were taught as states belonging to the four planes, being a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

## In the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī,
## the Explanation of the Classification of Aggregates is finished.
42:
## 2. Āyatanavibhaṅgo
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Now, desiring to show the Suttanta classification in the Description of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga), which follows the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga), the Buddha taught the twelve bases, such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and the form-base (rūpāyatana). Regarding these bases, first, by the method outside the Pāḷi text:

Atthalakkhaṇatāvatva, kamasaṅkhepavitthārā,
Tathā daṭṭhabbato ceva, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Among these decisions, to explain specifically (visesa) first: It is called 'cakkhu' (eye) because it delights exceedingly or because it manifests clearly. The meaning is that it delights in the form-object or makes it manifest. It is called 'rūpa' (form) because it is formed (rūpayati); the meaning is that it manifests the intention in the heart by undergoing changes in color. It is called 'sota' (ear) because it hears. It is called 'sadda' (sound) because it is uttered. It is called 'ghāna' (nose) because it smells. It is called 'gandha' (odor) because it indicates its own source. It is called 'jivhā' (tongue) because it is as if calling for life, which is the cause of longevity, such as taste. It is called 'rasa' (taste) because beings enjoy it. It is called 'kāya' (body) because it is the source (āya) of loathsome (kucchita) taints (āsava). The 'source' means the place of origin or the cause of arising. It is called 'phoṭṭhabba' (tangible) because it is touched. It is called 'mana' (mind) because it knows. They are called 'dhammā' (mental objects/phenomena) because they bear their own characteristics.

In a general sense (sāmañña), however, it should be known as 'āyatana' (base) because it exerts, because it extends the arising mind and mental factors, and because it leads to the long suffering of saṃsāra. In the eye, form, and so on, the mind and mental factors that have those respective doors and objects exert themselves, arise, and strive through their respective functions such as experiencing. This is what is meant by 'exerting' (āyatanato). Furthermore, these bases extend (tanonti) or expand those mental phenomena that have arisen. This is what is meant by 'extending' (tananato). And as long as the very long suffering of saṃsāra, which has occurred in the beginningless saṃsāra, does not cease, these bases lead (nayanti) or continue it. This is what is meant by 'leading' (nayanato). Thus, all these phenomena are called 'āyatana' because of exerting, extending, and leading the long suffering.

In another way, 'āyatana' should be understood in the sense of an abode, a mine (source), a meeting place, a birthplace, and a cause. Accordingly, in the world, in such terms as 'issarāyatana' (the abode of the Lord/Brahma) and 'vāsudevāyatana' (the abode of Vasudeva/Vishnu), the abode is called 'āyatana'.
43:
(The word āyatana) is used. In terms such as 'suvaṇṇāyatana' (gold mine) and 'rajatāyatana' (silver mine), the source (ākara) is called āyatana. In the Dispensation, however, in such passages as 'Birds resort to that banyan tree, the delightful meeting place (āyatana),' the meeting place (samosaraṇaṭṭhāna) is called āyatana. In 'Dakkhināpatha is the birthplace (āyatana) of cattle,' the birthplace (sañjātidesa) is called āyatana. In 'When the cause (āyatana) exists, one attains the state of a witness in those respective phenomena to be realized,' the cause (kāraṇa) is called āyatana.

In the eye, form, and so on, those respective mind and mental factors reside because their existence depends on them; therefore, the eye and so on are their abode (nivāsaṭṭhāna). In the eye and so on, those mind and mental factors are found in abundance because they depend on the eye, etc., and take form, etc., as objects; therefore, the eye and so on are their source (ākara). The eye and so on are also their meeting place (samosaraṇaṭṭhāna), because they meet there by way of base, door, and object. The eye and so on are also their birthplace (sañjātidesa), because they arise right there with those as support and object. The eye and so on are also their cause (kāraṇa), because in the absence of the eye, form, etc., the mind and mental factors cannot arise. Thus, because of these reasons—the sense of abode, the sense of source, the sense of meeting place, the sense of birthplace, and the sense of cause—these phenomena are called 'āyatana, āyatana'. Therefore, in the sense already stated, it is the eye and it is a base, thus it is the 'eye-base' (cakkhāyatana)... etc... it is a mental object and it is a base, thus it is the 'mental-object base' (dhammāyatana). In this way, first, the decision should be known by way of 'meaning' (attha).

By way of 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) means that the decision should also be known by way of the characteristics of the eye and so on in these eye-bases, etc. The characteristics of those eye and other bases should be understood in the same manner as stated below in the Description of the Materiality Section (Rūpakaṇḍaniddesa).

By way of 'quantity' (tāvatva) means by way of being of that much quantity, namely twelve. This is what is meant: The eye and other phenomena are indeed just 'dhammā' (phenomena). This being so, why are twelve bases taught instead of saying only 'dhammāyatana'? It is because of the definition of the doors and objects for the arising of the six groups of consciousness. Because they are defined here as the doors and objects for the six groups of consciousness, this distinction alone exists; therefore, twelve are taught. For the group of consciousness included in the eye-consciousness process, only the eye-base is the door of arising, and only the form-base is the object. Likewise for the others. For the sixth group of consciousness (mind-consciousness), however, only a part of the mind-base known as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind is the door of arising, and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) is the specific object not shared with other types of consciousness.
44:
Object means - the twelve bases (āyatanas) were taught to define the doors and objects of the six classes of consciousness. Thus, in this Āyatana-vibhaṅga, the decision 'by number' (tāvatvato) should be understood.

'By order' (kamato) means - in this Āyatana-vibhaṅga as well, among the orders such as the order of arising mentioned previously, only the order of teaching (desanākkama) is appropriate. Among the internal bases, the eye base (cakkhāyatana) is prominent because it has a visible and resistant object (sappaṭigha-visaya); therefore, it is taught first. After that, the ear base (sotāyatana) and others, which have non-visible but resistant objects, are taught. Alternatively, because they are very helpful as causes for the 'unsurpassed seeing' (dassanānuttariya) and 'unsurpassed hearing' (savanānuttariya), the eye base and ear base are taught first among the internal bases. Then the three beginning with the nose base (ghānāyatana) are taught. The mind base (manāyatana) is taught last because it is the resort of all five. Among the external bases, because they are the objects of the eye and so on, the form base (rūpāyatana) and others are taught immediately after their respective internal bases. Furthermore, this order should also be understood for the purpose of defining the causes for the arising of consciousness. As it was taught: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises... dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.' Thus, the decision 'by order' (kamato) should be understood here.

'By brief and detailed' (saṅkhepavitthārā) means - briefly, because the mind base and a portion of the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) are included as 'mind' (nāma), and the remaining bases are included as 'matter' (rūpa), all twelve bases are merely mind and matter (nāma-rūpa).

In detail, among the internal bases, the eye base is merely eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) by type, but it has infinite varieties according to cause (paccaya), destination (gati), group (nikāya), and person (puggala). The four beginning with the ear base are the same. The mind base has eighty-one varieties according to the divisions of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness in the three planes; however, it has infinite varieties according to the divisions of physical base (vatthu), practice (paṭipadā), and so on. The bases of form, smell, and taste have four varieties each according to their origin (samuṭṭhāna); the sound base has two varieties. According to the divisions of similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga), all bases have infinite varieties. The tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) has three varieties by way of the elements of earth, fire, and air; four varieties by origin; and many varieties by way of similar and dissimilar. The mental-object base has many varieties by way of the mental objects in the three planes. Thus, the decision 'by brief and detailed' (saṅkhepavitthārā) should be understood.

'By how they should be regarded' (daṭṭhabbato) means - here, all these bases should be regarded as not coming from anywhere and not going anywhere. Indeed, they do not come from anywhere before their arising, nor do they go anywhere after their dissolution; rather, before arising, they have not yet attained their nature (they do not exist).
45:
All bases do not come from anywhere before the arising (uppāda), nor do they go anywhere after the dissolution (bhaṅga); they have the nature of non-existence before arising and the nature of destruction where nothing remains after dissolution. In the middle of arising and dissolution, they occur without being under anyone's control, as they are dependent on causes such as kamma. Therefore, those bases should be regarded as not coming from anywhere and not going anywhere. Furthermore, they should be regarded as being without effort (nirīha) and without activity (abyāpāra). In reality, in the eye-sensitivity, forms, and so on, there is no activity such as 'O, may consciousness arise due to our union.' Those eyes, forms, and so on do not make an effort as a door, a physical base, or an object for the purpose of producing consciousness, nor do they engage in activity. Rather, it is the natural law (dhammatā) of things that when there is a union of the eye, forms, and so on, eye-consciousness and so forth arise accordingly. Therefore, they should be regarded as being without effort and without activity. Furthermore, the internal bases should be regarded as an empty village (suññagāma) because they are devoid of the nature of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The external bases should be regarded as village-attacking dacoits (gāmaghātakacorā) because they afflict the internal bases. As the Buddha taught: 'Monks, the eye is afflicted by agreeable and disagreeable forms,' and so on in detail. Moreover, the internal bases should be regarded as six animals, and the external bases as their hunting grounds. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of how they should be regarded.

Now, to show the manner in which those bases should be contemplated with insight (vipassanā), the Blessed One began with 'The eye is impermanent' and so on. Therein, the eye-sensitivity should be understood as impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. Furthermore, it is called impermanent for four reasons: because it has arising and passing away, because of change, because it is temporary, and because it excludes permanence. That same eye is called suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressive. Or, because after arising it reaches a state of presence, and in that presence it is worn out by aging (jarā), and having reached aging it inevitably breaks up; therefore, it is called suffering for four reasons: because of constant oppression, because it is difficult to endure, because it is the basis of suffering, and because it excludes happiness. It is called non-self (anattā) in the sense of not being under one's control. Or, because no one can exercise control over the eye that has arisen, saying, 'Let it not reach the state of presence; having reached presence, let it not age; having reached aging, let it not break up'; and because it is devoid of the manner of being under such control; therefore, it is called non-self for four reasons: because it is empty, because it is ownerless, because it cannot be made to act according to one's will, and because it excludes self. It is of the nature of change (vipariṇāmadhamma) because it reaches destruction, because of the transition of natural phenomena from one state to another in the sequence of before and after, and because of abandoning its original nature. This is a synonym for impermanence. The same method applies to the passages such as 'Forms are impermanent.' Furthermore, in this context, excluding the eye, the things belonging to the three planes are only 'impermanent,' not 'the eye.' But the eye is both 'the eye' and 'impermanent.' Likewise, the remaining things are only 'suffering,' not 'the eye.' But the eye is both 'the eye' and 'suffering.'
46: The eye is indeed the eye, and it is suffering. The remaining states are non-self; they are not the eye. The eye is indeed the eye, and it is also non-self. This same method applies to forms and so on. In this Suttanta-bhājanīya, what did the Blessed One show? He showed the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) of the twelve bases (āyatana). Indeed, when the Perfectly Enlightened One wishes to show the characteristic of non-self, he shows it through impermanence (anicca), or through suffering (dukkha), or through both impermanence and suffering. Among those three, if someone were to say, 'The eye is the self,' that statement is not tenable. Both the arising and the vanishing of the eye are evident. Since arising and vanishing are evident, if one holds that view, it would follow that 'My self arises and vanishes.' Therefore, it is not tenable to say 'The eye is the self.' Thus, the eye is non-self. In this sutta, he showed the characteristic of non-self through impermanence. 'Monks, form is non-self. Monks, if this form were the self, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain [one's wish] regarding form: "Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus." But monks, because form is non-self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain [one's wish] regarding form: "Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus."' In this sutta, he showed the characteristic of non-self through suffering. 'Monks, form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen as "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."' In such passages, he showed the characteristic of non-self through impermanence and suffering. Why? Because impermanence and suffering are obvious. Indeed, when a bowl, a cup, or any vessel falls from the hand and breaks, people say, 'Oh, it is impermanent!' Thus, impermanence is said to be obvious. In this body, when boils, abscesses, and so on appear, or when one is pierced by a stump or a thorn, people say, 'Oh, it is painful!' Thus, suffering is said to be obvious. But the characteristic of non-self is not obvious; it makes the eye of wisdom blind, it is not clear to knowledge, it is difficult to penetrate, difficult to illustrate, and difficult to make others understand. The characteristics of impermanence and suffering are evident in the world whether Tathāgatas arise or not. But the characteristic of non-self is not evident apart from the arising of a Buddha; it is evident only when a Buddha arises. Even powerful and influential ascetics and wanderers like the teacher Sarabhaṅga can speak of 'impermanence and suffering,' but they cannot speak of 'non-self.' If they were able to speak of 'non-self' to the assembled audience, the penetration of the paths and fruits would occur for that audience. Indeed, making the characteristic of non-self known is not the domain of anyone else; it is the domain of the Omniscient Buddhas alone. Thus, this characteristic of non-self is not obvious. Therefore...
47:
When the Teacher wishes to show the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa), He shows it by way of impermanence (anicca), or by way of suffering (dukkha), or by way of both impermanence and suffering. In this Suttanta classification (Suttantabhājanīya), it should be understood that He shows the characteristic of non-self by way of impermanence and suffering.

Indeed, why do these characteristics not appear? Due to the non-attention to and non-penetration of what, and due to being concealed by what? The characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to and non-penetration of arising and passing away (udayabbaya), and because it is concealed by continuity (santati). The characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to and non-penetration of constant oppression, and because it is concealed by the postures (iriyāpatha). The characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to and non-penetration of the resolution into various elements, and because it is concealed by compactness (ghana). However, when arising and passing away are discerned and continuity is broken, the characteristic of impermanence appears according to its true nature. When constant oppression is attended to and the postures are exposed, the characteristic of suffering appears according to its true nature. When the various elements are resolved and compactness is broken down, the characteristic of non-self appears according to its true nature.

In this context, the distinction between impermanence (anicca) and the characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa), suffering (dukkha) and the characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa), and non-self (anatta) and the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) should be understood. Therein, impermanence refers to the group of five aggregates. Why? Because they have the nature of arising, passing away, and transformation, or because they do not exist after having been. Arising, passing away, and transformation is called the characteristic of impermanence. Or, the variation of mode known as non-existence after having been is called the characteristic of impermanence. According to the statement, "That which is impermanent is suffering," those same five aggregates are called suffering. Why? Because they are constantly oppressed. The mode of being constantly oppressed is called the characteristic of suffering. According to the statement, "That which is suffering is non-self," those same five aggregates are called non-self. Why? Because they do not follow one's will. The mode of not following one's will is called the characteristic of non-self. Thus, impermanence, suffering, and non-self are one thing, while the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, and the characteristic of non-self are another. This whole set of the five aggregates, the twelve bases (āyatana), and the eighteen elements (dhātu) is called impermanence, suffering, and non-self. The aforementioned variations of modes are called the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, and the characteristic of non-self.

Briefly, here, ten bases are of the sense-sphere, and two belong to the three planes. It should be understood that the sequence of contemplation with insight knowledge (vipaśśanā-ñāṇa) is taught for all bases.

## Explanation of the Suttanta Classification (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā).
48:
## 2. Exposition of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya

In the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, unlike in the Suttanta-bhājanīya below where the bases were taught in pairs such as "eye-base and visible-data-base" for the benefit of those practicing insight, the internal and external bases are taught by way of defining them as "eye-base, ear-base," and so on, in order to show their nature in all aspects through the method of distinguishing internal and external.

In the Niddesavāra (Exposition Section) of those bases, the passages beginning with "Among them, what is the eye-base?" should be understood in the same manner as already stated below (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary).

In the exposition of the dhammāyatana (mental-object base), it is stated: "Among those states, what is the unconditioned element? It is the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion." Regarding this, the meaning is as follows: The unconditioned element is Nibbāna, which has an unconditioned nature. However, because greed and other defilements are destroyed upon reaching this Nibbāna, it is described as "the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion." This is the uniform explanation of the teachers in this context.

A Vitandavādin (sophist), however, says: "There is no such thing as Nibbāna separately; the destruction of defilements itself is Nibbāna." When told, "Bring forth a Sutta [to support this]," he cites the Jambukhādaka Sutta: "Friend Sāriputta, it is said, 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna.' What, friend, is Nibbāna? Friend, that which is the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this is called Nibbāna." Citing this, he says, "By this Sutta, it should be known that there is no separate Nibbāna; the destruction of defilements alone is Nibbāna."

That Vitandavādin should be asked: "Is the meaning exactly as this Sutta appears?" He will certainly reply: "Yes, there is no meaning apart from the Sutta." Then he should be told: "You have brought this Sutta; now bring the immediately following Sutta." The immediately following Sutta is: "Friend Sāriputta, it is said, 'Arahattaphala, Arahattaphala.' What, friend, is Arahattaphala? Friend, that which is the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this is called Arahattaphala." This is the Sutta brought forth immediately after the previous one.

When this subsequent Sutta is brought forth, they say to that Vitandavādin: "Nibbāna is a state included within the dhammāyatana, whereas Arahattaphala consists of the four aggregates. One who dwells having realized Nibbāna..."
49:
Whether the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, was asked about Nibbāna or about Arahattaphala, he answered only as the destruction of defilements. How is it then? Are Nibbāna and Arahattaphala one and the same, or are they different? [The Vitandavādin says:] "Whether they are one or different, what benefit is there for you who are making such excessive distinctions in this matter of Nibbāna?" [The Sakavādin replies:] "Do you not know whether they are one or different? Is it not good to know now?" Being thus questioned repeatedly, the Vitandavādin, unable to deceive, had to say: "Because it occurs at the end of the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga) where greed and other defilements are destroyed, Arahattaphala is called the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion."

Then the Sakavādins said to him: "You have done a great task. Even one who wants someone to speak by giving a bribe would have him say only this. Just as you have explained these terms such as 'destruction of greed' by distinguishing them, please also note this meaning: Because greed and others are destroyed upon reaching Nibbāna, Nibbāna is called the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. In fact, all three of these are merely synonyms for Nibbāna."

If he understands when this is said, that is good. If not, he should be made to understand by showing the fault that many Nibbānas would then exist. How should he be made to understand? First, he should be asked: "Is what is called 'destruction of greed' only the destruction of greed, or is it also the destruction of hatred and delusion? Is 'destruction of hatred' only the destruction of hatred, or also the destruction of greed and delusion? Is 'destruction of delusion' only the destruction of delusion, or also the destruction of greed and hatred?"

Then the Vitandavādin will certainly say: "The destruction of greed is only the destruction of greed; the destruction of hatred is only the destruction of hatred; the destruction of delusion is only the destruction of delusion."

Then it should be said to him: "In your doctrine, the destruction of greed would be one Nibbāna, the destruction of hatred another, and the destruction of delusion another. With the destruction of the three unwholesome roots, there would be three Nibbānas; with the destruction of the four graspings, four Nibbānas; with the destruction of the five hindrances, five Nibbānas; with the destruction of the six groups of craving, six Nibbānas; with the destruction of the seven underlying tendencies, seven Nibbānas; with the destruction of the eight wrongnesses, eight Nibbānas; with the destruction of the nine things rooted in craving, nine Nibbānas; with the destruction of the ten fetters, ten Nibbānas; and with the destruction of the one thousand five hundred defilements, if each is a separate Nibbāna, there would be many Nibbānas. Then there would be no limit to the number of your Nibbānas. Therefore, do not hold such a view, but accept that because greed and others are destroyed upon reaching Nibbāna, the single Nibbāna is called the destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. All three of these are merely synonyms for the one Nibbāna."
50:
If, even when spoken to in this way, he does not comprehend, he should be made to understand by way of the grossness (of his view of Nibbāna). How? (By saying): "Even animals such as bears, leopards, deer, and monkeys, who lack the eye of wisdom and are blind and foolish, indulge in sexual intercourse when overcome by defilements. At the end of such indulgence, their defilements subside. According to your doctrine, such animals as bears, leopards, deer, and monkeys would be said to have reached Nibbāna. Indeed, your Nibbāna is so gross and crude that it is not even fit to be worn as an ornament on the ear." However, without holding such a view, one should understand that the single Nibbāna is called "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion," referring only to the fact that lust and so on are exhausted because of reaching Nibbāna. Take it that all three are merely synonyms for Nibbāna.

If, even when spoken to in this way, he does not comprehend, he should be made to understand by way of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). How? First, he should be asked: "Do you say there is such a thing as gotrabhū?" If he answers, "Yes, I do," then he should be asked: "At the moment of gotrabhū, are the defilements already destroyed, being destroyed, or will they be destroyed?" He will likely answer: "They are not already destroyed, nor are they being destroyed; rather, they will be destroyed (in the future)." When asked, "What does gotrabhū take as its object?" he will answer, "It takes Nibbāna as its object." (Then it should be said): "At your moment of gotrabhū, the defilements are not yet destroyed, nor are they being destroyed, but will be destroyed later. You are designating Nibbāna as the destruction of defilements even while the defilements are not yet destroyed; you are designating Nibbāna as the abandonment of latent tendencies (anusaya) even while the latent tendencies have not yet been abandoned. Such a designation is inconsistent with your previous statement. However, without holding such a view, one should understand that the single Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, referring only to the fact that lust and so on are exhausted because of reaching Nibbāna. Take it that all three are merely synonyms for Nibbāna."

If, even when spoken to in this way, he does not comprehend, he should be made to understand by way of the Path (magga). How? First, he should be asked: "Do you say there is such a thing as the Path?" If he answers, "Yes, I do," then he should be asked: "At the moment of the Path, are the defilements already destroyed, being destroyed, or will they be destroyed?" Then the wise vitandavādī (sophist) will answer: "It should not be said they are already destroyed or will be destroyed; it should only be said they are being destroyed." (Then it should be asked): "If that is so, what is Nibbāna, the destruction of defilements, which is the object of the Path? Which are the defilements being destroyed by the Path? What kind of Nibbāna as the destruction of defilements does the Path take as an object to exhaust which defilements?" Therefore, do not hold such a view. The single Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion, referring only to the fact that lust and so on are exhausted because of reaching Nibbāna. These three are merely synonyms for Nibbāna.

When spoken to in this way, he asks: "You keep saying 'āgamma, āgamma' (having reached/depending on); from where did you get this word 'āgamma'?" (The answer is): "I got it from the Sutta."
51:
Regarding the word "laddha" (obtained), when it is said, "Bring the Sutta," (the reply is): "Thus ignorance and craving arise depending on (āgamma) that Nibbāna; they are destroyed in that, they are broken in that, and nothing remains at any time." When this was recited, the opponent was reduced to silence.

In this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method also, the ten bases (āyatana) are of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). The two bases (mind and mental objects), however, should be understood as being mixed mundane and supramundane, belonging to the four planes.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya
## 3. Commentary on the Question Section (Pañhāpucchaka)
In this Question Section also, all terms that are applicable and not applicable in the explanation (vissajjanā) are asked, and the answer is given only by way of what is applicable. This is the method not only here, but in the Question Sections of all the Vibhaṅgas. Here, the ten bases should be understood as indeterminate (abyākata) by way of being matter (rūpa). The two bases should be understood as being wholesome and so on, just like the four aggregates mentioned in the Khandha-vibhaṅga. Indeed, the four aggregates are only conditioned (sappaccaya) and constructed (saṅkhata) states. The mental-object base (dhammāyatana), however, is stated as: "It may be unconditioned (appaccaya), it may be unconstructed (asaṅkhata)."

In the Triads of Objects (ārammaṇattika) also, the mental-object base known as subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa), which does not take an object, belongs to the "not-to-be-declared" (navattabba) category. Furthermore, it belongs there only because it does not take an object, and not because it has an object that is not-to-be-declared as limited and so on. This is the distinction here.
