The rest is exactly the same (as in the Khandha-vibhaṅga). For in this Āyatana-vibhaṅga also, just like the four aggregates, the two bases are "limited objects" (parittārammaṇa) for one who is lusting, hating, deluded, restraining, contemplating, or reviewing with regard to the fifty-five sense-sphere states; all these statements are identical to what was said in the Khandha-vibhaṅga.

## The Commentary on the Analysis of the Bases (Āyatana-vibhaṅga)
## in the Sammohavinodanī is finished.
52:
## 3. Dhātuvibhaṅga
## 1. Commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya

Now, in this Dhātuvibhaṅga which follows immediately after the Āyatanavibhaṅga, the Teacher said, "The elements are six," and so forth, desiring to show the Suttantabhājanīya method by summarizing all elements into three groups of six elements each. In that context, "six" is a delimitation by number. "Elements" (dhātuyo) is a designation of the delimited phenomena. In terms such as the earth element (pathavīdhātu), the meaning of 'element' (dhātu) is the sense of intrinsic nature (sabhāvaṭṭha); the sense of intrinsic nature is the sense of voidness (suññataṭṭha); the sense of voidness is the sense of non-being (nissattaṭṭha). Thus, because it is the earth itself that is an element in the sense of intrinsic nature, voidness, and non-being, it is called the 'earth element'. The same method applies to the water element (āpodhātu) and others. Having thus understood the compound of these terms, the meaning should be understood as follows: the earth element is the element of foundation; the water element is the element of cohesion; the fire element is the element of maturation; the air element is the element of support; the space element is the element that is uncontacted (by the great essentials); the consciousness element is the element of cognizance.

"Two kinds of earth element" means that this earth element is of two types. This earth element is not of one kind only, but is indeed of two kinds by way of the division into internal (ajjhatta) and external (bāhira). Therefore, it is said: "There is the internal earth element, and there is the external earth element." Therein, "internal" refers to those things belonging to the continuity of living beings, which are one's own and internal. "External" refers to those things belonging to the continuity of formations, which are not connected with the sense faculties. Both "internal" (ajjhatta) and "personal" (paccatta) are synonyms for what is one's own and internal. Now, to show that earth element by way of its natural mode, the words "hard" (kakkhaḷa) and so forth are said. Therein, "kakkhaḷa" means stiff or hard. "Kharigata" means rough. "Kakkhaḷattā" means the state of being hard. The state of being hard is the very nature of hardness. "Internal clung-to" (ajjhattaṃ upādinnaṃ) means that which is called internal to oneself and is clung to by craving and views. What is called "clung-to" (upādinna) is the collection of matter situated in the body. Whether the matter situated in the body is originated by kamma (kammasamuṭṭhāna) or not, with reference to that matter, there is both the clung-to (upādinna) and the not-clung-to (anupādinna). However, to show that all matter in this body is indeed "clung-to" in the sense of being taken, grasped, and misapprehended as 'my body' through craving, conceit, and views, it is said: "internal clung-to."

Now, to show that same earth element by way of its physical basis, the words "as follows: head hairs, body hairs" and so forth are said. Therein, "seyyathidaṃ" is an indeclinable. Its meaning is: what is that internal earth element? Or, what is that which is called the internal, personal, hard nature? "Head hairs, body hairs," and so forth is the demonstration of the divisions of that internal earth element according to its physical basis. This is what is meant: head hairs are a distinct part (koṭṭhāsa) in this body, which are internal, clung-to, situated in the body, and characterized by hardness.
53:
Head hairs are one part. Body hairs are... (and so forth) ... feces are one part. Although not explicitly mentioned here, the brain (matthaluṅga), which is included in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, should also be included. The brain is a distinct part in this body, which occurs in the internal continuity, is taken as kamma-born matter, is situated in the body, and is characterized by hardness. In the explanation of the water element and others to be shown later, the same method should be understood for bile and so forth.

What is shown by this Pali text? It shows the attention to elements (dhātumanasikāra). What should be done by one who, having applied effort in this attention to elements and having established insight (vipassanā), desires to reach the supreme goal, Arahantship? One should purify the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). For it is only for one who possesses virtue that the development of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā) succeeds. The procedure for purifying that virtue should be understood in the same way as the method described in the Visuddhimagga. Having established oneself in virtue, one with purified virtue should cut off the ten prior impediments (palibodha). The procedure for cutting off those impediments should also be understood in the same way as the method described in the Visuddhimagga. One who has cut off the impediments should learn the meditation subject of attention to elements. The teacher, when teaching the meditation subject of attention to elements, should explain the sevenfold skill in acquisition (uggahakosalla) and the tenfold skill in attention (manasikārakosalla). The student also should perform recitation (sajjhāya) many times in the presence of the teacher to make the meditation subject free from tangles and proficient. For it is said in the Commentary: "A monk who is a beginner, desiring to be liberated from aging and death, should desire skill in acquisition through seven ways, and should desire skill in attention through ten ways."

Therein, 'skill in acquisition' in this meditation subject of attention to elements should be desired through these seven ways: verbally, mentally, by way of color, by way of shape, by way of direction, by way of location, and by way of delimitation. 'Skill in attention' should be desired through these ten ways: in order, not too fast, not too slow, by warding off distraction, by transcending concepts, by gradual dropping, by way of characteristic, and the three Suttas. Both of these will become clear later in the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga.

One who has thus learned the meditation subject, avoiding the eighteen faults of a dwelling mentioned in the Visuddhimagga, living in a dwelling endowed with five factors, and being himself endowed with the five factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga), should go to a secluded place after returning from the alms round after the meal and attend to the meditation subject. And while attending to it—
54:
By way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, one should reflect on each part, such as the hair of the head, and finally, reflection should be developed in this way: These hairs of the head grow on the skin that wraps the skull. Just as, regarding the short grass (kunda-grass) growing on top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know, "Short grass has grown upon me," nor does the short grass know, "We have grown upon the top of an anthill"; in the same way, the skin wrapping the skull does not know, "Hairs have grown upon me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown upon the skin wrapping the skull." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "hair of the head" is a separate part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, void, non-sentient, hard, and is the earth element.

The hairs of the body grow on the skin that wraps the body. Just as, regarding the dabba-grass growing in a deserted village site, the village site does not know, "Dabba-grass has grown upon me," nor does the dabba-grass know, "We have grown in a deserted village site"; in the same way, the skin wrapping the body does not know, "Body hairs have grown upon me," nor do the body hairs know, "We have grown upon the skin wrapping the body." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "body hair" is a separate part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, void, non-sentient, hard, and is the earth element.

The nails grow on the tips of the fingers and toes. Just as, when children play by piercing Madhuka seeds with small sticks, the sticks do not know, "Madhuka seeds have been placed upon us," nor do the Madhuka seeds know, "We are situated on the sticks"; in the same way, the fingers do not know, "Nails have grown on our tips," nor do the nails know, "We have grown on the tips of the fingers." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "nails" is a separate part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, void, non-sentient, hard, and is the earth element.

The teeth grow in the jawbones. Just as, regarding the posts that carpenters have fixed and placed in stone mortars with some kind of resin, the mortars do not know, "Posts are situated in us," nor do the posts know, "We are situated in the mortars"; in the same way, the jawbones do not know, "Teeth [have grown] in us..."
55:
...nor do the teeth know, "We have grown in the jawbones." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "teeth" is a separate part in this body, an inanimate thing, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a non-sentient thing, a hard earth element.

The skin stands wrapping the entire body. Just as, regarding a large lute covered with wet ox-hide, the large lute does not know, "I am covered with wet ox-hide," nor does the wet ox-hide know, "The large lute is covered by me"; in the same way, the body does not know, "I am covered by skin," nor does the skin know, "The body is covered by me." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "skin" is a separate part in this body, an inanimate thing, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a non-sentient thing, a hard earth element.

The flesh stands plastered over the collection of bones. Just as, regarding a wall plastered with fine clay, the wall does not know, "I am plastered with fine clay," nor does the fine clay know, "The large wall is plastered by me"; in the same way, the collection of bones does not know, "I am plastered with flesh consisting of nine hundred pieces of flesh," nor does the flesh know, "The collection of bones is plastered by me." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "flesh" is a separate part in this body, an inanimate thing, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a non-sentient thing, a hard earth element.

The sinews stand binding the bones together inside the body. Just as, regarding wall timbers bound with creepers, the wall timbers do not know, "We are bound with creepers," nor do the creepers know, "The wall timbers are bound by us"; in the same way, the bones do not know, "We are bound with sinews," nor do the sinews know, "The bones are bound by us." These things are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called "sinews" is a separate part in this body, an inanimate thing, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a non-sentient thing, a hard earth element.

Among the bones, the heel bone stands supporting the ankle bone. The ankle bone stands supporting the shin bone. The shin bone stands supporting the thigh bone. The thigh bone [stands supporting] the hip bone...
56:
(The bones) exist. The hip bone stands supporting the backbone. The backbone stands supporting the neck bone. The neck bone stands supporting the skull. The skull rests on the neck bone. The neck bone rests on the backbone. The backbone rests on the hip bone. The hip bone rests on the thigh bone. The thigh bone rests on the shin bone. The shin bone rests on the ankle bone. The ankle bone rests on the heel bone.

Among those bones, just as in a heap of bricks, wood, or cow dung, the lower parts do not know, "We stand supporting the upper parts," nor do the upper parts know, "We rest upon the lower parts"; in the same way, the heel bone does not know, "I stand supporting the ankle bone," the ankle bone does not know, "I stand supporting the shin bone," the shin bone does not know, "I stand supporting the thigh bone," the thigh bone does not know, "I stand supporting the hip bone," the hip bone does not know, "I stand supporting the backbone," the backbone does not know, "I stand supporting the neck bone," the neck bone does not know, "I stand supporting the skull," the skull does not know, "I rest on the neck bone," the neck bone does not know, "I rest on the backbone," the backbone does not know, "I rest on the hip bone," the hip bone does not know, "I rest on the thigh bone," the thigh bone does not know, "I rest on the shin bone," the shin bone does not know, "I rest on the ankle bone," and the ankle bone does not know, "I rest on the heel bone." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called 'bone' is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element (pathavīdhātu).

Bone marrow exists inside various bones. Among that bone marrow and those bones, just as steamed rattan shoots placed inside bamboo joints do not know, "Rattan shoots are placed within us," nor do the rattan shoots know, "We exist within bamboo joints"; in the same way, the bones do not know, "Bone marrow exists within us," nor does the bone marrow know, "I exist within the bones." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called 'bone marrow' is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The kidneys (vakka) have a single root originating from the throat, and after going a short distance, they are bound by a thick nerve that divides into two, and they stand surrounding the heart. Among those (kidneys and nerves)...
57:
Just as between two mangoes tied to a stalk, the stalk does not know, "Two mangoes are tied by me," nor do the two mangoes know, "We are tied by a stalk"; in the same way, the thick nerve does not know, "The kidneys (vakka) are tied by me," nor do the kidneys know, "I am tied by a thick nerve." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called 'kidneys' is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The heart stands in the interior of the body, depending on the center of the chest cavity. Among that heart and the chest cavity, just as a piece of meat placed inside an old palanquin cage—the palanquin cage does not know, "A piece of meat is placed depending on me," nor does the piece of meat know, "I stand depending on an old palanquin cage"; in the same way, the chest cavity does not know, "The heart stands depending on me," nor does the heart know, "I stand depending on the chest cavity." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called 'heart' is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The liver stands in the interior of the body, depending on the right side between the two breasts. Among that liver and the side, just as a lump of meat stuck to the side of a potsherd—the potsherd does not know, "A lump of meat is stuck to me," nor does the lump of meat know, "I am stuck to the side of a potsherd"; in the same way, the right side between the breasts does not know, "The liver stands depending on me," nor does the liver know, "I stand depending on the right side between the breasts." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called 'liver' is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

Among the membranes, the concealing membrane stands surrounding the heart and kidneys. The unconcealing membrane stands wrapping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the whole body. Among those membranes and the flesh, just as meat wrapped in a rag—the meat does not know, "I am wrapped in a rag," nor does the rag know, "I have wrapped the meat"; in the same way, the kidneys, heart, and the flesh of the whole body do not know, "We are covered by the membrane," nor does the membrane know, "The kidneys, heart, and the flesh of the whole body are covered by me." Mutually...
58:
These things are devoid of conscious reflection (ābhoga-paccavekkhaṇā). Thus, what is called the membrane (kilomaka) is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element (pathavī-dhātu).

The spleen (pihaka) is situated on the left side of the heart, relying on the upper side of the stomach-membrane. Between the spleen and the stomach-membrane, just as a lump of cow dung that is placed relying on the upper side of a granary does not know, 'The lump of cow dung is relying on me,' nor does the lump of cow dung know, 'I am relying on the upper side of the granary'; in the same way, the upper side of the stomach-membrane does not know, 'The spleen is situated relying on me,' nor does the spleen know, 'I am situated relying on the upper side of the stomach-membrane.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, what is called the spleen is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The lungs (papphāsa) are situated inside the body between the two breasts, hanging over and covering the heart and liver from above. Between the lungs and the interior of the body, just as a bird's nest hanging inside an old granary does not know, 'A bird's nest is hanging in me,' nor does the bird's nest know, 'I am hanging inside an old granary'; in the same way, the interior of the body does not know, 'The lungs are situated hanging in me,' nor do the lungs know, 'I am situated hanging in such an interior of the body.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, what is called the lungs is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The large intestine (anta) is situated inside the body from the throat to the end of the passage for excrement. Between the large intestine and the interior of the body, just as the body of a headless snake coiled and placed in a blood trough does not know, 'I am situated in a blood trough,' nor does the blood trough know, 'A snake's body is situated in me'; in the same way, the interior of the body does not know, 'The large intestine is situated in me,' nor does the large intestine know, 'I am situated inside the body.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, the large intestine...
59:
...is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The small intestine (antaguṇa) is situated binding the twenty-one coils of the large intestine. In that regard, just as when a rope ring for wiping the feet is sewn with small strings, the rope ring does not know, 'The small strings are situated sewing me,' nor do the small strings know, 'We are situated sewing the rope ring'; in the same way, the large intestine does not know, 'The small intestine is situated binding me,' nor does the small intestine know, 'I am situated binding the large intestine.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, what is called the small intestine is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The undigested food (udariya) is what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, situated in the stomach. In that regard, just as with dog's vomit in a dog's bowl, the dog's bowl does not know, 'Dog's vomit is situated in me,' nor does the dog's vomit know, 'I am situated in a dog's bowl'; in the same way, the stomach does not know, 'Undigested food is situated in me,' nor does the undigested food know, 'I am situated in the stomach.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, what is called the undigested food is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The feces (karīsa) is situated at the end of the large intestine, in what is called the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya), which is like a bamboo joint about eight finger-breadths long. In that regard, just as with fine yellow clay that is pressed and put into a bamboo joint, the bamboo joint does not know, 'Yellow clay is situated in me,' nor does the yellow clay know, 'I am situated in a bamboo joint'; in the same way, the receptacle for digested food does not know, 'Feces is situated in me,' nor does the feces know, 'I am situated in the receptacle for digested food.' These things are devoid of mutual conscious reflection. Thus, what is called the feces is a distinct part in this body, inanimate, indeterminate, empty, non-being, and is the solid earth element.

The brain (matthaluṅga) is situated inside the skull. In that regard, just as with a lump of dough put into an old gourd shell, the gourd shell does not know, 'A lump of dough is situated in me,' nor does the lump of dough know, 'I am situated in a gourd shell'; in the same way, the interior of the skull does not know, 'The brain is situated in me,' nor does the brain...
60:
(The brain) does not know, "I am situated inside the skull." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called the brain is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate (avyākata), void, non-being, and is the solid earth element (pathavīdhātu).

By the phrase "whatever else there is," He shows the earth element contained in the other three groups, such as the water group, by way of the characteristic of hardness, making it "whatever-else-earth-element" (yevāpanaka-pathavī).

In explaining the external earth element: *Ayo* means black iron. *Loha* is of four types: natural metal (jātiloha), hybrid metal (vijātiloha), artificial metal (kittimaloha), and inferior metal (pisācaloha). Among these four, the seven types—iron, silver, gold, white tin, black lead, copper, and steel—are called natural metals. *Nāganāsika* metal is called hybrid metal. The three types—bronze, lead-alloy (or *te*), and brass—are called artificial metals. The eight types—*morakkhaka*, *puthuka*, *malinaka*, *capalaka*, *selaka*, *āṭaka*, *bhallaka*, and *dūsiloha* (rust)—are called inferior metals. Among these metals, five types of natural metals have been separately mentioned in the Pāḷi. Along with the two natural metals, copper and steel, all the rest should be understood here as *loha*.

*Tipu* means white lead (tin). *Sīsa* means black lead. *Sajju* means silver. *Muttā* means pearls produced in the ocean. *Maṇi* means all types of gems such as *jotirasa* and others, excluding beryl (veḷuriya) and others mentioned in the Pāḷi. *Veḷuriya* means a gem the color of bamboo (cat's eye). *Saṅkha* means a conch shell produced in the ocean. *Silā* means all types of stones such as black stone, yellow stone, and white stone. *Pavāဠa* means coral. *Rajata* means coins (kahāpaṇa). *Jātarūpa* means gold. *Lohitaṅka* means red ruby. *Masāragalla* means variegated gem. Among grass and such, those with external heartwood, at the lowest being coconut trees and the like, are also called grass (tiṇa). Those with internal heartwood, at the lowest being a piece of wood, are called wood (kaṭṭha). *Sakkharā* means gravel ranging from the size of a mung bean to the size of a fist. Stones smaller than a mung bean are called sand (vālikā). *Kaṭhala* means any kind of potsherd. *Bhūmi* means earth. *Pāsāṇa* means a stone that cannot be held within a fist up to a stone not yet reaching the size of an elephant. A stone from the size of an elephant upwards...
61:
...is called a mountain (pabbata). By the phrase "or whatever else," He includes other collections of the earth element such as palmyra seeds, coconuts, and fruits. By the phrase "internal earth element and external earth element," He shows that both types of earth element are indeed one single earth element because they share the same characteristic of hardness.

In the explanation of the water element (āpodhātu) and so on, it should be understood in the same manner as mentioned below. In the words "āpo, āpogata," etc., it is called *āpo* because of its function of cohesion (ābandhana). Because it has reached the nature of *āpo*, it is called *āpogata*. Because of its function of viscosity, it is called *sneha*. Because it has reached the nature of viscosity, it is called *snehagata*. "Cohesion of matter" means the state of binding together inseparable matter (avinibbhogarūpa). Bile, phlegm, and so on should also be contemplated as elements by defining them through their color, shape, direction, location, and boundaries.

In this regard, this is the method: Among the types of bile, non-localized bile (abaddha-pitta) is connected with the life faculty (jīvitindriya) and exists pervading the entire body. Localized bile (baddha-pitta) is situated in the gallbladder (pittakosaka). Just as the oil pervading a cake does not know, "I exist pervading the cake," nor does the cake know, "The oil exists pervading me," even so, the body does not know, "Non-localized bile exists pervading me," nor does the non-localized bile know, "I exist pervading the body." And just as in a luffa fruit (kosātakī) filled with rainwater, the luffa fruit does not know, "Rainwater exists in me," nor does the rainwater know, "I exist in the luffa fruit," even so, the gallbladder does not know, "Localized bile exists in me," nor does the localized bile know, "I exist in the gallbladder." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called bile is a separate part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void, non-being, a liquid, and is the water element characterized by cohesion.

Phlegm (semha) is about the measure of a handful and is situated in the stomach lining (udara-paṭala). Just as in a cesspool with a layer of foam on top, the cesspool does not know, "A layer of foam exists in me," nor does the layer of foam know, "I exist in the cesspool," even so, the stomach lining does not know, "Phlegm exists in me," nor does the phlegm know, "I exist in the stomach lining." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus...
62:
Phlegm is a separate part in this body; it is without consciousness, indeterminate (avyākata), void, not a living being, a liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) characterized by cohesion.

Pus has no permanent location. It stays in those places where blood collects and putrefies in a part of the body struck by a stump, a thorn, a weapon, a flame, etc., or where boils and pimples arise. In this regard, to give an analogy: just as in a tree where resin is oozing due to an axe-cut, etc., the parts of the tree where the axe-cut is do not know, 'Resin is staying in us,' nor does the resin know, 'I am staying in the axe-cut parts of the tree'; even so, the parts of the body struck by a stump, a thorn, etc., do not know, 'Pus is staying in us,' nor does the pus know, 'I am staying in those parts.' These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, pus is a separate part in this body; it is without consciousness, indeterminate, void, not a living being, a liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) characterized by cohesion.

Among the types of blood, circulating blood (saṃsaraṇa-lohita) stays pervading the whole body like unconfined bile (abaddha-pitta). Stored blood (sannicita-lohita) stays filling the lower part of the liver's location to the extent of one bowlful, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. Regarding that circulating blood, the judgment is the same as for unconfined bile. Regarding the other, stored blood, to give an analogy: just as when water in a cracked pot is moistening clods of earth below, the clods of earth do not know, 'We are being moistened by water,' nor does the water know, 'I am moistening the clods of earth'; even so, the place below the liver or the kidneys, etc., do not know, 'Blood is staying in me,' or 'It is staying moistening us,' nor does the blood know, 'I am staying filling the lower part of the liver and moistening the kidneys, etc.' These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, blood is a separate part in this body; it is without consciousness, indeterminate, void, not a living being, a liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) characterized by cohesion.
63:
Sweat stays filling the pores of the hair and body hair and flows out during times of heat from fire, etc. In this regard, just as when bundles of lotus roots, lotus stalks, white lilies, or reeds (nala) are just pulled out of the water, the openings of the bundles of lotus stalks, etc., do not know, 'Water is flowing from us,' nor does the water flowing from the openings of the bundles of lotus stalks, etc., know, 'I am flowing from the openings of the bundles of lotus stalks, etc.'; even so, the pores of the hair and body hair do not know, 'Sweat is flowing from us,' nor does the sweat know, 'I am flowing from the pores of the hair and body hair.' These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, sweat is a separate part in this body; it is a separate part, a thing without life-faculty, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a thing that is not a living being, a liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) with the nature of cohesion.

Fat (meda) is the thick oil that stays pervading the whole body of a stout person, and relying on the flesh of the calves, etc., of a thin person. In this regard, just as when a heap of meat is covered with a cloth dyed with turmeric, the heap of meat does not know, 'The turmeric-dyed cloth stays relying on me,' nor does the turmeric-dyed cloth know, 'I stay relying on the heap of meat'; even so, the flesh in the whole body or in the calves, etc., does not know, 'Fat stays relying on me,' nor does the fat know, 'I stay relying on the flesh in the whole body or in the calves, etc.' These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, fat is a separate part in this body; it is a separate part, a thing without life-faculty, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a thing that is not a living being, thick oil, a thick liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) with the nature of cohesion.

Tears, when they are produced, stay filling the eye sockets or flow out. In this regard, just as in the cavities of young palm nuts filled with liquid, the cavities of the young palm nuts do not know, 'Liquid stays in us,' nor does the liquid know, 'I stay in the cavities of the young palm nuts'; even so, the eye sockets do not know, 'Tears stay in us,' nor do the tears know, 'I stay in the eye sockets.' These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, tears are a separate part in this body; it is a separate part, a thing without life-faculty, an indeterminate state, a void thing, a thing that is not a living being, a liquid, and is the water element (āpo-dhātu) with the nature of cohesion.

Skin-oil (vasā) is the melted grease that stays on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the points of the shoulders during times of heat from fire, etc. In this regard, for example, like oil poured on...
64: Just as in clear oil that has been sprinkled with oil, the clear oil does not know, "The oil stands pervading me," nor does the oil know, "I stand pervading the clear oil"; similarly, the area of the palms and so forth does not know, "The fat (vasā) stands pervading me," nor does the fat know, "I stand pervading the area of the palms and so forth." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called fat (vasā) is a separate portion in this body, insentient, indeterminate (abyākata), void (suñña), not a being, liquid, and of the nature of cohesion (ābandhanākāra), which is the water element (āpodhātu). Saliva (kheḷo), when there is a cause for its production, descends from both sides of the cheeks and stays on the tongue. There, just as in a small well dug on a riverbank with a continuous flow of water, the bottom of the well does not know, "Water stays in me," nor does the water know, "I stay at the bottom of the well"; similarly, the surface of the tongue does not know, "Saliva, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stays on me," nor does the saliva know, "I, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stay on the surface of the tongue." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called saliva (kheḷo) is a separate portion in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void, not a being, liquid, and of the nature of cohesion, which is the water element. Snot (siṅghāṇikā), when it arises, fills the nostrils and either stays or flows out. There, just as in a shell filled with putrid curd, the shell does not know, "Putrid curd stays in me," nor does the putrid curd know, "I stay in the shell"; similarly, the nostrils do not know, "Snot stays in us," nor does the snot know, "I stay in the nostrils." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called snot (siṅghāṇikā) is a separate portion in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void, not a being, liquid, and of the nature of cohesion, which is the water element. Synovial fluid (lasikā) stays in the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the bones. There, just as in an axle lubricated with oil, the axle does not know, "Oil stays lubricating me," nor does the oil know, "I stay lubricating the axle"; similarly, the one hundred and eighty joints do not know, "Synovial fluid stays in us..."
65: Just as the axle does not know, "It stays lubricating me," the synovial fluid (lasikā) does not know, "I stay lubricating the one hundred and eighty joints." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called synovial fluid (lasikā) is a separate portion in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void, not a being, liquid, and of the nature of cohesion, which is the water element. Urine (mutta) stays inside the bladder. There, just as when cesspool water is poured into a water pot turned upside down (or without an opening), the water pot does not know, "Cesspool water stays in me," nor does the cesspool water know, "I stay in the water pot"; similarly, the bladder does not know, "Urine stays in me," nor does the urine know, "I stay in the bladder." These things are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called urine (mutta) is a separate portion in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void, not a being, liquid, and of the nature of cohesion, which is the water element. The phrase "or whatever else" (yaṃ vā pana) is said in reference to the water element contained in the remaining three groups (earth, fire, air). In the explanation of the external water element, the liquid produced depending on the root is called root-juice (mūlarasa). The same method applies to trunk-juice and so forth. Milk and so forth are well-known. However, there is no restriction here as in the medicinal training rule (bhesajja-sikkhāpada). Any milk is just milk. The same method applies to the rest, such as curd and so forth. "Bhummāni" refers to waters staying in pits and so forth. "Antalikkhāni" refers to rainwaters that have not yet reached the ground. "Yaṃ vā panā" refers to snow-water, world-destroying rainwater, water supporting the earth, and so forth, which enter the "yevāpanaka" category here. In the explanation of the fire element (tejodhātu), it is called "tejo" because of its sharp power. It is called "tejógata" because it has reached the state of fire. "Usmā" is the mode of heat. It is called "usmāgata" because it has reached the state of heat-vapor. "Usuma" is intense vapor. It is called "usumagata" because it has reached that state of vapor. By which disturbed fire element this body is heated (santappati), and heat arises through one-day fevers and so forth. By which fire element this body decays (jīrīyati), reaching the state of deficiency of the faculties, loss of strength, wrinkling of the skin, graying of the hair, and so forth. By which disturbed fire element this body is consumed (pariḍayhati), that person...
66:
That person, lamenting 'I am burning, I am burning,' longs for the application of butter washed a hundred times, Gosīta sandalwood, and the like, as well as the breeze from a palm-leaf fan. By which [fire element] what is eaten (rice, etc.), drunk (beverages, etc.), chewed (pastries, etc.), and tasted (ripe mango, honey, molasses, etc.) is properly digested, meaning it reaches a state of separation into juices and so forth. Among these four types of fire element, the first three are produced by four causes. The last one, the digestive fire (pācaka-tejo), is produced only by kamma (kamma-samuṭṭhāna). This is the explanation of the terms here.

The method of attention (manasikāra) is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk reflects: 'That by which [this body] is heated—this santappana-tejo is a distinct part in this body, insentient, indeterminate (abyākata), void of self, not a living being, a fire element with the characteristic of maturing.' He reflects: 'That by which [this body] is aged, that by which it is consumed by heat, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested—these are distinct parts in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void of self, not a living being, a fire element with the characteristic of maturing.' 'Or whatever else' (yaṃ vā pana) refers to the natural fire element (utu-tejo) in this body, which is included in the 'whatever else' (yevāpanaka) category.

In the description of the external fire element: fire that burns depending on wood and has wood as its fuel is called 'wood-fire' (kaṭṭhaggi). The same method applies to bark-fire and so on. 'Rubbish-fire' (saṅkāraggi) is fire made by gathering and burning rubbish. 'Indra's fire' (indaggi) is lightning. 'Heat of fire' (aggisantāpa) is the heat of a flame or of glowing coals without flame. 'Heat of the sun' (sūriyasantāpa) is the heat of sunlight. 'Heat of a woodpile' (kaṭṭhasannicayasantāpa) is the heat in a place where wood is stacked. The same method applies to the rest. 'Or whatever else' includes the fire of petas, the fire that destroys the world-cycle (kappa-vināsaggi), the fire of hell, and so on, in this description of the external fire element.

In the description of the air element: it is called 'air' (vāyo) because of its blowing force. It is called 'gone to air' (vāyogata) because it has reached the state of air. 'The stiffness of form' (thambhitattaṃ rūpassa) is the stiff state of inseparable material form (avinibbhoga-rūpa). 'Upward-going winds' (uddhaṅgamā vātā) are winds that move upwards, causing belching, hiccups, and so forth. 'Downward-going winds' (adhogamā vātā) are winds that move downwards, expelling feces, urine, and so forth. 'Winds in the belly' (kucchisayā vātā) are winds outside the intestines. 'Winds in the bowels' (koṭṭhāsayā vātā) are winds inside the intestines. 'Winds coursing through the limbs' (aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā) are winds that spread through the major and minor limbs of the whole body, following the network of veins.
67:
...are winds that cause bending, stretching, and so forth. 'Knife-like winds' (satthakavātā) are winds that occur as if cutting the joints and ligaments with a pair of scissors. 'Razor-like winds' (khurakavātā) are winds that split the heart as if with a razor. 'Lotus-extracting winds' (uppalakavātā) are winds that pull out the heart-flesh itself. 'In-breath' (assāsa) is the nasal air entering within. 'Out-breath' (passāsa) is the nasal air exiting without. Among these, all the previously mentioned winds are produced by four causes. The in-breath and out-breath, however, are produced only by consciousness (citta-samuṭṭhāna). This is the explanation of the terms here.

This is the method of attention: In this Dispensation, a monk, having grasped the various winds such as the upward-going winds by way of their upward-going nature, etc., reflects: 'Upward-going winds are a distinct part in this body, insentient, indeterminate, void of self, not a living being, a wind element with the characteristic of supporting (vitthambhana).' The same method applies to the rest. By the phrase 'or whatever else' (yaṃ vā pana), the winds that follow the groups of air elements other than those specifically mentioned fall into the 'whatever else' (yevāpana) category.

In the description of the external air element: 'Easterly winds' (puratthimā vātā) are winds coming from the eastern direction. The same method applies to the west, north, and south. 'Dusty winds' (sarajavātā) are winds with dust. 'Dustless winds' (arajavātā) are pure winds free from dust. 'Cold winds' (sītavātā) are those produced by the cold season, arising amidst cold clouds. 'Hot winds' (uṇhavātā) are those produced by the hot season, arising amidst hot clouds. 'Minor winds' (parittavātā) are slow, thin winds. 'Great winds' (adhimattavātā) are strong winds. 'Black winds' (kāḷavātā) are those arising amidst black clouds; when struck by these, the skin color becomes black. Some teachers say this is a name for winds that blow so as to make the skin black. 'Verambha winds' (verambhavātā) are winds blowing above one league (yojana). 'Wing winds' (pakkhavātā) are winds produced by the flapping of wings, even of a fly. 'Garuda winds' (supaṇṇavātā) are winds caused by the force of the wings of Garudas. In truth, these are also wing-flapping winds, but they are mentioned separately because of their great force. 'Palm-leaf fan winds' (tālavaṇṭavātā) are winds produced by palm leaves or other circular fans. 'Fan winds' (vidhūpanavātā) are winds produced by a fanning leaf. These palm-leaf fans and fanning leaves can produce wind that has not yet arisen and can circulate wind that has already arisen. 'Or whatever else' (yaṃ vā pana) means that, excluding the winds mentioned in the Pali text here, the remaining winds fall into the 'whatever else' (yevāpana) category.

In the description of the space element: it is called 'space' (ākāsa) because it is not scratched, in the sense of being non-resistant. It is called 'gone to space' (ākāsagata) because it has reached the state of space.
68:
It is called 'agha' because it is not struck (untouched). Because it has reached the state of a void, it is called 'aghagata'. 'Vivara' means an aperture or gap. Because it has reached the state of an aperture, it is called 'vivaragata'. 'Untouched by flesh and blood' means an opening free from flesh and blood. The phrase 'ear-hole' etc., is to show the different types of such openings. The 'ear-hole' is the aperture in the ear, a space untouched by flesh and blood. The same method applies to the remaining nose-hole, etc.

'Yena' (by which) refers to the opening through which one swallows various kinds of food and brings them inside. 'Yattha' (where) refers to the place called the inner abdominal lining where the four types of food remain. 'Yena' (by which) refers to the opening through which all the digested food, having become dregs, exits. That path of exit for old food, from the stomach-lining to the rectum, measuring about a span and four finger-breadths, should be known as the space element (ākāsadhātu) which is free and untouched by flesh and blood. In this explanation of the space element, 'Yaṃ vā pana' (or whatever else) includes all gaps such as the space between skin, flesh, tendons, bones, and hair, which belong to the 'yevāpanaka' (miscellaneous) category.

In the description of the external space element, 'untouched by the four great elements' refers to openings in walls, windows, etc., which are free from the four great elements. By this Pali, the space in which one performs preliminary work (parikamma) and gives rise to the fourth and fifth jhānas is taught.

In the description of the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu), the element called eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu). The same applies to the remaining consciousness elements. Thus, when these six elements are grasped, the eighteen elements are already grasped. How? By grasping the earth, fire, and air elements, the tangible-object element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu) is already grasped. By grasping the water and space elements, the mental-object element (dhammadhātu) is grasped. By grasping the consciousness element, the mind element (manodhātu) is grasped because it precedes and follows that consciousness. Eye-consciousness element etc., appear directly in the Sutta. The remaining nine elements should be brought in and shown. For by grasping the eye-consciousness element, its support, the eye element (cakkhudhātu), and its object, the visible-form element (rūpadhātu), are already grasped. In this way, by grasping ear-consciousness etc., all eighteen elements, including the ear element etc., are grasped.

Among those elements, the grasping of materiality (rūpa) is taught through ten elements. The grasping of mentality (arūpa) is taught through seven elements. Through the mental-object element (dhammadhātu), there may be grasping of materiality or mentality. Thus, the grasping of materiality and mentality is taught as the grasping of materiality through eleven and a half elements, and the grasping of mentality through seven and a half elements. Materiality and mentality are the five aggregates. That is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). The craving from the previous life that produces that Truth of Suffering is the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca).
69:
...is the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin is the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca). The Path that knows that Truth of Cessation in various ways is the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca). Thus, it should be understood that for a monk who applies his mind to this meditation subject of the Four Truths by way of the eighteen elements, the conclusion is stated, having brought him to the summit, which is the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala).

Now, to show the second group of six elements, he said "Aparāpi cha dhātuyo" (There are another six elements), etc. Among those elements, the pleasure element (sukha-dhātu) and the pain element (dukkha-dhātu) are shown as a pair by way of their opposition, having their basis in body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda). This is because the feeling of pleasure is the opposite of the feeling of pain, and the feeling of pain is the opposite of the feeling of pleasure. To whatever extent an area is pervaded by the feeling of pleasure, to that same extent the feeling of pain can pervade. To whatever extent an area is pervaded by the feeling of pain, to that same extent the feeling of pleasure can pervade. The terms "joy element" (somanassa-dhātu) and "displeasure element" (domanassa-dhātu) are also treated as a pair in the same way. This is because the feeling of joy is the opposite of the feeling of displeasure, and the feeling of displeasure is the opposite of the feeling of joy. To whatever extent an area is pervaded by the feeling of joy, to that same extent the feeling of displeasure can pervade. To whatever extent an area is pervaded by the feeling of displeasure, to that same extent the feeling of joy can pervade.

The pair consisting of the equanimity element (upekkhā-dhātu) and the ignorance element (avijjā-dhātu) is treated as a pair by way of their similarity. Both of these are similar because they are unmanifest. Among those, by taking the pleasure and pain elements, the body-consciousness element (kāyaviññāṇa-dhātu) associated with them, the body element (kāya-dhātu) which is their basis, and the tangible element (phoṭṭhabba-dhātu) which is their object, are also taken. By taking the joy and displeasure elements, the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu) associated with them is taken. By taking the ignorance element, the mental-object element (dhamma-dhātu) is taken. By taking the equanimity element, the eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, and mind element, as well as the eye element, visible-data element, etc., which are their bases and objects, are also taken. In this way, the eighteen elements are also taken. Now, among those eighteen elements, the entire procedure, such as the grasping of materiality by way of the ten elements, should be understood in the same manner as stated below. Thus, it should be understood that for the benefit of a certain monk, the conclusion is stated, having brought him to the summit, which is the Fruition of Arahantship. Among those elements, the terms such as "What is the pleasure element? That which is bodily ease..." are just as stated below.

11. In the third group of six elements, regarding the term "kāma" (sensuality), there are two kinds of sensuality: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma). Among those two, the element associated with defilement-sensuality, with reference to defilement-sensuality, is called the sensuality element (kāma-dhātu); this is a name for sensual thought (kāma-vitakka). With reference to objective sensuality, the very objects of the five cords of sensual pleasure are the sensuality element; this is a name for the sense-sphere states (kāmāvacara-dhamma). The element associated with ill-will is called the ill-will element (byāpāda-dhātu); this is a name for the thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka). Ill-will itself is the ill-will element because it is an element,
70:
This name (element of ill-will) is the name for anger (dosa) based on the ten grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu). The element associated with cruelty is called the element of cruelty (vihiṃsādhātu); this is the name for the thought of cruelty (vihiṃsāvitakka). Cruelty itself is the element, thus it is called the element of cruelty; this is the name for anger that harms others. Since this element of cruelty has not been mentioned below, its meaning and so forth should be understood by distinguishing them as follows: It is called cruelty (vihiṃsā) because beings are harmed by this quality, or because it is the nature of harming beings. That cruelty has the characteristic of harming, or the characteristic of being the opposite of compassion (karuṇā). It has the function of causing terror in the continuum of others, or the function of destroying compassion in one's own continuum. It manifests as the basis of suffering; it should be understood as having anger as its proximate cause.

Non-greed (alobha) is called renunciation (nekkhamma) because it is the departure from greed (lobha). The first jhāna is called renunciation because it is the departure from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); all wholesome states are called renunciation because they are the departure from all unwholesome states. The element associated with renunciation is called the element of renunciation (nekkhammadhātu); this is the name for the thought of renunciation (nekkhammavitakka). Renunciation itself is the element, thus it is called the element of renunciation; this is the name for all wholesome states. The element associated with non-ill-will is called the element of non-ill-will (abyāpādadhātu); this is the name for the thought of non-ill-will (abyāpādavitakka). Non-ill-will itself is the element, thus it is called the element of non-ill-will; this is the name for loving-kindness (mettā). The element associated with non-cruelty is called the element of non-cruelty (avihiṃsādhātu); this is the name for the thought of non-cruelty (avihiṃsāvitakka). Non-cruelty itself is the element, thus it is called the element of non-cruelty; this is the name for compassion (karuṇā).

Now, to show that very meaning, the word-analysis beginning with "Therein, what is the element of sensuality?" is commenced. Therein, "associated" (paṭisaṃyutta) means association by way of conjunction (sampayoga). Words such as "thought" (takka) and "applied thought" (vitakka) have the meanings already mentioned. "Viheṭheti" means it oppresses, it causes suffering. "Heṭhanā" is the oppression or the causing of suffering by means of striking with the hand and so forth. Intense harming is called "viheṭhanā". It is called "hiṃsanā" because it harms by means of this quality. Intense harming is called "vihiṃsā". "Rosanā" is irritation (ghaṭṭanā), and "virosanā" is intense irritation. Or, in all these words, it is merely an intensification of the word by the prefix "vi-". It is called "upaghāta" because it strikes closely by means of this quality; striking others closely is "parūpaghāta".

It is called "metti" because one loves by means of this quality. The mode of loving is "mettāyanā". The state of one endowed with loving-kindness is "mettāyitatta". The liberation of the mind that is freed from ill-will is "cetovimutti" (liberation of mind). Here, by the first three terms, both loving-kindness that has reached access (upacāra) and that which has reached absorption (appanā) are spoken of; by the last term, only loving-kindness that has reached absorption is spoken of.
71:
It is called compassion (karuṇā) because it feels pity for the suffering of beings by means of this quality. The mode of being compassionate is "karuṇāyanā". The state of one endowed with compassion is "karuṇāyitatta". The liberation of the mind that is freed from cruelty (vihiṃsā) is "cetovimutti". In this exposition of the element of non-cruelty as well, the distinction between access compassion and absorption compassion should be understood in the same way as before. In both the expositions of the element of non-ill-will and the element of non-cruelty, the terms "loving-kindness" and "compassion" are spoken of in the final term for the purpose of specifying "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti).

Here, sensual thought (kāmavitakka) occurs both with respect to beings and with respect to formations (saṅkhāra). Although it occurs in both, it is only a variety of the unwholesome course of action (kammapatha). Ill-will (byāpāda), however, can only break the course of action when it occurs with respect to beings; ill-will occurring with respect to formations other than beings cannot break the course of action. The same method applies to cruelty (vihiṃsā). Here, the discourse is of two kinds: the all-inclusive discourse (sabbasaṅgāhikakathā) and the unmixed discourse (asambhinna-kathā). By taking the element of sensuality (kāmadhātu), the element of ill-will and the element of cruelty are also taken. However, those two are shown by extracting them from the element of sensuality. This is called the all-inclusive discourse here. Setting aside the element of ill-will and the element of cruelty, to say that all remaining elements are only the element of sensuality is called the unmixed discourse. By taking the element of renunciation (nekkhammadhātu), the element of non-ill-will and the element of non-cruelty are also taken. Showing those two by extracting them from the element of renunciation is called the all-inclusive discourse here. Setting aside the element of non-ill-will and the element of non-cruelty, to say that the remaining elements are the element of renunciation is called the unmixed discourse.

By these six elements thus defined, the eighteen elements are already included. When all those elements are obtained by extracting them from the sensual element (as the eye-element and so forth), they are just the eighteen elements. Thus, by way of three sets of six, they become eighteen. Without taking it this way, if one makes eighteen for each set of six according to the method mentioned, and then condenses all those sets of eighteen into one, it should be understood that they are only eighteen. Thus, in this Suttanta-bhājanīya, sixteen elements belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and two elements belong to the three planes (tebhūmika); it should be understood that in this Suttanta-bhājanīya method, only the range of comprehension-knowledge (sammasana-ñāṇa) is spoken of.

## Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājanīya.
72:
## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Classification

In the Abhidhamma classification (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya), wishing to show all the elements (dhātu) in their specific nature, the Buddha spoke of the eighteen elements, beginning with the eye element and the form element. Among those eighteen elements, first in the summary section (uddesavāra):

The determination (vinicchaya) should be known by way of meaning (attha), by way of characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so forth, by way of order (kama), by way of measure and number (tāvatva), by way of condition (paccaya), and further by way of how they are to be seen (daṭṭhabba).

Among these, 'by way of meaning' (attato) is as follows: It is called 'eye' (cakkhu) because it sees clearly. It is called 'form' (rūpa) because it manifests the nature of being established in the mind. It is called 'eye-consciousness' (cakkhu-viññāṇa) because it is the consciousness of the eye-sensitivity. In this way, the determination should be known by the specific meanings of the terms such as 'eye' and so forth. However, in a general sense without distinction, it is called 'element' (dhātu) because it arranges (vidahati), because it is borne (dhīyate), because it is an arrangement (vidhāna), because it is arranged by this (vidhīyate), or because it is placed in this (dhīyati).

Indeed, just as the well-known elements in the world, such as the gold element and the silver element, being established as causes, arrange various things like gold and silver, so too these mundane elements arrange the suffering of saṃsāra in its many forms. They are borne by beings just as a burden is borne by carriers. These are merely the arrangement of suffering because they are not subject to anyone's will. By these elements, which are the instruments, the suffering of saṃsāra is arranged by beings. And that suffering of saṃsāra thus arranged is placed in these very elements. Thus, each individual state, such as the eye and so forth, is called an 'element' by virtue of meanings such as arranging and being borne, as applicable.

Furthermore, unlike the 'Self' (atta) of the sectarians which does not exist by nature, these elements are not non-existent. These are called 'elements' because they bear their own nature. Just as in the world, the various components of stone such as yellow orpiment (haritāla) and red arsenic (manosilā) are called 'elements', these states such as the eye and so forth are called 'elements' because they are similar to those elements. This is because these states are diverse components to be known by wisdom.

Alternatively, just as the name 'element' is known in the case of the liquid element, blood element, etc., which are components of the collection called the 'body' and are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics, so too the name 'element' should be known in these states such as the eye and so forth, which are components of the individual existence (attabhāva) called the five aggregates. This is because they are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics. Moreover, the word 'element' is a designation for that which is merely soulless (non-living). This is true; the Blessed One taught the discourse on elements in such passages as, 'Bhikkhu, this person consists of six elements,' in order to abolish the perception of a soul (living being). Therefore, by the meanings already mentioned, because it is both the eye and an element, it is called the 'eye element'. Because it is both mind-consciousness and an element, it is called the 'mind-consciousness element'. In this way, the determination by way of meaning should be known in this summary section.
73:
Indeed, these elements such as the eye and so forth are components of the knowledge that knows, and components of the states to be known. (Alternatively) They are states that are components to be known unerringly by wisdom. Or, just as the name 'element' is known in the case of the liquid element, blood element, etc., which are components of the collection called the 'self' and are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics, so too the name 'element' should be known in these states such as the eye and so forth, which are components of the individual existence (attabhāva) called the five aggregates. In truth, those states such as the eye and so forth are delimited by mutually dissimilar characteristics. Furthermore, this word 'dhātu' is a term that expresses a nature that is merely soulless (non-living). This is true; the Blessed One taught the discourse on elements in such passages as, 'Bhikkhu, this person (being) consists of six elements,' in order to abolish the perception of a 'being'. Therefore, according to the meanings and definitions mentioned, because it is both the eye and an element, it is called the 'eye element'. Similarly, because it is both mind-consciousness and an element, it is called the 'mind-consciousness element'. In this way, first, the determination by way of meaning should be known in this context.

'By way of characteristics and so forth' (lakkhaṇādito) means that the determination in these elements should also be known by way of the characteristics and so forth of the elements such as the eye. Their characteristics and so forth should be understood exactly in the manner already described below.

'By way of order' (kamato) means that in this Dhātuvibhaṅga as well, among the types of order such as the order of arising (uppatti-kkama) mentioned previously, only the order of teaching (desanā-kkama) is appropriate. That order of teaching is stated by way of the sequential determination of cause and effect. For these two, the eye element and the form element, are the cause, and the eye-consciousness element is the effect. In this way, the determination by way of order should be known in all elements.

'By way of measure and number' (tāvatvato) means [the determination should be known] by way of the state of having a measure of eighteen. This means that in various Sutta and Abhidhamma teachings, other elements are also seen, such as: the light element (ābhā-dhātu), the beautiful element (subha-dhātu), the element of the sphere of infinite space, the element of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the element of the sphere of nothingness, the element of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling, the sensual element (kāma-dhātu), the element of ill-will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill-will, the element of non-cruelty, the pleasure element, the pain element, the joy element, the grief element, the equanimity element, the ignorance element, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of endeavor, the low element, the medium element, the refined element, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element, the conditioned element, the unconditioned element, and 'the world of many elements, of various elements'.

This being so, if it is asked, 'Why was this delimitation of only eighteen made, without making a delimitation by way of all elements?' the answer is: because all elements that exist in the ultimate sense are included within those eighteen elements. Indeed, the light element is just the form element. The beautiful element, however, is connected with form and so forth. Why? Because it is a beautiful sign (subha-nimitta). For the beautiful sign is the beautiful element. And that beautiful sign does not exist apart from form and so forth; or rather, form and so forth which are the objects of wholesome resultant [consciousness] are themselves the beautiful element; thus, this beautiful element is merely form and so forth. In the element of the sphere of infinite space and so forth, all consciousness is the mind-consciousness element, and the remaining mental states are the dhamma element. The element of the cessation of perception and feeling, however, does not exist as a separate ultimate reality; it is merely the cessation of the two elements, namely, the mind-consciousness element and the dhamma element. The sensual element is merely the dhamma element; as it is said: 'Therein, what is the sensual element? It is the thought (takka) ... wrong intention associated with sensuality.' Or, all eighteen elements...
74:
In another way, there are eighteen elements. Regarding this, it has been taught: "Taking the Avīci hell as the lower limit and the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas as the upper limit, the aggregates, elements, and bases—namely, matter, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—that occur within this interval and are included therein, are called the kāmadhātu (sensual element)." The element of renunciation (nekkhamma-dhātu) is indeed the mental-object element (dhammadhātu). Or, because it is taught that "all wholesome states are the element of renunciation," it can also be the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). The elements of ill-will, cruelty, non-ill-will, non-cruelty, pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, ignorance, exertion, endeavor, and striving are all just the mental-object element.

The low, medium, and superior elements are just the eighteen elements themselves. In fact, the low eye-element and so on are called the low element (hīna-dhātu). The medium and superior eye-elements and so on are called the medium element (majjhima-dhātu) and superior element (paṇīta-dhātu). Strictly speaking, however, the unwholesome mental-object element and mind-consciousness element are the low element. Both the mundane wholesome and indeterminate mental-object and mind-consciousness elements, as well as the eye-element and so on, are the medium element. But the supramundane mental-object and mind-consciousness elements are the superior element. The earth, fire, and air elements are just the tangible-object element (phoṭṭhabbadhātu). The water element and space element are just the mental-object element. The consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu) is a summary of the seven consciousness elements, such as the eye-consciousness element. Seventeen elements and a portion of the mental-object element are conditioned elements (saṅkhata-dhātu). The unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu, i.e., Nibbāna) is only a portion of the mental-object element. The world of many elements and various elements is merely a differentiation of the eighteen elements. Thus, because all elements existing in reality are included within these eighteen, only eighteen were taught.

Furthermore, the eighteen elements were taught for the purpose of removing the perception of a "soul" (jīva) in those beings who perceive a soul in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. For there are beings who perceive a soul in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. To them, the Blessed One revealed the eighteen elements, wishing to remove the long-underlying perception of a soul by demonstrating the multiplicity of that consciousness through the divisions of eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, body-consciousness element, and mind-consciousness element, and its impermanence due to its occurrence in dependence on causes such as the eye and forms. What else? Likewise, they were revealed as eighteen according to the disposition of those to be led (veneyya), and according to the disposition of those beings who are to be guided by this teaching which is neither too brief nor too detailed.
75:
In brief and in detail,
This Blessed One reveals the Dhamma in such and such ways.
In whatever way He reveals it,
The darkness dwelling in the hearts of beings to be led,
Being struck by the power of the True Dhamma,
Reaches destruction in an instant.

Thus, the decision regarding these elements should be understood by way of "extent" (tāvatvato).

Regarding "number" (saṅkhato): First, the eye-element, being of one kind as eye-sensitivity, is counted as only one state. Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, smell, and taste elements are each counted as one state by way of ear-sensitivity and so on. The tangible-object element, however, is counted as three states by way of the divisions of earth, fire, and air. The eye-consciousness element is counted as two states by way of wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness elements are each counted as two. The mind-element is counted as three states by way of five-door adverting, wholesome-resultant receiving, and unwholesome-resultant receiving. The mental-object element is counted as twenty states by way of the three mental aggregates, sixteen kinds of subtle matter, and the unconditioned element (Nibbāna). The mind-consciousness element is counted as seventy-six states by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousnesses. Thus, the decision regarding these elements should be understood by way of "number."

Regarding "cause" (paccayā): The decision should be understood by way of the eye-element and so on being causes for the eye-consciousness element and so on. Their nature as causes will be made clear in the Niddesavāra (Exposition Section).

Regarding "how they should be regarded" (daṭṭhabbā): The meaning is that the decision should be understood by way of how they are to be regarded. For all conditioned elements should be regarded as void of a beginning and an end, as void of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self, and as occurring in dependence on causes.

Specifically, among these elements, the eye-element should be regarded like the surface of a drum, the form-element like the drumstick, and the eye-consciousness element like the sound. Likewise, the eye-element is like the surface of a mirror, the form-element like a face, and the eye-consciousness element like the reflection of the face. Alternatively, the eye-element is like sugarcane husks or sesame dregs, the form-element like the press-machine's axle, and the eye-consciousness element like the sugarcane juice or oil. Likewise, the eye-element is like the lower fire-stick, the form-element like the upper fire-stick, and the eye-consciousness element like the fire. This method applies to the ear-element and so on as well.

The mind-element, however, should be regarded as the precursor and follower of the eye-consciousness element and so on, as the case may be. In the mental-object element, the aggregate of feeling should be regarded as a dart, as a stake...
76:
Perception and the aggregate of mental formations should be seen like patients suffering from pain through association with the thorns and spikes of feeling. Alternatively, the perception of worldlings (puthujjanas) should be seen like an empty fist because it produces suffering by craving for what is pleasant, and like a forest deer because it grasps false signs. Mental formations should be seen like a man throwing someone into a pit of coals because they cast one into rebirth; like thieves pursued by royal officers because they are followed by the suffering of birth; and like the seeds of a poison tree because they are the cause of the continuum of aggregates that brings all harm. The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be seen like a razor-wheel because it is the cause of various dangers.

The unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu, Nibbāna), however, should be seen as the deathless, the peaceful, and the secure. Why? Because it is the opposite of all harm. The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should be seen like a forest monkey because it arises by letting go of a grasped object and taking another; like a wild horse because it is difficult to tame; like a stick thrown into the air because it falls wherever it wishes; and like a dancer because it is associated with various defilements such as greed and hatred.

In the section of the description (Niddesavāra), 'dependent on the eye and forms' means dependent on these two, and also on the other, the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) and the three associated mental aggregates. For, to the eye-consciousness element, the eye is the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya), the form is the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), the functional mind-element is the disappearance-condition (vigata-paccaya), and the three mental aggregates are the co-nascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya). Therefore, that eye-consciousness element is said to arise dependent on these four. The same method applies to the ear, etc.

'Immediately after ceasing' (niruddhasamanantarā) means immediately after it has ceased. 'The corresponding mind-element' (tajjā manodhātu) is the mind-element with the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana-kicca), which is twofold as wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. 'Or the first attention among all dhammas' means the first attention when all these dhammas such as eye-consciousness etc. arise; or it should be understood as the first attention to all dhammas known as the objects of eye-consciousness element, etc. By this statement, it should be understood that the functional mind-element with the function of five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana-kicca) is taken.

In the phrase 'immediately after the mind-element also has arisen and ceased', the word 'pi' (also) has the sense of inclusion. Therefore, it should be understood to mean 'after the mind-element and also after the mind-consciousness element'. By that, the resultant mind-consciousness element with the function of investigating (santīraṇa-kicca) which arises immediately after the resultant mind-element has arisen and ceased; the functional mind-consciousness element with the function of determining (votthabbana-kicca) which arises immediately after that investigating [consciousness] has arisen and ceased; and [the mind-consciousness element] which arises after that determining [consciousness] has arisen and ceased...
78:
## 4. Saccavibhaṅga (Analysis of the Truths)
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Suttanta Classification)
Now, in the Saccavibhaṅga, which follows the Dhātuvibhaṅga, the word "four" is a numerical limitation. The term "Noble Truths" is a designation of the states thus defined. In the section of the brief exposition (uddesavāra) beginning with "The Noble Truth of Suffering" —

By way of classification, and by way of definition, characteristics, and so forth,
By way of extracting the meaning, and likewise by way of being neither less nor more.
By way of order, and by way of the function of knowledge regarding the Noble Truths,
By way of the variety of included states, by way of simile, and by way of the groups of four.
By way of emptiness, the singlefold nature, and so forth, and by way of similarity and dissimilarity,
The wise should understand the decision in the sequence of the Teaching.

Among those mnemonic verses, "by way of classification" means the four distinct meanings each of suffering and so forth, which are true, not false, and not otherwise, and which must be penetrated by those who penetrate suffering and so forth. As it is said: "The meaning of oppressing, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of tormenting, the meaning of changing — these four are the meanings of suffering, which are true, not false, and not otherwise. The meaning of accumulating, the meaning of source, the meaning of conjunction, the meaning of impediment [for the origin]... (pe)... the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of being unconditioned, the meaning of deathlessness [for cessation]... (pe)... the meaning of leading out, the meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, the meaning of predominance — these four are the meanings of the path, which are true, not false, and not otherwise" (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga). Furthermore, it is said: "The meaning of oppressing, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of tormenting, the meaning of changing, the meaning of penetration," and so forth. Thus, suffering and the other truths should be understood by way of these four distinct meanings. This is the decision by way of classification in this context.

In the phrase "by way of definition, characteristics, and so forth," first, by way of definition (nibbacana) — here, the sound "du" is seen in the sense of vile (kucchita); for they call a vile son "duputta." The sound "kha" is in the sense of empty (tuccha); for they call the empty sky "kha." This first truth is vile because it is the site of many dangers, and it is empty because it is devoid of the nature of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self as imagined by the foolish. Therefore, because of being vile and because of being empty, it is called "dukkha." The sound "saṃ"...
79:
This sound "saṃ" indicates the sense of conjunction (saṃyoga) in such words as "samāgamo sametaṃ." This sound "u" indicates the sense of arising (uppatti) in such words as "uppannaṃ uditaṃ." The word "aya" indicates the sense of cause (kāraṇa). This second truth (the origin) is the cause of the arising of suffering when there is the conjunction of the remaining conditions such as ignorance. Thus, because it is the cause of the arising of suffering in conjunction, it is called "dukkhasamudaya" (the origin of suffering).

In the third truth (the cessation), the word "ni" indicates absence (abhāva), and the word "rodha" indicates a prison (cāraka). Therefore, it is called "dukkhanirodha" (the cessation of suffering) because in this Nibbāna there is the absence of the prison of saṃsāra known as the bond of suffering, and because it is empty of all destinations (gati). Alternatively, when that Nibbāna is attained (by the path-knowledge), the prison of saṃsāra known as the bond of suffering no longer exists because it is the opposite of that Nibbāna; thus it is called "dukkhanirodha." Or, because it is the condition for the cessation of suffering in the sense of non-arising, it is called "dukkhanirodha." The fourth truth (the path) is called "dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā" (the practice leading to the cessation of suffering) because it goes towards that cessation of suffering by way of taking it as an object and being directed towards it, and because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering.

Furthermore, because the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha, penetrate these, they are called "Noble Truths" (Ariyasaccāni). As it is said: "Monks, these four are the Noble Truths. Which four? ... (pe) ... Monks, these four are the Noble Truths. The Noble Ones penetrate these truths; therefore, they are called Noble Truths." Alternatively, they are the "Truths of the Noble One" (the Buddha), thus they are Noble Truths. As it is said: "Monks, in the world with its devas ... (pe) ... among the generation of devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore, they are called Noble Truths." Or else, because of the attainment of the state of a Noble One through the full awakening to these, they are Noble Truths.
