As it is said: "Monks, because of fully awakening to these four Noble Truths as they really are, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, is called 'Noble'." Furthermore, they are Noble Truths because they are noble truths; "noble" here means real, not false, and not deceptive. As it is said: "Monks, these four Noble Truths are real, not false, and not otherwise; therefore, they are called Noble Truths." Thus, the decision by way of definition (nibbacana) in these four truths should be understood.

What is meant by "by way of characteristics and so forth"? Here, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppressing (bādhana), the function of tormenting (santāpana), and the manifestation of occurrence (pavatti). The truth of origin has the characteristic of originating (pabhava), the function of preventing interruption (anupacchedakaraṇa), and the manifestation of impediment (palibodha). The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace (santi), the function of deathlessness (accuti),
80:
## Decision by Distinction of Characteristics

The Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) has the manifestation of non-occurrence as its essence. The Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) has the characteristic of leading out from saṃsāra, the function of abandoning the defilements, and the manifestation of emergence (from formations). Alternatively, they have the characteristics of occurrence (pavatti), causing occurrence (pavattaka), cessation (nivatti), and causing cessation (nivattaka) respectively. Likewise, they have the characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhata), craving (taṇhā), the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and seeing (dassana). Thus, in these four truths, the decision 'by distinction of characteristics' should be understood.

In the phrase 'by way of meaning and by way of extracting the meaning,' first, regarding the meaning: What is the meaning of 'truth' (sacca)? It is not deceptive like a magic trick to those who investigate with the eye of wisdom, not misleading like a mirage, and not non-existent in nature like the 'self' (atta) of the sectarians. Rather, it is indeed the object of the knowledge of the Noble Ones (ariyas) by way of being real, non-distorted, and existing in the modes of oppression, origin, peace, and liberation. This real, non-distorted, and existing nature should be understood as the meaning of truth, just like the hot characteristic of fire or the nature of the world. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, this suffering is real, it is not unreal, it is not otherwise," and so on in detail. Furthermore—

Suffering is not non-oppressive, and nothing other than suffering is oppressive. Because of the certainty of the nature of oppression, this is known as a truth.

Apart from craving, suffering does not arise from elsewhere, nor does that suffering not arise from that craving (it indeed does). Because of the certainty of the cause of suffering, craving is called a truth.

There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is that Nibbāna not of a peaceful nature. Because of the certainty of the nature of peace, this Nibbāna is known as a truth.

There is no liberation other than the Path, nor is that Path not a means of liberation. Because of the nature of true liberation, it is recognized as a truth.

Thus, the wise say that the meaning of truth is the real, non-distorted, and existing nature in all four truths, such as suffering, without distinction. Thus, the decision 'by way of meaning' should be understood.

How is it 'by way of extracting the meaning' (atthuḍḍhāra)? Here, this word 'truth' (sacca) is seen in many senses. For example—in the sense of truthful speech (vācā-sacca) in such passages as: "One should speak the truth, one should not get angry"; in the sense of the truth of abstinence (virati-sacca) in such passages as: "Ascetics and Brahmins standing in truth"; in the sense of...
81:
"Why do they speak various truths, those skilled in debate who claim to be experts?"—in such passages, it is seen in the sense of the truth of views (diṭṭhi-sacca). "Truth is one, there is no second"—in such passages, it is seen in the sense of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), referring to Nibbāna and the Path. "Of the four Noble Truths, how many are wholesome?"—in such passages, it is seen in the sense of the Noble Truth (ariya-sacca). This word 'truth' here also refers to the sense of the Noble Truth. Thus, in these four truths, the decision 'by way of extracting the meaning' should also be understood.

Regarding the heading 'by way of neither less nor more' (anūnādhikato): Why did the Blessed One teach exactly four Noble Truths, neither less nor more? Because no other truth is possible and because none of the four can be removed. Indeed, no other truth can be added to these, nor can even one of these be removed. As He said: "Monks, it is impossible that any ascetic or Brahmin in this world should come and say: 'This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama; there is another Noble Truth of Suffering. I will set aside this Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama and point out another Noble Truth of Suffering.'" And as He said: "Monks, it is impossible that any ascetic or Brahmin should say: 'This is not the first Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama; I will reject this first Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama and point out another first Noble Truth of Suffering,'" and so on.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One explained the occurrence (pavatti) of the round of rebirth, He explained it together with its cause (samudaya); and He explained the cessation (nivatti) from the round together with its means (magga). Thus, because the occurrence, the cessation, and the causes of both are limited to these four, only four are taught. Likewise, only four are taught by virtue of: that which is to be fully understood (dukkha), that which is to be abandoned (samudaya), that which is to be realized (nirodha), and that which is to be developed (magga); by virtue of the basis of craving (dukkha), craving (samudaya), the cessation of craving (nirodha), and the means to the cessation of craving (magga); and by virtue of the object of attachment (dukkha), delight in that object (samudaya), the total uprooting of attachment (nirodha), and the means to uproot attachment (magga). Thus, the decision 'by way of neither less nor more' should be understood.

Regarding the heading 'by way of order' (kamato): This sequence is also the order of teaching (desanākkama). Among these four truths, the Truth of Suffering is taught first because it is gross and common to all beings, and thus easy to understand. The Truth of the Origin is taught immediately after it to show the cause of that suffering. The Truth of Cessation is taught after that to make it known that when the cause (origin) ceases, the effect (suffering) ceases. The Truth of the Path is taught at the end to show the means for attaining that cessation. Alternatively, He taught suffering first to produce a sense of urgency (saṃvega) in beings who are infatuated with the enjoyment of worldly happiness. That suffering does not arise spontaneously without a cause, nor is it created by a Lord (Issara) or Brahma, etc.; rather, it arises because of this (craving/origin)...
82:
To make it known that this suffering arises because of this origin of craving, the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya-sacca) was taught immediately after that suffering. After that, for the purpose of generating relief by showing the escape to those whose minds are terrified, being oppressed by suffering along with its cause, and who are seeking an escape from suffering, the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca) was taught. After that, for the purpose of attaining cessation, the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca) which leads to cessation was taught. Thus, the decision regarding the 'order' should be understood here.

'In the Noble Truths, whatever knowledge there is, by way of its function' means that the decision should also be understood by way of the function of the knowledge of the truths. Indeed, the knowledge of the truths is twofold: knowledge of conformity (anubodha-ñāṇa) and knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). Among these, the knowledge of conformity is mundane and occurs in the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path by way of hearsay and so on. The knowledge of penetration is supramundane and, having cessation (Nibbāna) as its object, penetrates all four truths by way of its function. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the way leading to the cessation of suffering'—all this should be stated.

As for that mundane knowledge, therein, the knowledge of suffering prevents personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) which occurs by way of being overwhelmed by the outbursts of defilements. The knowledge of the origin prevents annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi); the knowledge of cessation prevents eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi); and the knowledge of the path prevents the view of the inefficacy of action (akiriya-diṭṭhi). Alternatively, the knowledge of suffering prevents the misconception regarding the result (phala), which is the perception of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self in the aggregates that are devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The knowledge of the origin prevents the misconception regarding the cause (hetu), which is the assumption of a cause in what is not a cause, occurring as the belief that the world proceeds because of causes such as a creator (Issara), a primal substance (Padhāna), time (Kāla), or nature (Sabhāva). The knowledge of cessation prevents the misconception regarding cessation, which is the taking of the formless world or the 'pinnacle of the world' (lokathūpikā) as Nibbāna. The knowledge of the path prevents the misconception regarding the means (upāya), which is the taking of a path that is not the path to purity—such as devotion to sensual indulgence or self-mortification—as the path to purity. Therefore, it is said:

'A man is confused about the world, the origin of the world,
The cessation of the world, and the peaceful means thereto,
So long as he does not understand the Truths.'

Thus, the decision regarding the 'function of knowledge' should be understood here.

'By the classification of what is included' means that in the Truth of Suffering, excluding craving and the taintless (anāsava) states, all remaining states are included. In the Truth of the Origin, the thirty-six modes of craving are included. The Truth of Cessation is unmixed Nibbāna alone. In the Truth of the Path, with Right View as the head, the base of power of investigation (vīmaṃsid dhipāda), the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), the power of wisdom (paññā-bala), and the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) are included. Under the designation of Right Intention, the three such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) are included; under the designation of Right Speech, the four types of good verbal conduct; under the designation of Right Action, the three types of good bodily conduct; and by way of Right Livelihood, fewness of wishes (appicchatā) are included.
83:
Contentment (santuṭṭhitā) is also included; or because all these—Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood—are virtue loved by the Noble Ones (ariyakanta-sīla), and because virtue is to be received with the hand of faith, and because of the existence of those who possess that virtue, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), the power of faith (saddhā-bala), and the base of power of desire (chandiddhipāda) are included (in the Truth of the Path). Under the designation of Right Effort, the four right endeavors (sammappadhāna), the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the energy enlightenment factor are included. Under the designation of Right Mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the mindfulness enlightenment factor are included. Under the designation of Right Concentration, the three types of concentration such as that with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra) and so on, and the concentration of mind (citta-samādhi), the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the enlightenment factors of joy (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) are included. Thus, the decision regarding the 'classification of what is included' should be understood here.

'By way of similes' means: the Truth of Suffering should be seen as a burden; the Truth of the Origin as the taking up of the burden; the Truth of Cessation as the laying down of the burden; and the Truth of the Path as the means of laying down the burden. Also, the Truth of Suffering is like a disease; the Truth of the Origin like the cause of the disease; the Truth of Cessation like the curing of the disease; and the Truth of the Path like the medicine. Or, the Truth of Suffering is like a famine (dubbhi kkha); the Truth of the Origin like bad rain (dubbuṭṭhi); the Truth of Cessation like plenty (subhikkha); and the Truth of the Path like good rain (suvuṭṭhi). Furthermore, these truths should be understood by way of similes by connecting them with: an enemy, the root of the enemy, the total destruction of the enemy, and the means for the total destruction of the enemy; a poison tree, the root of the tree, the cutting off of the root, and the means for cutting off that root; fear, the root of fear, the state of fearlessness, and the means for attaining that fearlessness; the near shore, the great flood, the far shore, and the effort to reach that far shore. Thus, the decision 'by way of similes' should be understood here.

'By way of the tetrad' means: in these truths, there is that which is suffering but not a Noble Truth; there is that which is a Noble Truth but not suffering; there is that which is both suffering and a Noble Truth; and there is that which is neither suffering nor a Noble Truth. This same method applies to the Origin and so on. Therein, the states associated with the Path and the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are suffering because of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā) according to the saying 'whatever is impermanent is suffering', but they are not the Noble Truth (of Suffering). Cessation (Nibbāna) is a Noble Truth but not suffering. The other two Noble Truths (Origin and Path) may be suffering by way of impermanence, but they are not suffering in the true sense for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the purpose of full understanding (pariññā). However, in every way, the five aggregates of clinging, excluding craving, are both suffering and the Noble Truth. The states associated with the Path and the fruits of recluseship are neither suffering nor the Noble Truth in the true sense for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the purpose of full understanding of that Truth of Suffering. Thus, having connected them appropriately in the Origin and so on, the decision 'by way of the tetrad' should be understood here.
85:
Alternatively, it is threefold by way of the division into the three aggregates, such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). For this supramundane path, being partial, is included within the three aggregates (which include both mundane and supramundane) which are complete, just as a city is included within a kingdom. As it is said:

“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not included within the Noble Eightfold Path. But, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is included within the three aggregates. Friend Visākha, whatever is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Whatever is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). Whatever is right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).” (M. Ni. 1.462).

Among these eight path factors, the three factors beginning with right speech are virtue itself. Therefore, they are included in the aggregate of virtue by way of their common nature. Although in the Pali text the designation is made in the locative case as “in the aggregate of virtue,” the meaning should be understood by way of the instrumental case. Among the three factors beginning with right effort, concentration (samādhi) by its own nature is not able to reach absorption (appanā) by way of one-pointedness on the object; however, it is able to do so when it has received the appropriate assistance when effort (vīriya) performs the function of exerting and when mindfulness (sati) performs the function of not floating away (non-forgetfulness) from the object.

In this regard, there is this simile: Suppose three friends enter a park intending to enjoy a constellation festival. One of them sees a Champaka tree in full bloom but is unable to reach the flowers even by raising his hand. Then his second friend bends down and offers his back. Even standing on his back, he is still unsteady and unable to reach them. Then the other third friend offers his shoulder for support. Standing on the back of one and leaning on the shoulder of the other, he picks the flowers as he pleases, wears them, and enjoys the festival. This illustration should be understood as being accomplished without fail in the same way.

The three states beginning with right effort, which arise together, are like the three friends who entered the park together. The object is like the Champaka tree in full bloom. Concentration (samādhi), which cannot enter fixedly into the object by its own nature like the one who cannot pick the flowers even by raising his hand. Effort (vīriya) is like the friend who bends down and offers his back. Mindfulness (sati) is like the friend who stands offering his shoulder...
86:
Mindfulness is like a companion. For example, just as among such persons, one might stand on the back of another and, leaning on the shoulder of a second, a third is able to pick flowers as he pleases; even so, while effort (vīriya) performs the function of upholding, and mindfulness (sati) performs the function of non-forgetting (not letting the object slip away), concentration (samādhi), having gained such support, is able to fixate on the object with one-pointedness. Therefore, in this context, only concentration is included in the Concentration Aggregate (samādhikkhandha) by way of its own nature. Effort and mindfulness, however, are included by way of their activity (kiriya).

Regarding Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) and Right Thought (sammā-saṅkappa), wisdom (paññā) by its own nature is unable to determine the object as 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self'; however, it is able to do so only when thought (vitakka) strikes the object again and again. How is this? For example, a treasurer, though wishing to examine a coin on all sides after placing it in his palm, cannot turn it over with his eyes alone; he can only examine it from this side and that after turning it over again and again with his fingers. Even so, wisdom by its own nature cannot determine the object in terms of impermanence and so on; it can only determine the object that is taken up and given to it by vitakka, which acts as if striking and turning the object over with its characteristic of directing the mind onto the object and its function of repeated striking.

Therefore, here too, only Right View is included in the Wisdom Aggregate (paññākkhandha) by way of its own nature, while Right Thought is included by way of its activity. Thus, the Path is included within these three aggregates. With reference to this, it is said: "It is threefold by way of the division of the three aggregates." It is fourfold by way of the Path of Stream-entry and so on.

Furthermore, all the Truths are of one kind because they are not otherwise (undeviating) or because they are to be fully known. They are of two kinds by way of mundane and supramundane, or conditioned and unconditioned. They are of three kinds by way of being abandoned by vision, being abandoned by cultivation, and being neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation. They are of four kinds by way of the divisions of the tasks such as full comprehension (pariññeyya) and so on. Thus, the determination should be understood here 'by way of being of one kind' and so on.

'By way of similarity and dissimilarity' means: all the Truths are similar to one another in being undeviating, in being void of self, and in being difficult to penetrate. As it is said:

"What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult or more hard to achieve—that a man from afar should shoot arrow after arrow through a narrow keyhole without missing, or that he..."
87:
"...should pierce the tip of a hair split seven times (or a hundred times) with another hair tip?" When asked thus, [Ānanda replied:] "Venerable Sir, this indeed is more difficult and more hard to achieve—that one should pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with another hair tip." [The Buddha said:] "Ānanda, those who penetrate as it really is, 'This is suffering'... [and] those who penetrate as it really is, 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' penetrate something even more difficult than that piercing of hair tips." (Saṃ. Ni. 5. 1115).

The Truths are dissimilar (visabhāga) due to the definition of their individual characteristics. The first two Truths (Suffering and Origin) are similar (sabhāga) in being deep because they are difficult to fathom with wisdom, in being mundane, and in being accompanied by taints (āsavas). They are dissimilar due to the distinction between result and cause, and because one is to be fully comprehended while the other is to be abandoned. The latter two Truths (Cessation and Path) are also similar in being deep because their meaning is difficult to fathom, in being supramundane, and in being without taints. They are dissimilar due to the distinction between the object and the subject (knower), and because one is to be realized while the other is to be developed. The first and third Truths are also similar in being designated as results, but they are dissimilar in being conditioned (saṅkhata) and unconditioned (asaṅkhata). The second and fourth Truths are also similar in being designated as causes, but they are dissimilar in being entirely unwholesome and entirely wholesome. The first and fourth Truths are also similar in being conditioned, but they are dissimilar in being mundane and supramundane. The second and third Truths are also similar in being neither-trainee-nor-adept (nevasikkhānāsikkha), but they are dissimilar in being with an object and without an object.

Thus, in these ways and methods, the wise person
Should know the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths.

## The Explanation of the Summary of the Suttanta Analysis is finished.

## 1. Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

## Exposition of Birth

Now, in order to show the detailed analysis of Suffering and so on, which were indicated in brief, this exposition (niddesavāra) is begun: "Therein, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is also suffering," and so on. In that exposition, birth (jāti) should be understood, and the meaning of suffering in birth should be understood. Aging (jarā), death (maraṇa)...
88:
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair, association with the unloved, and separation from the loved should be understood. The nature of suffering in association with the unloved and separation from the loved should be understood. Not getting what one desires (icchā) should be understood; the nature of suffering in not getting what one desires should be understood. The aggregates should be understood; the nature of suffering in the aggregates should be understood.

This matrix (mātikā) exists for the purpose of explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering. This so-called suffering is manifold and of various kinds, namely: suffering as suffering (dukkha-dukkha), suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), suffering due to formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), concealed suffering (paṭicchanna-dukkha), exposed suffering (appaṭicchanna-dukkha), indirect suffering (pariyāya-dukkha), and direct suffering (nippariyāya-dukkha).

Among these, bodily and mental painful feeling is called 'suffering as suffering' because it is painful both by nature and by name. Pleasant feeling is called 'suffering due to change' because it causes the arising of pain through its change and destruction. Equanimous feeling and the remaining formations of the three planes are called 'suffering due to formations' because they are oppressed by rise and fall. Such oppression also exists in the Paths and Fruits. Therefore, these [Paths and Fruits] should be understood as 'suffering due to formations' because they are included within the Truth of Suffering.

Bodily and mental ailments such as earache, toothache, the fever of lust, and the fever of hatred are called 'concealed suffering' (paṭicchanna-dukkha) because they can only be known by asking and because the effort of their occurrence is not obvious; it is also called 'unmanifest suffering' (apākaṭa-dukkha). Ailments arising from the thirty-two types of torture and punishment, etc., are called 'exposed suffering' (appaṭicchanna-dukkha) because they can be known without asking and because the effort of their occurrence is obvious; it is also called 'manifest suffering' (pākaṭa-dukkha). Excluding 'suffering as suffering', all other forms of suffering such as birth (jāti) mentioned in the Analysis of the Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasacca-vibhaṅga) are called 'indirect suffering' (pariyāya-dukkha) because they are the basis and cause for various sufferings. 'Suffering as suffering' is called 'direct suffering' (nippariyāya-dukkha).

Among those, the Noble Truth of Suffering should be explained based on these two terms: indirect suffering and direct suffering. This Noble Truth appears in the Pali texts both in brief and in detail. Where it appears in brief, it is appropriate to explain it both briefly and in detail. But where it appears in detail, it should be explained only in detail, not briefly. In this context, since it appears in detail, it should be explained only in detail. Therefore, in the section of exposition (niddesavāra), taking the words such as "What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering," it is said: "Birth should be understood, the nature of suffering in birth should be understood," and so on. In that statement, birth and so on should be understood by way of this word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya): "What is birth? The birth, the being born of various beings in various orders of beings..."
89:
In that [word-by-word commentary], the explanation of the meaning is as follows: The phrase 'of those various beings' (tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ) is a general indication pertaining to many beings in brief. How so? Even if one were to speak all day long, saying 'the birth of Devadatta, the birth of Somadatta,' the beings would not be exhausted, nor would the explanation of the birth of others be completed. However, by these two words [tesaṃ tesaṃ], there is no being who is not included, and the explanation of the birth of others is completed. Therefore, it is said: 'of those various beings'. The phrase 'in various [orders]' (tamhi tamhi) is a general indication pertaining to many collections of beings by way of birth and destination (gati). 'In the order of beings' (sattanikāye) means in the group of beings, in the assembly of beings.

The word 'birth' (jāti) has various meanings. To elaborate: In the passage 'one birth, two births,' it occurs in the sense of 'existence' (bhava). In the passage 'Visākhā, there are those of the ascetic order (jātika) called Nigaṇṭhas,' it occurs in the sense of 'group' or 'order' (nikāya). In the passage 'The type of grass (jāti) called Tiriyā grew from the navel and stood touching the sky,' it occurs in the sense of 'designation' (paññatti). In the passage 'Birth is included in two aggregates,' it occurs in the sense of the 'characteristic of the conditioned' (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa). In the passage 'Monks, starting from the first mind, the first consciousness that arises in the mother's womb, that is his birth,' it occurs in the sense of 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi). In the passage 'Ānanda, the Bodhisatta is just born (sampatijāta),' it occurs in the sense of 'parturition' (pasūti). In the passage 'Not to be blamed because of talk about birth,' it occurs in the sense of 'clan' or 'lineage' (kula). In the passage 'Sister, since I was born in the Noble Birth (ariya-jāti),' it occurs in the sense of 'Noble Virtue' (ariya-sīla).

In this context, however, this [word birth] refers to the aggregates that first arise along with their transformations (vikāra). Therefore, 'jāti' (birth) in the sense of 'being born' is the term for the intrinsic nature here. The term is expanded with a prefix as 'sañjāti' in the sense of 'being fully born'. It is called 'okkanti' in the sense of 'descent'. Or else, it is called 'jāti' due to the sense of arising, and it is associated with the incomplete sense bases (āyatana). It is called 'sañjāti' due to the sense of being fully born, and it is associated with the complete sense bases. It is called 'okkanti' due to the sense of descent, and it is associated with egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings. For they descend into the egg-shell and the womb, and in descending, they take rebirth-linking as if entering [a room]. It is called 'abhinibbatti' due to the sense of manifestation, and it is associated with moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings. For they are born with their bodies already manifest. This is just conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā).
90:
Now is the discourse on the ultimate sense (paramattha). Truly, in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates (khandhas) manifest, not beings (sattā). In the phrase 'of the aggregates', it should be understood that one aggregate is taken in the realm of one constituent (ekavokāra-bhava), four in the realm of four constituents (catuvokāra-bhava), and five in the realm of five constituents (pañcavokāra-bhava). 'Manifestation' (pātubhāvo) means arising (uppatti). In the word 'of the bases' (āyatanānaṃ), the inclusion by way of the bases arising in various realms should be understood. 'Acquisition' (paṭilābho) is the manifestation itself in the continuity (santati). When those bases manifest, they are said to be acquired. This nature is called birth (jāti). That birth has the characteristic of first manifestation in various existences, the function of handing over, the manifestation of emerging here from a past existence, or the manifestation of the diversity of suffering through its results.

Now, regarding the statement 'the meaning of suffering in birth should be understood', this birth is not suffering (dukkha-vedanā) in itself, but it is called 'suffering' because it is the basis and cause for the arising of suffering. For what suffering is it the basis? It is the basis for all suffering, such as the suffering in the states of deprivation (apāya) which the Blessed One has illustrated by way of similes in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta and other discourses, and the various sufferings such as those rooted in the descent into the womb in the human world, which is a happy destination. Among those, this is the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb: when this being is born in the mother's womb, he is not born in places such as blue, red, or white lotuses. Rather, he is born like a worm in rotting fish, rotting dough, or a cesspool, in the region of the belly which is extremely cramped, pitch dark, permeated by various foul odors of corpses, and circulated by impure, extremely foul-smelling winds, between the stomach (āmasaya) below and the mature-food receptacle (pakkāsaya) above, and between the abdominal membrane and the backbone. Born there, for ten months, he is cooked like a dish of meat in a pot by the heat of the mother's womb, steamed like a ball of dough, and experiences intense suffering, unable to bend or stretch. This is 'suffering rooted in descent into the womb' (gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ).

That being experiences intense suffering through the effort of being pulled, dragged, and shaken, like a sheep in the hands of a drunkard or a young snake in the hands of a snake charmer, when the mother suddenly stumbles, walks, sits, rises, or turns. When the mother drinks cold water, he feels like one fallen into a cold hell; when she swallows hot gruel or rice, he feels as if scattered with a rain of embers; when she swallows salty or sour things, he feels like one undergoing the torture of having salt water poured on a flayed wound. This is 'suffering rooted in the maintenance of the fetus' (gabbhapariharaṇamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ).
91:
The suffering that arises for a mother with a malpresented fetus, through cutting and tearing in the delivery room—a place of suffering which even friends, ministers, and loved ones should not behold—is called 'suffering rooted in fetal calamity' (gabbhavipattimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ). When the mother is about to give birth, the winds born of kamma turn the fetus upside down and propel it toward the birth canal, which is as terrifying as a pit of hell. The suffering that arises while being dragged through the extremely narrow birth canal, like a great elephant through a keyhole, or like a denizen of hell being crushed by the Saṅghāṭa mountains, is called 'suffering rooted in childbirth' (vijāyanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ). The suffering that arises for the newborn, whose body is as delicate as a tender wound, when being handled, bathed, washed, or wiped with cloth—feeling as if being pierced by the point of a needle or cut by the edge of a razor—is called 'suffering rooted in emerging from the mother's womb' (bahi-nikkhamanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ). The suffering that occurs in the subsequent course of life for one who harms himself, who devotes himself to the practice of self-mortification such as the naked ascetic's practice (acelaka-vata), who does not eat out of anger, or who hangs himself, is called 'suffering rooted in one's own exertion' (attūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ).

The suffering that arises for one who experiences torture, imprisonment, etc., caused by others, is called 'suffering rooted in the exertion of others' (parūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ). Thus, for all this suffering, this birth (jāti) is indeed the foundation. Therefore, it is said:

If a being were not born in the hells,
Where would that unbearable suffering, such as burning by fire, find a footing?
Therefore, in this Dispensation, the Sage said that birth is suffering.

In the animal realm, there is manifold suffering
Arising from being struck by whips, goads, and sticks.
How could that suffering exist there without birth?
Therefore, birth is the cause of suffering in that realm as well.

Among the petas, there is diverse suffering
Arising from hunger, thirst, wind, and heat.
Since that does not exist for one who is not born there,
The Sage said that birth is suffering for that reason too.
92:
In the Lokantarika hell, which is intensely dark and unbearably cold, and among the Asuras, there is suffering. If there were no birth (jāti) in those places, that suffering would not exist. Therefore, this birth is indeed suffering.

In the mother's womb, which is like a cesspool of excrement, a being must dwell for a long time and then emerge from it, thereby reaching extremely terrible suffering. This suffering, too, would not exist without birth. Therefore, this birth is indeed suffering.

What is the use of much speaking? Whatever suffering exists anywhere in this world, it never exists in the absence of birth. Therefore, the Great Sage (the Buddha) declared birth as "suffering" first among all sufferings.

## Description of Old Age (Jarāniddesa)

In the description of old age, the term "jarā" (old age) refers to the nature itself. The term "jīraṇatā" (decay) is a description of its mode. The three terms beginning with "khaṇḍicca" (brokenness) are descriptions of its function upon the passing of time. The last two are descriptions of its natural state. This old age is indicated by the term "jarā" according to its nature; thus, it is the nature itself. It is indicated by the term "jīraṇatā" according to its mode; thus, it is a description of its mode. It is indicated by the term "khaṇḍicca" by way of the function of causing the broken state of teeth and nails upon the passing of time. It is indicated by the term "pālicca" (greyness) by way of the function of causing the greyness of head hair and body hair. It is indicated by the term "valittacatā" (wrinkled skin) by way of the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to wrinkle. Therefore, these three terms beginning with "khaṇḍicca" are descriptions of the function upon the passing of time. By showing these transformations through those terms, "evident old age" (pākaṭajarā) is shown.

Just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire becomes evident through the uprooting of grass and trees or through charring—yet that path is not the water, wind, or fire itself—likewise, the path taken by old age becomes evident through the brokenness of teeth and so on, and can be grasped even by opening the eyes. However, the brokenness of teeth and so on are not old age itself. For old age is not an object of eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññeyya).
93:
By the terms "decline of life" and "ripening of the faculties," the natural state of old age is shown, which is characterized by the exhaustion of life and the ripening of the eye-faculty and so on, becoming fully manifest only upon the passing of time. Therefore, it should be understood that these last two are descriptions of the natural state of old age. Among them, because the life of one who has reached old age declines, old age is called the "decline of life" by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), attributing the effect to the cause. The faculties such as the eye, which in youth are very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become over-ripe, disturbed, and unclear when one reaches old age, and they become incapable of grasping even gross objects. Therefore, old age is called the "ripening of the faculties" also by way of metonymy.

All such old age thus described is of two kinds: evident old age (pākaṭajarā) and concealed old age (paṭicchannajarā). Among them, the old age that occurs in material phenomena (rūpadhamma), which is seen through the broken state of teeth and so on, is called "evident old age." But the old age in immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) is called "concealed old age" because such a transformation is not visible. The broken state of teeth and so on that is seen there is merely the appearance (vaṇṇa) of those teeth, which is easily cognizable. Having seen that appearance with the eye and reflecting with the mind-door, one knows old age, thinking, "These teeth have been struck by old age." This is like seeing the signs of ox horns tied in a place where there is water and thereby knowing the existence of water below. Furthermore, this old age is of two kinds: continuous old age (avīci-jarā) and discontinuous old age (savīci-jarā). In gems, gold, silver, pearls, the moon, and the sun, etc., and in the stages of life such as the "slow decades" (manda-dasaka) of living beings, and in non-living things such as flowers, fruits, and shoots, the distinction of appearance at various intervals is difficult to discern; therefore, that old age is called "avīci-jarā" (uninterrupted old age). In other things besides those, the distinction of appearance at various intervals is easily discerned; therefore, it is called "savīci-jarā" (interrupted old age).

Among those two, discontinuous old age (savīci-jarā) should be illustrated by way of the animate (upādinna) and the inanimate (anupādinna) as follows: In young children, first, what are called milk teeth arise, but they are not permanent. When those teeth fall out, new teeth arise again. They are white at first, but when struck by the wind of old age, they become black. Hair, too, may be red, black, or white at first. The skin has a reddish hue, but as one grows older, the whiteness in a fair person and the blackness in a dark person become prominent, and when struck by the wind of old age, wrinkling occurs. All crops are white at the time of sowing, then green, and when struck by the wind of old age, they become yellowish (pale). This can also be illustrated by mango shoots. This is what is called old age.
94:
This nature is called aging (jarā). This aging has the characteristic of the ripening of the aggregates; its function is leading to death; it manifests to the yogi's knowledge as the destruction of youth.

In the statement "the nature of suffering in aging should be understood," this aging is not suffering in itself, but it is called suffering because it is the basis for suffering. For which suffering is it the basis? It is the basis for both bodily suffering (kāya-dukkha) and mental grief (domanassa-dukkha). Indeed, the physical body of an aged person is as weak as an old cart; intense bodily suffering arises for one who strives to stand, walk, or sit. When children and wives do not recognize or respect them as before, mental grief arises. Thus, because it is the basis for these two kinds of suffering, aging should be understood as suffering. Furthermore—

Due to the looseness of the limbs, and due to the alteration of the senses,
Due to the destruction of youth, and due to the impairment of strength.
Due to the separation from one's own mindfulness and other qualities,
Due to the lack of devotion from children and wives, and due to reaching extreme second childhood.
Whatever suffering a mortal reaches, both bodily and mental,
All that has aging as its cause; therefore, aging is called suffering.

## Maraṇaniddesa (Exposition of Death)

In the exposition of death, it is called "passing away" (cuti) by way of shifting. This word "passing away" is a general term for the passing away of beings with one, four, or five aggregates. By the abstract term "shifting" (cavanatā), the characteristic of passing away is shown. "Breaking up" (bheda) is the demonstration of the arrival at the dissolution of the aggregates at the time of passing away. "Disappearance" (antaradhāna) is the demonstration of the lack of any place for the dissolved aggregates of passing away, just as there is no place for a broken pot. "Death as Mara" (maccu-maraṇa) is death known as Mara. "Time" (kāla) is the end-maker; his action is called "doing one's time" (kālakiriyā). By this much, death is shown according to worldly convention.

Now, to show it in the ultimate sense, he says "the breaking up of the aggregates" and so on. In the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break up; no being as such dies. But when the aggregates are breaking up, there is the conventional expression "a being is dying," and when they have broken up, "he is dead." Here, the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of the four-constituent and five-constituent existences, and the discarding of the carcass (kaḷevara) by way of the one-constituent existence. Or, the breaking up of the aggregates by way of the four-constituent existence, and the discarding of the carcass by way of the remaining two, the one-constituent and five-constituent existences.
95:
The discarding of the carcass should also be understood. Why? Because in both the one-constituent and five-constituent existences, the carcass known as the material body is clearly present. Alternatively, in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so on, the aggregates merely break up, and there is no discarding of any carcass. Therefore, by way of those devas and Brahmas, it is called "the breaking up of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ bheda). Among humans and so on, however, it is called "the discarding of the carcass" (kaḷevarassa nikkhepo). Since the discarding of the carcass occurs among these humans and so on, death is called "the discarding of the carcass."

By the phrase "the cutting off of the life faculty," he shows that death occurs only for living beings connected with the senses such as the eye, etc.; there is no such thing as death for inanimate matter not connected with the senses. Saying "the crop is dead" or "the tree is dead" is merely a conventional expression. In the actual sense, such words only indicate the state of exhaustion and disappearance of crops and so on. By the phrase "this is called death," all this, including passing away (cuti) and so on, is called death.

Furthermore, in this context of death, the distinctions of momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa), conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa), and death by cutting off (samuccheda-maraṇa) should also be understood. Among these, the breaking up of material and immaterial states during the course of existence is called "momentary death." This death expressed as "Tissa is dead" or "Phussa is dead" is called "conventional death." The passing away of an Arahant (khīṇāsava) which is without further rebirth is called "death by cutting off." In this context of "death is also suffering," only conventional death is intended. The names such as death by the exhaustion of birth (jātikkhaya-maraṇa), death by violence (upakkama-maraṇa), natural death (sarasa-maraṇa), death by the exhaustion of life-span (āyukkhaya-maraṇa), and death by the exhaustion of merit (puññakkhaya-maraṇa) are also names for that same conventional death. That death has the characteristic of passing away (cuti), the function of separation (viyoga) from the aggregates of existence, and it manifests as being parted (vippavāsa) from life.

In the statement "the nature of suffering in death should be understood," this death is also not suffering in itself; it is called suffering only because it is the basis for suffering. Indeed, the bodily feelings that occur near death burn the body like flaming grass torches held against the wind. When the signs of hell and so on appear, intense mental grief arises. Thus, because it is the basis for these two kinds of suffering—bodily and mental—death should be understood as suffering. Furthermore—

To the wicked person who repeatedly sees the signs of evil kamma and so on at the time of death,
And to the good person who cannot endure the separation from beloved objects,
Whatever mental suffering arises without distinction;
And to all people, due to causes such as the severing of the sinews that bind the joints,
Whatever bodily suffering arises, as if being pierced in mortal spots,
Which is unendurable and incurable;
Because this death is the basis for both that mental and bodily suffering,
Therefore, this death is spoken of (by the Buddha) as suffering.
97:
'Anyataraññatarena' means by one or another of the five ruins already mentioned, or by one or another of the ruins not yet mentioned, such as the ruin of friends and associates. 'Samannāgatassa' means one who is intensely and continuously bound, unable to be liberated. 'Anyataraññatarena dukkhadhammena' means [one who encounters] some cause for the arising of the suffering of sorrow. 'Soko' (sorrow) is called so because of the act of sorrowing; this is the individual essence of sorrow that arises from those causes. 'Socanā' is the manner of sorrowing. 'Socitattaṃ' is the state of being sorrowful. 'Antosoko' is sorrow within the mind. The second term (antoparisoko) increases the meaning by way of the prefix 'pari-'. Because that sorrow arises as if drying up or intensely parching the interior, it is called 'antosoko antoparisoko'.

'Cetaso parijjhāyanā' is the mode of the mind's burning. For sorrow, when it arises, burns the mind like fire, scorching it all around; it makes one say, "My mind is scorched; nothing appears to me anymore." A mind that is suffering is called 'dummana' (dejected), and the state of that mind is 'domanassa' (mental distress). Sorrow itself is called a dart (salla) because it enters and pierces [the heart] sequentially, thus it is 'sokasallaṃ'. This is what is called sorrow. Although this sorrow is essentially the feeling of mental distress (domanassa-vedanā), it has the characteristic of inner burning, the function of scorching the mind all around, and is manifested as continual grieving (in accordance with the ruins).

In the phrase 'the suffering aspect of sorrow should be understood,' this sorrow is called 'dukkha' because it is suffering by nature and because it is a basis for suffering. Of what suffering is it the cause? It is the cause of both physical suffering (kāyika-dukkha) and the mental distress (domanassa-dukkha) that occurs at the moment of the impulsion (javana). Indeed, due to the force of sorrow, a great boil arises in the heart, matures, and bursts; or dark blood issues from the mouth; and powerful physical suffering arises. For one who thinks, "So many of my relatives have perished, so much of my wealth [is gone]," powerful mental distress arises. Thus, because it is the basis for these two kinds of suffering, it should be understood as 'dukkha'. Furthermore:

Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a dart;
Like an arrow heated by fire, it burns intensely again and again.
Since it brings about various kinds of suffering,
Including disease, aging, and death, it is therefore called 'dukkha'.
98:
## Exposition of Lamentation

In the exposition of lamentation (parideva), it is called 'wailing' (ādeva) because people cry out with this sound of weeping, repeatedly referring to things such as "my daughter, my son." It is called 'lamentation' (parideva) because they cry out with this sound of weeping, repeatedly proclaiming various virtues. The two pairs of terms following these (ādevanā, paridevanā, ādevitatta, paridevitatta) are spoken by way of indicating the mode and nature of the first two terms. 'Speech' (vācā) means speaking. 'Vain talk' (palāpa) is empty and meaningless speech. 'Incoherent speech' (vippalāpa) is distorted vain talk by way of speaking partially or speaking other meanings, etc., due to being unable to speak fully because of excessive grief. 'Prattling' (lālappa) is repeated speaking. The mode of repeated speaking is 'the act of prattling' (lālappanā). The state of a person who prattles repeatedly is 'the state of prattling' (lālappitatta). This nature is called lamentation (parideva). That lamentation has the characteristic of repeated prattling, the function of repeatedly proclaiming virtues and faults, and it is manifested as mental agitation (or trembling).

Regarding the statement, "The suffering nature of lamentation should be understood," here, this lamentation is not suffering in itself. However, it is called suffering because it is the basis for bodily pain (kāya-dukkha) and mental distress (domanassa-dukkha). Indeed, a person who laments beats their own body with fists, strikes and rubs their chest with both hands, and hits their head against a wall. Because of such actions, intense bodily pain arises in them. They think, "So many of my relatives have reached destruction and ruin," and so forth. Because of such thoughts, intense mental distress arises in them. Thus, lamentation should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for both these types of suffering. Furthermore—

One who laments, being struck by the arrow of sorrow,
Experiences unbearable suffering born of the drying up of the throat, lips, palate, and gullet,
And indeed reaches even more excessive pain;
Therefore, the Blessed One called lamentation 'suffering'.

## Exposition of Pain and Grief

196-7. The expositions of pain (dukkha) and grief (domanassa) are clear, as they have been explained below in the Commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. Their characteristics and so forth are also spoken of in that same commentary.

Regarding the statement, "The suffering nature of pain should be understood, the suffering nature of grief should be understood," here, both of these are called suffering because they are suffering in themselves and because they are the basis for bodily and mental suffering. Indeed, through the suffering of having hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off...
99:
...for a person who is suffering, lying in a shelter for the destitute with a bowl for scraps placed before them, intense bodily pain arises as maggots emerge from the openings of their wounds. Seeing a great crowd of people celebrating a festival, adorned with pleasant ornaments and clothes dyed in various colors, intense mental distress arises. Thus, first, pain (dukkha) should be understood as the basis for both bodily and mental suffering. Furthermore—

This bodily pain oppresses,
And it causes mental pain to increase further;
Therefore, that [bodily pain] is specifically called 'suffering' (dukkha).

Those who have reached mental suffering dishevel their hair and beat their chests; they roll and writhe; they fall down like a broken cliff; they take up a sword; they eat poison; they hang themselves with a rope; they jump into a fire. They think of various distorted objects in various ways, with a remorseful and burning mind. Thus, grief (domanassa) should also be understood as the basis for both types of suffering. Furthermore—

Because grief oppresses the mind,
And brings about the oppression of the body,
Therefore, grief is also called 'suffering' (dukkha).

## Exposition of Despair

In the exposition of despair (upāyāsa), it is called 'trouble' (āyāsa) in the sense of mental exhaustion. This is a name for the mental exhaustion that occurs by way of sinking and despondency in objects such as the loss of relatives. Intense trouble is 'despair' (upāyāsa). The state of one who is excessively mentally exhausted is 'the state of being troubled' (āyāsitatta). The state of one who is intensely mentally exhausted is 'the state of despair' (upāyāsitatta). This nature is called despair (upāyāsa). That despair has the characteristic of distorted attachment to an object, the function of moaning, and it is manifested as dejection and sinking.

Regarding the statement, "The suffering nature of despair should be understood," here, this despair is also not suffering in itself, but it is called 'suffering' because it is the basis for both types of suffering. In truth, for those who, out of fear of an angry king who has stripped them of their position and ordered the killing of their sons and brothers, enter and hide in a forest, intense bodily pain arises due to standing, lying, and sitting miserably in a place of suffering while in a state of great mental exhaustion. For those who think, "So many of our relatives have perished, so many of our possessions are lost," intense mental distress arises. Thus, despair should be understood as 'suffering' because it is the basis for both these types of suffering. Furthermore—
100:
Because of the burning of the mind and the exhaustion of the body, despair (upāyāsa) produces suffering of extreme measure; therefore, despair is called suffering (dukkha).

Among these (sorrow, lamentation, and despair), sorrow (soka) should be understood like the cooking of oil and so forth in a vessel by a slow fire. Lamentation (parideva) should be understood like the overflowing of oil from a vessel when cooked by a fierce fire. Despair (upāyāsa) should be understood like the cooking of the remaining oil that has not overflowed, which is unable to come out and continues to cook inside the vessel until it is exhausted.

## Exposition of Association with the Unloved

In the exposition of association with the unloved (appiyasampayoga-niddesa), "yassa" is analyzed as "ye assa" (those objects of his). "Aniṭṭha" means those that are unsought. Whether sought or unsought, the name "aniṭṭha" refers only to disagreeable objects. They are called "akantā" (unlovely) because they do not enter or penetrate the mind. They are called "amanāpā" (disagreeable) because they do not please the mind or increase its well-being. The words "rūpā" (forms) and so forth indicate the nature of those unpleasant objects. They are called "anatthakāma" (wishing harm) because they desire ruin (dukkha), which is the opposite of prosperity. They are called "ahitakāma" (wishing misfortune) because they desire what is not beneficial. They are called "aphāsukakāma" (wishing discomfort) because they desire an uncomfortable and painful dwelling. They are called "ayogakkhemakāma" (wishing lack of security) because they do not desire Nibbāna, which is the security from the four bonds (yoga) and is free from fear, but instead desire for them only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) which is accompanied by fear.

Furthermore, they are "anatthakāma" because they do not desire the welfare (attha) consisting of the growth of faith (saddhā) and so forth, but desire the harm (anattha) consisting of the decline of that faith and so forth. They are "ahitakāma" because they do not desire the benefit (hita) which is the means for faith and so forth, but desire the non-benefit (ahita) which is the means for the decline of faith and so forth. They are "aphāsukakāma" because they do not desire a comfortable dwelling but desire an uncomfortable dwelling. They are "ayogakkhemakāma" because they do not desire any kind of security but desire fear; thus should the meaning be understood here.

"Saṅgati" means joining by going (to enemies). "Samāgama" means joining with those who have come. "Samodhāna" means being together in postures such as sitting and lying down. "Missībhāva" means performing all activities together. This is the application in terms of beings (satta). In terms of formations (saṅkhāra), whatever meaning is obtainable should be taken. This (association, etc.) is called "association with the unloved" (appiyasampayoga). That association with the unloved has the characteristic of meeting with disagreeable beings and formations, the function of distressing the mind, and the manifestation of a harmful state.
101:
In the ultimate sense, this association with the unloved is not a single distinct phenomenon (dhamma). It is called suffering (dukkha) simply because it is the basis for the two kinds of suffering (physical and mental) for those associated with unloved beings and formations. For when unpleasant objects are met with, they produce physical suffering through stabbing, cutting, burning, and so forth, and mental suffering by generating agitation. Therefore, the former teachers said:

"In this world, upon seeing the unloved, suffering first arises in the mind. Thereafter, physical suffering arises due to the efforts of that unloved one. Therefore, because that association with the unloved is the basis for both kinds of suffering, it should be understood that the Great Sage called it 'suffering'."

## Exposition of Separation from the Loved

The exposition of separation from the loved (piyavippayoga-niddesa) should be understood by the method opposite to the aforementioned exposition of association with the unloved. The words "whether it be a mother" and so forth are stated here to specifically show the persons who desire one's welfare. In that context, she is called "mother" (mātā) because she regards one as "mine" (mamāyati). He is called "father" (pitā) because he loves (piyāyati). He is called "brother" (bhātā) because he associates (bhajati). Likewise for "sister" (bhaginī). One is called "friend" (mittā) because of showing loving-kindness (mettā) or because of including one in all secrets. They are called "companions/ministers" (amaccā) because of being together (amā) in duties to be performed. They are called "relatives" (ñātī) because they are known or recognized as "this person is our internal person." They are called "blood-relations" (sālohita) because they are connected by blood. Thus should the meaning of these words be understood. "This is called" means this separation from these loved things is termed "separation from the loved" (piyavippayoga). That separation from the loved has the characteristic of being parted from desirable objects, the function of producing sorrow, and the manifestation in wisdom as the ruin of relatives and so forth.

This separation from the loved also is not a single distinct phenomenon in the ultimate sense. It is called suffering (dukkha) simply because it is the basis for the two kinds of suffering that arise for those separated from loved things. For when one is separated from desirable objects, it produces physical suffering by way of drying up and withering the body, and so forth. It also produces mental suffering by causing one to grieve repeatedly: "That which we formerly had, we have no longer." Therefore, it is said:

"Due to separation from relatives, wealth, and so forth, fools are severely tormented and suffer, being pierced by the arrow of sorrow. Therefore, that separation from the loved is known as 'suffering'."

## Exposition of Desire

In the exposition of desire (icchā-niddesa), "jātidhammānaṃ" means those who have the nature of birth, whose natural state is being born. "Desire arises" means craving (taṇhā) arises. "O, indeed..." (aho vata) expresses a wish. "We are subject to birth; O, if only we were not subject to birth! Indeed, if only birth and so forth would not come to us!"—thus they wish. One should desire that state of not being subject to birth which is manifest in the virtuous who have abandoned the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), and the non-coming of birth which is manifest in the Arahants who have attained Parinibbāna. Although one wishes for that absence of birth and the non-coming of birth, it cannot be obtained by mere wish because it cannot be attained without developing the Path (magga), and because it can be attained by developing the Path even without wishing. In the phrase "this also" (yampicca), the syllable "pi" is for the purpose of including the desire for the absence of aging and so forth mentioned above.
102:
“O, that we were not subject to birth! O, that birth would not come to us!”—this cannot be attained by mere wish. The state of not being subject to birth, which exists in the virtuous who have abandoned the origin (samudaya), and the non-coming of birth, which exists in the Arahants who have attained Parinibbāna, are desired. Even if one desires it, it cannot be reached without the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā); and even if one does not desire it, it can be reached through the development of the Path. Therefore, it is not something to be attained by mere wish alone.

“Idampi” means “this also.” The word “pi” is used to include the remaining items mentioned above. “Yampicchaṃ” refers to not obtaining an object that is unattainable, even when desiring it through the factor of craving (lobha). That craving which longs for an unattainable object should be understood as suffering (dukkha). The same method applies to the terms “jarādhammānaṃ” (subject to aging) and so on. Thus, the desire for unattainable objects is stated as: “Not getting what one wants is also suffering.” That desire (icchā) has the characteristic of wanting an unattainable object, the function of seeking that object, and the manifestation of the non-attainment of those objects.

It is called suffering because it is the basis for the two kinds of suffering: bodily suffering and mental suffering. Indeed, a certain person is praised, “I will become king.” Surrounded by a group of shameless fools, he hides in rugged mountains or thick forests. Then, the king, learning of this, sends his forces. That person, whose followers are suppressed by the king’s men, is himself struck and flees, entering among trees or rocks. At that time, a great storm arises, and there are dark, black rain clouds. Then, insects such as black ants surround and bite him from all sides. Because of that, intense bodily suffering arises in him. When he thinks, “Because of me alone, so many relatives and so much wealth have been destroyed,” intense mental distress (domanassa) arises. Thus, this desire (icchā) should be understood as suffering because it is the basis for these two kinds of suffering. Furthermore—

For beings in this world who long for various things,
Because of the non-attainment of those various desired things,
That suffering consisting of distress arises.
Since the longing for unattainable objects is the cause of that,
The Victor (Jina) declared that not getting what one wants is suffering.

## Description of the Aggregates of Clinging

In the description of the aggregates of clinging, the phrase “in brief” (saṅkhittena) is said with reference to the teaching (desanā). Although it is not possible to summarize suffering as being this many hundreds or this many thousands or this many...
103:
...hundreds of thousands of instances, it is possible to summarize the teaching (desanā). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to summarize the teaching, said: “There is no other suffering (apart from the five aggregates of clinging); in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.” “Seyyathidaṃ” is an indeclinable (nipāta). Its meaning is: “If one asks, ‘What are those five?’” The meaning of the terms “rūpūpādānakkhandha” (the aggregate of clinging to form) and so on has already been explained in the Khandha-vibhaṅga.

Regarding the statement, “The suffering nature of the aggregates should be understood”—

The Buddha, endowed with the quality of Tādi, has taught in this description of the truth of suffering such pains as birth and so on.
Whatever other suffering has not been specifically mentioned, all that does not exist apart from these aggregates.
Therefore, the Great Sage (Mahesi), the teacher of the end of suffering, has declared these aggregates of clinging, in brief, as “suffering.”

To explain this further: Just as fire oppresses fuel, as weapons strike a target, as gadflies and mosquitoes harass a herd of cattle, as reapers destroy a field, and as robbers plunder a village, so too birth and the other states oppress the group of the five aggregates of clinging in various ways. Just as grass and creepers grow on the earth, and as flowers, fruits, and sprouts grow on trees, so too they arise only in the aggregates of clinging. The initial suffering of the aggregates of clinging is birth (jāti), the middle suffering is aging (jarā), and the final suffering is death (maraṇa). Sorrow (soka) is the suffering of being consumed all around due to the impact of the suffering at the time of death. Lamentation (parideva) is the suffering of repeated wailing due to the inability to bear that sorrow. Then, pain (dukkha) is the suffering that severely afflicts the body due to contact with undesirable touches, known as the disturbance of the elements. Grief (domanassa) is the suffering that afflicts the mind due to the arising of resentment in that bodily pain among worldlings (puthujjana) who are oppressed by it. Despair (upāyāsa) is the suffering of repeated moaning in those who are exhausted by the increase of sorrow and so on. Not getting what one wants (icchitālābha) is the suffering caused by the frustration of desire in those whose wishes are destroyed. Thus, when examined in various ways, only the aggregates of clinging are the causes of suffering. In this way, if one wished to teach by showing each one individually, it would not be possible to finish teaching all that suffering even in many aeons. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” in order to show all that suffering summarized within the five aggregates of clinging, just as the taste of the entire ocean’s water is shown in a single drop of water.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Suffering is Finished.
104:
## 2. Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of the Origin

In the exposition of the truth of the origin, "yāyaṃ taṇhā" means "yā ayaṃ taṇhā" (which is this craving). "Ponobhavikā" means it is called so because it has the habit of creating renewed existence. Alternatively, it is called "ponobhavikā" because it gives renewed existence, because it leads to renewed existence, or because it causes birth in existence again and again. That craving may be a giver of renewed existence or not; it may lead to renewed existence or not; or it may merely provide the functional result (pavattivipāka) in the physical basis (upadhi) of a rebirth already given by another kamma. However, whether that craving gives renewed existence or not, leads to it or not, or merely provides the functional result in the physical basis of a given rebirth, it still receives the name "ponobhavikā."

It is called "nandirāgasahagatā" because it arises together with delight and lust (nandirāga), which is called extreme pleasure. It means it has reached the state of being one with delight and lust in terms of essence. "Tatratatrābhinandinī" means it is called so because it takes great delight in whatever existence (attabhāva) it is born into. Alternatively, it is called "tatratatrābhinandinī" because it takes great delight in various objects such as visible forms. It means one who takes great delight in visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

"Seyyathidaṃ" is an indeclinable. It has the meaning of asking, "What is that craving?" "Kāmataṇhā" is craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure, and it is a name for the lust (rāga) that occurs in the five cords of sensual pleasure. Craving for existence is called "bhavataṇhā." It is a name for the lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) that arises through the power of longing for existence, as well as for the lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, and for the attachment to jhāna. Craving for non-existence is called "vibhavataṇhā." It is a name for the lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi).

Now, to show in detail the object-basis of that craving, the phrase beginning with "sā kho panesā" is stated. In that passage, "uppajjati" means it arises. "Nivisati" means it establishes itself through the power of repeated occurrence. "Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ" means whatever in the world has an endearing nature and a pleasurable nature.

In the passages beginning with "cakkhuṃ loke," beings in the world who are attached to the eye and so forth as "mine," while established in prosperity, regard their own eye as having a clear five-colored sensitivity (pasāda) by following the perception of their reflection in mirrors and so forth. They also regard it as being like a jeweled lion-window opened in a golden mansion. They regard the ear as being like a silver tube or like a thread of an ornament (pāmaṅgasuttaka). They regard the nose, which is called a "prominent nose," as being like a rounded rod of yellow orpiment and realgar. They regard the tongue as being like a layer of red blanket, and as giving a soft, smooth, and sweet taste. They regard the body as being like a sal-tree trunk or like a golden archway. They regard their own mind as being noble and unlike the minds of others. They regard visible forms as being like the color of golden flowers or the kaṇikāra flower and so forth.
105:
...and so forth. They regard sounds as being like the song of an intoxicated karavīka bird or cuckoo, or like the sound of a melodiously and gently blown jeweled flute. Regarding smells and so forth, which are produced by the four causes—kamma, consciousness (citta), temperature (utu), and nutriment (āhāra)—and which they have obtained, they think, "Who else besides me has such smells, tastes, and tangibles?" To those beings who think in this way, those doors and objects such as the eye are indeed endearing and pleasurable. Because of this, craving that has not yet arisen arises in those doors and objects such as the eye, and craving that has already arisen settles and establishes itself through the power of repeated occurrence. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "The eye in the world is endearing and pleasurable. Here this craving, when arising, arises," and so forth. In that passage, "when arising" means at whatever time it arises, at that time it arises in this eye-sensitivity. This method applies to all other instances as well.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of the Origin is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

In the exposition of the truth of cessation, regarding the phrase "yo tassāyeva taṇhāya" (the [fading away] of that very craving), it should have been said "yo tasseva dukkhassa" (of that very suffering). This is because suffering ceases only through the cessation of the origin, and not otherwise. As it is said:

"Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its root is unharmed and firm, so also, when the latent tendency (anusaya) of craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again" (Dhammapada 338).

Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the cessation of that suffering, showed it by way of the cessation of the origin, and thus spoke in this way. For the Tathāgatas have behavior like that of a lion (sīhasamānavutti). When they wish to cause the cessation of suffering and to show the cessation of suffering, they deal with the cause (the origin), not the effect. However, the sectarians outside the Dispensation have behavior like that of a dog (suvānavutti). When they wish to cause the cessation of suffering and to show the cessation of suffering, they deal only with the effect through the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) and through the teaching of that very practice, not with the cause. Being of lion-like behavior, the Teacher, dealing with the cause, spoke the words beginning with "yo tassāyeva."

In that passage, "tassāyeva" (of that very [craving]) refers to that very craving which was explained below by way of its arising and establishing itself. All the terms beginning with "asesavirāganirodho" (fading away and cessation without remainder) are synonyms for Nibbāna. Indeed, because craving fades away and ceases without remainder upon reaching and taking Nibbāna as an object, that Nibbāna is called "the fading away and cessation of that craving without remainder." Furthermore, because craving is given up, relinquished, released, and no longer clung to upon reaching Nibbāna, Nibbāna is called giving up (cāga), relinquishment (paṭinissagga), release (mutti), and non-attachment (anālaya).

Although Nibbāna is essentially one, its names are many by way of being the opposite of the names of conditioned things (saṅkhata).
106:
All these terms are indeed synonyms for Nibbāna. Because of attaining Nibbāna, craving fades away and ceases without remainder. Therefore, Nibbāna is called "the fading away and cessation of that very craving without remainder." Because of attaining Nibbāna, craving is given up, relinquished, liberated, and no longer adhered to. Therefore, Nibbāna is called "giving up, relinquishment, liberation, and detachment."

Although Nibbāna is only of one kind, there are many synonyms for Nibbāna because it is the opposite of the names of all conditioned things (saṅkhata). They are: fading away and cessation without remainder, giving up, relinquishment, liberation, detachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, the desireless, non-accumulation, non-rebirth, non-reappearance, the non-destination, the unborn, the unaging, the ailment-free, the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentation-free, the despair-free, and the undefiled.

Now, in order to show that craving—which has been cut by the Path and has reached the state of non-occurrence upon attaining Nibbāna—no longer exists in those objects where its arising was previously shown, the Buddha said "Sā kho panesā" and so on. In this regard, for example: if a man sees a bitter gourd vine growing in a field and, starting from the tip, searches for the root and cuts it, that vine will gradually wither and reach a state of disappearance. Then, it can be said that the bitter gourd plant in that field has ceased and has been abandoned. In the same way, when craving that exists in objects such as the eye—like the bitter gourd vine in the field—is cut at the root by the Noble Path, it reaches the state of non-occurrence upon attaining Nibbāna. Having reached this state, that craving is no longer perceived in those objects, just like the bitter gourd vine in the field.

Alternatively: bandits from a forest might be captured and executed at the south gate of a city. Then, it can be said that the bandits in the forest are dead or have been killed. In the same way, craving that exists in the eye and so on—like the bandits in the forest—has ceased in Nibbāna because it ceased upon attaining Nibbāna, like the bandits at the south gate. Having ceased in this way, that craving is no longer perceived in those objects, just like the bandits in the forest. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the cessation of that craving in those very objects, said: "The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasant; here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; here, when ceasing, it ceases," and so on. The remaining meanings are clear.

## The Exposition of the Description of the Truth of Cessation is finished.
