## 4. Description of the Exposition of the Truth of the Path

In the exposition of the Truth of the Path, the phrase "this path alone" (ayam-eva) is a restriction to exclude the claim of other sectarians that their practices lead to cessation. It is called "Noble" (Ariya) because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it makes one a Noble One, and because it brings about the attainment of the Noble Fruit. It is called "Eightfold" (Aṭṭhaṅgika) because it has eight factors. This path is merely the factors themselves, like an army with four divisions or an orchestra with five instruments; there is no path separate from its factors. It is called "Path" (Magga) because it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna, or because it seeks Nibbāna, or because it goes along killing the defilements. "Seyyathidaṃ" means "What is that path?"

Now, wishing to show that the path is merely the factors and that there is no path separate from the factors, the Buddha said "Sammā-diṭṭhi... pe... Sammā-samādhi." In that text, Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi) has the characteristic of correct seeing. Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa) has the characteristic of correct directing. Right Speech (Sammā-vācā) has the characteristic of correct embracing. Right Action (Sammā-kammanta) has the characteristic of correct originating. Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) has the characteristic of correct purification. Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma) has the characteristic of correct upholding. Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) has the characteristic of correct establishing. Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi) has the characteristic of correct placing.

Among those eight path factors, each factor has three functions. What are those functions? Firstly, Right View abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements, takes cessation (Nibbāna) as its object, and sees the associated states without delusion by dispelling the delusion that covers that Truth of Cessation. Right Intention and the other factors likewise abandon wrong intention and so on, and take cessation as their object. Specifically, among these factors, Right Intention directs the associated states toward the object of cessation; Right Speech correctly embraces the associated states; Right Action correctly sets up the associated states; Right Livelihood purifies the associated states; Right Effort upholds the associated states; Right Mindfulness establishes the associated states upon the object; and Right Concentration correctly places the associated states.

Furthermore, this so-called Right View has various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage (pubba-bhāga). At the moment of the Path, however, it has a single moment and a single object. In terms of function, it receives four names such as "knowledge regarding suffering" and so on. Right Intention and the others also have various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the Path, they have a single moment and a single object. Among those factors, Right Intention, in terms of function, is called "intention of renunciation" and so on...
108:
(Right Thought) obtains three names. The three path factors beginning with Right Speech, in the preliminary stage of the Path, are not the same in terms of moment or object; they are both abstinences (virati) and volitions (cetanā). However, at the moment of the Path, they are only abstinences. This pair, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, also each obtain four names by virtue of the four Right Strivings (sammappadhāna) and the four Foundations of Mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) respectively, according to their functions. Right Concentration, however, is called only Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path.

Thus, among these eight path factors, the Blessed One taught Right View first because it is of great benefit to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. This Right View is also called "the light of wisdom" and "the weapon of wisdom." Therefore, by means of this Right View, known as insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in the preliminary stage of the Path, the practitioner (yogāvacara) destroys the darkness of ignorance (avijjā), slays the insurgents of defilements (kilesa), and reaches Nibbāna safely. Thus it is said: "Right View was taught first because it is of great benefit to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna."

Right Thought is also of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, Right Thought was taught immediately after Right View. Indeed, just as a goldsmith, turning a coin over and over in his hand and looking at it with his eyes, knows, "This is counterfeit, this is genuine," so too the practitioner, thinking with initial application (vitakka) in the preliminary stage and looking with the wisdom of insight, knows, "These states belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), these states belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and so on." Or, just as a carpenter takes a large log rolled towards him by a man from one end, and by hewing it with an adze, makes it useful for work such as building a house, so too the practitioner, taking the states presented by repeated thinking with initial application, defines them with wisdom as "These states belong to the sense sphere, these states belong to the fine-material sphere," and so on, making them useful for the task of full understanding (pariññā). Thus it is said: "Right Thought is of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, Right Thought was taught immediately after it."

Just as that Right Thought is beneficial to Right View, it is also beneficial to Right Speech. As it is said: "Householder, having first thought and pondered, one afterwards breaks into speech." Therefore, Right Speech was taught immediately after Right Thought.

Since people in the world first arrange with speech, saying, "We shall do this and that work," and then engage in activities, speech is beneficial to bodily action. Therefore, Right Action was taught immediately after Right Speech.
109:
Right Livelihood is taught after those two (Right Speech and Right Action) because the morality of "livelihood as the eighth" (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) is fulfilled only by one who abandons the four types of verbal misconduct and the three types of bodily misconduct and fulfills both good bodily and verbal conduct, and not by anyone else.

One who has such pure livelihood should not be content with just this much, thinking "My livelihood is pure," and live in negligence. Rather, to show that this effort must be undertaken in all postures, Right Effort was taught immediately after that (Right Livelihood).

Next, to show that one who has undertaken effort must also firmly establish mindfulness in the four objects such as the body, Right Mindfulness was taught immediately after that (Right Effort).

It should be understood that Right Concentration was taught immediately after Right Mindfulness because mindfulness thus well-established is able to investigate the tendencies of states that are beneficial or unbeneficial to concentration, and to settle the mind on a single object.

In the explanation of Right View, the meditation on the Four Noble Truths is shown starting with "knowledge of suffering." Among these four truths, the first two are the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), and the last two are the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). Between the round and the cessation, the monk applies his mind to the meditation on the round; there is no such application in the cessation. Having learned the first two truths from a teacher, both in brief as "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin," and in detail as "What are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form," and so on, the practitioner monk performs the task of meditation by reciting them repeatedly with his voice. Regarding the other two truths, however, he performs the task of meditation merely by hearing that "the truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing."

That practitioner monk, while performing the task of meditation in this way, penetrates the Four Truths with a single penetration; he realizes them with a single realization (ekābhisamaya). He penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā), the origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna), cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā), and the path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā). He realizes suffering through the realization of full understanding... the path through the realization of development.

Thus, for that monk, in the preliminary stage of the Path, there is penetration through learning, questioning, hearing, memorizing, and examining the two truths (suffering and origin). Regarding the other two truths, there is only penetration through hearing. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration by way of function (kicca) regarding the three truths, and penetration by way of object (ārammaṇa) regarding the truth of cessation. Among these knowledges, all penetration-knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) is supramundane (lokuttara); the knowledge of hearing, memorizing, and examining is mundane (lokiya) belonging to the sense sphere. Reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa), however, occurs to one who has reached the truths. Since this monk is a beginner (ādikammika), that reviewing knowledge is not mentioned here. For this monk, in the stage prior to full understanding, "Suffering...
111:
Regarding the three types of thought such as sensual thought, among the thirty-eight meditation objects (kammaṭṭhāna) analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali, there is not even one that is not an opposite. Specifically, however, the opposite of sensual thought is only the first jhana on the object of foulness (asubha). The opposites of the thought of ill will are the triple and quadruple jhanas on the object of loving-kindness (mettā). The opposites of the thought of cruelty are the triple and quadruple jhanas on the object of compassion (karuṇā). Therefore, for one who attains jhana after performing preliminary work (parikamma) on the object of foulness, at the moment of attainment, the intention associated with jhana arises as the opposite of sensual thought by way of suppression (vikkhambhana). For one who establishes insight by making jhana the basis, at the moment of insight, the intention associated with insight arises as the opposite of sensual thought by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga). For one who urges insight forward and reaches the path, at the moment of the path, the intention associated with the path arises as the opposite of sensual thought by way of eradication (samuccheda). It should be understood that the thought thus arisen is called the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa). In the cases of attaining jhana by performing preliminary work on the object of loving-kindness or performing preliminary work on the object of compassion, etc., all should be applied in the same manner as the previous method. It should be understood that the thought thus arisen is called the intention of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa) and the intention of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa). Thus, these factors such as the intention of renunciation are distinct in the preliminary stage because their modes of arising by way of insight and jhana are different. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of unwholesome intention through the cutting off of its cause in these three instances. This is called Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa).

In the description of Right Speech (sammā-vācā-niddesa) also, because the mind that abstains from false speech is of one kind, and the minds that abstain from malicious speech and so forth are each of different kinds, those four abstinences (veramaṇī) are distinct in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome abstinence called Right Speech arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of the fourfold unwholesome intention of immorality known as wrong speech through its total eradication. This is called Right Speech.

In the description of Right Action (sammā-kammanta-niddesa) also, because the mind that abstains from killing living beings is of one kind, the mind that abstains from taking what is not given is of another, and the mind that abstains from sexual misconduct is of yet another, those three abstinences (veramaṇī) are distinct in the preliminary stage. At the moment of the path, however, a single wholesome abstinence called Right Action arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of the threefold unwholesome intention of immorality known as wrong action through its total eradication. This is called Right Action.
113:
—the Path that arises is associated with the first jhāna. In this Path, the eight path factors and the seven factors of enlightenment are fully present. For one who practices insight after emerging from the second jhāna, the Path that arises is associated with the second jhāna. In this Path, there are seven path factors (excluding Right Thought/Sammā-saṅkappa). For one who practices insight after emerging from the third jhāna, the Path that arises is associated with the third jhāna. In this Path, there are seven path factors and six factors of enlightenment (excluding rapture/pīti). This same method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), the fourth and fifth jhānas arise. These jhānas are said to be only supramundane (lokuttara) and not mundane (lokiya). How should this be understood? In this formless realm also, for one who, after emerging from any jhāna such as the first jhāna, has attained the Path of Stream-entry and then developed the formless attainments and is born in the formless realm, the three higher Paths arise for him there associated with that same jhāna. Thus, it is the basis jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) alone that determines the jhāna factors of the Path. However, some Elders say, "The aggregates (khandhas) which are the objects of insight determine them." Some say, "The inclination of the person (puggalajjhāsaya) determines them." Others say, "Insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) determines them." The decision on their views should be understood according to the method stated below in the commentary on the Supramundane Section (Lokuttara-pada-bhājanīya) of the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa). In the phrase "This is called Right Concentration," it refers to the one-pointedness (ekaggatā) of mind present in these four jhānas. This one-pointedness is mundane in the preliminary stage and is called supramundane Right Concentration in the subsequent Path moment. Thus, the Blessed One taught the Truth of the Path by way of the mundane and the supramundane.

Among those mundane and supramundane Paths, in the mundane Path, all path factors have one of the six sense objects as their object as appropriate. In the supramundane Path, however, for the Noble person (ariya) who proceeds toward the penetration of the Four Truths, the wisdom-eye that takes Nibbāna as its object and absolutely uproots the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) is called Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi). For the Noble person thus endowed with Right View, the thought (vitakka) associated with that Right View, which absolutely uproots the three types of wrong thought and directs the mind toward the state of Nibbāna, is called Right Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa). For the Noble person who thus sees and thinks, the abstinence from wrong speech associated with that Right Thought, which absolutely uproots the four types of verbal misconduct, is called Right Speech (Sammā-vācā). For the Noble person who thus abstains, the abstinence from the three types of bodily misconduct associated with that abstinence (virati), which absolutely cuts off wrong action, is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta). The abstinence from wrong livelihood associated with those very Right Speech and Right Action, which is the purification of them and absolutely cuts off scheming (kuhana) and so forth, is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva). For the Noble person established in this ground of virtue (sīla-bhūmi) called Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood, that which is appropriate to that virtue and associated with that abstinence—
114:
Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma) is the exertion of energy that completely cuts off laziness (kosajja), and accomplishes the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the maintenance of arisen wholesome states. For the Noble One who exerts effort in this way, the non-confusion of mind (asammosa) which is associated with that energy, which removes wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati), and which accomplishes mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so forth regarding objects such as the body, is called Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati). For the Noble One whose mind is well-guarded by such unsurpassed mindfulness, the one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) which is associated with that Right Mindfulness and which completely uproots wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi) should be understood as Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi). This is the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path, which, together with the mundane path, is known as the 'Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā).

That Noble Eightfold Path is called both 'Knowledge' (vijjā) and 'Conduct' (caraṇa) because Right View and Right Thought are included in Knowledge, while the remaining path factors are included in Conduct. Similarly, it is called both 'Serenity' (samatha) and 'Insight' (vipassanā) because those two (Right View and Right Thought) are included in the vehicle of insight, while the remaining factors are included in the vehicle of serenity. Alternatively, it is called the 'Three Aggregates' (khandha) and the 'Three Trainings' (sikkhā) because those two are included in the Aggregate of Wisdom (paññā-kkhandha), the next three in the Aggregate of Virtue (sīla-kkhandha), and the remaining three in the Aggregate of Concentration (samādhi-kkhandha), as well as in the trainings of Higher Wisdom (adhipaññā), Higher Virtue (adhisīla), and Higher Mind (adhicitta). The Noble Disciple endowed with these path factors is like a traveler endowed with eyes capable of seeing and feet capable of walking; being endowed with knowledge and conduct, he avoids the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) by means of the vehicle of insight, and devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) by means of the vehicle of serenity. Practicing the Middle Way (majjhima paṭipadā), he breaks through the mass of delusion with the Aggregate of Wisdom, the mass of hatred with the Aggregate of Virtue, and the mass of greed with the Aggregate of Concentration. Reaching the three attainments (sampatti)—the attainment of wisdom through the training of higher wisdom, the attainment of virtue through the training of higher virtue, and the attainment of concentration through the training of higher mind—he realizes Nibbāna, the deathless ambrosia. He enters the Noble Ground known as the 'Certainty of Rightness' (sammattaniyāma), which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, and adorned with the thirty-seven jewels of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma).

## Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

206-214. Now, the Abhidhamma Exposition is presented. In that Abhidhamma Exposition, the Buddha did not say 'Noble Truths' (ariya-saccāni) but said 'Four Truths' (cattāri saccāni) in order to show the Origin (samudaya), which is described as the cause of suffering without exception.
115:
It has been stated. If it were stated as 'Noble Truths' (ariya-saccāni), the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots accompanied by taints (sāsava), and the remaining wholesome states accompanied by taints would not be included. It is not craving alone that produces suffering; these remaining causes such as defilements also produce suffering. Thus, because these causes also produce suffering, the Buddha said 'Four Truths' (cattāri saccāni) instead of 'Noble Truths' (ariya-saccāni) to show the Origin (samudaya) as the cause without exception.

In the Section of Exposition (niddesa-vāra), among those four truths, the Origin of Suffering is explained first without explaining the Truth of Suffering in detail, for the purpose of easily indicating that very suffering. When that Origin of Suffering is indicated, the Truth of Suffering is easily indicated by the method of 'the remaining defilements' and so forth. In this section, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is also indicated in five ways by means of the abandoning of the Origin as previously stated, such as 'the abandoning of craving' and 'the abandoning of craving and the remaining defilements.' The Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), however, is indicated by showing only a mere outline of the method of teaching analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī by means of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) associated with the first jhāna. In that Truth of the Path, the variety of methods should be understood. We shall clarify this later.

Since the eightfold path is not the only practice (paṭipadā), but the fivefold path is also taught as the practice according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of the individual—based on the statement, 'Even before the path, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are very pure'—the Section on the Fivefold Path (pañcaṅgika-vāra) is also indicated to show that method. Furthermore, since not only the eightfold and fivefold paths are the practice, but the more than fifty associated states are also the practice, the third All-inclusive Section (sabba-saṅgāhika-vāra) is also indicated to show that method. In that All-inclusive Section, the statement 'the remaining states are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' is omitted. The rest of the arrangement is the same in all sections.

Among those three sections, in the first of the five portions (koṭṭhāsa) of the Eightfold Section, such as 'the abandoning of craving and the remaining defilements,' there are ten methods by means of the two methods each—the fourfold and fivefold—in these five sections: Pure Practice (suddhika-paṭipadā), Pure Emptiness (suddhika-suññata), Practice of Emptiness (suññata-paṭipadā), Pure Desireless (suddhika-appaṇihita), and Practice of Desireless (appaṇihita-paṭipadā), within the passage where jhānas are applied to the Path of Stream-entry. In this same manner, there are two hundred methods across the twenty applications (abhinivesa). Those two hundred methods are multiplied by four by means of the four predominant factors (adhipati)...
116:
Thus, there are two hundred pure methods without predominance and eight hundred methods with predominance; in this way, there are one thousand methods in total. Just as there are one thousand methods in the Path of Stream-entry, so it is with the remaining three paths; thus, there are four thousand methods in the four paths. Just as there are four thousand methods in the first section, so it is with the remaining sections; thus, there are twenty thousand methods in the five sections of the Eightfold Cycle. Similarly, there are twenty thousand methods each in the Fivefold Cycle and the All-inclusive Cycle; thus, the Teacher has analyzed and taught sixty thousand methods in total. In the Pali text, however, it appears only in brief. Thus, it should be understood that this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, consisting of three Great Cycles and fifteen sections, adorned with sixty thousand methods, has been explained.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya

## 3. Commentary on the Questionnaire

In the Questionnaire (Pañhāpucchaka), the nature of the four truths as wholesome and so forth should be understood in the same way as stated in the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandha-vibhaṅga). Regarding the Triad of Objects: the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) has a limited object for one who enjoys sense-sphere states; it has an exalted object for one who enjoys exalted states; it has an indescribable object (not to be called limited, exalted, or immeasurable) for one who enjoys concepts. The Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) has a limited object when it arises by taking sense-sphere states as its object; it has an exalted object when it arises by taking fine-material or immaterial-sphere states as its object; it has an immeasurable object when reviewing the nine supramundane states; it has an indescribable object when reviewing concepts. The Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) is always 'caused by the path' (magga-hetuka) by way of conascent cause; when developing the path by making either energy or investigation predominant, it is 'path-predominant' (maggādhipati); however, when either desire or consciousness is the predominant factor, it is simply 'indescribable' (not to be called 'caused by the path' or 'path-predominant'). The Truth of Suffering is a 'path-object' (maggārammaṇa) when Noble Ones review the path; it is 'path-predominant' when reviewing that same path with esteem; however, when reviewing the remaining states, it is 'indescribable' (not to be called 'path-object' or 'path-predominant').

The 'two truths' refer to the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin. These truths have past objects and so forth when they arise by taking states distinguished as past and so forth as their objects. The Truth of the Origin has an internal object and so forth for one who enjoys states distinguished as internal and so forth; it should be understood that the Truth of Suffering also has an indescribable object (not to be called internal or external) when the attainment of the sphere of nothingness occurs. Thus, in this Questionnaire, two truths are mundane and two truths are supramundane.
117:
Just as there are mundane and supramundane truths in this Questionnaire method, so it is in the two preceding methods. Indeed, the Blessed One taught only mundane and supramundane truths in all three methods, such as the Suttanta-bhājanīya. Thus, this Analysis of the Truths (Sacca-vibhaṅga) is also shown by analyzing it through the rotation of the three methods.

## 5. Indriyavibhaṅga
## 1. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

Now, in the Indriyavibhaṅga, which immediately follows the Saccavibhaṅga, the term "twenty-two" refers to the delimitation by number. "Faculties" (indriya) refers to the indication of the delimited phenomena. Now, wishing to show those faculties in their specific nature, he said "eye-faculty" (cakkhundriya) and so on.

In that context, it is called the eye-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the eye-door. It is called the body-faculty (and so on) because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the ear-door, nose-door, tongue-door, and body-door. It is called the mind-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of cognizing. It is called the female-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in femininity. It is called the male-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in masculinity. It is called the life-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of maintaining. It is called the pleasure-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of pleasure. It is called the equanimity-faculty (and so on) because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristics of pain, joy, grief, and equanimity. It is called the faith-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of decision (adhimokkha). It is called the energy-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of exertion. It is called the mindfulness-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of establishing [on the object]. It is called the concentration-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of non-distraction. It is called the wisdom-faculty because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing. It is called the 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty (aññātaññassāmītindriya) because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the characteristic of knowing that arises as "I shall know the Four Noble Truths that are not yet known." It is called the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in knowing again those very things that have been known. It is called the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) because it exercises the sense of sovereignty in the state of one who has already known.

In this Indriyavibhaṅga, the Suttantabhājanīya is not included. Why? Because in the Suttas, these twenty-two faculties do not appear in this sequence. For in the Suttas, in some places two faculties are taught, in some places three, and in some places five. Thus, there is no instance where the twenty-two appear continuously in this order. This is the method of the Commentary in this regard.

This is another method—among these faculties, the decision should be known by way of meaning (attha), by way of characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and so on, by way of order (kama), by way of division and non-division, and likewise by way of function (kicca) and by way of plane (bhūmi).

Therein, the meaning of the eye and so on has already been explained by the method beginning with "it is called the eye (cakkhu) because it sees (cakkkhati)." Among the last three, the first is called the 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty because it arises in the continuity of one who is practicing with the thought, "In the preliminary stage, I shall know Nibbāna or the Four Noble Truths which are not yet known," and because of the presence of the sense of a faculty. The second is called the faculty of final knowledge because of the act of knowing and because of the presence of the sense of a faculty. The third is called the faculty of one who has known because it arises only in the continuity of an Arahant who has known the Four Noble Truths, and because of the presence of the sense of a faculty.
119:
...because it arises only in the continuity of an Arahant whose task of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths is completed, and because the sense of a faculty is possible.

What is this "sense of a faculty" (indriya-attha)? The sense of being a sign of the Lord (Inda), the sense of being taught by the Lord, the sense of being seen by the Lord, the sense of being created by the Lord, and the sense of being cultivated by the Lord—these are the senses of a faculty. All of these are applicable here as appropriate. For the Blessed One, the Fully Enlightened One, is the Lord (Inda) because of His supreme sovereignty. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is also the Lord because there is no sovereign over kammas. Therefore, among these faculties, those produced by kamma indicate wholesome and unwholesome kamma. And they are created by that kamma. Thus, they are faculties in the sense of being a sign of the Lord and in the sense of being created by the Lord. Furthermore, all of these are faculties in the sense of being taught by the Lord and in the sense of being seen by the Lord, because they were explained according to reality and were fully realized by the Blessed One. For that very reason, they are faculties in the sense of being cultivated by the Lord, because some were cultivated by the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages (Muninda), through the cultivation of the objective field, and some through the cultivation of mental development (bhāvanā). Moreover, these faculties are also called "indriya" in the sense of sovereignty, which is called predominance (ādhipatya). For the sovereignty of the eye and so on is established in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so on; because when they are keen, [consciousness] is keen, and when they are dull, it is dull. This is the decision by way of "meaning" in this context.

'By way of characteristics and so on' means that the decision regarding the eye and so on should be known by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Their characteristics and so on are just as mentioned below. For the four beginning with the wisdom-faculty are, in terms of meaning, only non-delusion (amoha). The remaining ones appear there in their own nature.

'By way of order' refers to the order of teaching. Therein, because the attainment of the Noble plane occurs after fully understanding internal phenomena (ajjhatta-dhamma), the eye-faculty and so on, which are included in the individual existence (attabhāva), are taught first. To show that this individual existence is designated as "female" or "male" depending on certain phenomena, the female-faculty and the male-faculty are taught next. To make it known that both these types of individual existence proceed in dependence on the life-faculty, the life-faculty is taught next. As long as that life-faculty persists, there is no cessation of these feelings. To make it known that whatever is felt is all [included in] pleasure and pain, the pleasure-faculty and so on are taught next. To show the practice (paṭipatti) that these phenomena such as faith should be developed for the cessation of those feelings, faith and so on are taught next. To show the fruitfulness of the practice, that through this practice, this 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty first appears in oneself, the 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty is taught next. Because it is the fruit of that [first one] and because it should be developed immediately after it, the faculty of final knowledge is taught next. After this faculty of final knowledge, the faculty of one who has known is attained through mental development; and once this faculty of one who has known is attained, there is nothing further to be done...
120:
To make it known that there is still a higher task to be done, the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya), which is the supreme relief, is taught at the end. In this way, the order of these faculties should be understood.

Regarding 'Distinction and Non-distinction' (bhedābheda), among these faculties, only the life faculty (jīvitindriya) has distinction. That life faculty is of two types: the physical life faculty and the mental life faculty. The remaining faculties have no such distinction. Thus, the decision regarding distinction and non-distinction among these faculties should be understood.

Regarding 'Function' (kicca), if it is asked, 'What is the function of the faculties?' Firstly, for the eye faculty (cakkhundriya), according to the statement, 'The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states by way of faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya),' its function is to make the states such as eye-consciousness follow its own mode, characterized as sharp or dull, which is accomplished through its status as a faculty-condition. The functions of the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties are the same. However, the function of the mind faculty (manindriya) is to make conascent states follow its own will. The function of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) is to protect conascent states. The function of the femininity faculty (itthindriya) and the masculinity faculty (purisindriya) is to regulate the signs, behavior, and appearance of females and males respectively. The function of the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief (sukha, dukkha, somanassa, domanassindriya) is to overpower conascent states and lead them to their respective gross characteristics. The function of the equanimity faculty (upekkhindriya) is to lead to a peaceful, sublime, and neutral state. The function of the faculties such as faith (saddhā) is to overpower opposing states and lead associated states to a state of clarity and so forth. The function of the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is the abandoning of the three fetters (saṃyojana) and directing associated states toward that abandonment. The function of the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is the reduction and abandoning of sensual lust, ill-will, and so forth, and making conascent states follow its own will. The function of the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is the abandoning of effort in all tasks and being the condition for associated states to face the Deathless Nibbāna. Thus, the decision regarding function among these faculties should be understood.

Regarding 'Plane' (bhūmi), the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, masculinity, pleasure, pain, and grief are only of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) here. The mind faculty, life faculty, equanimity faculty, and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom pertain to all four planes. The joy faculty (somanassindriya) pertains to three planes: the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the supramundane. The final three faculties are exclusively supramundane. Thus, the decision regarding planes should be understood. One who understands thus—

A monk with much sense of urgency, established in sense restraint,
Having fully understood the faculties,
Reaches the end of suffering.
121:
In the Exposition Section (niddesavāra), everything beginning with 'The eye which is of the four great elements' should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Word-by-Word Commentary (padabhājanīya) of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. In the expositions of the energy faculty, concentration faculty, and so forth, terms such as right effort, wrong effort, right concentration, and wrong concentration are not mentioned. Why? Because of their all-inclusiveness. For the faculties taught here in this Indriya-vibhaṅga are all-inclusive. This being so, in this Indriya-vibhaṅga, ten faculties such as the eye faculty are mundane and belong only to the sense-sphere; three are exclusively supramundane; and nine, such as the mind faculty, are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma Classification

## 2. Commentary on the Interrogation

In the Interrogation (pañhāpucchaka), the distinction of all faculties into wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the method of the Pali text.

In the Triplets on Objects (ārammaṇattika), the statement 'seven faculties have no object' is said with reference to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, and masculinity faculties (which are purely physical). The life faculty (jīvitindriya), however, is not included among these objectless states because it is mixed with the mental life faculty. 'Two faculties' refers to the pleasure and pain faculties. These two have exclusively sense-sphere objects. The grief faculty (domanassindriya) may have a sense-sphere object when it arises with reference to sense-sphere states; it has a sublime (mahaggata) object when it arises with reference to fine-material or immaterial states; and it has an 'indescribable' object when it arises with reference to concepts (paññatti). The statement 'nine faculties may have sense-sphere objects' is said with reference to the mind, life, joy, and equanimity faculties, and the five faculties beginning with faith. Although the life faculty is included among objectless physical states because it is mixed with matter, it is included in the 'it may be' (siyā) portion by way of its mental life faculty component.

'Four faculties' refers to the pleasure, pain, grief, and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). These do not fall within the Triplet on Path as Object (maggārammaṇattika). The term 'Path as Cause' (maggahētuka) is said with reference to the conascent cause. When energy (vīriya) and investigation (vīmaṃsā) are predominant, it may be 'Path as Predominant' (maggādhipati). However, when desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) are predominant, it may be 'indescribable' (neither maggahētuka nor maggādhipati).
122:
"The ten faculties may be arisen, may be about to arise" (Dasindriyā siyā uppannā, siyā uppādino)—this statement is made with reference to the seven physical faculties and the three resultant faculties. These ten faculties are the same as the nine faculties mentioned below along with displeasure (domanassa). Among those ten faculties, when the faculty of displeasure (domanassindriya) occurs by taking a concept (paññatti) as an object, it has an object that cannot be described (as arisen or about to arise). The remaining nine faculties also have objects that cannot be described when reflecting on Nibbāna or when taking a concept as an object.

"Three faculties have external objects" refers to the three supramundane faculties. "Four faculties" refers to the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, and the faculty of displeasure. These faculties occur by taking internal phenomena or external phenomena as objects. "Eight faculties" refers to the mind faculty, the life faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the five faculties beginning with faith. Among these eight faculties, it should be understood that they have objects that cannot be described when the jhāna of the sphere of nothingness occurs.

Thus, in this question-and-answer section (pañhāpucchaka) as well, only the ten sense-sphere faculties, the three supramundane faculties, and the nine faculties that are a mixture of mundane and supramundane have been taught. This method of the question-and-answer section has the same scope as the Abhidhamma classification (abhidhamma-bhājanīya). However, this Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga) has been shown by extracting and classifying the two cycles (the Abhidhamma classification and the question-and-answer section) [without the Suttanta classification].

## In the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga named Sammohavinodanī,
## the Explanation of the Analysis of the Faculties is finished.
123:
## 6. Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga
## 1. Explanation of the Suttanta Classification Brief Exposition

Now, in the Analysis of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga) which immediately follows that [Analysis of the Faculties], a teacher who wishes to provide the commentary on the text laid down by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations," should enter the assembly of the Vibhajjavādins with wisdom. Without disparaging the former teachers, without deviating from his own tradition, without striving for the traditions of others, without contradicting the Suttas, in accordance with the Vinaya, observing the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa), illuminating the Dhamma, grasping the meaning, and repeatedly revolving that same meaning to point it out in detail through other methods, he should provide the commentary. The commentary on the meaning of Dependent Origination is inherently difficult to perform. Therefore, the former teachers said:
"Truth, the being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditions—these four things are hard to see and extremely difficult to teach."

Therefore, having repeatedly reflected, "Except for the Arahants who have attained learning (pariyatti) and penetration (paṭivedha), it is not easy for others to provide the commentary on Dependent Origination," [it is said]:
"Though I wish to speak today on the commentary of the mode of conditions, I find no footing, like one who has plunged into the ocean. However, this Dispensation is adorned with various methods of instruction, and the path of the former teachers continues uninterrupted. Therefore, relying on both of these, I shall undertake the commentary on this Dependent Origination; listen to that commentary with a concentrated mind."

The former teachers also said:
"Whoever listens to this, taking it to heart (or making it their own benefit), will gain a distinction of knowledge of what comes before and after. Having gained that distinction of knowledge, they will reach Nibbāna, which the King of Death cannot see."

In the texts beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations," the meaning should be understood from the beginning by way of the variety of instruction, by way of meaning and characteristic, etc., and by the delimitation of the factors. Regarding the variety of instruction: just as four men gathering creepers pull them, the Blessed One taught Dependent Origination in four ways, starting from the beginning, or from the middle to the end, and likewise from the end, or from the middle to the beginning.

Among those four men, one man first sees the root of the creeper, cuts it at the root, pulls the whole thing, and uses it for his work. Similarly, the Blessed One taught Dependent Origination from the beginning to the end, saying, "Monks, thus with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be... with birth as condition, aging and death come to be." Among those four men, another man first sees the middle of the creeper, cuts it in the middle, and pulls only the upper part...
124:
In the passages beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations," first of all:

The decision should be understood by way of the diversity of teaching, by way of meaning, characteristic, unity, and so forth, and by way of the determination of the factors.

Therein, "by way of the diversity of teaching" means: The Blessed One's teaching of Dependent Origination is fourfold, like the taking of a vine by four men gathering vines: starting from the beginning or from the middle and continuing to the end; likewise, starting from the end or from the middle and continuing to the beginning.

How so? Just as among four men gathering vines, one man first sees only the root of the vine; having cut it at the root and pulled it all out, he takes it and uses it for his work. Similarly, the Blessed One teaches Dependent Origination starting from the beginning to the end, thus: "So it is, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations... with birth as condition, aging and death."

Among those men, one man first sees the middle of the vine; having cut it in the middle, he pulls out only the upper part, takes it and uses it for his work. Similarly, the Blessed One teaches from the middle to the end, thus: "For him who finds delight in that feeling, who welcomes it and remains attached to it, delight (nandī) arises. That delight in feelings is clinging (upādāna); with clinging as condition, existence (bhava); with existence as condition, birth (jāti)."

Among those men, one man first sees the tip of the vine; holding the tip, he takes the whole vine following from the tip to the root and uses it for his work. Similarly, the Blessed One teaches Dependent Origination from the end to the beginning, thus: "Bhikkhus, it has been said: 'With birth as condition, aging and death.' Now, bhikkhus, is there aging and death with birth as condition, or not? Or how is it in this case?" They reply: "Venerable Sir, there is aging and death with birth as condition. Thus it is for us in this case: with birth as condition, aging and death." [He continues:] "With existence as condition, birth... with ignorance as condition, volitional formations. It has been said: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations.' Now, bhikkhus, are there volitional formations with ignorance as condition, or not? Or how is it in this case?" They reply: "Venerable Sir, there are volitional formations with ignorance as condition. Thus it is for us in this case: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations." Thus he teaches Dependent Origination from the end to the beginning.

Among those men, one man first sees only the middle of the vine; having cut it in the middle, descending downwards and taking it to the root for his work...
125:
...Similarly, the Blessed One teaches starting from the middle and continuing to the beginning, thus: "Monks, these four nutriments, what is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their production? Monks, these four nutriments have craving as their source, craving as their origin, craving as their birth, craving as their production. And this craving, monks, what is its source? It has feeling, contact, the sixfold sense base, name-and-form, and consciousness as its source. What is the source of formations?... Formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, ignorance as their production."

Why does he teach in this way? It is because Dependent Origination is all-beneficent and because the Blessed One himself has attained mastery of teaching (desanāvilāsa). Indeed, Dependent Origination, through various teachings, leads only to the penetration of the method [of the Dhamma]. And the Blessed One has attained mastery of teaching through his possession of the four kinds of fearlessness (vesārajja) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and by his attainment of the fourfold depth. Having attained mastery of teaching, he teaches the Dhamma by various methods. Specifically, the forward teaching (anuloma-desanā) starting from the beginning should be understood as being set forth for the purpose of showing the process of occurrence through their respective causes and for showing the order of arising, having seen venayable beings who are confused about the analysis of the causes of existence.

The reverse teaching (paṭiloma-desanā) starting from the end, aging and death, is for the purpose of showing the cause discovered by himself for this or that suffering such as aging and death, following the penetration of the preceding parts, while repeatedly observing the world that has fallen into distress in the manner beginning: "Alas, this world has fallen into distress; it is born, it ages, and it dies." The teaching starting from the middle and continuing to the beginning is for the purpose of showing the sequence of cause and effect starting from the past, having traced back to the past time following the definition of the source of nutriments. The teaching starting from the middle and continuing to the end is for the purpose of showing the future time, starting from the production of the cause of the future time in the present time. Among these four types of teachings, it should be understood that the forward teaching starting from the beginning—which is for the purpose of showing the process of occurrence through their respective causes and for showing the order of arising to venayable beings confused about the causes of existence—is the one presented here in this Paṭiccasamuppāda-vibhaṅga.

Why is ignorance mentioned at the beginning here? Is ignorance a causeless root-cause of the world, like the "Prakṛti" of the Proponents of Primordial Matter (Pakativādīs)? It is not a causeless root-cause. For the cause of ignorance has been stated thus: "With the arising of taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance."
126:
There is also a method of exposition by which ignorance (avijjā) may be the root cause. What is that method? It is by being the head/primary element in the discourse on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭakatha). For the Blessed One, when teaching the discourse on the cycle, taught by making two dhammas the head: either ignorance or craving for existence (bhavataṇhā). As he said: "Monks, the first beginning of ignorance is not known, such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist; it only came into being afterwards.' Even though this is said, monks, it is nevertheless known that 'ignorance has this as its condition' (idappaccaya)." (A. Ni. 10.61). Regarding craving for existence, he said: "Monks, the first beginning of craving for existence is not known, such that one could say, 'Before this, craving for existence did not exist; it only came into being afterwards.' Even though this is said, monks, it is nevertheless known that 'craving for existence has this as its condition'." (A. Ni. 10.62).

Why does the Blessed One, when teaching the discourse on the cycle, make only these two dhammas the head? Because they are the specific causes of kamma that lead to happy destinations (sugati) and miserable destinations (duggati). Ignorance is the specific cause of kamma leading to miserable destinations. Why? Because a worldling (puthujjana) overwhelmed by ignorance—just like a cow being slaughtered, tormented by the heat of fire and the blows of a stick, who in her distress drinks hot water which is neither pleasurable nor beneficial to her—undertakes various kammas leading to miserable destinations, such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), which are devoid of pleasure due to the heat of defilements and bring about his own harm by causing a fall into miserable destinations.

Craving for existence is the specific cause of kamma leading to happy destinations. Why? Because a worldling overwhelmed by craving for existence—just like the aforementioned cow, out of thirst for cold water, drinks cold water which is pleasurable and relieves her fatigue—undertakes various kammas leading to happy destinations, such as abstaining from killing living beings, which are pleasurable because they are free from the heat of defilements and relieve the fatigue of the suffering of miserable destinations by bringing about arrival at a happy destination.

Among these dhammas which are the heads of the discourse on the cycle, in some teachings the Blessed One teaches with a single dhamma as the root, such as: "Thus, monks, volitional formations have ignorance as their proximate cause; consciousness has volitional formations as its proximate cause," etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 2.23). Likewise: "Monks, in one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that can be clung to, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises," etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 2.52). In some teachings, he teaches with both as the root, such as: "Monks, for the fool who is hindered by ignorance and joined with craving, this body has been produced. Thus there are this body and external name-and-form."
127:
"Thus there is this pair; dependent on this pair there is contact, and the six bases through which the fool, being touched, experiences pleasure and pain," etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 2.19). Among those various teachings, this teaching here in this Vibhaṅga Pali, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," should be understood as a teaching with a single dhamma as the root by way of ignorance. Thus, first, the decision should be understood by way of the variety of teachings in this Dependent Origination.

'By way of meaning' means (the decision should be understood) by way of the meaning of the terms such as ignorance (avijjā). That meaning is as follows: Because it is improper to fulfill, evil conduct of body, etc., is called 'avindiya' (that which is not to be found/attained); the meaning is that it should not be acquired. Because it finds that 'avindiya', it is 'avijjā'. Conversely, good conduct of body, etc., is called 'vindiya' (that which is to be found/attained). Because it does not find that 'vindiya', it is 'avijjā'. Because it makes unknown the meaning of 'group' for the aggregates (khandha), the meaning of 'base' for the bases (āyatana), the meaning of 'voidness' for the elements (dhātu), the meaning of 'truth' for the truths (sacca), and the meaning of 'predominance' for the faculties (indriya), it is 'avijjā'. Because it makes unknown the fourfold meanings of suffering, etc., such as 'oppression' (pīḷana), it is also 'avijjā'. Because it causes beings to run through all types of birth (yoni), destination (gati), existence (bhava), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) in the endless cycle of birth (saṃsāra), it is 'avijjā'. Because it occurs in regard to women, men, etc., which do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha), and does not occur in regard to the aggregates, etc., which do exist, it is 'avijjā'. Furthermore, because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness, etc., and the dhammas of Dependent Origination and those dependently arisen, it is 'avijjā'.

That which a fruit depends upon to arise is a 'condition' (paccaya). 'Dependent' (paṭicca) means not without that; the meaning is without discarding that. 'Arises' (eti) means it both arises and proceeds. Furthermore, the meaning of 'assisting' is the meaning of condition. Because it is both ignorance and a condition, it is 'ignorance-condition' (avijjāpaccaya). Therefore, 'with ignorance as condition' (volitional formations arise).

Because they process/construct the conditioned fruit, they are called 'volitional formations' (saṅkhāra). Furthermore, there are two kinds of formations: formations caused by ignorance and formations occurring by the term 'saṅkhāra'. Among them, the three—meritorious formations (puññābhisankhāra), demeritorious formations (apuññābhisankhāra), and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisankhāra)—and the three—bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations—these six are the formations caused by ignorance. All of them are merely mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā).

As for these four—saṅkhata-saṅkhāra, abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra, abhisaṅkharaṇa-saṅkhāra, and payogābhisaṅkhāra—they are the formations occurring by the term 'saṅkhāra'.
128:
Among those (four types of formations), all conditioned things mentioned in the scriptures such as "All formations are indeed impermanent" are called 'conditioned formations' (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra). The mental and physical phenomena in the three realms produced by kamma are called 'formed formations' (abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra) in the Commentaries. These formed formations are also included in the phrase "All formations are indeed impermanent." However, their specific occurrence elsewhere is not found. The wholesome and unwholesome volitions occurring in the three realms are called 'formative formations' (abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra). The occurrence of these formative formations is evident in such scriptures as: "Monks, if this person who is possessed of ignorance performs a meritorious formation..." Physical and mental effort is called 'effort-based formation' (payogābhisaṅkhāra). This effort-based formation appears in such scriptures as: "As far as the momentum of the effort goes, it proceeds that far and then stands still like a wheel struck by an axle."

Not only these four types of formations, but there are also many other formations mentioned by the term saṅkhāra, such as: "Friend Visākha, for a monk entering the cessation of perception and feeling, first the verbal formation (vaci-saṅkhāra) ceases, then the bodily formation (kāya-saṅkhāra), and then the mental formation (citta-saṅkhāra)." Among these formations, there is no formation that is not included within 'conditioned formations' (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra). From here on, in the phrases such as "With formations as condition, consciousness arises," what has been said should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

Regarding the terms not yet explained: It is called 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) because it cognizes. It is called 'mentality' (nāma) because it bends towards an object. It is called 'materiality' (rūpa) because it is deformed. It is called 'base' (āyatana) because it extends (mental factors) and because it leads to the long suffering of the round of rebirths. It is called 'contact' (phassa) because it touches. It is called 'feeling' (vedanā) because it feels. It is called 'craving' (taṇhā) because it thirsts all around. It is called 'clinging' (upādāna) because it grasps. It is called 'existence' (bhava) because it comes to be (through kamma) and because it causes (rebirth) to be. Birth is 'jāti'. Aging is 'jarā'. It is called 'death' (maraṇa) because one dies by this (nature). Sorrow is 'soka'. Lamentation is 'parideva'. It is called 'suffering' (dukkha) because it causes pain, or because it destroys in two ways through the power of arising and staying. Being in a bad mental state is 'displeasure' (domanassa). Intense exhaustion is 'despair' (upāyāsa).

'Sambhavanti' means 'they arise.' The word 'sambhavanti' should be connected not only with terms like sorrow (soka) but with all the preceding terms. Otherwise, when it is said "With ignorance as condition, formations," it would not be clear what those formations do. When the word 'sambhavanti' is connected, the definition of cause and effect is established as: "Ignorance is the condition; therefore, with ignorance as condition, formations arise." This method applies to all instances.
129:
The word "evam" (thus) indicates the method already pointed out. By this word, it is shown that (effects like formations) arise only due to causes such as ignorance, and not due to the creation of a Lord (God) or other such causes. "Etassa" (of this) refers to the aforementioned (mass of suffering). "Kevalassa" (whole) means unmixed or entire. "Dukkhakkhandhassa" (of the mass of suffering) means the cause of the mass of suffering, not of a being, nor of happiness or beauty. "Samudayo" means arising. "Hoti" means it clearly comes into being. Thus, the decision regarding the meaning here should be understood.

"Lakkhaṇādito" means (the decision should be understood) by way of the characteristics and so forth of ignorance and the other factors. To wit: Ignorance has the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of non-knowing (aññāṇa), the function (rasa) of deluding (sammohana), manifests (paccupaṭṭhāna) as concealing (chādana), and has the taints (āsava) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Formations have the characteristic of forming (abhisaṅkharaṇa), the function of striving (āyūhana), manifest as volition (cetanā), and have ignorance as their proximate cause. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing (vijānana), the function of preceding (pubbaṅgama), manifests as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and has formations as its proximate cause, or else has the base and object as its proximate cause. Mentality has the characteristic of bending (namana), the function of association (sampayoga), manifests as inseparability (avinibbhoga), and has consciousness as its proximate cause. Materiality has the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana), the function of dispersing (vikiraṇa), manifests as indeterminate (abyākata), and has consciousness as its proximate cause. The sixfold base (saḷāyatana) has the characteristic of extending (āyatana), the function of seeing and so forth, manifests as the state of base and door, and has mentality-materiality as its proximate cause. Contact has the characteristic of touching (phusana), the function of impacting (saṅghaṭṭana), manifests as meeting (sangati), and has the sixfold base as its proximate cause. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing (anubhavana), the function of enjoying the flavor of the object (visayarasasambhoga), manifests as pleasure and pain, and has contact as its proximate cause. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause (hetu), the function of delighting (abhinandana), manifests as insatiability (atittibhāva), and has feeling as its proximate cause. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping (gahaṇa), the function of not releasing (amuñcana), manifests as the intensification of craving or as wrong view, and has craving as its proximate cause. Existence has the characteristic of kamma and its fruit (kammakamma-phala), the function of causing to be and being (bhāvana-bhavana), manifests as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and has clinging as its proximate cause. The characteristics and so forth of birth and the rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the Saccavibhaṅga. Thus, the decision here should also be understood by way of characteristics and so forth.

In the phrase "Ekavidhādito," ignorance is one-fold (ekavidha) by way of its nature as non-knowing, non-seeing, delusion, etc. It is two-fold by way of non-practice (appaṭipatti) and wrong practice (micchāpaṭipatti). Likewise, it is two-fold by way of being with-formation (sasaṅkhāra) and without-formation (asaṅkhāra). It is three-fold by way of association with the three feelings. It is four-fold by way of non-penetration of the Four Truths. It is five-fold by way of concealing the danger of the five destinations (gati). By way of doors and objects, it should be understood that there are six varieties in all mental phenomena.

Formations are one-fold by way of being with taints, being of the nature of resultant dhammas, and so forth. They are two-fold by way of being wholesome and unwholesome. Likewise, they are three-fold by way of being limited (paritta), sublime (mahaggata), or inferior, medium, and superior; or by way of being of certain wrongness (micchattaniyata) or uncertain (aniyata). They are three-fold by way of being meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth. They are four-fold by way of leading to the four modes of birth (yoni). They are five-fold by way of leading to the five destinations (gati).
130:
Consciousness is of one kind by way of being mundane resultant consciousness and so forth; of two kinds by way of being with roots and rootless and so forth; of three kinds by way of being included in the three planes of existence, by way of association with the three feelings, and by way of being rootless, two-rooted, and three-rooted; and of four or five kinds by way of the modes of birth (yoni) and destinations (gati).

Name-and-form is of one kind by way of having consciousness as its support and having kamma as its condition; of two kinds by way of having an object (sārammaṇa) and not having an object (anārammaṇa); of three kinds by way of the periods of time such as the past; and of four or five kinds by way of the modes of birth and destinations.

The six sense bases are of one kind by way of being the place of arising and meeting; of two kinds by way of being the sensitive matter dependent on the great elements and consciousness and so forth; of three kinds by way of having spheres of activity (gocara) that are reached, not reached, and neither; and of four or five kinds by way of being included in the modes of birth and destinations. In this manner, the classification into one kind and so forth should also be understood for contact and the rest. Thus, in this [Summary Section], the decision should be understood by way of the classification into one kind and so forth.

In the [matrix clause] "And the definition of the factors," sorrow and so forth are mentioned for the purpose of showing the uninterrupted nature of the wheel of existence. For these [sorrow etc.] occur to the fool who is oppressed by aging and death. As it was said: "Monks, an uninstructed worldling, when touched by a painful bodily feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into utter confusion." As long as these [sorrow etc.] continue to occur, ignorance also continues to occur. Therefore, once again, "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and thus the wheel of existence is continuously connected. Therefore, those [sorrow etc.] should also be understood as being summarized together with aging and death, so that there are only twelve factors of dependent origination. Thus, in this [Summary Section], the decision should be understood by way of the definition of the factors. This is the brief explanation by way of the Summary Section (Uddesavāra) in this [Vibhaṅga on Dependent Origination].

## The Explanation of the Summary Section is finished.

## Exposition of the Term Ignorance

Now follows the detailed explanation by way of the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra). It was said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]." There, when the volitional formations that have ignorance as their condition are to be shown—just as when a son is to be spoken of, the father is spoken of first—this being so...
131:
When one says "Mitta's son, Datta's son," the son is well-described. Therefore, the Teacher, skilled in teaching, in order to first show ignorance, which is like a father because it generates volitional formations, said: "What is that ignorance? It is non-knowledge (aññāṇa) regarding suffering," and so forth.

In that text, because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the true nature, essence, and characteristics of the truth of suffering, but remains covering, shrouding, and binding, it is called "non-knowledge regarding suffering." Likewise, because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the true nature, essence, and characteristics of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (the truth of the path), but remains covering, shrouding, and binding, it is called "non-knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." In these four bases, non-knowledge is called ignorance according to the Suttanta method.

In the Nikkhepakaṇḍa, however, by the Abhidhamma method, non-knowledge is also taken in four other bases, such as "non-knowledge regarding the past." There, "the past" (pubbanta) means the past time, the past aggregates, elements, and bases. "The future" (aparanta) means the future time, the future aggregates, elements, and bases. "The past and the future" (pubbantāparanta) means both of them. "Specific conditionality" (idappaccayatā) means the factors such as ignorance which are the causes of volitional formations and so forth. "Dependently arisen phenomena" (paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma) means the phenomena such as volitional formations that are produced by ignorance and so forth. There, because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the true nature, essence, and characteristics of the past aggregates and so forth, but remains covering, shrouding, and binding, it is called "non-knowledge regarding the past." Likewise, because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the true nature, essence, and characteristics of the future aggregates and so forth, the past and future aggregates and so forth, and specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena, but remains covering, shrouding, and binding, it is called "non-knowledge regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena." In these eight bases, non-knowledge is called ignorance according to the Abhidhamma method.

In this way, what is meant to be taught? Ignorance is said to be taught by way of its function and by way of its place of arising (jāti). How? Because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate these eight bases, it is taught by way of its function; and because when it arises, it arises in these eight bases, it is also taught by way of its place of arising. Having taught thus, once again...
132:
The twenty-five terms beginning with "such non-knowing (aññāṇa), non-seeing (adassana)" are taken to demonstrate the characteristic of ignorance (avijjā).

In that [Summary Section (Nikkhepakaṇḍa)], although this ignorance is spoken of by these eight terms, it is not yet considered 'well-explained' as long as its characteristic has not been stated by the twenty-five terms; it is only when the characteristic is stated that it is considered 'well-explained.' For example, a man searching for a lost ox might ask people, "Sirs, have you seen a white ox, or have you seen a red ox?" Those people might say, "In this country, there is no end to white and red oxen; what is the mark (lakkhaṇa) of your ox?" Then, only when that owner of the ox says, "It has horns that meet (saṅghāṭi)" or "It has horns like a plow (naṅgala)" is the ox considered 'well-described.' In the same way, although this ignorance is spoken of by eight terms, it is not yet considered 'well-explained' as long as its characteristic has not been stated by the twenty-five terms; it is only when the characteristic is stated that it is considered 'well-explained.' Therefore, for the purpose of showing the characteristic of that ignorance, the twenty-five terms are spoken; and ignorance should be understood by means of those terms.

What are those twenty-five terms? — Knowledge (ñāṇa) is indeed wisdom (paññā). That wisdom makes the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which is the cause of various benefits, known and manifest. However, when this ignorance arises, it does not allow those truths to be known or manifest; thus, it is called 'non-knowing' (aññāṇa), the opposite of knowledge. 'Seeing' (dassana) is also wisdom. That wisdom also sees that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow that aspect to be seen; thus, it is called 'non-seeing' (adassana). 'Realization' (abhisamaya) is also wisdom. That wisdom realizes that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow that aspect to be realized; thus, it is called 'non-realization' (anabhisamaya). 'Understanding' (anubodha), 'full enlightenment' (sambodha), and 'penetration' (paṭivedha) are also wisdom. That wisdom understands accordingly, understands rightly, and penetrates that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow that aspect to be understood accordingly, understood rightly, or penetrated; thus, it is called 'non-understanding' (ananubodha), 'non-enlightenment' (asambodha), and 'non-penetration' (appaṭivedha). 'Grasping' (saṅgāhanā) is also wisdom. That wisdom, having entered that aspect, grasps it by rubbing against it. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow one to enter, rub against, and grasp that aspect; thus, it is called 'non-grasping' (asaṅgāhanā). 'Plunging into' (pariyogāhanā) is also wisdom. That wisdom plunges into that aspect and enters it sequentially to grasp it. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow one to plunge in and enter sequentially to grasp that aspect; thus, it is called 'non-plunging' (apariyogāhanā). 'Equable inspection' (samapekkhanā) is also wisdom. That wisdom looks at that aspect evenly and rightly. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow one to look at that aspect evenly and rightly; thus, it is called 'non-equable inspection' (asamapekkhanā). 'Reviewing' (paccavekkhaṇā) is also wisdom. That wisdom reviews that aspect. But when ignorance arises, it does not allow one to review that aspect; thus, it is called 'non-reviewing' (apaccavekkhaṇā).
133:
For this ignorance, there is no action that is perceived; and because it is an action performed without self-investigation or reflection, it is called 'unperceived action' (apaccakkhakamma). Because of the state of being unwise, it is called 'foolishness' (dummejjha). Because of the state of being unskilled, it is called 'stupidity' (bālya).

That which knows well and in various ways is wisdom. That wisdom called clear comprehension (sampajañña) rightly understands benefit and non-benefit, cause and non-cause, and the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. However, when ignorance arises, it does not allow one to understand those aspects such as cause and effect in various ways; thus it is called 'lack of clear comprehension' (asampajañña). By way of deluding, it is 'delusion' (moha). By way of intense deluding, it is 'great delusion' (pamoha). By way of complete deluding, it is 'thorough delusion' (sammoha). By way of the meaning such as obtaining what should not be obtained, like bodily misconduct, it is called 'ignorance' (avijjā). Because it delights in the round of suffering and causes one to sink into it, it is called the 'flood of ignorance' (avijjogha). Because it yokes one to the round, it is the 'yoke of ignorance' (avijjāyoga). Because it has not been abandoned by the Path and arises again and again, it is the 'latent tendency of ignorance' (avijjānusaya). Just as rebels rising up on a road plunder travelers, it plunders, seizes, and loots the wholesome mind; thus it is the 'obsession of ignorance' (avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna). Just as when the door-bolt (called laṅgī) at a city gate has fallen, the exit of people inside the city and the entry of people outside the city are cut off; even so, when this ignorance falls upon the city of the five aggregates of a person, the movement of knowledge that leads to Nibbāna is cut off. Thus it is called the 'bolt of ignorance' (avijjālaṅgī). Because it is both unwholesome and a root, or because it is the root of unwholesome states, it is called 'unwholesome root' (akusalamūla). That unwholesome root is no other than the delusion intended here; thus delusion is the unwholesome root. Such a state with these characteristics is called 'ignorance'. In this way, the characteristics of ignorance should be understood by way of these twenty-five terms.

Although this ignorance with such characteristics is called 'non-knowledge' (aññāṇa) regarding suffering and so on, it is a part of the Truth of Suffering, it arises together with it, takes it as an object, and conceals it. It is not a part of the Truth of the Origin, but it arises together with it, takes it as an object, and conceals it. It is neither a part of the Truth of Cessation nor does it arise together with it; it does not take it as an object but merely conceals it. It is also not a part of the Truth of the Path nor does it arise together with it; it does not take it as an object but merely conceals it. Ignorance arises with the Truth of Suffering as its object and conceals it. Ignorance arises with the Truth of the Origin as its object and conceals it. Ignorance does not arise with the Truth of Cessation as its object, yet it conceals it. Ignorance does not arise with the Truth of the Path as its object, yet it conceals it.

The two truths, the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin, are profound because they are difficult to see. The two truths, the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, are difficult to see because they are profound. Furthermore, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is both profound and difficult to see. Among those truths, suffering is evident, but it is called profound because its characteristic is difficult to see. The same applies to the Truth of the Origin. Just as extracting the essence by churning the great ocean is a heavy task,
134:
just as extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru is a heavy task, and just as squeezing a mountain to extract its juice is a heavy task, even so, the two truths (Cessation and Path) are difficult to see precisely because they are profound. The Truth of Cessation, however, is extremely profound and extremely difficult to see. Because they are thus difficult to see and profound, this darkness of delusion which conceals the four Noble Truths is called ignorance (avijjā).

## Exposition of the Term Ignorance (Avijjāpadaniddesa)

## Exposition of the Term Formations (Saṅkhārapadaniddesa)

In the term 'formations' (saṅkhāra), without considering the formations mentioned below under the general term 'formations', but wishing to show only the formations conditioned by ignorance, it is said: "Among those, what are the formations conditioned by ignorance? They are meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so on." Therein, it is called 'merit' (puñña) because it purifies the person who performs it, because it fulfills that person's aspiration, and because it brings about a worshipful happy state of existence (sugati).
