It is called 'volitional formation' (abhisaṅkhāra) because it constructs the resultant (vipāka) and the matter produced by kamma (kammaja-rūpa). Since merit itself is a volitional formation, it is called 'meritorious volitional formation' (puññābhisaṅkhāra). It is called 'non-merit' (apuñña) because it is the opposite of merit. Since non-merit itself is a volitional formation, it is called 'non-meritorious volitional formation' (apuññābhisaṅkhāra). It is called 'imperturbable' (āneñja) because it does not shake. Since the imperturbable itself is a volitional formation, and because it constructs an imperturbable state of existence, it is called 'imperturbable volitional formation' (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). It is called 'bodily formation' (kāyasaṅkhāra) because it is set in motion by the body, or it proceeds from the body, or it is a formation of the body. The same method applies to verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra) and mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra).

Among those two groups, the first triad is taken by way of the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta. Indeed, in that Sutta it is said: "If he constructs a meritorious formation, consciousness reaches merit. If he constructs a non-meritorious formation, consciousness reaches non-merit. If he constructs an imperturbable formation, consciousness reaches the imperturbable." The second triad is taken by way of the Vibhaṅga Sutta which immediately follows that Sutta; it can also be said to be taken by way of the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta. Indeed, in that Sutta it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three formations. Which three? Bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation." Why are they taken by way of those Suttas? This so-called Abhidhamma was not recently made, nor was it made by outside ascetics or disciples...
135:
This Abhidhamma Dhamma was not taught by devas or Brahmās, nor by hermits outside the dispensation, nor by disciples. Indeed, this Abhidhamma Dhamma was taught only by the Omniscient Buddha. In the Abhidhamma Pāḷi as well as in the Sutta Pāḷi, the same identical Pāḷi has been pointed out; it is for the purpose of explaining this meaning (that it should be understood thus).

Now, in order to show those formations (saṅkhāra) by way of classification, He said the passage beginning with: "Among those, what is meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra)?" In that passage, by the term "wholesome volition" (kusala cetanā), without specific restriction, volition occurring in the four planes is also taught. However, because it is restricted by the terms "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) and "fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacara), the thirteen volitions—namely, eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions and five fine-material sphere wholesome volitions—are called meritorious formations. By the terms "consisting in giving" (dāna-maya) and so on, the occurrence of those very volitions by way of the bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) is shown. Among those, only the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions are "consisting in giving" and "consisting in virtue" (sīla-maya). But "consisting in mental development" (bhāvanā-maya) applies to all thirteen. Just as a person reciting a well-mastered Dhamma does not even notice passing one or two connections, but knows it later when reflecting; similarly, for one performing the preliminary work for a kasiṇa, reflecting on a well-mastered jhāna, or attending to a well-mastered meditation subject, mental development dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta) also occurs. Therefore, it is said: "But consisting in mental development applies to all thirteen."

Among those "consisting in giving" and so on: "The volition, the act of willing, the state of having willed, which arises on account of giving, concerning giving—this is called meritorious formation consisting in giving. On account of virtue... On account of mental development, concerning mental development, the volition, the act of willing, the state of having willed, which arises—this is called meritorious formation consisting in mental development." This is the brief teaching.

Regarding the four requisites such as robes, or the six objects such as visible forms, or the ten objects of giving such as food; for one who gives those various things, the volition occurring in the three times—namely, in the preliminary stage starting from the production (collection) of those requisites before giving, at the time of giving, and in the time of reflecting with a joyful mind after giving—is called "consisting in giving". For the sake of fulfilling virtue, the volition occurring in the continuity of one who goes to the monastery thinking "I will ordain", one who is ordaining, one who has reached the peak of his desire and reflects "I have indeed become a monk, how good, how excellent!", one who restrains himself by the Pātimokkha, one who reflects on the requisites such as robes, one who restrains the eye-door and so on regarding visible forms and so on that have come into range, and one who purifies his livelihood—this is called "consisting in virtue". By the sequence of insight (vipassanā) taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, for one who develops insight into the eye-sensitivity...
136:
...into visible forms and so on up to mental objects, eye-consciousness and so on up to mind-consciousness, eye-contact and so on up to mind-contact, feeling born of eye-contact and so on up to feeling born of mind-contact, perception of forms and so on up to perception of mental objects, and aging and death, as impermanent (anicca), as suffering (dukkha), and as non-self (anatta)—the volition arising in the continuity of such a person is called "consisting in mental development". This is the detailed explanation.

In the description of demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra-niddesa), "unwholesome volition" refers to the volition associated with the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. Regarding the term "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara): although among those twelve unwholesome volitions, the remaining volitions—excluding the two associated with displeasure (domanassa)—can also arise in the fine-material and immaterial planes of existence, they cannot lead to rebirth in those planes. Since they cause results by way of rebirth only in the sense-sphere plane, they are called only "sense-sphere".

In the description of imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra-niddesa), "immaterial-sphere wholesome volition" refers to the four immaterial-sphere wholesome volitions. These four volitions are called "imperturbable formations" because they are imperturbable (aniñjana) in nature and because they form (prepare) an imperturbable result. In fact, starting from the fine-material sphere fourth jhāna, the three volitions (wholesome, resultant, functional) and the twelve immaterial-sphere volitions—thus fifteen states—are called "imperturbable" (āneñja) because they are motionless (aniccala) and unshakable (aphandana). Among those, although the fine-material sphere wholesome volition is imperturbable, it is not called "imperturbable formation" because it produces fine-material or immaterial existence that is either similar or dissimilar to itself, and either with motion or without motion. Resultant and functional volitions, being without fruit, do not "form" a result; likewise, the immaterial-sphere resultant and functional volitions do not "form" a result. Therefore, those eleven volitions are called only "imperturbable" and not "formations". But the four immaterial-sphere wholesome volitions are called "imperturbable formations" because, just as the shadow of elephants, horses, etc., is similar to them, they produce only an imperturbable immaterial result similar to themselves.

Thus, there are 13 by way of meritorious formations, 12 by way of demeritorious formations, and 4 by way of imperturbable formations; all these together make 29 volitions. In this way, the Blessed One, as if weighing with a great scale or measuring by putting into a measuring cup the wholesome and unwholesome volitions arising in the continuities of infinite beings in infinite universes, delimited them with His Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and showed only these 29 volitions.
137:
Now, in order to show the three doors of action (kammadvāra) through which countless beings in countless world-systems strive when accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, [the Blessed One] said: "Among those formations, what is bodily formation? It is bodily volition (kāyasañcetanā)," and so forth. In this context, bodily volition refers to the twenty volitions—namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions (kāmāvacarakusala cetanā) and the twelve unwholesome volitions (akusala cetanā)—which arise from the bodily door by originating bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). The twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions that arise while causing grasping, taking, and moving at the bodily door can also be called bodily formations.

Verbal volition (vacīsañcetanā) refers to those same twenty volitions which arise from the verbal door by originating verbal intimation (vacīviññatti). The twenty volitions that arise while causing the movement of the jaw and the breaking into speech at the verbal door can also be called verbal formations. Here, however, the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññācetanā) is not taken because it does not serve as a condition for [resultant] consciousness in the future. Just like the volition of direct knowledge, the volition of restlessness (uddhaccacetanā) also does not serve as a condition for consciousness. Therefore, that volition of restlessness should also be excluded from being a condition for consciousness. However, all of these arise due to ignorance (avijjā).

Mental volition (manosañcetanā) refers to all twenty-nine volitions that arise at the mind door without originating either of the two intimations. Thus, the Blessed One showed the doors of action by stating that countless beings in countless world-systems strive through these three doors when accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

The mutual association of these two triads should also be understood. How? Meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) can be bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) for one who abstains from bodily misconduct, and it can be verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra) for one who abstains from verbal misconduct. Thus, the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions are meritorious formations, and they are also bodily formations and verbal formations. However, the thirteen volitions arising at the mind door are both meritorious formations and mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra). Non-meritorious formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) can be bodily formation when occurring by way of bodily misconduct, verbal formation when occurring by way of verbal misconduct, and mental formation when occurring at the mind door, bypassing the two [physical] doors. Thus, non-meritorious formation is bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.

Bodily formation can be meritorious formation or non-meritorious formation, but it cannot be imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). Verbal formation is the same. Mental formation, however, can be...
138:
...can be meritorious formation, non-meritorious formation, or imperturbable formation. These are called formations conditioned by ignorance (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā).

How is it to be known that these formations are conditioned by ignorance? It is known because they exist when ignorance exists. For someone in whom the non-knowledge (aññāṇa) called ignorance regarding the truth of suffering and so forth has not been abandoned, that person—due to non-knowledge regarding the truth of suffering and the past, etc.—perceives the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) as happiness, clings to it, and undertakes the three types of formations which are the causes of that suffering. Due to non-knowledge regarding the truth of the origin (samudayasacca), they perceive formations that are the requisites of craving—which are the causes of suffering—as causes of happiness and undertake them. Regarding the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca) and the truth of the path (maggasacca), due to non-knowledge, they perceive specific destinations (gati) that are not the cessation of suffering as the cessation of suffering; and they perceive sacrifices (yañña), austerities for immortality (amaratapa), and so forth, which are not the path to cessation, as the path to cessation. Desiring the cessation of suffering, they undertake the three types of formations, starting with sacrifices and austerities for immortality.

Furthermore, because of that unabandoned ignorance regarding the four truths, they do not know suffering—namely, the result of merit which is interspersed with many faults such as birth, aging, sickness, and death—as suffering. To attain that result, they undertake meritorious formations consisting of bodily, verbal, and mental formations, like a man desiring a celestial nymph leaps from a mountain peak. Not seeing that the result of merit, though called happiness, causes great fever at its end, is the suffering of change (vipariṇāmadukkha), and provides little gratification, they undertake the aforementioned meritorious formations—the cause of that suffering—like a moth rushing into a flame, or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking a honey-smeared sword blade.

Not seeing the danger in the indulgence of sensual pleasures and so forth along with their results, they undertake non-meritorious formations occurring through the three doors, due to the perception of happiness and being overwhelmed by defilements, like a fool playing with excrement, or like one wishing to die eating poison. Regarding the results of the formless sphere, not penetrating the fact that they are the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkha) and the suffering of change, and with the perverted perception of permanence and so forth, they undertake imperturbable formations—which are mental formations—like a person who has lost their way heading toward a city of demons (pisāca).

Thus, since formations exist only when ignorance exists and do not exist when ignorance is absent, it should be known that these formations are conditioned by ignorance. This has also been stated by the Blessed One: "Monks, an ignorant person, one who has fallen into ignorance, accumulates meritorious formations, accumulates non-meritorious formations, and accumulates imperturbable formations."
139:
“Monks, when ignorance has been abandoned by a monk and true knowledge has arisen, that monk, due to the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, no longer constructs, performs, or exerts meritorious volitional formations.”

Here, an objector says: “First, let us accept this point that ‘ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.’ However, it should still be stated: ‘For which volitional formations and in what way is it a condition?’” In response to that problem, this is said:

(Ignorance) is a condition for meritorious (volitional formations) in two ways.
For others (demeritorious), it is a condition in many ways.
For the latter (imperturbable), it is known to be a condition in only one way.

In that verse, ‘for meritorious in two ways’ means it is a condition in two ways: by way of object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Indeed, when one contemplates that ignorance as ceasing and vanishing, it is a condition for meritorious volitional formations of the sense sphere by way of object condition. When one knows a mind associated with delusion through the mind of supernormal knowledge, it is a condition for meritorious volitional formations of the fine-material sphere (by way of object condition). For one who fulfills the meritorious bases of the sense sphere such as giving for the sake of overcoming ignorance, and for one who produces fine-material sphere jhānas, it is a condition for both those types of meritorious volitional formations by way of decisive support condition. Likewise, for one who, being deluded by ignorance, desires the attainments of the sense-sphere existence and fine-material sphere existence and performs those very merits, it is also (a condition by way of decisive support condition).

‘For others (demeritorious) in many ways’ means it is a condition for demeritorious volitional formations in many ways. How? When unwholesome states such as lust arise taking this ignorance as an object, it is a condition by way of object condition; when one enjoys it by giving it importance, it is a condition by way of object-predominance and object-decisive support. For one who, being deluded by ignorance and not seeing the danger, commits acts such as killing living beings, it is a condition by way of decisive support condition. For the second impulsion (javana) and so on, it is a condition by way of proximity, contiguity, proximity-decisive support, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions. For one who performs any unwholesome act, it is a condition by way of root, conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Thus, it is a condition in many ways.

‘For the latter (imperturbable), it is known to be a condition in only one way’ means it is known to be a condition for imperturbable volitional formations only by way of the single decisive support condition. The nature of that ignorance as a decisive support condition should be understood in the same manner as stated for meritorious volitional formations.

Here, an objector says: “Is this ignorance alone the cause of volitional formations, or are there other causes as well?” What of it? If it were only one, the theory of a single cause would follow. If there are other causes for volitional formations besides ignorance, then the indication of a single cause as “volitional formations because of ignorance” would no longer be appropriate, would it? It is not inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. Why?
140:
In this world, a single effect does not arise from a single cause,
Nor do many effects; nor from many causes does a single effect arise.
However, there is a specific purpose in demonstrating a single cause and a single effect together.

In truth, in this world, there is no single effect that arises from only a single cause, nor are there many effects from a single cause. Nor does a single effect arise from many causes. Rather, only many effects arise from many causes. That statement is very true. It is observed that from many causes known as climate, earth, seed, and water, many effects arise known as a sprout endowed with color, smell, taste, and so on. Nevertheless, in the teaching where a single cause and a single effect are shown in pairs, such as “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness,” there is a specific purpose and benefit.

For the Blessed One, in some places, shows only one cause or one effect because of its predominance, in some because of its obviousness, in some because of its uniqueness (not being shared with other states), and because of the elegance of the teaching and its suitability to the inclinations of the beings to be taught (veneyya). He taught only one cause and one effect as in “With contact as condition, feeling.” Indeed, contact is the predominant cause of feeling, because feeling is determined respectively according to contact. Feeling is also the predominant effect of contact, because contact is determined respectively according to feeling.

He taught only one obvious cause as in “Diseases arising from phlegm.” Here, phlegm is the obvious cause, while causes such as kamma are not obvious. He taught only one unique cause as in “Monks, whatever unwholesome states there are, all those are rooted in unwise attention.” Indeed, unwise attention is a unique cause only for unwholesome states, whereas the physical base and object are causes that are also shared with wholesome and indeterminate states.

Therefore, in this teaching of Dependent Origination, although other causes of volitional formations such as the physical base, object, and conascent states exist, ignorance is shown as the cause of volitional formations because of its predominance—being the root cause of other causes of volitional formations such as craving, according to the words “For one who frequently contemplates gratification, craving increases” and “With the arising of taints, ignorance arises”—and because of its obviousness and uniqueness, according to the teaching “Monks, an ignorant person, having arrived at ignorance, constructs even meritorious volitional formations.” By this explanation regarding the demonstration of a single cause and a single effect in pairs, the purpose of demonstrating a single cause and a single effect in all places should be understood.
141:
Here it is asked: Even if this is so, how can ignorance (avijjā), which is definitely of undesirable fruit and is blameworthy, be a condition for meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra)? For sugarcane does not grow from a neem seed. 

How can it not be fitting? For in the world:

Both contrary and non-contrary,
Likewise similar and dissimilar,
A condition for states is established,
And those are not merely resultants (vipāka).

In the world, both contrary and non-contrary conditions for states—by way of location (ṭhāna), nature (sabhāva), function (kicca), and so on—are established. For the preceding mind is a contrary condition for the succeeding mind by way of location. Prior training in arts and sciences is a condition for the subsequent performance of those arts and sciences. Kamma is a contrary condition for matter (rūpa) by way of nature, and milk, etc., are conditions for curd, etc. Light is a contrary condition for eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) by way of function, and molasses, etc., are conditions for liquor (āsava), etc. However, the eye-sensitivity and visible objects, etc., are non-contrary conditions for eye-consciousness, etc., by way of location. Preceding javanas, etc., are non-contrary conditions for succeeding javanas, etc., both by way of nature and function.

Just as contrary and non-contrary conditions are established, so too are similar and dissimilar ones. For matter known as temperature (utu) and nutriment (āhāra) is a condition for matter similar to itself. Rice seeds, etc., are conditions for rice fruit, etc. Even though dissimilar, matter is a condition for mentality (nāma), and mentality is a condition for matter. Cow hair, goat hair, horns, curd, and sesame powder, etc., are conditions for the growth of dabba grass, bhūti grass, and so on. For whatever states there are contrary, non-contrary, similar, and dissimilar conditions, those states are not merely the resultants (vipāka) of those conditions. Thus, although this ignorance is blameworthy by way of being a resultant and by way of its nature of having definitely undesirable fruit, it should be understood as a condition for all these formations—meritorious formations and so on—as appropriate, by way of contrary and non-contrary conditions in terms of location, function, and nature, and by way of similar and dissimilar conditions.

And its state as a condition has been stated in this manner: "For one in whom the non-knowledge known as ignorance regarding suffering and so on has not been abandoned, that person, through non-knowledge regarding suffering and regarding the past and so on, takes the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) as happiness and undertakes the three types of formations which are the cause of that suffering."

Furthermore, this is another method:

In death and rebirth, in the round of rebirths,
And in the characteristic of formations,
He who is deluded regarding states
That have arisen dependently;

Since he performs these
Three types of formations,
Therefore, ignorance is the condition
For those three types as well.
142:
If it is asked: "How does one who is deluded in these (death, rebirth, etc.) perform these three types of formations?" Firstly, one who is deluded regarding death (cuti), not grasping death in all states of existence as "the breaking up of the aggregates is death," speculates in various ways such as "a being dies" or "the migration of a being to another place." One who is deluded regarding rebirth (upapāta), not grasping rebirth in all states of existence as "the manifestation of the aggregates is birth (jāti)," speculates in various ways such as "a being is reborn" or "the manifestation of a new body for a being."

One who is deluded regarding the round of rebirths (saṃsāra)—
"The succession of aggregates,
Of elements and bases,
Proceeding without interruption,
Is called the round of rebirths."

Not grasping the round of rebirths thus described, he speculates in various ways such as "this being goes from this world to another world" or "he comes from another world to this world." One who is deluded regarding the characteristic of formations, not grasping the individual characteristic (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) and the general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) of formations, speculates on formations as self, as belonging to self, as permanent, as beautiful, and as pleasant.

One who is deluded regarding states that have arisen dependently (paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma), not grasping the occurrence of formations, etc., due to conditions such as ignorance, etc., speculates in various ways such as: "The self knows or does not know; that self itself acts and causes to act; that self is reborn in a new conception; for that self, persons such as atoms or a creator (Issara) establish the body in the form of the embryonic stage (kalala), etc., and complete the sense bases; that self, being endowed with sense bases, touches, feels, craves, clings, and exerts; that self again exists in another life"; or "All beings are transformed by the nature of destiny and association."

He, being thus blinded by ignorance and speculating in this way, just as a blind man wandering on the earth might follow a right path, a wrong path, high ground, low ground, even ground, or uneven ground; even so, he performs and undertakes meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations. Therefore, this is said:

Just as a man blind from birth,
Who has no guide,
Sometimes travels by the right path,
And sometimes by the wrong path.

So the fool wandering in the round of rebirths,
Likewise having no guide,
Sometimes performs merit,
And sometimes even demerit.
143:
When that being knows the Dhamma and penetrates the truths, then, through the cessation of ignorance, he will wander at peace.

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations."

## The Explanation of the Term 'With Ignorance as Condition, Volitional Formations' is Finished.

## Explanation of the Term 'Consciousness'

In the explanation of the term "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness," among eye-consciousness and so forth, eye-consciousness is of two kinds: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant. Likewise, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness are each of two kinds. Mind-consciousness, however, has twenty-two varieties: 2 mind-elements which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants, 3 rootless mind-consciousness elements, 8 sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses with roots, 5 fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses, and 4 immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses. Thus, by these six types of consciousness, all thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness are included. Supramundane resultants, however, are not included because they do not apply to a discourse concerning the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa).

Regarding the inclusion of these resultant consciousnesses, an objection might arise: "How should it be known that this consciousness of the aforementioned varieties arises because of the condition of volitional formations?" (It should be known) because in the absence of accumulated kamma, there is no resultant. For this consciousness is a resultant, and a resultant does not arise in the absence of accumulated kamma. If it were to arise (without kamma), then all resultants would arise for all beings; but in fact, they do not. Therefore, it should be known: "This consciousness arises because of volitional formations."

If it is asked: "Which consciousness arises because of which volitional formation?" Firstly, because of meritorious volitional formations of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra), there are sixteen: the five wholesome resultants such as eye-consciousness and so forth; within mind-consciousness, 1 mind-element, 2 mind-consciousness elements, and 8 sense-sphere great resultants. As it is said: "Due to the performance and accumulation of wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, a resultant eye-consciousness arises. Likewise, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness arise; a resultant mind-element arises; a mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy arises; a mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity arises; a mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge arises;
144:
(Due to the condition of meritorious volitional formations of the sense sphere) a consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and prompted (sasaṅkhārika); a consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge; a consciousness accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted; a consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge; a consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and prompted; a consciousness accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge; a consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted (these sixteen resultant consciousnesses arise).

Because of meritorious volitional formations of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra), five fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses arise. As it is said: "Due to the performance and accumulation of that same fine-material sphere wholesome kamma, being a resultant, quite secluded from sense pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna... the fifth jhāna."

Thus, because of meritorious volitional formations, there are twenty-one varieties of consciousness.

Because of demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), there are seven varieties of consciousness: the five unwholesome resultants such as eye-consciousness and so forth, 1 mind-element, and 1 mind-consciousness element. As it is said: "Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, a resultant eye-consciousness arises. Likewise, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, a resultant mind-element, and a resultant mind-consciousness element arise."

Because of imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), there are four varieties of consciousness, namely the four immaterial resultants. As it is said: "Due to the performance and accumulation of that same immaterial sphere wholesome kamma, being a resultant, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of material form... accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space... accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness... accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness... accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, through the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna."

Thus, having understood the consciousness that arises because of volitional formations, its occurrence should now be understood. All this consciousness occurs in two ways: by way of the course of existence (pavatti) and by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
145:
Among those consciousnesses, these thirteen—the ten-fold sense-consciousness (dve-pañcavijñāṇa), the two mind-elements (manodhātu), and the one rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata ahetuka-manovijñāṇadhātu)—occur only during the course of existence (pavatti) in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). The remaining nineteen consciousnesses occur as appropriate in the three planes of existence, both during the course of existence and at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

How is this so? Firstly, the five wholesome resultant consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and so on, arise in a person whose faculties (indriya) have matured in due order, whether due to wholesome or unwholesome resultant. They occur by performing the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, based on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and so on, in relation to desirable (iṭṭha) or neutral-desirable (iṭṭhamajjhatta) objects like visible forms and so on, which have come into the range of the eye and other senses. Similarly, the five unwholesome resultant consciousnesses also occur. The only distinction is that for these unwholesome resultants, the objects such as visible forms and so on are undesirable (aniṭṭha) or neutral-undesirable (aniṭṭhamajjhatta). These ten consciousnesses have fixed doors, objects, bases, and locations, and they also have fixed functions.

Immediately after those wholesome resultant consciousnesses like eye-consciousness and so on, the wholesome resultant mind-element (manodhātu) occurs, performing the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana-kicca), based on the heart-base (hadayavatthu) and taking the very same object as those sense-consciousnesses. Similarly, after the unwholesome resultants, the unwholesome resultant mind-element occurs. These two types of consciousness have unfixed doors and objects, but they have fixed bases, locations, and functions.

The rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, however, occurs immediately after the wholesome resultant mind-element, performing the function of investigating (santīraṇa-kicca), based on the heart-base and taking the very same object as that mind-element. Furthermore, in the six doors, when there is a strong object, it occurs once or twice by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) on the object grasped by the javana, usually at the end of javanas associated with greed (lobha-sampayutta-javana) in sense-sphere beings, after cutting the flow of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). In the counting of the occurrence of consciousness, only two turns of consciousness appear at the time of registration in all doors. This consciousness receives two names: 'registration' (tadārammaṇa) and 'posterior life-continuum' (piṭṭhibhavaṅga). It has unfixed doors and objects, a fixed base, and unfixed locations and functions. Thus, it should be understood that these thirteen consciousnesses occur only during the course of existence in the five-constituent existence. Among the remaining nineteen consciousnesses, there is not even one that does not occur as a rebirth-linking consciousness appropriate to itself.

During the course of existence, the two rootless mind-consciousness-elements, which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants, [occur] in the five doors immediately after the wholesome and unwholesome resultant mind-elements...
146:
...performing the function of investigating (santīraṇa-kicca) [immediately after the wholesome and unwholesome resultant mind-elements]; performing the function of registration (tadārammaṇa-kicca) in the six doors according to the method previously mentioned; performing the function of life-continuum (bhavaṅga-kicca) when there is no thought-arising (cittuppāda) that cuts the life-continuum above the rebirth-linking given by itself; and performing the function of death (cuti-kicca) at the end of life. Thus, they occur performing these four functions, having a fixed heart-base (hadayavatthu) and unfixed doors, objects, locations, and functions.

The eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses with roots (sahetuka-kāmāvacara-vipākacitta) also occur during the course of existence, performing three functions: the function of registration in the six doors according to the method already mentioned, the function of life-continuum when there is no life-continuum-cutting consciousness above the rebirth-linking given by themselves, and the function of death at the end. They have a fixed base and unfixed doors, objects, locations, and functions.

The five fine-material sphere resultants (rūpāvacara-vipāka) and the four immaterial sphere resultants (arūpāvacara-vipāka) occur performing two functions: the function of life-continuum when there is no life-continuum-cutting consciousness above the rebirth-linking given by themselves, and the function of death at the end. Among these, the fine-material sphere resultants have fixed bases and objects, but unfixed locations and functions. The other immaterial sphere resultants occur without a physical base, having fixed objects and unfixed locations and functions. In this way, the thirty-two types of consciousness occur during the course of existence due to formations (saṅkhāra). In that occurrence, those various formations serve as conditions by way of kamma-condition (kamma-paccaya) and decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

Among those thirty-two types of consciousness, of the eleven registration consciousnesses (tadārammaṇa) mentioned, not even one occurs as registration in the fine-material or immaterial planes. Why? Because of the absence of the seed (bīja). Indeed, the rebirth-linking seed known as sense-sphere resultant, which could produce that registration during the course of existence in relation to objects such as visible forms and so on, does not exist in those fine-material and immaterial planes. If it is asked, 'If registration does not occur because of the absence of the rebirth-linking seed, would it not also follow that eye-consciousness and so on do not occur in the fine-material plane?' The answer is: No, they occur due to the power of the occurrence of the faculties (indriya) and due to the fixed law of consciousness (citta-niyāma) in the various thought-processes (vīthi).

Just as this registration definitely does not occur in the fine-material and immaterial planes, so too it does not follow after non-sense-sphere (akāmāvacara) states. Why? Because those states cannot produce it, and because they are dissimilar to that which produces it. For example, just as a young child who wishes to leave the house and go outside follows his own father who produced him, or another relative who is like his father and desires his welfare, by holding his finger, but does not follow others such as king's men; similarly, when this registration wishes to go outside from the object of the life-continuum, because of similarity, it follows only the sense-sphere javana which is like its father and produces it, but it does not follow other sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara) javanas.
147:
Just as this registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) does not follow after sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) states, likewise, when these sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states arise having sublime objects, it does not follow after them at that time either. Why? Because it is an unfamiliar territory and because it has exclusively limited (paritta) objects. Indeed, just as a young child, even when following his father or a relative like his father, follows only in familiar places such as the house door, the alley, or the crossroads, but does not follow one going to the forest or the battlefield; in the same way, the tadārammaṇa following sense-sphere states follows only those states occurring in familiar objects like the non-sublime, but does not follow those states occurring with sublime or supramundane objects.

Since it has been stated regarding that tadārammaṇa that "all sense-sphere resultants (kāmāvacara-vipāka), the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu), and the rootless functional mind-consciousness-element (ahetuka-kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) accompanied by joy—these states have limited objects," thus having exclusively limited objects, it should be understood that this tadārammaṇa does not follow even sense-sphere states that have sublime or supramundane objects.

Or else, what is the use of this logical argument? For it is stated definitively in the Commentary: The eleven tadārammaṇa consciousnesses do not take the role of tadārammaṇa when the javana has run with reference to a name or lineage (nāmagotta). When the javana has run with reference to a concept (paññatti), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. In insight (vipassanā) taking the three characteristics as objects, tadārammaṇa is not obtained. In powerful insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. When the javana has run with reference to fine-material or immaterial states, tadārammaṇa is not obtained. In states of fixed wrongness (micchattaniyata), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. In states of fixed rightness (sammattaniyata), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. When the javana has run with reference to supramundane states, tadārammaṇa is not obtained. When the javana has run with reference to direct-knowledge (abhiññā), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. When the javana has run with reference to the knowledge of analytical insight (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), tadārammaṇa is not obtained. In the case of a weak object in the sense-sphere, tadārammaṇa is not obtained; it is obtained only when a powerful object has come into focus (āpāthagata) at the six doors, and even when obtained, it is obtained only with a sense-sphere object. In the fine-material and immaterial realms, there is no such thing as tadārammaṇa.

The statement I made, "Among the remaining nineteen consciousnesses, there is none that does not occur as a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) appropriate to itself," is difficult to understand because it is too brief. Therefore, to show the detailed method of that statement, it is said: "How many rebirth-linkings are there? How many rebirth-linking consciousnesses? By what consciousness and where does rebirth-linking occur? What is the object of rebirth-linking?"
148:
Including the material rebirth-linking in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), there are twenty rebirth-linkings. There are nineteen rebirth-linking consciousnesses of the types already mentioned. Among those nineteen rebirth-linking consciousnesses, rebirth-linking in the planes of misery (apāya) occurs by the rootless mind-consciousness-element which is an unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu [investigating consciousness]). Rebirth-linking of those born blind, deaf, insane, mute (with a dribbling mouth), or as eunuchs/neuters, etc., in the human world occurs by the rootless mind-consciousness-element which is a wholesome resultant. Rebirth-linking of meritorious persons among the sense-sphere devas and humans occurs by the eight great resultants with roots (sahetuka-mahā-vipāka). Rebirth-linking in the fine-material Brahma realms occurs by the five fine-material-sphere resultants (rūpāvacara-vipāka), and in the immaterial realms by the four immaterial-sphere resultants (arūpāvacara-vipāka). Whichever consciousness causes rebirth-linking in whichever realm, that rebirth-linking is called the "appropriate rebirth-linking" for that consciousness.

Briefly, there are three objects of rebirth-linking: kamma, kamma-nimitta (sign of kamma), and gati-nimitta (sign of destination). Among these three objects, kamma refers to the wholesome or unwholesome volitions (cetanā) that have been performed. The object which was taken as the basis for performing the kamma is called kamma-nimitta. Among these, even if the kamma was performed over a hundred thousand times ten million aeons ago, at the moment of death, either the kamma or the kamma-nimitta appears as if it were coming to the mind.

In the appearance of the kamma-nimitta, this story is an illustration: A man named Gopaka Sīvali built a stupa at the Tālapiṭṭhika Monastery. While he was lying on his deathbed, that stupa appeared to him. Taking that very sign (nimitta), he passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm. There is also another kind of death called "death with great confusion" (sammūḷha-kālakiriyā). For someone walking away, they cut off his head from behind with a sharp sword. For someone lying down and sleeping, they also cut off his head with a sharp sword. They kill by drowning in water. Even at such times, some kamma or kamma-nimitta tends to appear. There is also another kind called "sudden death" (lahuka-maraṇa). A small fly resting on the head of a chisel is struck and crushed with a mallet. Even at such a time, kamma or kamma-nimitta tends to appear.

For a fly being crushed in this way, first, the body-door adverting (kāyadvārāvajjana) cannot turn the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); only the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) can turn the life-continuum. Then, after the javana has run, it descends into the life-continuum. In the second turn, the body-door adverting (five-door adverting) turns the life-continuum. Then the cognitive series consciousnesses—body-consciousness, receiving, investigating, and determining (votthabbana)—arise. After the javana has run, it descends into the life-continuum. In the third turn, the mind-door adverting turns the life-continuum. Then, after the javana has run, it descends into the life-continuum. At the point where this third cognitive series falls into the life-continuum, death occurs. For what purpose is this explanation brought forward? It is to illustrate that the objects of mental states appear thus rapidly. Gati-nimitta refers to a certain vision that appears of the place where one is to be reborn. Among those places of future rebirth, if it appears in hell, it is said to be like a great iron cauldron...
149:
The sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) is the appearance of a certain color or image representing the place where one is to be reborn. If that sign of destiny is for rebirth in hell, it appears like a large iron cauldron. If it is for rebirth in the human world, it appears like a woolen garment in the mother's womb. If it is for rebirth in the celestial world, wish-fulfilling trees, celestial mansions, beds, and so on appear. Thus, in brief, there are three objects of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi): kamma, the sign of action (kamma-nimitta), and the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta).

In another way, the objects of rebirth-linking are threefold: a past object, a present object, and a conceptual object (paññatti) which cannot be described as past or present. Rebirth-linking in the non-percipient realm (asaññasatta) has no object. Among those rebirth-linkings, the objects of the rebirth-linking of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) are exclusively past. The objects of the ten sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) rebirth-linkings are either past or present. The objects of the remaining rebirth-linkings are conceptual objects which cannot be described as past or present. Thus, rebirth-linking occurring with these three types of objects arises only immediately after a death-consciousness (cuti-citta) that has either a past object or a conceptual object. There is no death-consciousness that has a present object. Therefore, one should understand the manner in which rebirth-linking, having one of the three types of objects, occurs by way of happy destinations (sugati) or woeful destinations (duggati) immediately after a death-consciousness that has one of the two types of objects.

For example: First, for a person who, while staying in a happy sense-sphere destination, has performed evil deeds, in accordance with the words, "At that time, those [deeds] hang down [before him]," etc., while lying on the deathbed, the evil kamma he has accumulated or the sign of action (kamma-nimitta) appears before the mind-door (manodvāra). Immediately after the impulsion process (javana-vīthi)—which arises taking that object and ends with registration (tadārammaṇa) or is a pure impulsion process without registration—the death-consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). When that death-consciousness ceases, the rebirth-linking consciousness belonging to a woeful destination arises, inclined by the power of unabandoned defilements (kilesa), taking that very kamma or sign of action that had appeared. This is a rebirth-linking with a past object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

For another person, at the time of death, due to the power of the aforementioned kamma, a sign of a woeful destination (duggati-nimitta) such as the color of flames in hell and so on appears before the mind-door. After the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice for that person, taking that object, one adverting (āvajjana), five impulsions (javana)—which are slow in momentum due to the proximity of death—and two registrations (tadārammaṇa) arise, making three types of process-consciousnesses. Thereafter, taking the object of the life-continuum...
150:
...one death-consciousness occurs. By this much, eleven thought-moments (cittakkhana) have passed. Thereafter, while that same object still has a life-span of five remaining thought-moments, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises. This is a rebirth-linking with a present object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

For another being, at the time of death, a lowly object which is a cause for lust (rāga) and so on appears at one of the five sense-doors. For that being, at the end of the determining consciousness (votthabbana) that arises in due order, five impulsions and two registrations arise, having slowed down in momentum due to the proximity of death. Thereafter, one death-consciousness occurs taking the object of the life-continuum. By this much, fifteen thought-moments have passed: two life-continuums, adverting, seeing (eye-consciousness), receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), determining (votthabbana), five impulsions, two registrations, and one death-consciousness. Thereafter, while that same object still has a life-span of one remaining thought-moment, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises. This rebirth-linking is also a rebirth-linking with a present object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object. This is the manner of the occurrence of a woeful rebirth-linking with a past or present object immediately after a happy death-consciousness with a past object.

For a being staying in a woeful destination who has accumulated unblamable (wholesome) kamma, in the same manner as described, that unblamable kamma or its sign of action appears at the mind-door. Thus, by substituting the dark side (unwholesome) with the bright side (wholesome), everything should be understood as in the previous method. This is the manner of the occurrence of a happy rebirth-linking with a past or present object immediately after a woeful death-consciousness with a past object.

For a person staying in a happy destination who has accumulated unblamable kamma, in accordance with the teaching, "Those [deeds] hang down before that person at that time," etc., while lying on the deathbed, the unblamable kamma he has accumulated or its sign of action appears at the mind-door. And that appearance occurs only for a person who has accumulated wholesome sense-sphere kamma. For a person who has accumulated sublime (mahaggata) kamma, however, only the sign of action (kamma-nimitta) appears. Immediately after the impulsion process—which arises taking that object and ends with registration or is a pure impulsion process without registration—the death-consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum. After that death-consciousness has ceased, the rebirth-linking consciousness belonging to a happy destination arises, inclined by the power of unabandoned defilements, taking that very kamma or sign of action that had appeared. This is a rebirth-linking with either a past object or a conceptual object (which cannot be called past or present) occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.
151:
At the time of death of another being, due to the power of sense-sphere wholesome kamma, a sign of a happy destination (sugati-nimitta)—consisting of the appearance of a mother's womb in the human world, or the appearance of gardens, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth in the celestial world—appears at the mind-door. Just as in the sequence shown for the sign of a woeful destination, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) arises immediately after the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). This is rebirth-linking with a present object following death-consciousness with a past object.

At the time of death of another person, relatives say, "Dear, we are performing this Buddha-pūjā for your sake; clarify your mind," and they present at the five doors: a visible object such as flower garlands, banners, or streamers; or an audible object such as listening to the Dhamma or musical offerings; or an olfactory object such as incense or fragrance; or a gustatory object such as honey or molasses, saying, "Dear, taste this; it is a gift to be given for your sake"; or a tangible object such as cloth from China or Sāmāra, saying, "Dear, touch this; it is a gift to be given for your sake." When those objects like visible forms come into range, at the end of the determining (votthapana) that arises in sequence, because of the proximity of death, the momentum is slow, so five impulsions (javanas) and two registration (tadārammaṇa) consciousnesses arise. Thereafter, taking the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its object, one death-consciousness arises. At the end of that death-consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises with that very object which lasts for only one thought-moment. This too is rebirth-linking with a present object following death-consciousness with a past object.

For another who has attained sublime states such as the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and dwells in a happy destination, at the time of death, one of the signs—kamma, kamma-nimitta, or gati-nimitta of sense-sphere wholesome kamma—such as the earth-kasiṇa sign or the sublime consciousness itself, appears at the mind-door. Or, a refined object that is the cause for the arising of wholesomeness appears at one of the doors, such as the eye or ear. At the end of the determining that arises in sequence, because of the proximity of death, the momentum is slow, so five impulsions arise. For those with a sublime destination, there is no registration (tadārammaṇa). Therefore, immediately after the impulsions, taking the object of the life-continuum as its object, one death-consciousness arises. At the end of that death-consciousness, a rebirth-linking consciousness arises, which is included in one of the happy destinations—either sense-sphere or sublime—and has one of the objects that have appeared. This is rebirth-linking with an object that is past, present, or cannot-be-said (concept/paññatti), following a happy-destination death-consciousness with a concept object.

In this same manner, rebirth-linking following death from the formless (arūppa) realm should also be understood. This is the way the rebirth-linking consciousness with a past, concept, or present object occurs following a happy-destination death-consciousness with a past or concept object.
152:
For an evil-doer dwelling in a woeful destination, in the same manner as described, that kamma, kamma-nimitta, or gati-nimitta appears at the mind-door. At the five doors, an object that is the cause for the arising of unwholesomeness comes into view. Then, at the end of the death-consciousness in sequence, a rebirth-linking consciousness arises, which is included in a woeful destination and has one of those objects. This is the way rebirth-linking with a past or present object occurs following a woeful-destination death-consciousness with a past object. By this much, the occurrence of the nineteen types of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking has been explained.

All that consciousness is thus:
When occurring at rebirth-linking, it proceeds in two ways due to kamma;
By way of divisions such as 'mixed' and so on, the twofold and other divisions of that resultant consciousness should be understood.

When these nineteen types of resultant consciousness occur at rebirth-linking, they proceed in two ways due to kamma. This is because the respective productive (janaka) kamma of this consciousness is a condition by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) and strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). For it was said: "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for the resultant by way of strong dependence condition." The twofold and other divisions of that resultant consciousness occurring in this way, by way of divisions such as 'mixed' and so on, should also be understood. Namely: although this consciousness is single by way of rebirth-linking, it is twofold by way of being mixed or unmixed with matter (rūpa); threefold by way of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial planes of existence; fourfold by way of the modes of birth: egg-born (aṇḍaja), womb-born (jalābuja), moisture-born (saṃsedaja), and spontaneous (opapātika); fivefold by way of destination (gati); sevenfold by way of stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti); and eightfold by way of abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Among those divisions:

The mixed [with matter] is twofold by the division of sex (bhāva);
Therein, the 'with-sex' (sabhāva) is also twofold.
Together with the initial mixed [consciousness],
at minimum, two or three decads (dasaka) arise.

"Mixed is twofold by the division of sex" means that here, excluding the immaterial existence, when rebirth-linking consciousness mixed with matter arises, it is twofold: "with-sex" (sabhāva) and "without-sex" (abhāva). This is because in the fine-material existence, it arises without the sex-materiality (bhāva-rūpa) called the feminine faculty (itthindriya) and masculine faculty (purisindriya), while in the sense-sphere existence, it arises with sex-materiality, excluding the rebirth-linking of those born as eunuchs (jāti-paṇḍaka).

"Therein, the with-sex is also twofold" means that among those two types, with-sex and without-sex, the rebirth-linking consciousness that occurs with sex-materiality is twofold because it arises with either the feminine sex or the masculine sex.
153:
In this verse, 'Dve vā tayo vā dasakā, omato ādinā saha,' among the two types—mixed (missa) with matter and unmixed (amissa) without matter—there is the initial rebirth-consciousness mixed with matter. Along with that rebirth-consciousness, at the minimum, two decads arise by way of the base decad (vatthu-dasaka) and body decad (kāya-dasaka), or three decads arise by way of the base decad, body decad, and sex decad (bhāva-dasaka). There is no reduction of matter less than these two or three.

This matter, arising in such minimum measure, in the two modes of birth called egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja), takes the name 'kalala' (embryonic stage), being the size of a drop of clear oil or ghee taken up by a single hair of a newborn lamb. In the context of that rebirth-consciousness mixed with matter, the variety of its arising should be understood by way of the five destinations (gati). Indeed, among these destinations:

Niraye bhummavajjesu, devesu ca na yoniyo,
Tisso purimikā honti, catassopi gatittaye.
(In hell and among the devas, excluding the earth-bound deities (bhumma), the first three modes of birth do not exist. In the remaining three destinations, all four modes of birth exist.)

In that verse, by the word 'ca' in 'devesu ca,' it should be understood that just as the first three modes of birth do not exist in hell and among the devas excluding the earth-bound ones, they also do not exist among the hungry ghosts consumed by thirst (nijjhāmatanhika-peta). They are only of spontaneous birth (opapātika). In the remaining three destinations—namely, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the human realm—as well as among the previously excluded earth-bound deities, all four modes of birth exist.

Among those beings:
Tiṃsa nava ceva rūpīsu, sattati ukkaṃsato rūpāni,
Saṃsedajopapātīsu, atha vā avakaṃsato tiṃsa.
(In the fine-material brahma realms, 39 material phenomena arise. In moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, at the maximum, 70 material phenomena arise; or at the minimum, 30 material phenomena arise.)

Firstly, in the fine-material brahma realms (rūpa-brahmā) who have spontaneous birth, 39 material phenomena arise along with the rebirth-consciousness by way of four groups (kalāpa): the eye decad (cakkhu-dasaka), the ear decad (sota-dasaka), the base decad (vatthu-dasaka), and the life nonad (jīvita-navaka). Excluding the fine-material brahma realms, in other moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, at the maximum, 70 material phenomena arise by way of the decads of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, sex, and base. These 70 material phenomena always occur among the devas.

Among those decads, this collection of matter consisting of ten material phenomena—namely, color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, the four great elements, eye-sensitivity, and life-faculty—is called the eye decad (cakkhu-dasaka). The remaining decads should be understood in the same way. At the minimum, in the continuity of those who are born blind, deaf, without a nose, or as eunuchs (napuṃsaka) from birth, 30 material phenomena arise by way of the tongue decad (jivhā-dasaka), body decad (kāya-dasaka), and base decad (vatthu-dasaka). Between the maximum and minimum, the variation should be understood as appropriate.

Having understood this, again:
Khandhārammaṇagatīhetu-vedanāpītivitakkavicārehi,
Bhedābhedaviseso, cutisandhīnaṃ pariññeyyo.
(The distinction of difference or non-difference between death and rebirth should be fully understood by way of aggregates, objects, destinations, roots, feelings, zest, initial application, and sustained application.)
154:
This means that the distinction of difference or non-difference by way of aggregates and so on should be known between the two types of rebirth—mixed and unmixed—and the death-consciousness (cuti) that immediately preceded it in the past.

How? Sometimes, immediately after an immaterial death-consciousness (arūpa-cuti) with four aggregates, there is a rebirth-consciousness that also has four aggregates and is non-different even in terms of object. Sometimes, after a death-consciousness with a non-exalted external object, there is a rebirth-consciousness with an exalted internal object. This is the method within the immaterial planes themselves. Sometimes, however, immediately after an immaterial death-consciousness with four aggregates, there is a sense-sphere rebirth-consciousness (kāmāvacara-paṭisandhi) with five aggregates. Sometimes, immediately after a sense-sphere death-consciousness or a fine-material-sphere death-consciousness (rūpāvacara-cuti) with five aggregates, there is an immaterial rebirth-consciousness with four aggregates. In this way, after a death-consciousness with a past object, there is a rebirth-consciousness with a past, ineffable (concept), or present object. After some death-consciousness in a happy destination, there is some rebirth-consciousness in an unhappy destination. After a rootless death-consciousness, there is a rooted rebirth-consciousness; after a two-rooted death-consciousness, a three-rooted rebirth-consciousness; after a death-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, a rebirth-consciousness accompanied by joy; after a death-consciousness without zest, a rebirth-consciousness with zest; after a death-consciousness without initial application, a rebirth-consciousness with initial application; after a death-consciousness without sustained application, a rebirth-consciousness with sustained application; after a death-consciousness without both initial and sustained application, a rebirth-consciousness with both initial and sustained application. Thus, by the reverse of each method, whatever is applicable should be applied.

Having obtained its conditions, this mere phenomenon of mind and matter reaches another existence;
There is no migration from that [previous life], nor does it occur without a cause from that.

Thus, it is said that this mere phenomenon of mind and matter, having obtained its conditions and arising, reaches another existence; it is not a 'being' (satta), nor a 'soul' (jīva). There is no migration of it from the past existence to this one, nor is there a manifestation in this life without causes such as kamma from that past existence. We shall explain this meaning through the clear sequence of human death and rebirth:

In the past existence, for one who is near death either by natural causes or by effort, unable to endure the onset of the weapons of death-terminating feelings that cut the joints and ligaments of all limbs and organs, as the body gradually withers like a green palm leaf cast in the sun, and when the faculties such as the eye have ceased (become weak), while the body-faculty, mind-faculty, and life-faculty remain established in the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) alone, at that moment, the consciousness dependent on the remaining heart-base proceeds by taking as its object either kamma—known as formations (saṅkhāra) having obtained the remaining conditions from among weighty (garuka), habitual (āciṇṇa), proximate (āsanna), or stored (kaṭattā) kamma—or the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or sign of destination (gati-nimitta) manifested by that kamma. For that consciousness proceeding in this way, because craving and ignorance have not been abandoned, craving [arises] for that object whose faults are concealed by ignorance...
155:
Craving inclines [the consciousness], and the co-nascent volitional formations propel it. That [consciousness], being inclined by craving through the force of continuity and propelled by volitional formations, abandons its previous support and—like a man crossing a ditch by clinging to a rope tied to a tree on this bank—proceeds by means of conditions such as objects, whether enjoying or not enjoying the new support produced by kamma.

In this context, the preceding mind is called 'death' (cuti) because of falling away, and the succeeding mind is called 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) because it connects to the beginning of a new existence. It should be understood that this consciousness neither comes here from the previous life, nor does it appear without causes such as kamma, volitional formations, the inclining [craving], and objects from that previous life.

In this matter, echoes and so forth serve as illustrations. Because of the connection of the continuity, there is neither identity nor absolute difference. In the arising of this rebirth-linking consciousness due to causes included in the past life without migrating from the previous life, things such as echoes, lamps, seals, and reflections are illustrations. Just as echoes, lamps, seals, and shadows arise due to causes like the original sound without moving to another place, so too does this mind arise.

Regarding the statement 'Because of the connection of the continuity, there is neither identity nor absolute difference': if there were absolute identity in the connection of the continuity, curd would not be produced from milk. If there were absolute difference, curd would not arise dependent on milk. This is the method in all things produced by causes. If it were otherwise, all worldly conventions would be destroyed. Such destruction is not desired. Therefore, in this matter, one should not conclude with absolute identity or absolute difference.

Here, an objector says: "If there is no migration but only appearance [of consciousness], then since the aggregates in this human existence have ceased and the kamma which is the cause of the fruit does not go to that new life, would the fruit not belong to one person while the kamma was done by another? And if there is no enjoyer, for whom would that fruit be? Therefore, this explanation is not good."

To that objection, this is said:

The fruit that arises in a single continuity belongs neither to another nor [comes] from another. The cultivation of seeds is the proof of this meaning.

When a fruit arises in a single continuity, because absolute identity and difference are refuted, it is not said to belong to another or to come from another. The cultivation of seeds is the proof of this meaning. When the cultivation of mango seeds and so forth is performed, the specific fruit that arises in the continuity of that seed after a long time, having obtained conditions, does not belong to other seeds, nor does it arise due to other cultivations. And those seeds, and those cultivations...
156:
...those seeds or those cultivations do not reach the place where the fruit is. Thus, this unerring illustration should be understood. This meaning should also be understood through the example of arts, crafts, medicine, and so forth, which, when applied to a young body, give results in the grown body and so forth at a later time.

Regarding the statement, "If there is no enjoyer, for whom would that fruit be?":

By the very arising of the fruit, the convention of an 'enjoyer' is established; just as by the production of fruit, the convention that a tree 'bears fruit' is established.

Indeed, just as when a fruit, which is a part of the phenomena called a 'tree', arises, it is said that 'the tree bears fruit' or 'the tree has fruited', so too, when the result of pleasure or pain, called 'enjoyment' and being a part of the aggregates called 'deva' or 'human', arises, it is said that 'the deva or human enjoys' or 'is happy' or 'is suffering'. Therefore, in this matter, there is no need for a person called an 'enjoyer' apart from the arising of the fruit.

If someone should say: "Even so, do these volitional formations act as causes for the fruit while they exist, or while they do not exist? If they act as causes while existing, they must give their result at the very moment of their occurrence. If they act as causes while not existing, they would always bring results both before and after their occurrence."

To such a person, it should be said:

These volitional formations are causes because they have been done, but they do not always bring results. The illustration of a guarantor and so forth should be understood in this matter.

Indeed, volitional formations become causes for their own fruit simply because they have been done, not because of their existence or non-existence. As it is said: "Because of having done and accumulated wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness arises" (Dhs. 431). Having become the cause for their own appropriate fruit, they do not bring results again because the result has already ripened. To clarify this meaning, the illustration of a guarantor and so forth should be understood.

In the world, when someone becomes a guarantor to repay something for another's benefit, or buys goods, or takes a debt, the mere performance of that action is the cause for the repayment of that benefit. It is not the existence or non-existence of the action [at the time of repayment]. Even after the repayment of that benefit...
157:
(Just as a guarantor who has repaid the debt) is no longer the one performing the action. Why? Because the handing over (repayment) and so forth have been completed. Because they have been completed in this way, the formations (saṅkhāras) also act as conditions for their own results, but they do not continue to bring about results after having given results as appropriate. By this much of the discourse, the occurrence of rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhivijñāna) arising by way of the condition of formations, which occurs in two ways as mixed and unmixed, has been shown.

Now, in order to dispel confusion regarding all these thirty-two types of consciousness—

By way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence, in the realms and so forth,
these formations should be understood, as to how and for which [resultants] they are conditions.

In that verse, the three realms (bhava), the four modes of birth (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) are called 'realms and so forth'. The meaning is that it should be understood how these formations act as conditions for which resultant consciousnesses (vipākavijñāna) during the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence (pavatti) in those realms and so forth.

Among those formations, first, regarding meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra): the meritorious volitional formation consisting of eight types of sense-sphere volitions (kāmāvacara cetanā) acts as a condition in two ways—by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaya) and strong dependence condition (upanissayapaccaya)—for the nine resultant consciousnesses at the time of rebirth-linking in the happy destinations of the sense-sphere (kāma-sugati), without distinction. The meritorious volitional formation consisting of five types of fine-material sphere wholesome volitions (rūpāvacara kusala cetanā) acts as a condition only for the five resultant consciousnesses at the time of rebirth-linking in the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava). However, the aforementioned sense-sphere meritorious volitional formation of eight types acts as a condition in the two ways mentioned for the seven types of limited resultant consciousnesses (parittavipākavijñāna), excluding the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity, during the course of existence in the happy destinations of the sense-sphere; it does not act as a condition at the time of rebirth-linking. That same sense-sphere meritorious volitional formation acts as a condition in the same way for the five resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material realm during the course of existence; it does not act as a condition at the time of rebirth-linking. In the unhappy destinations of the sense-sphere, however, it acts as a condition in the same way for the eight types of limited resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence; it does not act as a condition at the time of rebirth-linking.

In those unhappy destinations, such as in hell, when the Elder Mahāmoggallāna traveled to hell and encountered desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa), that meritorious volitional formation acts as the condition. Among animals, also, desirable objects are indeed obtained by Nāgas, Garuḍas, and Petas of great power. That same sense-sphere meritorious volitional formation acts as a condition in the same way for the sixteen types of wholesome resultant consciousnesses in the happy destinations of the sense-sphere, both during the course of existence and at the time of rebirth-linking. Without distinction, the meritorious volitional formation acts as a condition in the same way for the ten resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material realm, both during the course of existence and at the time of rebirth-linking.

Demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) consisting of twelve types of unwholesome volitions act as a condition in the same way for one consciousness at the time of rebirth-linking in the unhappy destinations of the sense-sphere, but not during the course of existence; they act as a condition for six consciousnesses during the course of existence, but not at the time of rebirth-linking; and for all seven unwholesome resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence and...
158:
...also at the time of rebirth-linking. In the happy destinations of the sense-sphere, however, it acts as a condition in the same way for those same seven (unwholesome resultants) during the course of existence, but not at the time of rebirth-linking. In the fine-material realm, it acts as a condition in the same way for four resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence, but not at the time of rebirth-linking. Such conditioning occurs by way of seeing undesirable forms and hearing undesirable sounds in the sense-sphere. In the Brahma world, however, there are no such things as undesirable forms and so forth; likewise, they do not exist in the sense-sphere celestial realms.

Imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) act as a condition in the same way for the four resultant consciousnesses in the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava), both during the course of existence and at the time of rebirth-linking.

By way of the all-inclusive method of sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome volitions, bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra), which consists of twenty types of volitions, acts as a condition in two ways—by way of asynchronous kamma condition and strong dependence condition—for the ten resultant consciousnesses at the time of rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere. That same bodily formation acts as a condition in the same way for thirteen resultant consciousnesses in the sense-sphere and nine resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material realm during the course of existence, but not at the time of rebirth-linking. That same bodily formation acts as a condition in the same way for twenty-three resultant consciousnesses in the sense-sphere, both during the course of existence and at the time of rebirth-linking. The same method applies to verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra).

Mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra), which consists of twenty-eight or twenty-nine types of volitions, acts as a condition in the same way for nineteen resultant consciousnesses in the three realms at the time of rebirth-linking, but not during the course of existence. That same mental formation acts as a condition in the same way for the twenty-two resultant consciousnesses mentioned above (thirteen and nine) in the two realms during the course of existence, but not at the time of rebirth-linking. In the three realms, however, it acts as a condition in the same way for all thirty-two resultant consciousnesses, both during the course of existence and at the time of rebirth-linking. Thus, first, it should be understood how those formations act as conditions for which resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence in the realms. In this same way, they should be understood in the modes of birth and so forth.

Herein, the brief explanation from the beginning is as follows: Among these formations, first, the meritorious volitional formation gives rebirth-linking in two realms and produces all its own results. Likewise, it produces results in the four modes of birth such as the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and so forth; in the two destinations called devas and humans; and in the four stations of consciousness called 'beings with diversity of body and diversity of perception', 'beings with diversity of body and unity of perception', 'beings with unity of body and diversity of perception', and 'beings with unity of body and unity of perception', by way of humans and the planes of the first, second, and third jhānas. In the abode of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), however, this meritorious volitional formation produces only materiality; therefore, it gives rebirth-linking and produces all its own results in only four abodes of beings. Therefore,
159:
