This meritorious volitional formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) is a condition, in the manner already stated, for the 21 (or 23) types of resultant consciousness (vipākaviññāṇa) at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and during the course of existence (pavatti), as appropriate, in the two states of existence—namely, the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and the fine-material existence (rūpabhava)—the four modes of birth (yoni), the two destinations (gati), the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the four abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The demeritorious volitional formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), however, because it yields results through rebirth-linking in only one state of existence, the sense-sphere existence; in the four modes of birth; in the three remaining destinations (excluding the human and celestial destinations); in the one station of consciousness known as 'diversity of body and unity of perception' (nānattakāya-ekattasaññī); and in one such abode of beings—therefore, this demeritorious volitional formation is a condition, in the manner already stated, for the 7 types of resultant consciousness at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence in one state of existence, four modes of birth, three destinations, one station of consciousness, and one abode of beings.

The imperturbable volitional formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), because it yields results through rebirth-linking in one immaterial existence (arūpabhava), one mode of birth (spontaneous birth), one destination (celestial), the three stations of consciousness beginning with the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), and the four abodes of beings beginning with the sphere of infinite space—therefore, this imperturbable volitional formation is a condition, in the manner already stated, for the 4 types of resultant consciousness at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence in only one state of existence, one mode of birth, one destination, three stations of consciousness, and four abodes of beings.

The bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) also, because it gives rebirth-linking in one sense-sphere existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, two stations of consciousness, and two abodes of beings, produces all its own results. Therefore, this bodily formation is a condition, in the same manner, for the 23 types of resultant consciousness at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence in one state of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, two stations of consciousness, and two abodes of beings. The same method applies to the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra).

The mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra), however, because it does not fail to yield results anywhere except in one abode of beings (the non-percipient beings)—therefore, this mental formation is a condition, in the same manner, for the 32 types of resultant consciousness, as applicable, at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence in the three states of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and eight abodes of beings. However, in the abode of beings without consciousness (non-percipient beings), there is no consciousness conditioned by formations.

Even though there is no consciousness there, meritorious volitional formation is a condition for kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa) in the realm of non-percipient beings by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaya). Thus—
160:
Thus, it should be understood how and for which [resultant consciousnesses] these formations are conditions in the states of existence and so forth, by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.

## Explanation of the Clause: Consciousness Conditioned by Formations

## Explanation of the Clause: Name and Form

In the explanation of name and form conditioned by consciousness, the decision should be understood by way of: diversity of teaching (desanābheda), occurrence in all states of existence and so forth, inclusion (saṅgaha), and the method of conditioning.

'By way of diversity of teaching' means: 'Therein, what is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.' In this way, because the term 'form' (rūpa) is not differentiated, the teaching is identical in both the Suttanta and here in the Abhidhamma. However, there is a difference in the term 'name' (nāma).

In the Suttanta, it is said: 'Therein, what is name? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention.' Here in the Abhidhamma, however, it is said: 'The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate.' In that Suttanta, the mental phenomena that arise due to eye-consciousness, the mental phenomena that are the cause for the duration of the arisen mind, and the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of immaterial states are only evident when taught in dependence on other states. Therefore, wishing to show those mental phenomena, the formations aggregate was divided into three—volition, contact, and attention—and taught together with the [other] two aggregates. But here in the Abhidhamma, wishing to include all name-states, both those mentioned and those not mentioned in the Suttanta, it is said: 'The three aggregates—the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate.'

If it is asked, 'Are only these three aggregates name? Is consciousness not called name?' The answer is: It is not that it is not [name]. However, if that consciousness were included in 'name and form,' there would be the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses: the resultant consciousness included in 'name' and the conditioning consciousness. Therefore, placing consciousness in the position of the condition, only the three aggregates are mentioned to show the 'name' that is produced by the condition of consciousness. Thus, the decision should be understood 'by way of diversity of teaching.'

In the phrase 'by way of occurrence in all states of existence and so forth,' 'name' occurs in all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and the remaining abodes of beings, excluding the one abode of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta).
161:
Matter occurs in the two types of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the first four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the five abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). While mind and matter are thus occurring, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) and egg-born (aṇḍaja) beings who lack the sex-decad (bhāva-rūpa), two starting points of material continuity—namely, the base-decad (vatthu-dasaka) and the body-decad (kāya-dasaka)—and the three mental aggregates appear. Therefore, for these beings, in detail, these 23 states—20 material phenomena and 3 mental aggregates—should be understood as 'mind-and-matter with consciousness as condition.' However, by the method of taking what was not taken (or excluding what was taken), if 9 material phenomena are removed from one material group, there are 14; for those with the sex-decad, by adding the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), there are 33; and then, by removing 18 material phenomena from the two material continuities, there are 15.

This is because, among spontaneously born beings (opapātika), at the moment of rebirth-linking for Brahmas such as those of the Brahmakāyika realm, four starting points of material continuity—namely, the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka), the ear-decad (sota-dasaka), the base-decad, and the life-nonad (jīvitindriya-navaka)—and the three mental aggregates appear. Therefore, for these Brahmas, in detail, these 42 states—39 material phenomena and 3 mental aggregates—should be understood as 'mind-and-matter with consciousness as condition.' By the agahitaggahaṇa method, if 27 material phenomena are removed from the three material continuities, there are 15.

In the sensual existence (kāmabhava), however, at the moment of rebirth-linking for the remaining spontaneously born beings or moisture-born (saṃsedaja) beings whose sense bases (āyatana) are complete, seven starting points of material continuity and the three mental aggregates appear. Therefore, for these beings, in detail, these 73 states—70 material phenomena and 3 mental aggregates—should be understood as 'mind-and-matter with consciousness as condition.' By the agahitaggahaṇa method, if 54 material phenomena are removed from the six material continuities, there are 19. This is the presentation according to the maximum. At the minimum, for those beings who lack certain material continuities, the 'mind-and-matter with rebirth-linking consciousness as condition' should be understood in brief and in detail by reducing them according to their respective deficiencies. For formless Brahmas, only the three mental aggregates occur. For non-percipient Brahmas (Asaññasatta), only the life-nonad occurs in terms of matter. This is the method at the time of rebirth-linking.

During the course of existence (pavatti), in all places where matter occurs, at the static phase (ṭhitikkhaṇa) of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the pure octad group (suddhaṭṭhaka-kalāpa) born of temperature (utu-samuṭṭhāna) appears due to the temperature that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. The rebirth-linking consciousness itself, however, does not produce matter. Indeed, just as a man falling down a precipice cannot support another, that rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter because of the weakness of its physical base and its own weakness. From the first life-continuum (bhavaṅga) after the rebirth-linking consciousness onwards, the pure octad group born of mind arises. At the time when sound becomes manifest, the sound-nonad group (sadda-navaka) arises due to temperature and mind occurring after the moment of rebirth-linking. There are those womb-born beings who live depending on physical nutriment; for those beings, the nutriment...
162:
The rebirth-linking consciousness cannot produce matter. Indeed, just as a man falling down a precipice cannot be a support for another, it is unable to produce matter because of the weakness of its physical base and its own weakness. From the first life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga) after the rebirth-linking consciousness onwards, the pure octad group born of mind becomes manifest. At the time when sound becomes manifest, the sound-nonad group (sadda-navaka) arises due to temperature and mind occurring after the moment of rebirth-linking. There are those womb-born beings who live depending on physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra). Regarding those beings, it is said in the Saṃyutta Nikāya: 'The man in his mother's womb subsists there on the food and drink that his mother eats.' According to this statement, the pure octad group born of nutriment arises in the body permeated by the nutriment swallowed by the mother. For spontaneously born beings (opapātika), it arises when they first swallow the saliva that has entered their mouths. Thus, among the pure octad born of nutriment, the matter born of temperature, and the matter born of mind, there are 26 types of matter through the power of two nonad groups at the maximum. When combined with the 70 kamma-born material phenomena (kammaja-rūpa), which were previously stated in the Khandha-vibhaṅga to arise three times in every mind-moment, there are 96 types of matter. Combining these 96 types of matter with the 3 mental aggregates, there are 99 states in brief. Alternatively, because the word 'or' (vā) implies uncertainty and sound arises only occasionally, by excluding those two types of sound-matter, these 97 states should be understood as 'mind-and-matter with consciousness as condition' for all beings as they occur. For those beings—whether sleeping, negligent, walking, eating, or drinking—these mind-and-matter phenomena occur day and night with consciousness as the condition. We shall explain later how they have consciousness as their condition.

Among these material phenomena, there is kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa). Although it is established first of all in the existences, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, it cannot stand firmly if it is not supported by matter born of the other three causes (mind, temperature, and nutriment). Nor can the matter born of the three causes stand without being supported by kamma-born matter. Rather, like sheaves of reeds that are struck by the wind but stand leaning against each other when set up in the four directions, or like lashed boats that have found a footing somewhere in the great ocean and stand without drifting away even when struck by the force of waves, these material phenomena born of the four causes (catusamuṭṭhānika-rūpa) stand well, supporting each other without falling. They continue to occur for one year, two years... even up to a hundred years, as long as the life-span or the merit of those beings lasts. Thus, the decision regarding these material phenomena born of the four causes should be understood here by the phrase 'because of occurrence in all existences, etc.'
163:
In this term "Saṅgaha" (Summary), it should be understood that "with consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter arises" by including them through the method of elision of similar forms (ekasesa-naya) as follows: there is only mind (nāma) caused by consciousness during the course of existence and at rebirth in the formless (arūpa) realms, and during the course of existence in the five-constituent (pañcavokāra) realms; there is only matter (rūpa) caused by consciousness at all times in the non-percipient (asaññasatta) realms, and during the course of existence in the five-constituent realms; and there is mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) caused by consciousness at all times in the five-constituent realms. All these—mind, matter, and mind-and-matter—are collectively termed "mind-and-matter."

If it is objected that "it is improper (to say mind-and-matter arises due to consciousness) because there is no consciousness in the non-percipient realms," that objection is not correct (it is indeed proper). The reason is:

That consciousness which is the cause of mind-and-matter is known to be of two kinds: resultant (vipāka) and non-resultant (avipāka). Therefore, this statement is indeed proper.

This is because the consciousness that is the cause of mind-and-matter is understood to be twofold, distinguished as resultant and non-resultant. In the non-percipient realm, this matter is kamma-produced (kamma-samuṭṭhāna), and thus it has as its cause the kamma-forming consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) that occurred in a five-constituent existence. Likewise, during the course of existence in the five-constituent realm, the kamma-produced matter at the moment of wholesome (kusala) and other consciousnesses (also has consciousness as its cause). Therefore, this statement is indeed proper. Thus, the decision herein should be understood by way of "Saṅgaha."

In this term "Paccayanaya" (Method of Conditions):

Resultant consciousness is a condition for mind in nine ways. It is a condition for the base-matter (vatthu-rūpa) in nine ways, and for the remaining matter in eight ways.
Kamma-forming consciousness is a condition for matter in one way. Other consciousnesses, however, are conditions for the respective mind-and-matter as is appropriate.

Whether at the moment of rebirth or during the course of existence, there is that mind called "resultant" (vipāka). That resultant consciousness, whether associated with matter or not, and whether at rebirth or at other times, is a condition for mind in nine ways through the conditions of: conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), resultant (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). For the base-matter at the moment of rebirth, it is a condition in nine ways through the conditions of: conascence, mutuality, support, resultant, nutriment, faculty, dissociation (vippayutta), presence, and non-disappearance. Excluding the base-matter, it is a condition for the remaining matter through eight conditions, by excluding the mutuality condition from these nine. Kamma-forming consciousness, however, is a condition for the matter of non-percipient beings or for the kamma-born matter in the five-constituent realm in only one way, by the power of decisive support (upanissaya) according to the Suttanta method. All other consciousnesses, starting from the first life-continuum (bhavaṅga), for the respective mind-and-matter...
164:
It should be understood that it assists accordingly. If the method of how it assists name-and-form were shown in detail, the entire Paṭṭhāna discourse would have to be expanded; therefore, we do not undertake that detailed method. Here, there might be a question: "How is it to be known that rebirth-linking name-and-form occurs because of consciousness?" It is known through both Sutta and logic. Indeed, in the Sutta texts, the fact that feeling and so on have consciousness as their condition is established by many methods, such as "states following consciousness." By logic: Through mind-produced matter seen here, the fact that consciousness is the condition for matter not seen is established. Indeed, when the mind is clear or not clear, mind-produced matter corresponding to that mind is seen to arise. From what is seen, there is an inference of what is not seen. Therefore, through the mind-produced matter seen here, it should be known that consciousness is the condition even for the rebirth-linking matter that is not seen. The fact that matter originating from kamma also has consciousness as its condition appears in the Paṭṭhāna text. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of the method of conditionality. And here, by saying "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form [arises]," the Blessed One makes it known to wise people who investigate that, in the ultimate sense, only name-and-form is occurring, not a "being," not a "person." Therefore, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion, which cannot be turned back by any recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.

## Explanation of the term: Conditioned by Consciousness, Name-and-Form.

## Explanation of the term: The Six Sense Bases

In the explanation of the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form: The three [mental] aggregates are known as "name" (nāma); the primary elements, the bases, and so on are known as "form" (rūpa). That name-and-form, treated as a single term (ekasesa), is the condition for such [six sense bases].
165:
In the context of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) which is the condition for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), 'mentality' (nāma) refers to the three mental aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā). 'Materiality' (rūpa) should be understood as the four great elements (mahābhūta), the six bases (vatthu), the life faculty (jīvitindriya), and so on, which are invariably included within one's own continuity. This mentality-materiality is an elided compound (ekasesa) meaning 'mentality and materiality which is mentality-materiality,' and it should be understood as the condition for the six sense bases, which is also an elided compound meaning 'the sixth base and the six bases which are the six sense bases.' Why? Because in the formless realm (arūpa), mentality alone is the condition. Furthermore, that mentality is the condition only for the sixth base, the mind base (manāyatana), and not for the others. For it will be stated in the section on the indeterminate (abyākata-vāra): "With mentality as condition, the sixth base arises." It should be understood that the mentality-materiality included here is what is analyzed and taught in that section on the indeterminate.

In this regard, if there is a question: "How can it be known that mentality-materiality is the condition for the six sense bases?" It can be known because the six sense bases exist only when mentality-materiality exists. Only when such-and-such mentality and materiality exist does such-and-such sense base arise; it cannot be otherwise. The nature of the six sense bases existing only when mentality-materiality exists will become clear when explaining the method of conditions (paccaya-naya). Therefore:

Whether at the moment of rebirth-linking or during the course of existence,
whichever mentality-materiality is the condition for whichever sense base,
and in whatever manner it is a condition,
that should be understood by the wise.

The meaning of that verse is:
In the formless realm, at the moments of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, mentality alone is the condition for the sixth base, the mind base, in at least seven ways.

How? At the moment of rebirth-linking, mentality is the condition for the mind base in at least seven ways through the conditions of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), association (sampayutta), resultant (vipāka), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). In some instances, it is also a condition through other conditions such as the root condition (hetu) or the nutriment condition (āhāra). Through these, the maximum and minimum (ukkaṃsa and avakaṃsa) should be understood.

During the course of existence, resultant mentality is also a condition in the same manner as mentioned. However, mentality other than resultant (wholesome, unwholesome, or functional) is a condition in at least six ways, excluding the resultant condition from the aforementioned conditions. Here too, in some instances, it is a condition through other conditions such as the root condition or the nutriment condition, and through these, the maximum and minimum should be understood.

In realms other than the formless realm (the five-constituent existence), at the moment of rebirth-linking, mentality is likewise the condition for the sixth base, the mind base. That same mentality is the condition for the other sense bases in six ways.
166:
In the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) other than the formless realm, that resultant mentality, being an associate of the heart-base (hadayavatthu), is a condition for the sixth base, the mind base, in at least seven ways, just as stated for the formless realm. For the other five sense bases beginning with the eye base (cakkhāyatana), however, this resultant mentality, having the four great elements as associates, is a condition in six ways by way of conascence (sahajāta), dependence (nissaya), resultant (vipāka), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Among these mentalities, some are conditions by way of the root condition (hetu), and some by way of the nutriment condition (āhāra), thus acting as conditions through other conditional forces as well. Through the power of those other conditional forces, the maximum and minimum (ukkaṃsa and avakaṃsa) should be understood.

During the course of existence (pavatti), it is the same: resultant mentality is a condition for resultant mentality.
Non-resultant mentality is a condition for the non-resultant sixth base, the mind base, in six ways.

During the course of existence in the five-constituent existence, just as at the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant mentality is a condition for the resultant sixth base in at least seven ways. Non-resultant mentality, however, is a condition for the non-resultant sixth base in at least six ways, by excluding the resultant condition from those seven conditions. In this context, the maximum and minimum should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

In that same five-constituent existence, resultant mentality is the condition for the remaining five sense bases.
Non-resultant mentality is also shown to be a condition in four ways in the same manner.

In that same five-constituent existence, during the course of existence, for the remaining five sense bases beginning with the eye base—whether they have the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) etc. as their base or the other heart-base as their base—resultant mentality is a condition in four ways through the conditions of post-nascence (pacchājāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Just as resultant mentality is shown, non-resultant mentality is also shown in the same way. Therefore, it should be understood that mentality of various types such as wholesome (kusala) etc. is also a condition for those five sense bases in four ways. Thus, it should be understood how mentality alone is the condition for whichever sense base and in whichever manner, whether at rebirth-linking or during the course of existence.

Materiality (rūpa), however, in this context, is not a condition for even a single sense base in the formless realm.
But in the five-constituent existence which has five aggregates, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the heart-base materiality (hadayavatthu-rūpa) is a condition for the sixth base, the mind base, in six ways.
The great elements (mahābhūta) are conditions for the five sense bases in four ways without distinction.

At the moment of rebirth-linking, the heart-base materiality is a condition for the sixth base, the mind base, in six ways through the conditions of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). The four great elements, without distinction, at the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, for whichever...
167:
Whichever sense base arises, by the power of that respective base, it assists the five bases such as the eye-base in four ways through the conditions of conascence (sahajāta), dependence (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).

Material life-faculty assists these five, such as the eye, in three ways; and nutriment also [assists] during the course of existence (in three ways).
These same five bases assist the sixth, the mind-base, in six ways; the heart-base assists that same mind-base in five ways.

To these five bases such as the eye, both at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and during the course of existence (pavatti), material life-faculty assists in three ways by the power of presence, non-disappearance, and faculty (indriya). By the words "and nutriment" (āhāro ca), material nutriment also assists in three ways by the power of presence, non-disappearance, and nutriment. And that nutriment assists only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking, in the bodies of beings who subsist on nutriment. Those five bases, such as the eye-base, assist the sixth mind-base—comprising eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness—in six ways by the power of dependence, prenascence (purejāta), faculty, dissociation (vippayutta), presence, and non-disappearance during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking. Excluding the five [sense] consciousnesses, the heart-base assists the remaining mind-base in five ways by the power of dependence, prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking. Thus, it should be understood how matter alone assists whichever sense base, in whatever manner, whether at rebirth-linking or during the course of existence.

Both name and form together assist whichever sense base in whatever manner;
The wise should understand that mode of assistance in all cases, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.

To explain: at the moment of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), name-and-form—consisting of the three mental aggregates and the heart-base—assists the sixth mind-base through the conditions of conascence, mutuality (aññamañña), dependence, resultant (vipāka), association (sampayutta), dissociation, presence, non-disappearance, and so on. This is merely a brief indication here. Since everything can be connected by following the method already stated, the detailed explanation is not shown here.

## Exposition of the Term "Sixfold Sense Base with Name-and-Form as Condition".
168:
## Exposition of the Term "Contact"

In explaining the arising of contact conditioned by the sixfold sense base, in brief, there are only six kinds of contact, such as eye-contact. In detail, however, they are thirty-two, just like consciousness.

Indeed, in the Pali text, only the six kinds of contact, such as eye-contact, are mentioned in brief. In detail, however, there are ten—five wholesome resultant contacts and five unwholesome resultant contacts starting with eye-contact—and the remaining twenty-two contacts associated with mundane resultant consciousness. Thus, all [contacts] are thirty-two, just like the consciousness mentioned as being conditioned by volitional formations (saṅkhāra). The condition for these thirty-two types of contact is the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana). Regarding that sixfold sense base:

The wise regard the internal bases, such as the eye, together with the sixth [the mind-base], as the "sixfold sense base"; and also [the internal bases] together with the six external bases, such as visible forms.

Among those [teachers], some teachers, considering that "this is a discourse on the occurrence [of phenomena] in a living being," show only the condition and the conditionally arisen states that are included within a single continuity (santati). Following the Pali "contact conditioned by the sixth base" (chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso), they hold that the sixth base (mind-base) in the formless realm, and the sixfold sense base in other realms by way of inclusive grouping, are the condition for contact. By forming a single term through the inclusion of a part in the whole (ekadesasarupekatthesa), they regard only the six internal bases, such as the eye together with the sixth mind-base, as the "sixfold sense base." Indeed, both the sixth base and the sixfold sense base come under the designation of "sixfold sense base" (saḷāyatana).

Other teachers, however, show only the conditionally arisen contact as being included within a single continuity, while showing the condition as potentially belonging to a different continuity. Wishing to show whatever base is a condition for contact, they include the external bases as well, and regard the internal bases together with the sixth mind-base, as well as the external bases such as the form-base, as the "sixfold sense base." Indeed, when the sixth base and the sixfold sense base are treated as a single term (ekasesa), they come under the designation of "sixfold sense base."

Here, an objector asks: "A single contact does not arise from all bases, nor do all contacts arise from a single base. Yet, it is stated as a single [term], 'contact conditioned by the sixfold sense base.' Why is that?" The answer is as follows: This is true. A single contact does not arise from all bases, nor do all contacts arise from one. However, a single contact does arise from several [bases]. For example, a single eye-contact arises due to the eye-base, the form-base, the mind-base (known as eye-consciousness), and the remaining associated states (dhammāyatana). This should be applied to all cases accordingly. Therefore...
169:
In this Vibhaṅga of Dependent Origination, the Blessed One, who is endowed with the attribute of Tādi, although pointing out 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact' (saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso) using the singular form, has shown that this single contact arises due to many bases.

'By the singular designation' (ekavacananiddesena) means that by this singular expression 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact', the Buddha, the Possessor of the Tādi attribute, shows that a single contact arises due to many bases. However, regarding the bases—

Among the bases, one should clearly demonstrate how the five (internal) bases condition in six ways, how the other one (mind base) conditions in nine ways, and how the six external bases condition this mind-contact accordingly.

The explanation of that verse is as follows: First, the five bases such as the eye base condition the fivefold contact such as eye-contact in six ways: as support (nissaya), pre-nascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), existence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Furthermore, the single resultant mind base conditions the manifold resultant mind-contact in nine ways: as co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), association (sampayutta), existence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).

Among the external bases, the form base is a condition for eye-contact in four ways: as object (ārammaṇa), pre-nascence (purejāta), existence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Similarly, the sound base and so on (condition ear-contact and so on in four ways). For mind-contact, those [bases] such as the form base as well as the mental-object base condition it by those four conditions mentioned above, and also by the object condition alone. Thus, one should clearly demonstrate how the six external bases condition this mind-contact accordingly.

## The explanation of the clause 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact' is finished.

## Explanation of the Clause on Feeling

In the explanation of 'With contact as condition, feeling' (phassapaccayā vedanā)—

Six types of feeling, such as feeling born of eye-contact, are spoken of by way of doors. These feelings are understood to be eighty-ninefold by way of their association with the eighty-nine types of consciousness.

Indeed, in the Pāḷi text, by the method starting with 'feeling born of eye-contact' (cakkhusamphassajā vedanā), these six feelings are spoken of by way of doors. These feelings are understood to be eighty-ninefold because they are associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness.

Among these eighty-nine feelings, in this text 'With contact as condition, feeling', the former teachers have said that only the thirty-two feelings associated with resultant (vipāka) consciousness are intended.
170:
Among those (feelings), in the five doors, (contact) conditions the five (feelings) in eight ways. For the remaining (feelings), contact conditions in one way. In the mind door also, that contact (conditions) in the same way.

In detail: In the five doors, for the five feelings that have the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and so on as their physical bases, contact such as eye-contact conditions as a basis in eight ways: as co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), association (sampayutta), existence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). For the remaining sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and registration (tadārammaṇa) in each door, contact such as eye-contact conditions as a basis in only one way: as decisive support (upanissaya).

'In the mind door also, that contact (conditions) in the same way' (manodvārepi so tathā) means: In the mind door also, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of registration, that contact known as co-nascent mind-contact conditions as a basis in the same way, in eight ways; and also for the resultant feelings of the three planes occurring by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti). As for those sense-sphere feelings occurring by way of registration in the mind door, the mind-contact associated with advertence (āvajjana) in the mind door conditions them as a basis in one way: as decisive support (upanissaya).

## The explanation of the clause 'With contact as condition, feeling' is finished.

## Explanation of the Clause on Craving

In the explanation of 'With feeling as condition, craving' (vedanāpaccayā taṇhā)—

Six types of craving, such as craving for forms (rūpataṇhā), are shown here (in this teaching). Each of those cravings is understood to be threefold according to its mode of occurrence.

In this explanation of 'With feeling as condition, craving', just as a son is named after his father, such as 'the merchant's son' or 'the brahmin's son', these six cravings are shown, manifested, and spoken of by way of their objects, as craving for forms... and so on... craving for mental objects (dhammataṇhā). Among them, the meaning of the term should be understood in this way: craving for forms is 'craving for forms' (rūpataṇhā).

Among those cravings, each single craving is understood to be threefold according to its mode of occurrence: as craving for sensual pleasures (kāmataṇhā), craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhavataṇhā). Indeed, craving for forms itself, when [it enjoys] a visible object that has entered the range of the eye by way of enjoying sensual pleasure...
171:
When craving arises while enjoying and delighting in an object, it is called sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā). When that same craving arises together with the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), occurring as "it is permanent, it is eternal," it is called craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). This is because lust (rāga) associated with the view of eternalism is called bhava-taṇhā. When that same craving arises together with the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi), occurring as "it is cut off, it perishes," it is called craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). This is because lust associated with the view of annihilationism is called vibhava-taṇhā. The same method applies to craving for sounds (sadda-taṇhā) and so forth; thus, there are eighteen types of craving.

These eighteen types of craving occur in relation to internal (ajjhatta) objects such as visible forms, and eighteen in relation to external (bahiddhā) objects, making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present, totaling one hundred and eight types of craving. Briefly, however, they should be understood as six types by way of objects such as visible forms, or as three types by way of sensual craving and so forth. Just as people, out of delight and affection for a son, cherish the nurse with a sense of "mine," so too, out of delight and affection for the feeling (vedanā) that arises by way of objects such as visible forms, they cherish with a sense of "mine" those who provide such objects—painters, lute players, perfumers, cooks, weavers, physicians who prepare elixirs, and so on—offering them great honor. Therefore, it should be understood that all this craving arises with feeling as a condition (vedanā-paccaya taṇhā).

In this context, resultant pleasant feeling (vipāka-sukha-vedanā) is intended. That resultant pleasant feeling is the cause of craving in a single way. "In a single way" means it is a cause by way of the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Alternatively:
One who is in pain longs for pleasure; one who is in pleasure desires even more pleasure.
Equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā), because of its peaceful nature, is also spoken of as pleasure.
Therefore, the Great Sage (the Buddha) taught that all three types of feeling are conditions for craving.
Even though feeling is a condition, craving cannot arise without latent tendencies (anusaya). Therefore, in the continuum of an Arahant who has fulfilled the holy life (vusi-manto), that craving does not arise.

## Exposition of the Term: Craving Conditioned by Feeling (Vedanāpaccayā Taṇhā)

In the opening of the exposition of grasping (upādāna): There are four types of grasping. These four types of grasping should be shown by way of the analysis of meaning, by way of the brief and detailed exposition of the states, and by way of their order. In this Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, the four types of grasping appear as: grasping at sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna), grasping at views (diṭṭhupādāna), grasping at rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), and grasping at the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). Among these four, the analysis of meaning is as follows: It is called kāmupādāna because it firmly grasps at the objects of sense-pleasure (vatthu-kāma). Since the defilement of sense-pleasure (kilesa-kāma) itself is the nature of firm grasping, it is also called kāmupādāna. Grasping (upādāna) means firm taking or the nature of firm taking.

In this context, the prefix "upa" expresses the meaning of "firmness" (daḷha), as in the words upāyāsa and upakkusa.
172:
## Exposition of the Term: Grasping (Upādāna)

In the exposition of grasping conditioned by craving (taṇhā-paccayā upādāna):

There are four types of grasping. These four types of grasping should be explained by way of the analysis of meaning, by way of the brief and detailed exposition of the states, and by way of their order.

In the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, these four types of grasping appear starting from kāmupādāna up to attavādupādāna. The analysis of their meaning is as follows: It is called kāmupādāna because it firmly grasps at the objects of sense-pleasure (vatthu-kāma). Since it is both the defilement of sense-pleasure and has the nature of firm grasping, it is called kāmupādāna. Grasping (upādāna) means firm taking or the nature of firm taking. In this word upādāna, the prefix "upa" expresses the meaning of "firmness" or "excessive," as in the words upāyāsa and upakaṭṭha.

Similarly, it is called diṭṭhupādāna because it is both a wrong view and has the nature of firm grasping. Alternatively, it is called diṭṭhupādāna because it firmly grasps a previously held wrong view. For instance, in views such as "the self and the world are eternal," a subsequent view firmly grasps the preceding view.

Similarly, it is called sīlabbatupādāna because it firmly grasps the practices of cattle (sīlabbata). Since that practice itself has the nature of firm grasping, it is called sīlabbatupādāna. Because of the firm conviction that "one is purified from defilements through the practices of cattle, the vows of cattle, etc.," those very practices are called grasping.

Similarly, it is called vāda (doctrine) because one speaks by means of this state; it is called upādāna because one firmly grasps by means of this state. What does one speak of or grasp? Only the self (atta). Because it is the state of speaking of and firmly grasping the self, it is called attavādupādāna. Or, because it is the means of firmly grasping the mere doctrine of self as the self, it is called attavādupādāna. This is the analysis of their meaning.

Regarding "the brief and detailed exposition of the states": Firstly, concerning kāmupādāna, the Pāḷi states: "Therein, what is kāmupādāna? It is the desire for sense-pleasures (kāmacchanda), the lust for sense-pleasures (kāmarāga), the delight in sense-pleasures (kāmanandī), the craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā), the affection for sense-pleasures (kāmasneha), the fever of sense-pleasures (kāmapariḷāha), the infatuation with sense-pleasures (kāmamucchā), and the total immersion in sense-pleasures (kāmajjhosāna)." Thus, briefly, it means the firmness of craving. The firmness of craving is simply the subsequent craving that arises firmly due to the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) of the preceding craving.

Some teachers, however, say: Craving (taṇhā) is the longing for an object not yet obtained, like a thief stretching out his hand in the dark toward goods. Grasping (upādāna) is the firm taking of an object already obtained, like that thief seizing the goods. These states of craving and grasping are the opposites of fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā). Likewise, they are the roots of the suffering caused by seeking and the suffering caused by guarding. The remaining three types of grasping are, briefly, just wrong views (diṭṭhi) only.

In detail, the firmness of the 108 types of craving previously mentioned in relation to visible forms and so forth is called kāmupādāna. Wrong view with ten bases is called diṭṭhupādāna. As it was said: "Therein, what is diṭṭhupādāna? The view that 'there is no merit in giving, no merit in sacrifice... etc.,' which they declare having realized for themselves."
173: Such a wrong view ... [pe] ... perverted grasping exists; this view is called clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). The misapprehension that purification comes through the practices of cattle or the practices of dogs is clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbatupādāna). Regarding this, it was said: 'Therein, what is clinging to rites and rituals? That which is such a wrong view ... [pe] ... perverted grasping of recluses and brahmins outside of this [Dispensation] that purification comes through virtue, through a vow, or through virtue and a vow—this is called clinging to rites and rituals.' Identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) consisting of twenty objects is clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). Regarding this, it was said: 'Therein, what is clinging to the doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling ... [pe] ... being untrained in the Dhamma of the Great Ones, regards form as self ... [pe] ... perverted grasping exists—this is called clinging to the doctrine of self.' This is the brief and detailed explanation of the states in this description of clinging (upādānaniddesa). In the word 'kamatō' (in terms of order), there are three kinds of order: the order of arising (uppattikkama), the order of abandonment (pahānakkama), and the order of teaching (desanākkama). Among these, because there is no first arising of these defilements in the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra), the order of arising of defilements is not stated in the primary sense (nippariyāyena). However, in a figurative sense (pariyāyena), generally in a single life, there is the perverted reflection of eternalism or annihilationism preceded by the grasping of a self. Thereafter, in the continuum of one who holds 'this self is eternal,' clinging to rites and rituals arises for the sake of purifying the self. In the continuum of one who holds 'it is annihilated' and has no regard for the next world, clinging to sensual pleasures arises. Thus, clinging to the doctrine of self arises first, followed by clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, and clinging to sensual pleasures. This is their order of arising in a single life. Among these, the three beginning with clinging to views are abandoned first because they are to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). Clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned later because it is to be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). This is their order of abandonment. Among these, clinging to sensual pleasures is taught first because it has a broad scope and is well-known in the world. Indeed, that clinging to sensual pleasures has a broad scope because it is associated with the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed. The others have a narrow scope because they are associated only with the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view. Generally, clinging to sensual pleasures is prominent among the multitude of beings who delight in their attachments (ālaya), while the others are not. One who has clinging to sensual pleasures often holds wrong views such as belief in festive omens (kotūhalamangala) for the sake of obtaining sensual objects; since it is said not to be eternalism, clinging to views is taught immediately after that. When that clinging to views is divided, it is of two kinds: clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to the doctrine of self. Between these two, clinging to rites and rituals is taught first because it is coarse and evident, being recognizable just by seeing the behavior of cattle or the behavior of dogs. Clinging to the doctrine of self is taught at the end because it is subtle. This is their order of teaching.
174:
Among these four types of clinging, craving is a condition that assists the first, clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), in one way. That same craving is a condition that assists the remaining three types of clinging in either seven ways or eight ways.

In this group of four types of clinging thus taught, craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā) is a condition that assists the first, clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), in only one way, by way of decisive support (upanissaya), because of its arising in the objects greatly delighted in through craving. To the remaining three types of clinging, however, it is a condition in seven ways by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), non-disappearance (avigata), and root (hetu); or in eight ways including decisive support (upanissaya). When that craving is a condition by way of decisive support, it is only non-conascent craving.

## Explanation of the term: "With Craving as condition, Clinging [arises]."
## Explanation of the term: "Existence" (Bhava).

In showing "With Clinging as condition, Existence [arises]":
The decision should be understood by way of meaning, by way of state, by way of purpose, by way of division, and by way of summary, as to which clinging is a condition for which existence and in what way.

In that verse, it is called "existence" (bhava) because it comes to be (bhavati). "Duvidhena" means because of occurring in two ways. Alternatively, the instrumental case "duvidhena" is used in the sense of the nominative case; it means "there are two kinds." "Atthi" means it exists or is found. Action itself is existence, thus it is "action-existence" (kamma-bhava). Rebirth itself is existence, thus it is "rebirth-existence" (upapatti-bhava). Between these two, rebirth-existence is called existence because it comes to be. As for action (kamma), just as the arising of the Buddhas is called "The arising of the Buddhas is happiness" (Dhammapada 194) because it is the cause of happiness, so too kamma should be understood as "existence" by naming the cause after the effect, because it is the cause of existence.

Among those two kinds of existence, the question "Which is action-existence?" means "What is that which is called action-existence?" Meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth have the meanings already stated. "Sabbaṃ" means all without exception. It is called "leading to existence" (bhavagāmi) because it goes to or leads to existence. By this term "bhavagāmi," supramundane (lokuttara) action is excluded. This is because this is a discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and supramundane action depends on Nibbāna, which is free from the round. It is called "action" (kamma) because it is performed.

Among the types of existence such as sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava), existence known as the sense-sphere is sense-sphere existence. This same method applies to fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava) and immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava). It is called "percipient existence" (saññā-bhava) because it is the existence of beings with perception, or because perception exists in this existence. Conversely, it is "non-percipient existence" (asaññā-bhava). Of the gross perception...
175:
Because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, in this existence, there is perception that is neither perception nor non-perception; therefore, it is called 'existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (nevasaññānāsaññābhava). Existence mixed with only the aggregate of form is called 'one-constituent existence' (ekavokārabhava). Or, because there is only one constituent spread out in this existence, it is called 'one-constituent existence'. The same method applies to 'four-constituent existence' (catuvokārabhava) and 'five-constituent existence' (pañcavokārabhava). These nine types of existence are called 'rebirth-existence' (upapattibhava). Thus, in this exposition of existence, the decision should first be understood 'by way of meaning' (attato).

Regarding the decision 'by way of nature' (dhammato): In this exposition of existence, meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) consist of 13 volitions (cetanā). Demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) consist of 12 volitions, and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) consist of 4 volitions. By the phrase "all karma leading to existence," all states associated with volition or called karma, which lead to rebirth because they are accumulated, are included. Sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) consists of the 5 appropriated aggregates (upādinnakkhandha). Likewise, fine-material existence (rūpabhava) consists of 5, immaterial existence (arūpabhava) of 4, percipient existence (saññābhava) of 4 or 5, non-percipient existence (asaññābhava) of 1 appropriated aggregate, and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception of 4. One-constituent existence and so forth consist of 1, 4, and 5 appropriated aggregates. Thus, in this exposition of existence, the decision should also be understood 'by way of nature'.

Regarding the decision 'by way of purpose' (sātthato): Just as meritorious formations and so forth are stated in the exposition of existence, they were also stated in the exposition of formations (saṅkhāraniddesa). Even though they are the same, the states taught in the previous exposition of formations were taught because they are the cause of rebirth in this life through the power of past karma. The states taught in this exposition of existence are taught because they are the cause of rebirth in the future through the power of present karma. Therefore, stating them again is indeed purposeful. Alternatively, previously, in the manner of "Therein, what is meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition of the sense sphere," etc., only volition itself was taught as formation. But in this exposition of existence, because it is said "all karma leading to existence," states associated with volition are also included. Previously, only karma that is the cause of consciousness was taught as formation; now, karma that brings about non-percipient existence is also taught. Or what is the use of many words? In the phrase "with ignorance as condition, formations," only wholesome and unwholesome states such as meritorious formations and so forth were taught. But in this phrase "with clinging as condition, existence," because rebirth-existence is also included, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate (abyākata) states are taught. Therefore, in every way, this restatement is indeed purposeful. Thus, in this exposition of existence, the decision should also be understood 'by way of purpose'.

Regarding the decision 'by way of classification and inclusion' (bhedasaṅgahato): It should be understood by way of the classification and inclusion of existence conditioned by clinging. For whatever karma is performed that brings about sense-sphere existence conditioned by sense-desire clinging (kāmupādāna), that is 'karma-existence' (kammabhava). The aggregates brought about by that karma are 'rebirth-existence' (upapattibhava). The same method applies to fine-material and immaterial existence. Thus—
176:
Due to sense-desire clinging (kāmupādāna), two types of sense-sphere existence—karma-existence and rebirth-existence—arise; within those two sense-sphere existences, percipient existence and five-constituent existence are included. Two types of fine-material existence arise; within those two fine-material existences, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, and five-constituent existence are included. Two types of immaterial existence arise; within those two immaterial existences, percipient existence, existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and four-constituent existence are included. Thus, there are six types of existence along with those included within. Just as there are six types of existence along with those included within due to sense-desire clinging, so there are six types each due to the remaining types of clinging. Thus, by way of classification, there are twenty-four types of existence along with those included within due to clinging.

By way of inclusion, however, by taking karma-existence and rebirth-existence together, there is one sense-sphere existence along with those included within due to sense-desire clinging; likewise, fine-material and immaterial existences arise, making three types of existence. Similarly, there are three types each due to the remaining types of clinging; thus, by way of inclusion, there are twelve types of existence along with those included within due to clinging. Furthermore, without specifying the four types of clinging, generally, karma that leads to sense-sphere existence due to clinging is called karma-existence; the aggregates brought about by that karma are called rebirth-existence. The same method applies to fine-material and immaterial existence. Thus, by another method of inclusion, there are six types of existence: two sense-sphere, two fine-material, and two immaterial existences along with those included within due to clinging. Or, without entering into the classification of karma-existence and rebirth-existence, there are three types of existence by way of sense-sphere existence and so forth, along with those included within. Without entering into the classification of sense-sphere existence and so forth, there are two types of existence by way of karma-existence and rebirth-existence. Without entering into the classification of karma and rebirth, there is only one existence by way of 'existence conditioned by clinging'. Thus, in this exposition of existence, the decision should be understood by way of the classification and inclusion of existence having clinging as its condition.

In the matrix clause 'And which is the condition for which' (yam yassa paccayo ceva), it means the decision should also be understood by way of the condition and the conditionally arisen, as in which clinging is the condition for which existence. Among these types of clinging, which clinging is the condition for which existence? Any clinging is indeed a condition for any existence. For an ordinary person (puthujjana) is like a madman. Without investigating 'this is proper, this is improper', by the power of any clinging, they long for any existence and perform any karma. Therefore, the statement of some teachers that 'fine-material and immaterial existences do not occur due to rule-and-ritual-clinging' should not be accepted. It should be accepted only that every type of existence occurs due to every type of clinging. How? In this world, some person, either by way of hearsay or by following what they have seen, thinks: 'These sense pleasures are abundant in the human world, in wealthy families such as the wealthy warrior-nobles (khattiyamahāsāla), and in the six sense-sphere deva worlds.' Being deceived by hearing false teachings and so forth for the sake of attaining those sense pleasures, they think: 'By this karma, sense pleasures will be fulfilled.'
177:
A person who thinks thus performs bodily misconduct and so forth due to the power of clinging to sense-desire (kāmupādāna). Because of the fulfillment of such misconduct, he is reborn in the states of deprivation (apāya). Alternatively, one who longs for sensual pleasures in the present life, or one who protects sensual pleasures already acquired, performs bodily misconduct and so forth due to the power of clinging to sense-desire. Because of the fulfillment of such misconduct, he is reborn in the states of deprivation. In those states of deprivation, the kamma that is the cause of his rebirth is called kamma-process existence (kamma-bhava); the aggregates generated by kamma are called rebirth-process existence (upapatti-bhava). Perceptive existence (saññā-bhava) and five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) are merely included within that sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava).

Another person, however, having wisdom increased by hearing the Good Dhamma and so forth, thinks, "Through this wholesome kamma, sensual pleasures will be fulfilled," and performs bodily good conduct and so forth due to the power of clinging to sense-desire. Because of the fulfillment of such good conduct, he is reborn among devas or humans. Among those devas and humans, the kamma that is the cause of his rebirth-process existence is called kamma-process existence; the aggregates generated by kamma are called rebirth-process existence. Perceptive existence and five-constituent existence are merely included within that sense-sphere existence. Thus, clinging to sense-desire is a condition for sense-sphere existence, together with its various types and its internal inclusions such as perceptive existence and five-constituent existence.

Another person, having heard or imagined that "Sensual pleasures are more perfect in fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava) and immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava) than in that sense-sphere existence," attains fine-material and immaterial meditative absorptions (samāpatti) solely through the power of clinging to sense-desire, and by the power of those absorptions, is reborn in the fine-material and immaterial Brahma worlds. In those Brahma worlds, the kamma that is the cause of his rebirth-process existence is called kamma-process existence; the aggregates generated by kamma are called rebirth-process existence. Perceptive existence, non-perceptive existence (asaññā-bhava), neither-perceptive-nor-non-perceptive existence (nevasaññānāsaññā-bhava), one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and five-constituent existence are merely included within that existence. Thus, clinging to sense-desire is also a condition for fine-material and immaterial existences, which have various types and internal inclusions.

Another person, clinging to the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi), thinking, "This self is annihilated, is well-annihilated, in the sense-sphere attainment existence or in one of the fine-material or immaterial existences," performs kamma that leads to such existence. For him, that kamma is called kamma-process existence; the aggregates generated by kamma are called rebirth-process existence. Perceptive existence and so forth are merely included within that existence. Thus, clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) is a condition for all three existences—sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial—together with their various types and internal inclusions.

Another person, through clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna), thinking, "This self is happy and free from fever in the sense-sphere attainment existence or in one of the fine-material or immaterial existences," performs kamma that leads to such existence. For him, that kamma is called kamma-process existence; the aggregates generated by that kamma are called rebirth-process existence. Perceptive existence and so forth are merely included within that existence...
178:
...Thus, clinging to the doctrine of self is a condition for the three existences, together with their various types and internal inclusions.

Another person, (having heard or imagined) that "This rite and ritual (sīlabbata), when fulfilled by one, leads to the perfection of happiness in the sense-sphere attainment existence or in one of the fine-material or immaterial existences," performs kamma that leads to such existence through the power of clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbatupādāna). For that person, that kamma is called kamma-process existence; the aggregates generated by that kamma are called rebirth-process existence. Perceptive existence and so forth are merely included within those existences. Thus, clinging to rites and rituals is also a condition for the three existences, together with their various types and internal inclusions. In this way, in this description of existence, the decision as to which clinging is a condition for which existence should be understood.

If it be asked: "In this context, which clinging is a condition for which existence, and in what way?"

It should be understood that clinging is a condition for fine-material and immaterial existences by way of decisive-support condition (upanissaya-paccaya);
And that clinging is a condition for sense-sphere existence by way of conascence (sahajāta) and so forth (as well as by way of decisive-support condition).

In fact, these four types of clinging are a condition in a single way, by way of decisive-support condition, for fine-material and immaterial existences, as well as for wholesome kamma-process existence and rebirth-process existence included within sense-sphere existence. However, for unwholesome kamma-process existence associated with itself in sense-sphere existence, it is a condition by way of conascence and other such types, namely: conascence, mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), non-disappearance (avigata), and root (hetu) conditions. But for unwholesome kamma-process existence not associated with itself, it is a condition by way of decisive-support condition only.

## The Description of Existence Conditioned by Clinging is finished.

## The Description of Birth, Aging, Death, etc.

In the description of birth conditioned by existence and so forth, the decision regarding the terms 'birth' (jāti) and so forth should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Saccavibhaṅga. In this context, by the term 'existence' (bhava), only kamma-process existence is intended. For that kamma-process existence alone is the condition for birth, not rebirth-process existence. And that kamma-process existence should be noted as being a condition in two ways: by way of kamma-condition and decisive-support condition.

In that regard, it may be asked: "How is it to be known that existence is the condition for birth?" It is known because of the observation of differences such as inferiority and superiority among beings, even when external conditions are equal. Indeed, even when external conditions such as the generating father and mother, semen and blood, and nutriment are equal, the difference of inferiority and superiority is seen even among twin beings. And that difference...
179:
The distinction such as being inferior or superior is not without a cause, because it is not the case that such distinctions do not exist at all times and in the continuity of all beings. Since there is no other cause in the internal continuity of beings produced by that kamma-process (kammabhava), it does not have a cause other than kammabhava; it has only kammabhava as its cause. Indeed, kamma is the cause that produces the distinction of beings as inferior, superior, and so on. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Kamma distinguishes beings, that is to say, as inferior and superior" (M. iii, 289). Thus, this meaning should be understood: "Becoming is the condition for birth."

Because when there is no birth, what is called aging and death does not occur, nor do states such as sorrow. But when there is birth, there occur aging and death, and also states such as sorrow—whether in a fool who is touched by the suffering known as aging and death and is connected with aging and death, or in one who is touched by various states of suffering but is not connected with aging and death. Therefore, it should be understood that this birth is the condition for aging and death, as well as for sorrow and so on. Furthermore, that birth is a condition in a single way, by way of the decisive support (upanissaya).

## Exposition of the terms beginning with 'Birth due to Becoming'

The meaning of the terms beginning with "evametassa" (thus of this) should be understood in the same way as stated in the section of the brief exposition (uddesavāra). Terms such as "saṅgati" (conjunction) are merely synonyms for "samudaya" (origination).

However, since in this context sorrow and so on are mentioned at the end, that ignorance (avijjā) which is mentioned at the beginning of this Wheel of Existence (bhavacakka) as "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," should be understood as follows:

Through sorrow and so on, ignorance is established; this Wheel of Existence is known to have an unknown beginning;
It is devoid of a doer or an experiencer; it is empty with the twelvefold emptiness.

It should be understood that it revolves continuously and perpetually. How, then, is ignorance established here through sorrow and so on? How is this Wheel of Existence said to have an unknown beginning? How is it devoid of a doer and an experiencer? And how is it empty with the twelvefold emptiness? In this Wheel of Existence, sorrow, pain, grief, and despair are inseparable from ignorance, and what is called lamentation occurs in the continuity of the confused person. Thus, when those states like sorrow are established, ignorance is also established. Furthermore, it is said: "With the arising of taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance." And these states like sorrow occur because of the arising of taints. How? Firstly, when there is separation from the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma), sorrow arises due to the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava). As it is said:
180:
"If the sensual pleasures of a person who desires and has generated longing for them fail, he suffers like one pierced by an arrow" (Sn. 773). And as it is said elsewhere: "From sensual desire, sorrow is born" (Dhp. 215). All these states also arise from the arising of the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), as it is said: "For one who dwells obsessed with the thought 'I am form, form is mine,' that form changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and alteration of form, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair" (S. iii, 1). Just as they arise from the arising of the taint of views, so they arise from the arising of the taint of existence (bhavāsava), as it is said: "Even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, enjoying much happiness, and dwelling for a long time in high mansions, when they hear the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, they for the most part fall into fear, agitation, and terror" (S. iii, 78; A. ii, 33). This is like the gods who are terrified by the fear of death upon seeing the five preceding omens. Just as they arise from the arising of the taint of existence, so they arise from the arising of the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava), as it is said: "Bhikkhus, that fool experiences three kinds of pain and grief in this very life" (M. iii, 246).

Thus, since these states like sorrow arise from the arising of the taints, the manifestation of these states like sorrow establishes the taints which are the cause of ignorance. When the taints are established as being present in the capacity of a condition, ignorance is also established. In this way, it should be understood that 'ignorance is established through sorrow and so on.'

However, when ignorance is established as being present in the capacity of a condition, and again there is the sequence of cause and effect as "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness," there is no end to this. Therefore, that twelve-factored Wheel of Existence, proceeding by way of the connection of cause and effect, is established as having an 'unknown beginning' (aviditādi).

If this is so, does it not contradict the statement "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations," which mentions it as the beginning? This is not a statement of an absolute beginning; rather, it is a statement of the predominant factor (padhāna). For among the three rounds (vaṭṭa), ignorance is the predominant factor. By grasping ignorance (not yet having abandoned it), the remaining round of defilements, the round of kamma, and the round of result wrap around the fool, just as when the head of a snake is caught, the rest of the snake's body wraps around the arm. But when the total destruction of ignorance is achieved, there is liberation from those rounds, just as when the head of a snake is cut off, there is liberation from the arm that was wrapped. As it is said: "Through the [fading away and cessation] of ignorance..."
181:
"With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease," and so forth (from Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidānavagga and Vinaya Mahāvagga). Thus, for one who holds onto this ignorance (by not yet abandoning it), there is the bondage of the round; for one who releases it (by abandoning it), there is liberation from the round. This is a statement of that principal state of ignorance, and not merely a statement of the beginning; thus should this Wheel of Existence be understood as starting with ignorance and so forth. Since the occurrence of formations and so forth is due to causes such as ignorance, this Wheel of Existence is devoid of any creator of the round such as a Brahmā or a Mahābrahmā who is imagined as "Brahmā is the best, the creator," and it is also devoid of a self (atta) that experiences pleasure and pain, which is imagined as "This self of mine speaks and experiences."

Furthermore, in this Wheel of Existence, ignorance is empty of a permanent state (dhuva-bhāva) because it has the nature of arising and passing away; it is empty of a beautiful state (subha-bhāva) because it is defiled and defiling; it is empty of a pleasant state (sukha-bhāva) because it is oppressed by arising and passing away; and it is empty of a self-state (atta-bhāva) that could be subject to one's will because its occurrence is dependent on conditions. Likewise, the factors such as formations and so forth are also empty. Or, just as ignorance is not the self, does not belong to the self, is not in the self, and does not possess a self, so too the factors such as formations and so forth are the same. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence should be understood as "empty by way of the twelvefold emptiness."

Having understood this, further:
Of that Wheel, ignorance and craving are the roots; the periods such as the past are three.
In those periods, the factors are two, eight, and two respectively according to their specific nature.

Of this Wheel of Existence, the two states called ignorance and craving should be understood as the roots. This Wheel of Existence is twofold: the one having ignorance as its root and ending with feeling, because it brings the present effect from the past cause; and the one having craving as its root and ending with aging and death, because it continues and expands into the future. Between these two, the former is taught by way of those of a speculative temperament (diṭṭhi-carita), and the latter by way of those of a craving temperament (taṇhā-carita). This is because for those of a speculative temperament, ignorance is the leader in the round of rebirth, and for those of a craving temperament, craving is the leader. Or, the first is taught to uproot the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by showing the non-interruption of causes for the arising of effects; the second is taught to uproot the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) by showing the aging and death of states that have arisen. Or, the first is taught by way of womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings to show the gradual occurrence; the second is taught by way of spontaneously born (opapātika) beings to show the simultaneous occurrence.

The periods of this Wheel of Existence are three: past, present, and future. Among these periods, as they appear by their specific nature in the Pali text, the two factors of ignorance and formations belong to the past period.
182:
The two factors, ignorance and formations, occur in the past period. The eight factors starting from consciousness (viññāṇa) and ending with existence (bhava) occur in the present period. The two factors, birth (jāti) and aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa), occur in the future period. This is how they should be understood. Furthermore:

This Wheel of Existence has three links—preceded by cause, preceded by result, and preceded by cause; it has four groups;
It has twenty spokes, three rounds, and revolves incessantly.

This is also how it should be understood. Among those links, between formations (saṅkhāra) and rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa), there is one link called the 'cause-result link' (hetu-phala-sandhi). Between feeling (vedanā) and craving (taṇhā), there is one link called the 'result-cause link' (phala-hetu-sandhi). Between existence (bhava) and birth (jāti), there is one link called the 'cause-result link' (hetu-phala-sandhi). Thus, this Wheel of Existence should be understood as having three links of cause and result. There are four groups (saṅgaha) defined by the beginning and end of the links, namely: ignorance and formations are one group; consciousness, mind-and-matter, the sixfold sense base, contact, and feeling are the second group; craving, clinging, and existence are the third group; birth and aging-and-death are the fourth group. Thus, this Wheel of Existence should be understood as having four groups.

Five causes in the past, five results now;
Five causes now, five results in the future.

By these twenty modes or spokes, it should be understood as 'the Wheel of Existence with twenty spokes' (vīsati-ākārāra). Among those spokes, regarding 'five causes in the past,' the two factors of ignorance and formations have already been mentioned. However, one who is ignorant craves; one who craves clings; and due to that clinging, existence (kamma-bhava) arises. Therefore, craving, clinging, and existence are also included among the past causes. Hence, it is stated (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga): "Delusion in the previous kamma-existence is ignorance; accumulation is formations; attachment is craving; approaching is clinging; volition is existence. These five factors in the previous kamma-existence are the causes for rebirth here."

In that Pāḷi text, 'in the previous kamma-existence' means at the time of performing the kamma-existence in a previous life. 'Delusion is ignorance' refers to the delusion regarding the truth of suffering, etc., at that time; performing kamma while deluded by that delusion is ignorance. 'Accumulation is formations' refers to the preceding volitions of one performing that kamma. For example, the preceding volitions that arise in the mind of one who, having thought 'I will give a gift,' prepares the requisites for the gift for a month or even a year. The volition at the moment of placing the gift in the hands of the recipients is called 'existence' (bhava). Alternatively, the volitions in the six javanas within a single process of adverting are called 'accumulating formations' (āyūhana-saṅkhāra). The seventh javana volition is called 'existence' (bhava). Or, any...
183:
Intention is called becoming; the efforts associated with that intention are called formations. 'Nikanti craving' refers to the desire and longing for the result of kamma in the state of rebirth-existence (uppatti-bhava) by one who is performing kamma; that desire and longing is called craving. 'Upagamana clinging' refers to the approaching, grasping, and misapprehending that arises through the kamma which is the cause of becoming, in such a way as: 'Having done this kamma, I shall enjoy sensual pleasures in such and such a place, or I shall be annihilated'; this is called clinging. 'Intention is becoming' means that the intention mentioned at the conclusion of the effort is to be understood as becoming.

'Now, the fivefold fruit' refers to the states beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, which indeed appear in the Pali text.
