Thus He said: 'In this case, rebirth is consciousness, descending is name-and-form, clarity is the sense base, touching is contact, experiencing is feeling. These five states in this rebirth-existence (uppatti-bhava) occur due to kamma performed in the past' (Paṭis. I. 47). In that Pali text, 'rebirth-consciousness' is the consciousness called rebirth because it arises by way of connecting one existence with another. 'Descending name-and-form' refers to the entry of mental and physical states into the mother's womb, like coming and entering; this is called name-and-form. 'Clarity as sense base' is said by way of the five sense bases such as the eye, etc. 'Touching as contact' is the contact that arises by touching the object. 'Experiencing as feeling' is the resultant experience that arises together with rebirth-consciousness or with contact having the sixfold sense base as its condition; thus the meaning should be understood.

'Now, the five causes' refers to craving, clinging, and becoming, which appear in the Pali text. When becoming is taken, the formations occurring in the preceding part of that becoming or associated with it are also taken. By taking craving and clinging, the ignorance associated with those states, or the ignorance through which one performs kamma while being deluded, is also taken. Thus there are five causes. Therefore He said: 'In this case, due to the maturity of the sense bases, the delusion is ignorance, the effort is formations, the desire is craving, the approaching is clinging, the intention is becoming. These five states in this kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) are the conditions for rebirth in the future' (Paṭis. I. 47). In that Pali text, 'due to the maturity of the sense bases in this case' shows the intense delusion at the time of performing kamma by one whose sense bases are mature. The remaining words are clear.

'The fivefold fruit in the future' refers to the five beginning with consciousness. These are mentioned by the inclusion of birth (jāti). Aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) are the aging and death of those very states. Therefore He said: 'In the future...'
185:
It should be understood that as long as the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) is not severed, because its causes are not severed, it does not stand still but keeps revolving again and again.

This wheel of becoming, which thus revolves—

By way of the truths from which they arise, and by way of function,
By way of prevention, and by way of similes,
And by way of the variety of profound methods, it should be understood as is appropriate.

In that verse, since in the Saccavibhaṅga Pāḷi, wholesome and unwholesome kamma are described without distinction as the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca), the formations (saṅkhāra) caused by ignorance (avijjā) are the second truth arising from the second truth. Consciousness (viññāṇa) caused by formations is the first truth arising from the second truth. The states beginning with mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) and ending with resultant feeling (vipākavedanā), which are caused by consciousness and so on, are the first truth arising from the first truth. Craving (taṇhā) caused by feeling is the second truth arising from the first truth. Clinging (upādāna) caused by craving is the second truth arising from the second truth. Becoming (bhava) caused by clinging is both the first and second truths arising from the second truth. Birth (jāti) caused by becoming is the first truth arising from the second truth. Aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) caused by birth is the first truth arising from the first truth. Thus, it should first be understood as is appropriate 'by way of the truths from which they arise'.

Furthermore, in this dependent origination, ignorance confuses regarding objects and is the cause for the manifestation of formations. Likewise, formations formulate conditioned things and are the cause for consciousness. Consciousness also cognizes the object and is the cause for mind-and-matter. Mind-and-matter also supports each other and is the cause for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). The six sense bases also operate in their respective spheres and are the cause for contact (phassa). Contact also touches the object and is the cause for feeling. Feeling also experiences the flavor of the object and is the cause for craving. Craving also lusts for lustful things and is the cause for clinging. Clinging also clings to clingable things and is the cause for becoming. Becoming also throws into various destinies (gati) and is the cause for birth. Birth also generates the aggregates (khandhas), and by way of their manifestation, it is the cause for aging and death. Aging and death also preside over the state of ripening and breaking of the aggregates, and are the cause for the appearance of another existence (as they are the basis for sorrow and so on). Therefore, in all factors, this wheel of becoming should also be understood as is appropriate by way of the twofold 'function'.
186:
In this Wheel of Existence, the statement 'with ignorance as condition, formations come to be' prevents the view that [existence] is created or managed by lords such as Brahmā or Viṣṇu. The statement 'with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be' prevents the view that a self (atta) transmigrates from one life to another. The statement 'with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality comes to be' prevents the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā) by showing the diversity of the objects of mentality and materiality which are imagined as a self. By the statements 'with mentality-materiality as condition, the six sense bases come to be' and so forth, views such as 'the self sees, knows, touches, feels, craves, clings, becomes, is born, ages, and dies' are prevented. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence should be understood as is appropriate 'by way of prevention' of wrong views.

Furthermore, in this Wheel of Existence, because of not seeing the individual characteristics (sa-lakkhaṇa) and universal characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) of phenomena, ignorance is like a blind person. Formations caused by ignorance are like the stumbling of a blind person. Consciousness caused by formations is like the fall of one who has stumbled. Mentality-materiality caused by consciousness is like the appearance of a boil on the one who fell. The six sense bases caused by mentality-materiality are like the small pustules on the boil that are about to burst. Contact caused by the six sense bases is like striking the pustules. Feeling caused by contact is like the pain from being struck. Craving caused by feeling is like the desire to cure the pain. Clinging caused by craving is like taking unsuitable medicine in the desire for a cure. Existence caused by clinging is like applying an unsuitable ointment. Birth caused by existence is like the aggravation of the boil due to the ointment. Aging and death caused by birth are like the bursting of the boil following its aggravation.

Alternatively, ignorance overwhelms beings like a cataract covering the eyes. The fool overwhelmed by it wraps himself in formations that cause rebirth, just as a silkworm wraps itself in its own silk threads. Consciousness, seized by formations, finds a footing in the destinies, just as a prince seized by a minister finds a footing in the kingdom. Consciousness, through imagining the sign of rebirth, brings about various kinds of mentality-materiality at the moment of rebirth-linking, just as a magician displays an illusion. The six sense bases, established in mentality-materiality, reach growth, increase, and full development, just as a forest thicket established on good soil. Contact arises from the impact of the sense bases, just as fire arises from the friction of the fire-drill and its base. Feeling manifests in one touched by contact, just as burning occurs in one touched by fire. Craving increases in one who feels, just as thirst increases in one who drinks salt water. One who is thirsty with craving longs for existences, just as a thirsty person longs for water. That longing itself is his clinging. Through clinging, he grasps existence, just as a fish seizes a hook out of greed for bait. When there is existence, there is birth, just as when there is a seed, there is a sprout. When there is birth, there is inevitably aging and death, just as when there is a tree, it must fall.

In another way, the Blessed One, referring to the depth of meaning, depth of phenomena, depth of teaching, and depth of penetration, taught: 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is deep and it appears deep.' Therefore, the Wheel of Existence should also be understood by way of the various modes of depth. Among those four kinds of depth, it is not that aging and death do not occur because of birth (indeed, they do occur).
187: It is like the falling of a tree that has arisen. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence (Bhavacakka) should be understood through appropriate similes. The Blessed One, referring to its depth in terms of meaning (attha), law (dhamma), teaching (desanā), and penetration (paṭivedha), said: 'Deep, indeed, Ānanda, is this Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and deep it appears.' Therefore, this Wheel of Existence should be understood through its various aspects of depth as appropriate. Among those four, it is not that aging-and-death does not occur because of birth, nor does it occur due to other causes without birth. Thus, aging-and-death arises sequentially because of birth. Because this nature of sequential arising due to the cause of birth is difficult to understand, the nature of aging-and-death arising from the cause of birth is deep. Similarly, the nature of birth arising from the cause of becoming... and formations arising from the cause of ignorance is deep. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence is called 'Attha-gambhīra' (Depth of Meaning). This is how it is Attha-gambhīra. The result of a cause is called 'Attha'. 'Knowledge of the result of a cause is Attha-paṭisambhidā' (Analytical Knowledge of Meaning) as it is said. In whatever manner and at whatever moment ignorance is the cause of various formations, because that manner is difficult to understand, the nature of ignorance being the cause of formations is deep. Similarly, the nature of formations... and birth being the cause of aging-and-death is deep. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence is called 'Dhamma-gambhīra' (Depth of Law). This is how it is Dhamma-gambhīra. The cause is named 'Dhamma'. 'Knowledge of the cause is Dhamma-paṭisambhidā' (Analytical Knowledge of Law) as it is said. Because it is taught in various ways due to various reasons, the teaching (desanā) of this Dependent Origination is also deep. In that teaching, no knowledge other than Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) can find a footing. That teaching is taught in some discourses in forward order (anuloma), in some in reverse order (paṭiloma), in some in both forward and reverse orders, in some starting from the middle in either forward or reverse order, in some with three connections and four groups (tisandhi catusaṅkhepa), in some with two connections and three groups (dvisandhi tisaṅkhepa), and in some with one connection and two groups (ekasandhi dvasaṅkhepa). Therefore, this Wheel of Existence is called 'Desanā-gambhīra' (Depth of Teaching). This is how it is Desanā-gambhīra. In this Wheel of Existence, there is a certain nature of ignorance and so on; by penetrating that nature, states such as ignorance are penetrated according to their own characteristics. Because that nature is difficult to delve into, it is deep. Therefore, this Wheel of Existence is called 'Paṭivedha-gambhīra' (Depth of Penetration). To elaborate on that—in this Wheel of Existence, the nature of ignorance, which is unknowing, non-seeing, and non-penetration of the Truths, is deep. The nature of formations—their constructing, their accumulating of causes, their being with lust, and their being without lust—is deep. The nature of consciousness—its emptiness of self, its lack of agency (byāpāra), and its manifestation at the moment of rebirth-linking without migrating from one life to another—is deep. The nature of name-and-form—their arising together, their being distinct, their being indistinct, their inclining towards an object, and their being subject to change—is deep.
188: The nature of ignorance—its unknowing, its non-seeing, and its non-penetration of the Four Noble Truths—is deep. The nature of formations—their constructing, their accumulating and grasping of causes, their being with lust, and their being without lust—is deep. The nature of consciousness—its emptiness of self, its lack of agency (byāpāra), and its manifestation at the moment of rebirth-linking without migrating from one life to another—is deep. The nature of name-and-form—their arising together, their being distinct, their being indistinct, their inclining towards an object, and their being subject to change—is deep. The nature of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana)—their being predominant by way of the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya), their being the doors of the world, their being like a field, and their being the basis for objects—is deep. The nature of contact (phassa)—its touching, its impacting, and the meeting and coincidence of the three factors: base, object, and consciousness—is deep. The nature of feeling (vedanā)—its experiencing the flavor of the object, its being pleasant, its being painful, its being neutral, and its experiencing without a living soul—is deep. The nature of craving (taṇhā)—its excessive delighting, its obsessive clinging, its moistening, its being like a creeper, its being like a river, and its being difficult to fill like the ocean of craving—is deep. The nature of clinging (upādāna)—its firm grasping through the four types of clinging, its taking hold of the cords of sensual pleasure, its firm preoccupation, its wrong misapprehension, and its being difficult to overcome—is deep. The nature of becoming (bhava)—its accumulating, its constructing, and its casting into the modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (ṭhiti), and the abodes where beings dwell—is deep. The nature of birth (jāti)—its being the beginning of the aggregates in a single life, its being the source of the sense bases, its descending, its being produced, and its manifestation—is deep. The nature of aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa)—its exhausting, its decaying, its breaking up, and its changing—is deep. This is the depth of penetration (paṭivedha-gambhīratā) in this Wheel of Existence. Since there are four methods of interpretation (naya) in this Wheel of Existence, namely: the Method of Unity (Ekattanaya), the Method of Diversity (Nānattanaya), the Method of Non-agency (Abyāpāranaya), and the Method of Natural Law (Evaṃdhammatānaya), this Wheel of Existence should be understood through these various methods as appropriate. Among these methods, 'the Method of Unity' (Ekattanaya) refers to the non-interruption of the continuum of mind and matter, like a seed reaching the state of a tree through the state of a sprout and so on, in the manner: 'With ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be.' One who sees this method correctly abandons the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) because of the understanding of the non-interruption of the continuum proceeding through the connection of cause and effect. One who sees it wrongly clings to the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) because of grasping as a unity the non-interruption of the continuum proceeding through the connection of cause and effect. 'The Method of Diversity' (Nānattanaya) refers to the defining of ignorance and so on according to their respective characteristics. One who sees this method correctly abandons the view of eternalism because of seeing the arising of ever-new phenomena. One who sees it wrongly clings to the view of annihilation because of grasping as diverse—as if they were separate continua—those things that fall within a single continuum. 'The Method of Non-agency' (Abyāpāranaya) refers to the absence of such effort (byāpāra) as 'I must produce formations' in ignorance, or 'Consciousness must be produced by us' in formations. One who sees this method correctly abandons the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi) because of the understanding of the absence of a doer (kāraka). One who sees it wrongly clings to the view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi) because of not grasping the causal status established by the natural law of ignorance and so on, even in the absence of effort. 'The Method of Natural Law' (Evaṃdhammatānaya) refers to the fact that only formations and so on arise from causes such as ignorance and so on, just as curd arises from milk and so on, and not other things. One who correctly...
189:
One who sees the effect in accordance with the cause abandons the view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi) and the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi). But one who sees wrongly, not grasping the occurrence of the effect in accordance with the cause, but grasping the impossibility of a certain effect from a certain cause, clings to the view of non-causality and the doctrine of fatalism (niyatavāda). Thus, this wheel of becoming—

By way of the truths from which they arise, and by way of function,
By way of prevention, and by way of similes,
And by way of the variety of profound methods,
It should be understood as is appropriate.

This wheel of becoming is bottomless due to its profundity and difficult to overcome because it must be grasped through various methods.

Without breaking this wheel of becoming—
Which, like a thunderbolt, is constantly crushing and churning—
There is no one, even in a dream,
Who has transcended the danger of saṃsāra.

And this was said by the Blessed One: "Ananda, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound. Ananda, because of not understanding and not penetrating this Dhamma [with full understanding of the known, full understanding by investigation, and full understanding by abandoning], this generation has become like a tangled ball of thread, like a bird's nest, like muñja grass and rushes, and does not transcend the four planes of misery, the unhappy destination, the ruinous state, and saṃsāra." Therefore, a wise person who strives for his own welfare or the welfare of others, should set aside other tasks and constantly strive with mindfulness to gain a foothold in the profound distinctions of dependent origination.

## Description of the Suttanta Classification

## 2. Description of the Abhidhamma Classification

Thus, the Teacher, whose knowledge is unimpeded in all things, as if spreading out the great earth or expanding the sky, having shown the untangled dependent origination in the Suttanta classification by way of various consciousnesses, now, because this dependent origination occurs not only in various consciousnesses but also in a single consciousness, [shows] the dependent origination occurring in a single mind-moment by way of the Abhidhamma classification...
190:
To show the Dependent Origination (paccaya-ākāra) occurring in a single thought-moment in various ways, the Matrix (mātikā) was first established starting with the method 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro). In the Matrix thus established:

There are nine methods with nine root terms starting with ignorance and so forth. In those methods, the tetrads (catukka) and the different cycles (vāra) should be shown.

The explanation in this verse is as follows: In this Matrix, by means of the nine root terms starting with ignorance—namely, ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name, the sixth sense-base, contact, feeling, craving, and clinging—there are nine methods: the method starting with ignorance, the method starting with volitional formations, the method starting with consciousness, the method starting with name, the method starting with the sixth sense-base, the method starting with contact, the method starting with feeling, the method starting with craving, and the method starting with clinging.

Among those nine methods, in the first method starting with ignorance, there are four tetrads: the tetrad of conditions (paccaya-catukka), the tetrad of causes (hetu-catukka), the tetrad of the associated (sampayutta-catukka), and the tetrad of mutuality (aññamañña-catukka). Just as there are four tetrads in this method starting with ignorance, so too are there in the remaining eight methods; thus, by way of four tetrads in each method, there are thirty-six tetrads in total. Among those thirty-six tetrads, since four cycles are included in each tetrad, by way of four tetrads, there are sixteen cycles in each method, making a total of one hundred and forty-four cycles.

## 1. The Tetrad of Conditions (Paccaya-catukka)

Among those four tetrads, in the tetrad of conditions within the very first method rooted in ignorance, the first cycle is called the twelve-factored cycle associated with two incomplete factors, because 'name' is stated in the place of 'name-and-form' and 'the sixth sense-base' is stated in the place of 'the six sense-bases'. The second cycle is called the eleven-factored cycle associated with one incomplete factor, because only 'name' is stated in the place of 'name-and-form' and no base is stated in the place of 'the six sense-bases'. The third cycle is called the twelve-factored cycle associated with one incomplete factor, because 'the sixth sense-base' is stated in the place of 'the six sense-bases'. The fourth cycle, however, is simply the complete twelve-factored cycle.

In this tetrad, there might be a question: "Is this cycle also associated with one incomplete factor because it is stated 'with the sixth sense-base as condition, contact arises'?" No, it is not so, because that sixth sense-base is not a factor (aṅga). Here, only contact is a factor, not the sixth sense-base. Therefore, because that sixth sense-base is not a factor, this fourth cycle is not one associated with an incomplete factor. In the Commentary, however, it is stated: "The first cycle is by way of universal inclusion, the second by way of specific conditions, the third by way of beings in the womb, the fourth..."
191:
(The fourth cycle) is taken by way of beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika). Likewise, the first cycle is taken in the sense of being all-inclusive (sabba-saṅgāhika); the second, in the sense of specific conditions (paccaya-visesa); the third, by way of incomplete sense bases (aparipuṇṇāyatana); and the fourth, by way of complete sense bases (paripuṇṇāyatana). Similarly, the first is taken as all-inclusive; the second, by way of the Mahānidāna Sutta; the third, by way of the fine-material plane of existence (rūpabhava); and the fourth, by way of the sensual plane of existence (kāmabhava) (so say the former teachers).

Among these four cycles, the first cycle is not excluded from any of the other three cycles, starting from the second; therefore, it is called "all-inclusive" (sabba-saṅgāhika). The distinction of the remaining cycles will become clear later. For the sake of making that distinction clear:

Whatever is stated differently in a certain cycle [from the Suttanta-bhājanīya method], and whatever is not stated in a certain cycle;
How a certain condition assists a certain effect—all that should be noted.

In this verse, this is the method: First, without distinction, in all four cycles, it is stated as "saṅkhāro" (formation—singular) instead of "saṅkhārā" (formations—plural) as in the Suttanta-bhājanīya. Why is it stated thus? Because it occurs in a single mind-moment (eka-cittakkhaṇika). In the Suttanta-bhājanīya, Dependent Origination occurring in various mind-moments is analyzed. In this [Abhidhamma-bhājanīya] method, Dependent Origination occurring in a single mind-moment is undertaken. In a single mind-moment, there are not many volitions (cetanā); therefore, it is stated as "saṅkhāro" and not "saṅkhārā."

In the first cycle, because of the inclusion of states belonging to a single mind-moment and because of being common to all places, matter (rūpa) is excluded and it is stated only as "viññāṇapaccayā nāmaṃ" (with consciousness as condition, mentality). That mentality belongs to a single mind-moment and is common to all places; it is not the case that it does not occur in any place where consciousness arises. Since contact (phassa) belonging to a single mind-moment is only one in this first cycle, wishing to take the sense base that is the appropriate condition for that contact, in the place of the sixfold sense base, only the single mind-base is stated as "nāmapapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ" (with mentality as condition, the sixth sense base). This is because that mind-base (manāyatana) is the appropriate condition for a single unwholesome contact. Although this state [the mind-base] is indeed already stated in the factor "saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ," it is taken again here [in "nāmapapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ"] for the sake of showing the distinction between cause and fruit, and for the sake of the completeness of the factors. In that [former factor], formation is the cause specifically, and mentality is the fruit generally. But here, mentality is the cause generally, and contact is the fruit specifically.

States such as sorrow (soka) and so on are not included because they cannot all occur in a single mind-moment, and they do not occur in every place where mind arises (existence) or in every mind. Birth, aging, and death (jāti, jarā, maraṇa), although they do not have the duration of even a single mind-moment, are included because they are contained within the mind-moment...
192:
(Birth, aging, and death) are taken to complete the twelve factors. Thus, in this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method, one should first understand what is stated in a different way and what is not stated.

The meaning of what is stated in the cycles following this first cycle should be understood just as stated in the Suttanta-bhājanīya. If any specific distinction appears in a particular cycle, I shall explain that distinction in its respective place.

In the passage "In what way is what state a condition for what state?", ignorance (avijjā) is a condition for formation (saṅkhāra) in seven ways: by the six conditions shared with associated states—conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata)—and by the root-cause condition (hetu-paccaya). Among those seven conditions, since the three tetrads starting with the root-cause tetrad (hetu-catukka) are stated later by way of non-disappearance, association, and mutuality conditions, here, having removed those three conditions, it should be understood that ignorance is a condition for formation in four ways by the power of the remaining conditions.

Formation is a condition for consciousness in eight ways: by the six shared conditions and by kamma and nutriment (āhāra) conditions. But here, removing those same three, it is in five ways. Consciousness is a condition for mentality in nine ways: by the six shared conditions and by faculty (indriya), nutriment, and predominance (adhipati) conditions. But here, removing the three, it is in six ways. Mentality is a condition for the sixth sense base in many ways: by the six shared conditions; and here, some mentality by predominance condition, some by nutriment condition, and so on. But here, removing those same three, it is in three, four, or five ways. The sixth sense base is to contact as consciousness is to mentality. Likewise, contact is a condition for feeling in seven ways: by the six shared conditions and by nutriment condition. But here, removing those same three, it is in four ways. Feeling is a condition for craving in eight ways: by the six shared conditions and by jhāna and faculty conditions. But here, removing those same three, it is in five ways. Craving is to clinging as ignorance is to formation. Likewise, clinging is a condition for existence in seven ways: by the six shared conditions and by path (magga) condition. But here, removing those same three, it is in four ways. In the case of existence being a condition for birth, since "birth" (jāti) here is intended as "arising" (uppāda), which is a characteristic of the conditioned (saṅkhata), it is a condition only by way of decisive support (upanissaya) in a figurative sense (pariyāyena). Likewise, birth is a condition for aging and death.

As for those teachers who say: "In this tetrad, ignorance and so on are conditions for formation and so on by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) only. For the first cycle was undertaken solely by way of conascence condition"—to those [teachers], the absence of such [conascence] in existence and so on, and the [nature] of the remaining conditions...
193:
The possibility (of conditions other than the co-nascence condition) is shown, and (the views of those teachers) are rejected. For becoming is not a co-nascence condition for birth, nor is birth a co-nascence condition for aging and death. Those conditions other than the co-nascence condition for volitional formations and so forth, which have been taught (in the Paṭṭhāna), are indeed possible. Therefore, they should not be discarded. In this way, in the first cycle, whatever is stated differently in a particular place, or whatever is not stated in a particular place, and how a certain cause becomes a condition for a certain effect—all this should be understood. The same method applies to the second cycle and others.

However, there is this distinction: In the second cycle, after saying "with name as condition, contact," nothing is stated in the place of the six sense bases. For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of showing the specific condition of contact and for the purpose of including the teaching of the Mahānidāna Sutta. Indeed, not only the sixth sense base (mind-base) is a condition for contact; the three (mental) aggregates, such as the feeling aggregate, are also conditions. In the Mahānidāna Sutta as well, it was said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, if it is asked, 'Is there contact due to this condition?' the answer should be 'There is.' If it is asked, 'Due to what condition is there contact?' the answer should be 'With name as condition, contact.'" Thus, omitting the six sense bases, the Dependent Origination with eleven factors is taught. Therefore, for the purpose of showing this specific condition of contact and for the purpose of including the teaching of this Mahānidāna Sutta, in the second cycle, after saying "with name as condition, contact," nothing is stated in the place of the six sense bases. This is the distinction in the second cycle.

In the third cycle, however, the fourth factor, which has already appeared in the Suttanta-bhājanīya as "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," is taught. If it is objected that this fourth factor is inappropriate in this (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya) method because Dependent Origination (here) consists of a single thought-moment, it is not inappropriate (it is appropriate). Why? Because it exists as a condition that can assist in its own moment. In fact, although within that group of name-and-form, form lasts longer than a thought-moment, that consciousness is still a condition for that form in its own moment. How? Firstly, it is a condition for the form produced by consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) that arose earlier, or for other forms, by way of post-nascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). This has been taught (in the Paṭṭhāna): "Post-nascent states of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of post-nascent condition." But for the form produced by consciousness that is simultaneous, it is a condition by way of support condition (nissaya-paccaya). As it is said: "States of consciousness and mental factors are a condition for forms produced by consciousness by way of support condition."
194:
If so, why was it not stated like this (as "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form") in the previous cycles? It is because it was taught with reference to the realm (plane) where forms arise. This teaching of Dependent Origination is taught in terms of womb-born beings in the sense-sphere, spontaneously born beings with incomplete sense bases, and the Fine-material sphere Brahmas. Therefore, in this context, instead of saying "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," it is stated as "the sixth sense base." Therein, "name" is according to the method already mentioned. "Form" should be understood as the heart-base (hadaya-rūpa). That heart-base assists that sixth sense base in two ways: by way of support condition and pre-nascent condition. This is the distinction in the third cycle.

The fourth cycle is taught in terms of spontaneously born beings by way of birth (yoni), those with complete sense bases by way of sense bases, and sense-sphere beings by way of becoming (bhava). Therefore, in this context, it is stated as "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases." Therein, "name" assists the sixth sense base by way of co-nascence and other conditions, and assists the eye-base and so forth by way of post-nascent condition. In "form," the heart-base assists the sixth sense base by way of support and pre-nascent conditions, and the four great elements assist the eye-base and so forth by way of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Since this fourth cycle is Dependent Origination occurring within a single thought-moment, instead of saying "with the six sense bases as condition," it is stated as "with the sixth sense base as condition, contact." This is the distinction in the fourth cycle.

Having understood the differences between these cycles, it should be further understood that among all of them, the first two cycles are specifically taught to show the occurrence of Dependent Origination in the formless realm (arūpabhava). In the formless realm, the factors of Dependent Origination occur unmixed with form. The third cycle is taught to show the occurrence of Dependent Origination in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava). In the fine-material realm, although there is a mixture with form, the (full) six sense bases do not occur. The fourth cycle is taught to show the occurrence of Dependent Origination in the sense-sphere realm (kāmabhava). For in the sense-sphere realm, all six sense bases occur. Alternatively, the third cycle is taught with reference to the moment of the occurrence of unwholesome states for those with incomplete sense bases in both the fine-material and sense-sphere realms. Alternatively, the fourth cycle is taught for those with complete sense bases in the sense-sphere realm. Alternatively, the first cycle is taught with reference to its universality in all places where consciousness occurs. For that first cycle does not fail to occur in any place where consciousness arises. The second cycle is taught with reference to a specific condition. In this second cycle, the presence of eleven factors and the fact that name is a condition for contact is the specific condition. The third cycle is taught with reference to the first two types of birth (egg-born and womb-born). For that cycle occurs in those first two births, where the six sense bases do not always occur. The fourth cycle is taught with reference to the last two types of birth (moisture-born and spontaneously born). For that cycle occurs in those last two births, where the six sense bases always occur.
195:
By this much sequence of words, the explanation of the meaning of the verse already stated in the four cycles (vāra) has been made:

"Whatever is stated differently in a certain place, and whatever is not stated in a certain place, and in what way a thing is a condition for another, all that should be noted."

Following this explanation of the meaning, in the subsequent tetrads (catukka) from this method, one should understand the whole of this method as well as any specific distinction if there is one.

## 2. Hetucatukkaṃ

Among the subsequent tetrads, the method stated here in the Paccayacatukka is evident everywhere. However, the distinction should be understood as follows: In the Hetucatukka, first, because ignorance (avijjā) is the cause of those formations (saṅkhāra), it is called "avijjāhetuka" (caused by ignorance). This means there is ignorance that exists and follows until the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga) because of its co-existence with those formations. By the words "avijjāpaccayā" (conditioned by ignorance), it is shown generally that ignorance is a condition for formations by way of conascence (sahajāta) and so on. Then, by the word "avijjāhetuko" itself, the state of being a non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) is shown specifically. In the passages such as "viññāṇaṃ saṅkhārahetukaṃ" (consciousness caused by formations), the method is the same.

Why is the term "hetuka" not included and taught in the factors starting with becoming (bhava)? It is because for becoming, the non-disappearance condition is not constant, and for birth etc., the non-disappearance condition is entirely absent. Because it is taught: "Among those, what is becoming conditioned by clinging (upādāna)? Excluding clinging, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—this is called becoming conditioned by clinging." Therefore, here, the four mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) conditioned by clinging are named "bhava". In the aggregate of formations, birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa) are included because of the words such as "birth is included within two aggregates".

Among those—becoming, birth, aging, and death—as long as there is clinging, birth, aging, and death cannot be obtained; therefore, clinging cannot always be a non-disappearance condition for becoming. Because of the words such as "whatever is the birth of those various phenomena," among the conditioned characteristics (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa), at the moment of birth, the portion of becoming called aging and death does not exist; therefore, birth cannot be a non-disappearance condition for aging and death. Similarly, at the moment of aging and death, birth does not exist...
196:
...because of its absence. Indeed, becoming is a condition for birth, and birth for aging and death, only by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Thus, it should be understood that because the non-disappearance condition is not constant in every way, and because the non-disappearance condition is entirely absent, the term "hetuka" (referring to the non-disappearance condition) is not included in the factors such as becoming.

Some teachers, however, say: Because of the teaching "becoming is of two kinds," kamma-becoming (kammabhava) is mixed with process-becoming (upapattibhava). Since clinging cannot be a non-disappearance condition for process-becoming, it is not taught as "upādānapaccayā bhavo upādānahetuko" but only as "upādānapaccayā bhavo". They say that because the term "hetuka" is discontinued here, it is not mentioned later either. That statement is inappropriate because here, becoming mixed with process-becoming is not intended. This is because here, only the mental aggregates are intended as becoming.

In this Pali "bhavapaccayā jāti" (conditioned by becoming, birth), it should be understood that becoming, excluding birth, aging, and death, is the condition for birth. Why? Because birth and so on are not conditions for a subsequent birth. If that is so, should it not be taught that becoming, excluding birth, aging, and death, is the condition for birth? Indeed, it should be so taught, but it is not taught because there is no specific place (in the Pali text) to state it. In the exposition of the tenth factor (bhava), becoming arising from clinging should be taught in detail. In the exposition of the eleventh factor (jāti), birth should be taught. As for the becoming that is the condition for birth, there is no specific place to teach it in detail, so it is not taught. Even though it is not taught, it should be accepted by way of logic. In the Pali passages such as "viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ," because consciousness and so on can be non-disappearance conditions, the terms such as "viññāṇahetuka" are used. This is the distinction in the Hetucatukka.

## 3. Sampayuttacatukkaṃ

In the Sampayuttacatukka also, by the words "avijjāpaccayā," it is shown that formations have ignorance as their condition by way of conascence and so on. Then, by the word "avijjā-sampayutto" (associated with ignorance), the state of being an association condition (sampayutta-paccaya) is shown. In the remaining terms also, the method is the same. However, since there is no association of mental phenomena with material phenomena, in the third and fourth cycles of "viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ" etc., only the mental phenomena that can be obtained by the method of "nāma associated with consciousness" etc. are taken. This is the distinction in the Sampayuttacatukka.
197:
## 4. The Tetrad of Mutuality (Aññamaññacatukka)
In the Tetrad of Mutuality as well, by the phrase 'avijjāpaccayā' (conditioned by ignorance), the state of volitional formations having ignorance as a condition by way of conascence and so forth is shown; then, by the phrase 'saṅkhārapaccayāpi avijjā' (ignorance is also conditioned by volitional formations), the state of mutual conditionality is shown. The same method applies to the remaining terms. However, because existence (bhava) is non-residual (nippadesa) and clinging (upādāna) is a partial (sappadesa) state, and while a partial state can be a condition for a non-residual state, a non-residual state cannot be a condition for a partial state, therefore it is not stated here as 'upādāna is also conditioned by bhava'. Alternatively, it is not so stated because the teaching was concluded in the preceding section. Although the sixfold sense base arises because of mind-and-matter, in a single mind-moment, mind-and-matter does not arise because of the sixfold sense base. If the sixfold sense base were a mutual condition, [mind-and-matter would arise]. Therefore, in the fourth section, only what is obtainable—namely, mind and the matter of accumulation (upacayaruūpa)—is taken as 'mind-and-matter is also conditioned by the sixth sense base'. This is the distinction of the Tetrad of Mutuality.

## Matrix of the Method Rooted in Ignorance.

## Matrix of the Method Rooted in Volitional Formations, etc.
Now, the method rooted in volitional formations, "ignorance conditioned by volitional formations," will begin. In this method as well, just as in the method rooted in ignorance, the four tetrads and sixteen sections (vāra) should be understood. In the first tetrad, only the first section is shown, and the teaching is summarized. As in this method rooted in volitional formations, the same applies to the methods rooted in consciousness and so forth. In all those eight methods starting from the one rooted in volitional formations, by the method "ignorance conditioned by volitional formations" and so forth, the state of ignorance having volitional formations and so forth as conditions by way of conascence and so forth is shown; then again, by the method "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" and so forth, the occurrence of the wheel of dependent origination even in a single mind-moment is shown.

Why is the method rooted in existence (bhava) or the method rooted in birth, aging, and death not taught? Is it because ignorance cannot be conditioned by existence? No, it is not that it cannot. However, when "ignorance conditioned by volitional formations" and so forth are taught, not a single state included within existence is left out as a condition for ignorance. Therefore, because there is no further condition for ignorance to be taught anew, the method rooted in existence is not taught. By the term "existence," ignorance is also included. Thus, if "ignorance conditioned by existence" were taught, it would amount to saying "ignorance conditioned by ignorance." In a single mind-moment, however, ignorance...
198:
...is called a condition. Since the teaching was concluded at that point (the term existence), the methods rooted in birth and rooted in aging and death are not taken. Furthermore, birth, aging, and death are also included within existence. These—birth, aging, and death—do not become conditions for ignorance in a single mind-moment. Therefore, the method rooted in existence, or the methods rooted in birth and rooted in aging and death, are not taught.

## Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā).
## Commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome (Akusalaniddesavaṇṇanā)

248-249. Just as in the preceding Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa), the wholesome states were first analyzed in detail according to the order of the matrix established starting with the Wholesome Triad; now, in this (Vibhaṅga on Dependent Origination), since a matrix is not (separately) established, without first considering wholesome states, the Buddha spoke "Which states are unwholesome?" and so forth, in order to show the factors of dependent origination such as ignorance by analyzing them in detail according to the order in which they are established in the matrix by way of unwholesome states as "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance." The meaning of those words should be understood in the same way as stated in the preceding Section on the Arising of Consciousness. However, since craving and clinging to sense pleasures (kāmupādāna) cannot occur in a single mind-moment, in this context, to show only that clinging which is obtainable through craving (such as clinging to views), He taught "view, the resort to views" and so forth.

In the exposition of existence (bhava), since clinging is included within the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), He taught "excluding clinging: the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, the aggregate of consciousness." Only when taught in this way does clinging not come to be the condition for clinging itself. This is because a state cannot be its own condition. In the expositions of birth and so forth, because these are the birth and so forth of mental states (nāmadhamma), it is not stated as "broken teeth, graying hair, wrinkled skin, decease, passing away."

Having thus concluded the first section, again in the second section, at the very same time when the mode of conditionality was shown by the first section, the teaching was given by way of the method "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" and so forth at that same time, without stating a separate section on the determination of the occasion (samayavavatthānavāra), in order to show the mode of conditionality by another method as well. In that teaching, the phrase "excluding contact" was spoken for the purpose of extracting contact from "mind" (nāma), because contact is also included within mind.
199:
In the third cycle, consciousness conditions mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). When that mind-produced matter arises, because the growth of karma-produced matter such as the eye base (cakkhāyatana), which is supported by that mind-produced matter, is evident, it is stated as "the growth of the eye base," and so on. It is also stated thus because consciousness conditions the karma-produced matter (kammaja-rūpa) existing at that time through the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). In that passage (concerning the growth of the eye base, etc.), although only the two lineages of karma-produced and mind-produced matter are taken, the remaining two lineages (temperature-produced and nutriment-produced) should also be taken. This is because consciousness is indeed a condition for those lineages of matter as well.

In the fourth cycle, however, even within a single thought-moment, the eye base and others arise due to the condition of the great primary elements (mahābhūta-rūpa); the sixth base (manāyatana) arises due to the condition of the heart-base (hadaya-rūpa); and all matter arises appropriately through the power of conditions such as post-nascence and co-nascence due to the condition of name (nāma). Therefore, in that cycle, it is stated: "What is 'sixfold sense base conditioned by name-and-form'? It is the eye base," and so on.

In the second tetrad, the entire explanation is clear.

In the third tetrad, in order to show separately that which does not have the state of being conditioned by consciousness through association (matter) and that which does (name), it is stated: "Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness; name is associated with consciousness," and so on.

In the fourth tetrad, in the designation of name conditioned by contact, although it is not explicitly stated as "excluding contact, the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate—this is called name conditioned by contact," yet, because it was already stated in the explanation of the preceding term "contact conditioned by name" as "excluding contact, the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate," it is considered as stated even if not repeated here. This is because just as the name excluding contact is a condition for contact, contact is also a condition for that same name.

Just as this first method rooted in ignorance (avijjā-mūlaka), consisting of sixteen cycles and four tetrads, is illustrated for this first unwholesome consciousness, so too should the other eight methods rooted in formations (saṅkhāra-mūlaka), etc., be understood. The Pali text, however, is shown only in brief. Thus, it should be understood that in that first unwholesome consciousness alone, there are nine methods, thirty-six tetrads, and one hundred and forty-four cycles.

Now, in order to show the mode of conditions in the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses by this same method, the text begins with "Which states are unwholesome?" and so on. Therein, because in consciousnesses disconnected from wrong view (diṭṭhivippayutta) there is no clinging (upādāna) conditioned by craving (taṇhā), in the place of the Pali for clinging, clinging is...
200:
...the passage is filled by resolve (adhimokkha), which habitually descends firmly upon the object, just like clinging. In consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure (domanassa-sahagata), since there is no craving conditioned by feeling, the passage is filled by aversion (paṭigha), which is a powerful defilement, just as craving would be in the place of craving. In the place of clinging, it is filled by resolve (adhimokkha) itself.

In consciousness associated with doubt (vicikicchā-sampayutta), since there is no decision, there is also no resolve; therefore, in the place of craving, the passage is filled by doubt (vicikicchā), which is a powerful defilement. The place for clinging is simply omitted. In consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sampayutta), since resolve exists, the passage is filled by restlessness (uddhacca), which is a powerful defilement, in the place of craving. In the place of clinging, it is filled by resolve itself. In all instances, the Pali text is abbreviated, showing only the distinctions. In these shown distinctions, only the description of resolve (adhimokkha-niddesa) is new. The rest of the arrangement has already appeared below.

In the description of resolve, it is called 'adhimokkha' by virtue of deciding or plunging into. Or, the mind reaches a decision on the object by means of that state, being free from doubt; thus it is 'adhimokkha'. The mode of deciding is 'adhimuccanā'. It is called 'tadadhimuttatā' because of the state of that mind being resolved, or being resolved upon that object. In all these consciousnesses, the distinctions of methods, tetrads, and cycles should be understood by the same method stated for the first consciousness. However, in consciousness associated with doubt, because the method rooted in clinging is absent, there are 8 methods, 32 tetrads, and 128 cycles.

## Commentary on the Description of Unwholesome States

## Commentary on the Description of Wholesome States

Now, in order to show the mode of conditions in wholesome consciousnesses and so on by this same method, the text begins with "Which states are wholesome?" and so on. However, unlike in the unwholesome states where the matrix (mātika) was laid down first and the description (niddesa) followed, it is not done so here. Why? Because differences must occur in the conclusion cycle (appanā-vāra). For in mundane wholesome states and others, because those states are included within the truth of suffering, the conclusion (appanā) is "thus is the [arising] of this entire mass of suffering." But in supramundane wholesome states and others, the conclusion is "thus is the [arising] of these states." Therefore, since it is not possible to set down a common matrix here, the description is made only after specifying the matrix for each of those respective wholesome states and others.

In that description of wholesome states, since ignorance (avijjā) does not exist together with wholesome formations (saṅkhāra) in a single thought-moment, that ignorance is not mentioned; instead, just as ignorance is mentioned as the root of unwholesome states, so too the wholesome root (kusala-mūla) is mentioned as the root of wholesome states.
201: Because of the absence of craving and clinging, in the place of craving, pasāda (the clarity of faith) is mentioned, which enters and sinks into the object like craving; and in the place of clinging, adhimokkha (decision) is mentioned, which falls firmly upon the object like clinging. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as the method stated below.  ## Explanation of the Exposition on the Wholesome (Kusalatidddesavaṇṇanā)  ## Explanation of the Exposition on the Indeterminate (Abyākataniddesavaṇṇanā)  The indeterminate (abyākata) is analyzed according to the sequence of the Pali text found in the Section on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) below. In all cycles, the methods rooted in ignorance are omitted. Why? Because there is nothing suitable to be placed in the position of ignorance. In wholesome consciousness, there is a wholesome root to be placed in the position of ignorance, but in eye-consciousness and so on, there is none. In rooted (sahetuka) consciousness, although there is [a root], it is not taken there in the indeterminate because it has been cut off here in eye-consciousness and so on. It should be understood that the teaching is given as it falls into the stream of the teaching on the fivefold consciousness.  Specifically, here in this exposition on the indeterminate, in consciousness such as eye-consciousness, the positions of craving and clinging are omitted. Why? Because there is no powerful state suitable for the position of craving, and because of the absence of adhimokkha. In the remaining rootless (ahetuka) consciousness, only the position of craving is omitted. In rooted consciousness, however, because pasāda (faith) is present, the factor is filled with pasāda in the position of craving. Thus, in this exposition on the indeterminate, in eye-consciousness and so on, which are results of wholesome and unwholesome actions, six methods each should be understood: those rooted in volitional formations, consciousness, name, the six sense-bases, contact, and feeling. In the remaining rootless consciousness, there are seven methods each, including the one rooted in adhimokkha. In rooted consciousness, there are eight methods each, including the one rooted in pasāda.  In that exposition on the indeterminate, even in eye-consciousness and so on, only the first cycle of the four tetrads is taught. Although the second cycle is obtainable by way of the specific condition, it is not taught. The third and fourth cycles are not taught simply because they are impossible. This is because those cycles are mixed with matter (rūpa), and eye-consciousness and so on cannot produce matter. Just as two cycles are obtained in the first tetrad, so it is in the remaining tetrads. Therefore, although the second cycle in the first tetrad and the two cycles each in the remaining tetrads are not explicitly taught, they should be understood as being taught. In the remaining rootless indeterminate consciousness, all cycles in all tetrads can be obtained. However, because they are cut off here, they are not taken further; the teaching is given as it falls into the stream of the teaching on the fivefold consciousness.
202:
In the remaining resultant consciousnesses with roots (sahetuka-vipāka), the method is the same, except for the immaterial-sphere resultants (arūpāvacara-vipāka). For in the immaterial-sphere resultants, only two cycles (vāra) are obtained.

## Explanation of the Description of the Indeterminate

## Explanation of the Description of the Wholesome with Ignorance as Root

Now, in order to show the mode of conditions in a single mind-moment by another method, the text begins again with "Which states are wholesome?" (katame dhammā kusalā), etc. Therein, "conditioned by ignorance" (avijjāpaccaya) is said with reference to the state of being a condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya-satti). Therefore, in the Section of Description (niddesavāra), without analyzing ignorance by asking "Therein, what is ignorance?", it analyzes by asking "Therein, what is the formation conditioned by ignorance?". This is because only the formation (saṅkhāra), known as wholesome volition (kusala-cetanā), arises together with the consciousness at that moment, not ignorance.

Therein, for mundane wholesome states, ignorance is a condition by the method already stated below in the Suttanta Classification (Suttantabhājanīya). However, since a person with unabandoned ignorance develops the supramundane path for the sake of abandoning ignorance, it is also a condition for that supramundane state by way of overcoming that ignorance. For the striving for the wholesome occurs only for one with ignorance, not for the other [the Arahant]. Therein, in the wholesome states of the three planes, striving is obtained both by way of delusion and by way of the development that leads to overcoming. In the supramundane, it is obtained by way of the development that leads to total eradication. The rest of the arrangement is just as already stated.

This, however, is the distinction: just as below, in each wholesome state, nine sets of sixteen (soḷasaka) were obtained by the power of the four tetrads, they are not obtained here. Why? Because ignorance does not assist the wholesome formation by way of non-disappearance (avigata), association (sampayutta), and mutuality (aññamañña) conditions. Here, only the first tetrad is obtained by the power of decisive support (upanissaya). Even that is summarized by showing only the first cycle (vāra). Nevertheless, it should be presented in detail.

## Explanation of the Description of the Wholesome with Ignorance as Root

## Explanation of the Description of the Resultant with Wholesome Roots

Now, in order to show the mode of conditions in indeterminate states also by another method, the text begins with "Which states are indeterminate?" (katame dhammā abyākatā), etc. Therein, the phrase "conditioned by wholesome roots" (kusalamūlapaccayā) is also said with reference to the state of being a condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya-satti). For the wholesome resultant...
203:
The wholesome root is a condition for wholesome resultants and unwholesome resultants by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Regarding the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya), there is nothing further to be said. Therefore, this wholesome root is a condition by way of both decisive support condition and asynchronous kamma condition. For this very reason, in the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra), without specifically analyzing "What is the wholesome root?", it was analyzed as "What is the volitional formation (saṅkhāra) caused by the wholesome root?" The same method applies to unwholesome resultants.

Just as in the exposition of the wholesome rooted in ignorance (avijjā), in this exposition of resultants, the fourfold set of conditions (paccaya-catukka) is first obtained. That fourfold set of conditions is also shown in the first section and then summarized. Therefore, in each resultant consciousness, the distinction of sections should be understood by way of each fourfold set, in the method with wholesome roots and the method with unwholesome roots. However, in functional states (kiriya-dhamma), since neither ignorance nor wholesome and unwholesome roots obtain the status of decisive support condition, it should be noted that the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) is not taught by way of functional states.

In this way—
Having taught in many ways regarding unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate states,
And regarding the resultants of the wholesome and unwholesome by way of decisive support,
The Buddha, the most excellent of speakers, taught the mode of conditions once again in a single way,
For the purpose of producing specific knowledge regarding the distinctions of conditions for states.

For those who are devoid of the sequence of learning (pariyatti), hearing (savana), reflection (cintana), and practice (paṭipatti),
Since specific knowledge in this Dependent Origination never arises,
A wise person should always strive in that Dependent Origination according to the sequence of learning, hearing, reflection, and practice.
There is no other task more worthy of being done in the Dispensation than such striving.

This mode of conditions is shown and analyzed through two rotations by way of the Suttanta classification (Suttanta-bhājanīya) and the Abhidhamma classification (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya).

## 7. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga
## 1. Commentary on the Summary Section of the Suttanta Classification
Now, in this Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga), which follows the Analysis of Dependent Origination, the word "four" is a numerical delimitation. By that word, the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness is shown: they are neither fewer than four nor more than four. "Satipaṭṭhāna" has three types: (1) the object which is the domain of mindfulness (satigocara), (2) the state of the Teacher, the Buddha, transcending resentment and attraction (paṭighānunaya-vītivattatā) towards disciples who practice in three ways, and (3) mindfulness itself.

"Monks, I will teach the origin and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that... Monks, what is the origin of the body? With the origin of nutriment, there is the origin of the body." In such Pali passages, the object which is the domain of mindfulness is called "Satipaṭṭhāna." Likewise, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "The body is the establishment (upaṭṭhāna), but not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness." The meaning of the word Satipaṭṭhāna when taking the object as the essence is: mindfulness stands (patiṭṭhāti) in this object, therefore that object is called paṭṭhāna (foundation/standing place). What stands? Mindfulness stands. The standing place of mindfulness is Satipaṭṭhāna. Alternatively, paṭṭhāna means a principal station. The principal station of mindfulness is Satipaṭṭhāna, like a station for elephants or a station for horses.

"The Blessed One resorts to three foundations of mindfulness, resorting to which the Teacher is worthy of instructing the group of disciples." In this Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, the state of the Buddha transcending resentment and attraction towards disciples who practice in three ways is called Satipaṭṭhāna. The meaning of the word Satipaṭṭhāna there is: it is called paṭṭhāna because it should be set forth (paṭṭhapetabba), meaning it should be set in motion. By what is it set forth? It is set forth by mindfulness. The state set forth by mindfulness is Satipaṭṭhāna.

"The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment." In such Pali passages, mindfulness itself is called Satipaṭṭhāna. The meaning of the word Satipaṭṭhāna there is: it is called paṭṭhāna because it stands firmly in the object. It means it occurs by entering and plunging into the object. Mindfulness itself is Satipaṭṭhāna in the sense of a foundation (paṭṭhāna). Alternatively, it is sati in the sense of remembering the object, and paṭṭhāna in the sense of standing firmly in the object. Thus, because it is both mindfulness and a foundation, it is Satipaṭṭhāna. In this Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga, it is this mindfulness that is intended as Satipaṭṭhāna. If that is so, why is it used in the plural as "foundations of mindfulness"? Because mindfulness is manifold. Indeed, those mindfulnesses are many by way of the distinction of objects.
205:
Why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), neither more nor less? It is for the benefit of those to be disciplined (veneyya). Among those with a craving-inclined temperament (taṇhācarita), a view-inclined temperament (diṭṭhicarita), those who follow the vehicle of calm (samathayānika), and those who follow the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyānika), each is divided into two: the dull-witted (manda) and the sharp-witted (tikkha). For the dull-witted craving-inclined person, the coarse and obvious foundation of mindfulness on the body (kāyānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the sharp-witted, the subtle foundation of mindfulness on feelings (vedanānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the dull-witted view-inclined person, the foundation of mindfulness on the mind (cittānupassanā), which is not overly diversified, is the path to purification; for the sharp-witted, the highly diversified foundation of mindfulness on mental objects (dhammānupassanā) is the path to purification.

For the dull-witted calm-vehicle practitioner, the first foundation of mindfulness, which provides a sign (nimitta) to be attained without difficulty, is the path to purification. For the sharp-witted, because they do not settle on coarse objects, the second foundation of mindfulness is the path to purification. For the dull-witted insight-vehicle practitioner, the third foundation of mindfulness with its not overly diversified objects is the path to purification; for the sharp-witted, the fourth foundation of mindfulness with its highly diversified objects is the path to purification. Thus, exactly four are taught, neither more nor less.

Alternatively, it is for the purpose of abandoning the perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty (subha), pleasure (sukha), permanence (nicca), and self (atta). Although the body is foul (asubha), beings perceive it as beautiful through the perversion of beauty. To abandon that perversion by seeing the foul nature therein, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught. Although feelings and so forth are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self, feelings are actually suffering (dukkha), the mind is impermanent (anicca), and mental objects are non-self (anattā). Beings are distorted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self regarding these. To abandon those perversions by seeing suffering and so forth, the remaining three foundations of mindfulness were taught. Thus, it should be understood that exactly four are taught to abandon the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. Furthermore, it should be understood that four are taught not only to abandon the perversions, but also to abandon the four floods (ogha), the four bonds (yoga), the four taints (āsava), the four ties (gantha), the four types of clinging (upādāna), the four wrong courses (agati), and for the full understanding of the four nutriments (āhāra). This is the method of the treatises (pakaraṇanaya).

In the Commentary (Atthakathā), however, it is stated: "By way of refuge (saraṇa) and by way of convergence into unity (ekattasamosaraṇa), there is only one foundation of mindfulness; but by way of objects (ārammaṇa), there are four." This is illustrated by the following simile: Just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east take goods originating in the east and enter the city through the eastern gate; those coming from the south, west, and north take goods originating in the north and enter the city through the northern gate—this should be understood in the same way. The city is like the great city of Nibbāna; the gate is like the Noble Eightfold Path; and the directions like the east are like the body and so forth.

Just as those coming from the east take goods originating in the east and enter the city through the eastern gate, similarly, yogis who begin with the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) develop it in fourteen ways and, through the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of the body, enter the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the south enter the city through the southern gate, similarly, yogis who begin with the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) develop it in nine ways and, through the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of feelings, enter the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the west enter the city through the western gate, similarly, yogis who begin with the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) develop it in sixteen ways and, through the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of the mind, enter the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the north enter the city through the northern gate, similarly, yogis who begin with the contemplation of mental objects (dhammānupassanā) develop it in five ways and, through the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of mental objects, enter the single Nibbāna. Thus, it should be understood that while the foundation of mindfulness is one by way of refuge and convergence into unity, it is four by way of objects.
206:
Yogis who proceed through the stages of knowledge, taking the contemplation of the body as their starting point, develop the fourteenfold contemplation of the body and, through the Noble Path arisen by the power of developing the contemplation of the body, arrive at the single Nibbāna alone. Just as those coming from the south take goods produced in the southern region and enter the city through the south gate, so too, those who come taking the contemplation of feelings as their starting point develop the ninefold contemplation of feelings and, through the Noble Path arisen by the power of developing the contemplation of feelings, arrive at the single Nibbāna alone. Just as those coming from the west take goods produced in the western region and enter the city through the west gate, so too, those who come taking the contemplation of the mind as their starting point develop the sixteenfold contemplation of the mind and, through the Noble Path arisen by the power of developing the contemplation of the mind, arrive at the single Nibbāna alone. Just as those coming from the north take goods produced in the northern region and enter the city through the north gate, so too, those who come taking the contemplation of phenomena as their starting point develop the fivefold contemplation of phenomena and, through the Noble Path arisen by the power of developing the contemplation of phenomena, arrive at the single Nibbāna alone. Thus, it should be understood that although the foundation of mindfulness is one in terms of refuge (saraṇa) and in terms of converging upon the single Nibbāna (ekattasamosaraṇa), it is said to be fourfold in terms of the objects (ārammaṇa).

In this phrase, \"Here, monks,\" although the Blessed One taught this Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga while residing in the celestial realm, there was not even a single monk seated in the presence of the Blessed One there. Even though there were no monks, he addressed them as \"Here, monks,\" because monks develop these four foundations of mindfulness, as these are the domain of monks. Do only monks develop these foundations of mindfulness, and not bhikkhunīs and others? Bhikkhunīs and others also develop them. However, because monks are the foremost assembly (aggaparisā), he addressed them as \"Here, monks.\" Alternatively, he spoke thus to show the state of being a monk through the practice. Whoever practices this practice is called a monk. Whether it be a deva or a human, one who practices indeed attains the designation of a \"monk.\" Therefore, the Blessed One said:

\"Even if one is adorned, if he practices equanimity,
Is peaceful, tamed, established [in the Path], and celibate,
Having laid aside the stick towards all beings,
He is a Brahmin, he is a Samana, he is a Bhikkhu.\"
208:
It has been said that (the word 'body' is mentioned a second time) for the purpose of showing the breaking down of the compact mass and so forth. In this phrase 'ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ', the meaning of the word 'ādi' (and so forth) should also be understood as follows: This monk dwells contemplating only the body in this physical body, not contemplating other phenomena. What does this mean? Just as people contemplate water in a mirage even though it is not water, so too, one does not dwell contemplating permanence, happiness, self, and beauty in this body which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Rather, it means that by contemplating the body, one dwells contemplating only the collection of aspects such as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.

Alternatively, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, it is said: "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest... he breathes out mindfully," and so forth, describing the body from the breath and the inward breath to the collection of bones. Also, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said: "Here, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent; likewise the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, the hair-body, the body-hair-body, the outer-skin-body, the inner-skin-body, the flesh-body, the blood-body, the tendon-body, the bone-body, and the marrow-body." Because of contemplating all these types of bodies within this very physical body, the meaning should be understood as 'kāye kāyānupassī' (contemplating the body in the body).

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as 'kāyānupassī' (contemplating the body) in the body, which is a collection of various phenomena such as hair and body hair, because one does not contemplate anything that could be taken as "I" or "mine" in the body, but contemplates only the collection of various phenomena like hair, body hair, and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning should be understood as 'kāye kāyānupassī' because of contemplating the body, which is defined as a collection of aspects such as the characteristic of impermanence, following the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "In this body, one contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent," and so forth.

To elaborate further: This bhikkhu who has entered upon the practice of contemplation of the body contemplates this physical body as impermanent, not as permanent, by virtue of the seven types of contemplation such as the contemplation of impermanence. He contemplates it as suffering, not as happiness. He contemplates it as non-self, not as self. He becomes disenchanted, not delighted. He becomes dispassionate, not lustful. He causes cessation, not arising. He relinquishes, not grasps. As he contemplates that physical body as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence. As he contemplates it as suffering, he abandons the perception of happiness. As he contemplates it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self...
209:
...he abandons the perception of self. When he is disenchanted, he abandons delight (nandi). When he is dispassionate, he abandons lust (rāga). When he causes cessation, he abandons arising (samudaya). When he relinquishes, he abandons grasping (ādāna). This should be understood (as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

The word 'viharati' (dwells) merely indicates being engaged in one of the four postures. It means that he carries and maintains the individual existence (attabhāva) so that it does not fall, by interrupting the discomfort of one posture with another posture.

'Bahiddhā kāye' means in the body of another. 'Ajjhattabahiddhā kāye' means contemplating in one's own body at times, and in the body of another at times. Indeed, by the first method, the comprehension of the body (kāyaparippaha) in one's own body is taught. By the second method, in the body of another. By the third method, the comprehension of the body in one's own body at times and in the body of another at times is taught. There is no such thing as an object that connects both the internal and external simultaneously. However, what is meant here is the time of alternating between the internal and external for one who has a proficient meditation subject. The word 'ātāpī' (ardent) indicates being endowed with the energy that comprehends the body. For at that time, he is endowed with that energy which is called 'ātāpa' because it burns away the defilements in the three realms of existence; therefore, he is called 'ātāpī'.

'Sampajāno' (clearly comprehending) means being endowed with the wisdom known as clear comprehension that comprehends the body. 'Satimā' (mindful) means being endowed with the mindfulness that comprehends the body. This monk, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it repeatedly with wisdom. Indeed, for one devoid of mindfulness, there is no such thing as contemplation (anupassanā). That is why the Blessed One said: "Monks, I say that mindfulness is useful in all things." Therefore, by this much, 'kāye kāyānupassī viharati', the meditation subject of the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body is taught. Alternatively, the mental contraction (sloth) of one who is not ardent (anātāpī) creates an obstacle to the meditation subject. One who lacks clear comprehension is confused about comprehending the right means and avoiding the wrong means. One who is forgetful (unmindful) is unable to abandon the wrong means and comprehend the right means. Therefore, the meditation subject does not succeed for him. Thus, it should be understood that 'ātāpī sampajāno satimā' is said to show those qualities by whose power that meditation subject succeeds. Having thus shown the factors associated with the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body, the Blessed One now says 'vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ' to show the factors that should be abandoned. In that phrase...
210:
Having thus shown the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) and its associated factors (sampayoganga), the phrase "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world" is now spoken to show the factor of abandoning (pahānanga). In that phrase, "vineyya" (having removed) means having removed either by removal by substitution of opposites (tadanga-vinaya) or by removal by suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). In the phrase "loke" (in the world), the collection of forms (kāya) distinguished as internal and so forth, which is grasped [by knowledge], is itself called "the world" here. The meaning is: having removed covetousness and displeasure in that world.
