Because covetousness (abhijjhā) includes sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and displeasure (domanassa) includes ill-will (byāpāda), it should be understood that by showing these two powerful states included among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the abandoning of all hindrances is stated.

Specifically, here, by the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of attraction (anurodha) based on the perfection of the body is stated; by the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of repulsion (virodha) based on the failure of the body is stated. Furthermore, by the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of excessive delight in the body is stated; by the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of lack of delight in the development of the body (kāya-bhāvanā) is stated. By the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of the attribution of beauty (subha) and happiness (sukha), etc., which do not truly exist in the body, is stated; by the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of the rejection of foulness (asubha) and suffering (dukkha), etc., which truly exist in the body, is stated. By thus abandoning attraction, repulsion, and so forth, the power of the yogi's meditation and their capability in meditation are demonstrated. For this is the power of meditation: to be free from attraction and repulsion, to be able to endure both delight and lack of delight, and to be devoid of attributing what is not there and rejecting what is there. That yogi who is free from attraction and repulsion, who endures delight and lack of delight, who does not attribute what is not there, and does not reject what is there, is one capable in meditation.

Alternatively—in the phrase "contemplating the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassī), the subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) is stated by way of contemplation. In the word "dwells" (viharati), the carrying of the body of one engaged in meditation by way of the stated mode of dwelling is mentioned. In the terms beginning with "ardent" (ātāpī), right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya) is stated by way of ardency (ātāpa); by mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), the all-beneficial meditation (or the means of carrying out the meditation) is stated. Or else, by mindfulness, the tranquility (samatha) obtained through the power of body-contemplation is stated; by clear comprehension, insight (vipassanā) is stated; and by the removal of covetousness and displeasure, the fruit of development (bhāvanā-phala) is stated. This is the explanation of the meaning of the Summary (uddesa) of the Contemplation of the Body.

## Explanation of the Summary of the Contemplation of Feelings, etc.

In the summaries of the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth, the terms such as "internal" (ajjhatta) should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Indeed, in these contemplations of feelings and so forth, there is a threefold division: in one's own feelings, etc.; in another's feelings, etc.; and sometimes in one's own and sometimes in another's feelings, etc.
211:
The grasping [of the object] has already been stated. In the sentences beginning with "contemplating feelings in feelings" (vedanāsu vedanānupassī), the purpose of repeating the word "feelings" and so forth should be understood in the same way as stated in the contemplation of the body.

In the passage "contemplating feelings in feelings, contemplating mind in mind, contemplating phenomena in phenomena," "feelings" (vedanā) refers to the three types of feelings. These feelings are only mundane (lokiya). The mind (citta) is also only mundane; likewise, the phenomena (dhammā) are only mundane. The detailed classification of these feelings and other states will become clear in the Exposition Section (niddesavāra). However, in this Summary Section (uddesavāra), a monk who contemplates feelings in whatever manner they should be contemplated is to be known as "one contemplating feelings in feelings." This same method applies to the mind and phenomena.

In what manner should feelings be contemplated? Firstly, pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) should be contemplated as suffering (dukkha); painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) as a dart (salla); and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā) as impermanent (anicca). As it is said:

"Whatever monk has seen pleasant feeling as suffering,
has seen painful feeling as a dart,
and has seen the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent,
that monk is indeed one who sees rightly; he shall wander in peace."

All these feelings should also be contemplated as suffering. Thus it has been said: "Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering, I say." They should also be contemplated by way of being pleasant or painful. As it is said: "Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes." All such passages should be expanded. Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations, such as impermanence (anicca) and so forth. The remaining details will become clear in the Exposition Section itself.

Regarding the mind and phenomena: the mind should be contemplated by way of its various distinctions such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), kamma, result (vipāka), and functional (kiriya), as well as by way of the contemplations of impermanence, etc., and by way of the distinctions such as "with lust" (sarāga), etc., that appear in the Exposition Section. Phenomena (dhammā) should be contemplated by way of individual essence (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), by way of the nature of emptiness (suññatā) which is void of self, by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence, etc., and by way of the distinctions such as "present" (santa) and "absent" (asanta) that appear in the Exposition Section. The rest is as previously stated.

Indeed, in this context, for someone who has abandoned covetousness and displeasure in the world called the "body," they are certainly abandoned in the worlds of feelings and so forth as well. However, it is stated in all [four foundations] by way of different individuals and by way of the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā) occurring in various thought-moments. Alternatively, when they are abandoned in one, they are abandoned in the rest as well. Therefore, it should be understood that it is stated this way for the purpose of showing the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure in feelings and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Summary Section is finished.
212:
## Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Body

Now (after teaching the summary section), just as a skilled bamboo worker, desiring to make utensils such as coarse mats, fine mats, flower baskets, caskets, and cases, obtains a large bamboo, cuts it into four parts, takes each part, splits it, and then makes those various utensils; or just as a skilled goldsmith, desiring to make various kinds of ornaments, obtains a very pure gold bar, divides it into four portions, takes each portion, and then makes those various ornaments; in the same way, the Blessed One, desiring to lead beings to the attainment of various distinctions through the teaching of the Satipaṭṭhāna, divided the single Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) into four by way of the object, according to the method beginning with, "There are four foundations of mindfulness: here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally," and then, desiring to explain each of those four foundations of mindfulness individually, he began the detailed explanation (niddesa-vāra) with the method beginning with, "And how, monks, does a monk [dwell contemplating the body] internally?"

In that detailed explanation, the word "Kathañca" (And how?) is a question asked with the desire to explain in detail. The summary of the meaning here is: In what manner and in what way does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body internally? This same method applies to the remaining question sections (on feelings, mind, and mental objects). "Idha bhikkhu" means a monk in this Dispensation (Sāsana). Here, the word "idha" (here) points to the Dispensation which is the support for the person who produces all forms of contemplation of the body, such as internal contemplation, and it excludes the existence of such a state in other dispensations. For it was said: "Monks, only here is there a recluse... other doctrines are void of recluses." Therefore, it is said, "a monk in this Dispensation."

"Ajjhattaṃ kāyaṃ" means one's own body. "Uddhaṃ pādatalā" means upwards from the soles of the feet. "Adho kesamatthakā" means downwards from the tips of the hair of the head. "Tacapariyantaṃ" means bounded all around by the skin. "Pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati" means he sees that this body is filled with various impurities such as hair and so forth. How? "In this body there are hairs of the head... urine." In that context, "atthi" means they exist or are found. "Imasmiṃ" means in this body which is said to be upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the tips of the hair, bounded all around by the skin, and full of various impurities. "Kāye" means in the physical body.
213:
The body is called 'kāya' because it is a collection (sañcaya) of loathsome things (kucchita) such as hair and the like, and because it is the place of origin (āyabhūta) for hundreds of diseases such as eye diseases and so forth.

These items such as hair of the head and body hair are the thirty-two parts (aspects). In this regard, the connection should be understood by joining each term with the word 'exists' (atthi), as in 'In this body there are hairs of the head, in this body there are hairs of the body.' Indeed, in this fathom-long carcass, from the soles of the feet upwards, from the tips of the hair downwards, and all around bounded by the skin, even when searching in every way, one does not find even an atom's weight of pure substance such as pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, aloe wood, saffron, camphor, or scented powder. Instead, one finds only various kinds of impurities such as hair and body hair, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and ungraceful in appearance. Therefore, it is said: 'In this body there are hairs of the head, hairs of the body... urine.' This is the explanation by way of the connection of words.

A noble son (kulaputta) who wishes to reach Arahantship by developing this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should first purify the fourfold virtue (sīla). Being established in perfectly pure virtue, he should cut off whichever of the ten impediments (palibodha) exist. Having produced the first jhāna through the meditation on the mindfulness of repulsiveness (paṭik္kūlamanasikāra), and using that jhāna as a basis to establish insight (vipassanā), he should learn the practice from a good friend (kalyāṇamitta). This good friend should be one who has reached at least the fruit of Arahantship or Anāgāmī, is well-versed in the Pali and the Commentaries, and is a teacher of the scriptures (tanti-ācariya). If such a pure good friend is not available in one's own monastery, one should go to where that teacher resides to learn. The purification of the fourfold virtue, the ten impediments, the cutting off of impediments, and the procedure for approaching a teacher are all explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, they should be understood according to the method stated there.

When a teacher explains the meditation subject, he should do so in three ways to suit the person. If a monk has naturally already learned the meditation subject, it should be taught to him by having him recite it during one or two sitting sessions. If a monk wishes to learn while living in the teacher's presence, it should be taught to him whenever he comes. If a monk wishes to learn and then go elsewhere, it should be taught without being too detailed or too brief, making it clear and uncomplicated (nigganṭhika).

How should it be taught? The seven skills in learning (uggahakosalla) and the ten skills in attention (manasikārakosalla) should be taught. Among them, the skills in learning should be taught by way of verbal recitation, mental reflection, color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. Indeed, in this meditation on repulsiveness, even if one is a bearer of the Three Pitakas, one should first perform verbal recitation when giving attention to it. For some people, the meditation subject becomes clear even while they are reciting. This is like the two elders who learned the meditation subject from the Elder Mahādeva who lived in the Malaya region. It is said that those elders...
214:
The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be taught to that monk in a way that is neither too detailed nor too brief, making it free from entanglement and complexity. How should the teacher explain it? The teacher should explain the sevenfold skill in acquisition (uggahakosalla) and the tenfold skill in attention (manasikārakosalla).

Among those skills, the sevenfold skill in acquisition should be explained as follows: verbally, mentally, by color, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation. Indeed, in this meditation on the foulness of the body (kāyanupassanā-kammaṭṭhāna), even one who knows the Tipitaka by heart should first perform verbal recitation (sajjhāya) when practicing attention. For some, the meditation subject becomes clear even while performing the recitation, as was the case with the two elders who learned the meditation subject from the Great Elder Mahādeva who lived in Malaya. When those two elders requested a meditation subject, the Great Elder gave them the text of the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra-pāḷi), saying, "Recite this in this manner for four months." Although those elders were proficient in two or three Nikāyas, because they respectfully followed their teacher's words, they became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) while reciting the thirty-two parts of the body during those four months.

Therefore, a teacher who explains the meditation subject should tell the pupil, "First, perform the verbal recitation." When reciting, one should recite in both forward (anuloma) and backward (paṭiloma) order, delimiting the groups such as the skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka). Having recited in forward order: "Hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin," one should then recite in backward order: "Skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head." Immediately after that, in the kidney-pentad (vakka-pañcaka), having recited: "Flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys," one should then recite in backward order: "Kidneys, bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head." After that, in the lung-pentad (papphāsa-pañcaka), having recited: "Heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs," one should then recite in backward order: "Lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head."

After that, although the brain (matthalunga) is not included in this canonical text, it is mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga; thus, placing it at the end of feces (karīsa) in the canonical list, in this brain-pentad (matthalunga-pañcaka), having recited: "Bowels, entrails, undigested food, feces, brain," one should then recite in backward order: "Brain, feces, undigested food, entrails, bowels, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head."
215:
Then, in the fat-sextet (meda-chakka), having recited: "Bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat," one should then recite in backward order: "Fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain, feces, undigested food, entrails, bowels, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head."

Then, in the urine-sextet (mutta-chakka), having recited: "Tears, grease, saliva, snot, oil of the joints, urine," one should then recite in backward order: "Urine, oil of the joints, snot, saliva, grease, tears, fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain, feces, undigested food, entrails, bowels, lungs, spleen, membranes, liver, heart, kidneys, bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, hair of the body, hair of the head." In this way, verbal recitation should be performed for a hundred times, a thousand times, or even a hundred thousand times. This is because through verbal recitation, the text of the meditation subject becomes thoroughly familiar; the mind does not wander here and there; the parts (koṭṭhāsa) become clear, appearing like fingers interlaced or like a row of fence posts. Just as one recites verbally, one should also recite mentally. Verbal recitation is the cause for mental recitation. Mental recitation is the cause for the penetration of characteristics (lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha). The penetration of characteristics is the cause for the penetration of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala-paṭivedha).

"By color" means the color of the hair and so forth should be defined. "By shape" means the shape of that same hair and so forth should be defined. "By direction" means that in this body, from the navel upwards is the upper direction, and downwards is the lower direction. Therefore, the direction should be defined as: "This part is in such and such a direction." "By location" means the location of each part should be defined as: "This part is situated in such and such a place." Regarding "by delimitation," there are two kinds of delimitation: delimitation of the similar (sabhāga-pariccheda) and delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāga-pariccheda). Therein, the delimitation of the similar should be known as: "This part is delimited below, above, and around by such and such." The delimitation of the dissimilar should be known by way of non-confusion, such as: "The hairs of the head are not the hairs of the body, and the hairs of the body are not the hairs of the head."
216:
A teacher who explains the sevenfold skill in learning should do so after knowing: "This meditation subject is taught in such-and-such a sutta by way of repulsiveness, and in such-and-such a sutta by way of elements." This meditation subject is taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta only by way of repulsiveness. In the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, it is taught by way of elements. In the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, however, the four jhanas are analyzed with reference to the person to whom [the parts] appear by way of color. Between these two, the meditation subject taught by way of elements is insight meditation (vipassanā), while that taught by way of repulsiveness is serenity meditation (samatha). It is also said that this meditation subject is taught in this Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga without distinction, as being common to all serenity meditation subjects.

After explaining the sevenfold skill in learning, the tenfold skill in attention should be explained as: "in order, not too fast, not too slow, warding off distraction, transcending concepts, gradual dropping, reaching absorption, and the three suttas." Among these ten, "in order" means that from the beginning of reciting this meditation subject, one should attend to it in order, not skipping any part. For a yogi who attends to it by skipping parts is like an unskilled man climbing a thirty-two-step ladder; if he skips a step while climbing, he falls with a weary body and fails to complete the climb. Similarly, because of not attaining the satisfaction that should be gained through the perfection of meditation, he falls with a weary mind and fails to complete the meditation.

Even when attending in order, one should attend "not too fast." For a yogi who attends too fast, it is like a man who, having set out on a three-league journey, travels with great speed seven times back and forth without noting the entrances and exits; although his journey is finished, he still has to ask for directions to go. Similarly, although the meditation subject reaches its end, it remains unclear and does not bring about distinction. Therefore, one should attend to it without being too fast.

Just as it should not be too fast, it should also be "not too slow." For a yogi who attends too slowly, it is like a man who wishes to travel a three-league journey in a single day but lingers among the trees, mountains, and thickets along the way; the journey does not end, and it takes two or three days to complete. Similarly, the meditation subject does not reach its end and cannot be a cause for attaining the distinction of jhana.

"Warding off distraction" means that one should abandon the meditation subject and ward off the mind's distraction toward many external objects. For a yogi who does not ward off distraction toward external objects, the meditation subject declines. For example, if a man walking along a narrow cliff path as wide as a footstep does not note his steps but looks here and there, he will miss his footing and fall into a cliff a hundred fathoms deep. Similarly, if the mind is distracted externally...
217:
Just as for a man who lingers by being attached to trees, mountains, or thickets along the way, the journey does not reach its end and must be completed in two or three days; similarly, the meditation subject does not reach its end and cannot be a cause for attaining distinction.

"Warding off distraction" (vikkhepapaṭibāhanato) means that one should ward off the mind's distraction toward various external objects by letting go of the meditation subject. If it is not warded off, it is like a man traveling a narrow path near a cliff only a foot wide; if he does not note his steps and looks here and there, he slips and falls into a cliff a hundred cubits deep. Similarly, if there is distraction toward external objects, the meditation subject declines and perishes. Therefore, one should attend by warding off distraction.

"Transcending concepts" (paṇṇattisamatikkamanato) means that one should transcend the concepts such as "hair of the head, body hair" and establish the mind on the aspect of "repulsiveness." For example, when water is scarce, people see a well in the forest and tie a sign such as a palm leaf there; they come to bathe and drink using that sign. However, when the path becomes clear through constant travel, the sign is no longer needed, and they go to bathe and drink whenever they wish. Similarly, for one who attends by way of the concepts "hair of the head, body hair" in the preliminary stage, when the aspect of repulsiveness becomes clear, he should transcend those concepts and establish the mind only on the aspect of repulsiveness.

"Gradual dropping" (anupubbamuncanato) means that whichever part (koṭṭhāsa) does not appear to the mind, one should drop that part and attend by dropping them in order. For a beginner, even when attending to "hair of the head," the attention may go and settle on the final part, "urine." When attending to "urine," the attention may go and settle on the first part, "hair of the head." While attending in this way, some parts appear and some do not. Therefore, one should work only on those parts that appear. If two parts appear, one should repeatedly attend to the one that is clearer of the two and bring about absorption (appanā) jhana.

There is this analogy for bringing about absorption through repeated attention: A hunter wishing to catch a monkey living in a palm grove of thirty-two palms shoots an arrow at the leaf of the first palm tree to scare it. That monkey jumps in order from tree to tree until it reaches the last palm tree. When the hunter does the same at the last tree, it returns to the first tree. In this way, after going back and forth repeatedly, the monkey eventually flees only from the place where it is scared and finally stays for a long time in one palm tree, firmly grasping the central leaf-bud of that tree...
218:
That monkey would jump to a palm tree and go only to the furthest palm tree. When it reaches that furthest palm tree, if the hunter does the same thing, it would return to the first palm tree in the same manner as before. As that monkey goes back and forth repeatedly in this sequence, it would run away only from the places where it is frightened, and then, crouching in one palm tree in due order, it would firmly grasp the needle-like bud of a palm leaf in the middle of that tree; even when shot at, it would not get up. In the same way, this illustration should be understood as being completed without deviation.

To correlate this simile—just as there are thirty-two palm trees in a palm grove, so there are thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) in this body. The mind is like the monkey. The yogī is like the hunter. Just as the monkey lives in a palm grove of thirty-two trees, the yogī's mind wanders repeatedly by way of the object in the body consisting of thirty-two parts. Just as when the hunter shoots an arrow at the leaf of the first palm tree to frighten it, the monkey jumps to various palm trees and goes to the furthest palm tree, so it should be noted that when the yogī begins the work of attention as 'hair of the head' (kesā), the mind proceeds in sequence and becomes well-established only in the final part. The same method applies when returning. Just as the monkey, going back and forth repeatedly, runs from the place of frightening, so it should be noted that for the yogī who practices attention repeatedly, when some parts appear and some do not, he should let go of those that do not appear and perform the preliminary work (parikamma) only on those parts that do appear. Just as the monkey, crouching in one palm tree in due order, firmly grasps the needle-like bud of a palm leaf in the middle of that tree and does not get up even when shot at, so it should be noted that when two parts appear at the end, the yogī attends repeatedly to the one that appears more clearly and brings about appanā absorption.

Another simile is as follows—just as a monk wandering for alms, living in dependence on a village of thirty-two houses, might receive two houses' worth of alms at the very first house and thus skip the next house; on the next day, he might receive three houses' worth and skip the next two; on the third day, he might receive a full bowl at the very first house and go to the rest-house to consume it; so this illustration should be understood. The village of thirty-two houses is like the thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa). The alms-collecting monk is like the yogī. That monk's living in dependence on the village is like the yogī's performing the preliminary work on the thirty-two parts. Receiving two houses' worth of alms at the first house and skipping the next, and receiving three houses' worth on the second day and skipping the next two, is like letting go of the parts that do not appear during repeated attention and focusing on those that do appear...
219:
...performing the preliminary work on the parts that appear until two parts remain; and just as on the third day, receiving a full bowl at the very first house and sitting in the rest-house (āsanasalā) to consume it, so it should be noted that one attends repeatedly only to the part that appears most clearly among those two and brings about appanā absorption.

'Appanāto' means from the portion of appanā. It should be understood that appanā absorption occurs in each of the parts such as the hair of the head; this is the meaning here.

'Tayo ca suttantā' refers to the Adhicitta Sutta, the Sītibhāva Sutta, and the Bojjhaṅgakosalla Sutta. These three suttas should be understood for the purpose of balancing energy (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi); this is the meaning here. Among those suttas—

"Bhikkhus, a monk devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta) should attend to three signs from time to time. He should attend to the sign of concentration (samādhi-nimitta) from time to time, the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta) from time to time, and the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta) from time to time. Bhikkhus, if a monk devoted to the higher mind should attend only to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind may lead to laziness (kosajja). Bhikkhus, if a monk devoted to the higher mind should attend only to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind may lead to restlessness (uddhacca). Bhikkhus, if a monk devoted to the higher mind should attend only to the sign of equanimity, his mind would not be well-concentrated for the destruction of the taints (āsavas). Bhikkhus, when a monk devoted to the higher mind attends from time to time to the sign of concentration, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity, then that mind becomes pliant, wieldy, and radiant; it is not fragile and becomes well-concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

"Bhikkhus, just as a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice prepares a furnace and lights the mouth of the furnace. Having lit the mouth of the furnace, he takes the gold with tongs and puts it into the mouth of the furnace. Having put it into the mouth of the furnace, he blows on it from time to time, sprinkles it with water from time to time, and from time to time..."
220:
...watches with equanimity. Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to blow on that gold exclusively, that gold would likely burn. Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to sprinkle that gold with water exclusively, that gold would likely be extinguished. Monks, if a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice were to only watch that gold with equanimity, that gold would likely not reach proper maturity.

Monks, when a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice blows on that gold from time to time, sprinkles it with water from time to time, and watches it with equanimity from time to time, then that gold becomes soft, malleable, and radiant; it is no longer brittle and becomes well-suited for work. Whatever kind of ornament the goldsmith wishes to create—whether a tiara, earrings, a necklace, or a gold garland—the gold serves that purpose for him.

Monks, in the same way, a monk devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta)... becomes well-concentrated for the destruction of the taints (āsavas). To whatever state realizable by direct knowledge (abhiññā) he inclines his mind for realization, he attains the ability to witness it for himself in each case, provided the necessary conditions are present. This discourse should be known as the 'Adhicitta Sutta'.

Monks, a monk endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed peace (Nibbāna). What are the six? Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk restrains the mind on the occasion it should be restrained; he exerts the mind on the occasion it should be exerted; he gladdens the mind on the occasion it should be gladdened; he watches the mind with equanimity on the occasion it should be watched with equanimity. He is also one of noble resolution (adhimutti) and one who greatly delights in Nibbāna. Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed peace. This discourse should be known as the 'Sītibhāva Sutta'.
221:
The Bojjhaṅgakosalla Sutta appears in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta of the Saṃyutta Mahāvagga as follows: "Monks, in the same way, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga)."

Thus, having well-learned this sevenfold skill in learning (uggahakosalla) and having thoroughly defined this tenfold skill in attention (manasikārakosalla), the meditator (yogī) should properly learn the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by means of both skills. If it is comfortable for that meditator to reside in the same monastery as the teacher, he should practice the meditation subject without having it explained in detail, and upon attaining distinction, he should have it explained further and further. One who wishes to reside elsewhere should have it explained in detail according to the stated method, recite it repeatedly to cut off all difficulties in the text, and then, leaving behind dwellings unsuitable for meditation practice—avoiding the eighteen faults such as being a large dwelling (mahāvāsa)—he should reside in a suitable dwelling. After cutting off minor impediments (palibodha), if he is one of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita), he should perform the preparatory work (parikamma) in the attention to the repulsive (paṭikkūlamanasikāra), since lust must be abandoned.

When performing the preparatory work, he should first take the sign (nimitta) in the hairs of the head. How? Having plucked one or two hairs and placed them on the palm of the hand, he should first define their color. It is also proper to look at the hairs in the place where they were cut; it is also proper to look at them in a bowl of water or a bowl of rice-gruel. Seeing them when they are black, he should attend to them as "black, black"; when they are white, as "white, white." When they are mixed, he should attend to them according to the predominant color. Just as with the hairs of the head, he should take the sign only after seeing all the parts of the skin-pentad (tacapañcaka). Having taken the sign in this way and defined all the parts by way of color, shape, direction, location, and boundary, he should then define them as repulsive in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, habitat (āsaya), and location (okāsa).

In this regard, the sequential explanation of all the parts is as follows: The hairs of the head are naturally black in color, like the color of wet ariṭṭhaka seeds. In shape, they are long and round, like the shape of a balance rod. In direction, they grow in the upper part of the body. In location, they are bounded on both sides by the ears, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by...
222:
They are bounded by the hollow of the nape of the neck. The moist skin covering the skull is the location of the hairs. In terms of delimitation, the hairs are established by entering the skin covering the skull to the depth of about a grain of paddy; they are bounded below by their own roots, above by space, and around the sides by each other. No two hairs are in the same place; this is the delimitation of the similar (sabhāga-pariccheda).

"Hairs are not body hairs, body hairs are not hairs"—thus, the delimitation of the hairs as a separate group, not mixed with the remaining thirty-one parts (koṭṭhāsa), is the delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāga-pariccheda). This is the definition of hairs by way of color and so on.

This is the definition of those hairs as repulsive in five ways by way of color and so on: hairs are repulsive in terms of color, shape, smell, habitat (āsaya), and location. Indeed, if one sees something the color of hair in a bowl of very delicious rice-gruel or rice, one becomes disgusted, saying, "This is mixed with hair; take it away." Thus, hairs are repulsive in terms of color. Even when eating at night, if people touch a fiber of swallow-wort or bowstring hemp which has the shape of a hair, they are likewise disgusted. Thus, they are repulsive in terms of shape.

The smell of hairs that are not treated with oil, flowers, incense, and so on, is extremely disgusting; the smell of hairs thrown into a fire is even more disgusting. Although hairs might not be repulsive in terms of color and shape, they are certainly repulsive in terms of smell. For example, an infant's excrement is the color of turmeric and has the shape of a piece of turmeric; and the bloated, blackish carcass of a dog thrown in a rubbish heap is the color of a ripe palmyra fruit and has the shape of a rounded mudinga drum, and its fangs are like jasmine buds—both might not be repulsive in terms of color and shape, but they are certainly repulsive in terms of smell. In the same way, hairs might not be repulsive in terms of color and shape, but they are certainly repulsive in terms of smell.

Just as vegetables grown from the sewage flowing from a village in an impure place are disgusting and unfit for consumption for city-dwellers, so too, hairs are extremely disgusting because they arise from the impurities of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so on. This is their repulsiveness in terms of habitat (āsaya). These hairs [are like mushrooms] on a heap of feces...
223:
These hairs are like mushrooms growing on a heap of the thirty-one parts. Because they grow in an impure place, like vegetables growing in a cemetery or a rubbish heap, or like red, white, blue, or white lotuses growing in a moat and so on, they are extremely disgusting. This is their repulsiveness in terms of location (okāsa).

Just as the repulsiveness of hairs is defined in five ways by color, shape, smell, habitat, and location, so too, the repulsiveness of all the parts (koṭṭhāsa) should be defined in five ways by color, shape, smell, habitat, and location. All the parts should also be defined individually by way of color, shape, direction (disā), location (okāsa), and delimitation (pariccheda).

Among those parts, body hairs (lomā) are not of a pure black color like head hairs in their natural color, but are brownish-black. In terms of shape, they have the shape of a palm root with a downward-curving tip. In terms of direction, they grow in two directions. In terms of location, they grow on the skin that covers the rest of the body, mostly excluding the location where head hairs are established and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. In terms of delimitation, they are established by entering the skin covering the body to the depth of about a louse's egg; they are bounded below by their own roots, above by space, and around the sides by each other. No two body hairs are in the same place. This is the delimitation of the similar for those body hairs. The delimitation of the dissimilar is just the same as for head hairs.

Nails (nakhā) is the name for the twenty nail-plates. All of them are white in color. In terms of shape, they have the shape of fish scales. In terms of direction, the toenails grow in the lower direction, and the fingernails grow in the upper direction; thus they grow in two directions. In terms of location, they are established on the tips of the backs of the fingers and toes. In terms of delimitation, they are bounded in two directions by the flesh of the tips of the fingers and toes, inside by the flesh of the back of the fingers and toes, outside and at the tip by space, and around the sides by each other. No two nails are in the same place. This is their delimitation of the similar. The delimitation of the dissimilar is just the same as for head hairs.

Teeth (dantā) are the thirty-two tooth-bones of a person with a full set of teeth. They are also white in color. In terms of shape, they have many shapes. Indeed, among them, the four teeth in the middle of the lower row have the shape of gourd seeds set in a row in a lump of soft clay. On both sides of those, there is one tooth each with one root and one tip, having the shape of a jasmine bud. Beyond those, there is one tooth each with two roots and two tips, having the shape of a carriage-axle support. Beyond those, there are two teeth each with three roots and three tips. Beyond those, there are two teeth each with four roots and four tips. The same applies to the upper row. In terms of direction, they grow in the upper direction. In terms of location, they are established in the two jawbones. In terms of delimitation, they are bounded below by their own roots established in the jawbone, above by space, and around the sides by each other.
224:
The method is: In terms of direction, they are in the upper direction. In terms of location, they are fixed in the two jawbones. In terms of boundary, they are delimited below by the surface of their own roots fixed in the jawbone, above by space, and transversely by one another. Two teeth do not exist in the same place. This is their delimitation by the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Their delimitation by the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair of the head.

Skin (taco) is the thick skin that stays enveloping the whole body. Above that skin is the thin skin called 'chavi', which has colors such as black, dark, or yellow. If this thin skin were gathered from the whole body, it would be only the size of a jujube seed. The thick skin, however, is white in color. Its white color becomes apparent when the thin skin is destroyed by the impact of flames, or by blows from weapons, etc. In terms of shape, it has the shape of the body itself. This is the summary regarding the skin.

In detail: The skin of the toes has the shape of a silkworm cocoon. The skin of the top of the foot has the shape of a sandal with a cover. The skin of the calf has the shape of a palm-leaf rice packet. The skin of the thigh has the shape of a long bag full of rice. The skin of the buttocks has the shape of a water-strainer cloth full of water. The skin of the back has the shape of leather stretched over a plank. The skin of the abdomen has the shape of leather stretched over the body of a lute. The skin of the chest is mostly square in shape. The skin of both arms has the shape of leather stretched over a quiver. The skin of the back of the hand has the shape of a razor case or a leather pouch. The skin of the fingers has the shape of a key case. The skin of the neck has the shape of a neck-collar. The skin of the face, being full of holes large and small, has the shape of an insect's nest. The skin of the head has the shape of an alms-bowl bag.

A meditator (yogāvacara) who grasps the skin should send their knowledge upwards starting from the upper lip, first defining the skin that covers the face. Then the skin of the forehead bone. Then, just as one might insert a hand between an alms-bowl and the bag it is placed in, they should send their knowledge between the skull and the scalp, separating the skin from the bone where they are joined, and define the scalp. Then the skin of the shoulders. Then, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right hand. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left hand. Then the skin of the back. Having defined each of those, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right foot. Then...
225:
...in the same way, the skin of the left foot. Then, in due order, the skin of the bladder, the abdomen, the heart (chest), and the neck should be defined. Then, immediately after the skin of the neck, the skin of the lower jaw should be defined, bringing it to an end at the lower lip. In this way, to the meditator who grasps the skin in its grosser aspects, even the subtle skin becomes clear.

In terms of direction, it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. In terms of location, it stays enveloping the whole body. In terms of boundary, it is delimited below by the surface on which it rests, and above by space. This is its delimitation by the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Its delimitation by the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair of the head.

Flesh (maဓsa) consists of nine hundred pieces of flesh. All those pieces of flesh are red in color, like the kiဓsuka flower. In terms of shape: the flesh of the calf has the shape of rice wrapped in a palm leaf. The flesh of the thigh has the shape of a pestle. The flesh of the buttocks has the shape of the corner of an oven. The flesh of the back has the shape of a layer of palm-fruit pulp. The flesh on both sides of the ribs has the shape of a thin coating of clay in a granary. The flesh of the breasts has the shape of a ball of clay that has been rounded and thrown down. The muscles of both arms have the shape of a large skinless rat placed double. In this way, to the meditator who grasps the flesh in its grosser aspects, even the subtle flesh becomes clear. In terms of direction, it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. In terms of location, it stays plastered upon the three hundred and more bones in due order. In terms of boundary, it is delimited below by the surface of the collection of bones on which it rests, above by the skin, and transversely by each other. This is its delimitation by the similar. Its delimitation by the dissimilar is just like that of the hair of the head.

'Sinews' (nhārũ) refers to nine hundred sinews. In terms of color, all sinews are white. In terms of shape, they have various shapes. Among them, starting from the upper part of the neck, five great sinews descend, binding the body together, by the front of the heart (chest), five by the back, five by the right side, and five by the left side. Also, those binding the right arm: five by the front of the arm and five by the back. Likewise for the left arm. Also, those binding the right leg: five by the front of the leg and five by the back. Likewise for the left leg. Thus, there are sixty great sinews called 'body-sustainers' that descend, binding the body together; these are also called 'kaဓကara'. All of them have the shape of a yam bud.
226:
Other tendons (nhārū) spread over and remain in various places. Those finer than the sixty main tendons are like small strings twisted from thread. Others finer than those are like rotten vines. Others finer still are like the strings of a large lute. Others are like thick small threads. The tendons on the back of the hands and feet are like birds' feet. The tendons of the head are like small nets worn on children's heads. The tendons of the back are like wet nets spread out in the sun. The remaining tendons following the various large and small limbs are like a mesh garment (coat of mail) worn on the body. In terms of direction, they arise in two directions: above and below. In terms of location, they remain binding the bones throughout the whole body. In terms of boundary, they are delimited below by the surfaces resting on the three hundred bones, above by the areas touching the flesh and skin, and transversely by each other. This is their similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda). Their dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

Regarding the bones (aṭṭhī): excluding the thirty-two teeth, there are sixty-four hand bones, sixty-four foot bones, sixty-four soft bones dependent on the flesh, two heel bones, two ankle bones in each foot, two shin bones, two knee bones, two thigh bones, two hip bones, eighteen backbone segments, twenty-four ribs, fourteen chest bones, one breastbone, two collarbones, two shoulder blade bones, two upper arm bones, two forearm bones each, seven neck bones, two jawbones, one nose bone, two eye-socket bones, two ear bones, one forehead bone, one crown bone, and nine skull bones—thus making three hundred bones.

All these bones are white in color. In shape, they have various forms. Among them, the tip bones of the toes are like kataka seeds. The middle toe-joint bones immediately following them are like jackfruit seeds. The base toe-joint bones are like small drums (paṇava). The bones of the back of the foot are like a heap of crushed lotus roots. The heel bone is like a single-seeded palm fruit. The ankle bones are like marbles joined together. The place where the shin bones rest on the ankle bones is like a bamboo shoot with its skin unpeeled. The small shin bone is like the handle of a small bow. The large shin bone is like the back of a withered snake. The kneecap bone is like a small piece of foam that is worn away on one side.

Among those, the place where the shin bone (the 'horse-head' bone) enters and rests is like a cow's horn with a blunt tip. The thigh bone is like the handle of a poorly carved knife or axe. The place where that thigh bone enters and rests in the hip bone is like a playing marble. The place where the hip bone supports the thigh bone is like a large punnāga fruit with its tip cut off. The two hip bones are joined together like a potter's kiln; individually, they are like the cord that binds a blacksmith's hammer. At the end...
227:
The pelvic/buttock bone is like the hood of a snake held facing downwards, and it has large and small holes in seven places. The backbone segments, when viewed from the inside, are like stacked lead plates (sīsakapaṭṭa); when viewed from the outside, they are like a row of rings. Between those backbone segments, there are two or three spines like saw teeth. Among the twenty-four ribs, the incomplete ones are like incomplete sickles, and the complete ones are like complete sickles. All the ribs together are like the spread wings of a white cock.

The fourteen chest bones are like an old, decayed palanquin frame. The breastbone is like the head of a ladle. The collarbones are like the handles of small copper axes. The shoulder blade bones are like a Sinhalese hoe worn down on one side. The upper arm bones are like mirror handles. The forearm bones are like a pair of palm roots. The wrist bones are like lead plates placed close to one another. The bones of the back of the hand are like a heap of crushed lotus roots. Among the fingers, the base joint bones are like small drums (paṇava), the middle joint bones are like incomplete jackfruit seeds, and the tip joint bones are like kataka seeds. The seven neck bones are like bamboo rings threaded on a stick. The lower jawbone is like the cord that binds a blacksmith's hammer, and the upper jawbone is like a small knife for scraping sugarcane.

The eye-socket and nose-socket bones are like young palm seeds with the kernels removed. The forehead bone is like a conch-shell water-cup placed face down. The ear-tuft bones are like a barber's razor case. The bone at the place where the diadem is bound above the forehead and ear-tufts is like a piece of cloth covering a water pot and hanging down in folds on two sides. The crown bone is like a crooked coconut with the opening cut off. The skull bones are like the shells of old, decayed gourds sewn together.

In terms of direction, the bones arise in two directions: above and below. In terms of location, they exist throughout the whole body without distinction. Specifically, among these bones, the head bones rest on the neck bones, the neck bones on the backbone, the backbone on the hip bones, the hip bones on the thigh bones, the thigh bones on the knee bones, the knee bones on the shin bones, the shin bones on the ankle bones, and the ankle bones on the bones of the back of the foot. In terms of boundary, they are delimited internally by the bone marrow, above by the flesh, and at the tips and bases by each other. This is their similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda). Their dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair.
228:
Bone marrow (aṭṭhimiñjaṃ) refers to the marrow situated inside various bones. In color, it is white. In shape, the marrow situated inside large bones is like a large rattan shoot that has been placed and steamed inside a bamboo tube. The marrow situated inside small bones is like a small rattan shoot that has been placed and steamed inside a small bamboo joint. In terms of direction (disā), it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. In terms of location (okāsa), it is situated inside the bones. In terms of delimitation (pariccheda), it is bounded by the inner surfaces of the bones. This is its similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda). Its dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Kidney (vakkaṃ) refers to two lumps of flesh bound by a single stalk. In color, it is slightly red, the color of the seed of the pālibhaddaka (coral tree). In shape, it is like a pair of children’s spinning tops, or like a pair of mango fruits attached to a single stalk. In terms of direction, it occurs in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated encircling the heart, being bound by a thick sinew that starts from the neck as a single root and branches into two after a short distance. In terms of delimitation, the kidney is bounded by its own parts. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Heart (hadayaṃ) refers to the heart-flesh. In color, it is red, the color of the back of a red lotus petal. In shape, it is like a lotus bud placed upside down with the outer petals removed. It is smooth on the outside and like the inside of a kosātakī (sponge gourd) fruit on the inside. In those with wisdom, it is slightly bloomed; in those with little wisdom, it remains a bud. Inside it, there is a small cavity about the size of a punnāga (Alexandrian laurel) seed, where about half a pasata of blood remains. Depending on this blood, the mind-element (manodhātu) and mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) occur. This blood is red in those of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), black in those of hateful temperament (dosacarita), like the water from washing meat in those of deluded temperament (mohacarita), the color of pea soup in those of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita), the color of kaṇikāra (pterospermum) flowers in those of faithful temperament (saddhācarita), and in those of wise temperament (paññācarita), it appears clear, translucent, undisturbed, white, pure, and radiant like a well-washed genuine ruby. In terms of direction, it occurs in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated in the middle of the two breasts inside the body. In terms of delimitation, the heart is bounded by its own parts. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Liver (yakanaṃ) refers to a twin layer of flesh. In color, it is a mixture of red and yellow, like the color of the back of a not-too-red kumuda (white water lily) petal. In shape, it is single at the base and divided into two at the tip...
229:
(The liver) has the shape of a kovidāra (mountain ebony) leaf. In dull-witted people, it is just one large piece, but in wise people, there are two or three small livers. In terms of direction, it occurs in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated inside the two breasts, leaning towards the right side. In terms of delimitation, the liver is bounded by its own parts. This is its similar delimitation (sabhāgapariccheda). Its dissimilar delimitation (visabhāgapariccheda) is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Pleura (kilomaka) refers to the membrane that wraps around, which is of two types: concealed and unconcealed. Both types of pleura are white in color, like the color of a fine white cloth. In shape, it takes the shape of its own location. In terms of direction, the concealed pleura occurs in the upper direction. The remaining (unconcealed) pleura occurs in both directions. In terms of location, the concealed pleura exists covering the heart and the kidney (vakka). The unconcealed pleura exists wrapping around the flesh beneath the skin throughout the whole body. In terms of delimitation, it is bounded below by the flesh, above by the skin, and laterally by its own parts. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Spleen (pihaka) refers to the flesh of the 'stomach-tongue'. In color, it is blue (dark), like the color of a nigguṇḍi (five-leaved chaste tree) flower. In shape, it is seven finger-breadths in size, unbound, and has the shape of a black calf's tongue. In terms of direction, it occurs in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, leaning against the upper side of the stomach-membrane (udarapaṭala). If this spleen is struck by a weapon and comes out, the life of beings comes to an end. In terms of delimitation, the spleen is bounded by its own parts. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Lungs (papphāsa) refer to the lung-flesh divided into thirty-two pieces. In color, it is red, like the color of a not-too-ripe udumbara (cluster fig) fruit. In shape, it is like a thick piece of cake cut unevenly. Because there is no food or drink inside, it is struck by the heat of the karma-born fire-element (kammaja-tejo) that rises upwards, and thus it is tasteless and nutrient-less like a well-chewed lump of straw. In terms of direction, it occurs in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated inside the body between the two breasts, hanging down and covering the heart and the liver. In terms of delimitation, the lungs are bounded by their own parts. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is the same as described for the hair of the head.

Large intestine (anta) refers to the intestinal coil which is thirty-two cubits long in a man and twenty-eight cubits long in a woman, situated coiled in twenty-one places. In color, it is white...
230:
(The large intestine) has the color of mortar made with gravel. In shape, it is like a decapitated snake coiled and placed in a blood trough. In terms of direction, it is found in both directions. In terms of location, because it is connected above to the throat and below to the anus, it is situated inside the body from the throat to the end of the anus. In terms of boundary, it is delimited by its own parts. This is its similar boundary (sabhāgapariccheda). Its dissimilar boundary (visabhāgapariccheda) is like that of the hair.

Antaguṇa (mesentery) refers to the binding in the places where the large intestine is coiled. In color, it is white, like the color of the root of the white water-lily (dakastītalika). In shape, it is like the shape of the white water-lily root itself. In terms of direction, it is found in both directions. In terms of location, it is situated in twenty-one places between the coils of the large intestine, like the rope of a machine that pulls the machine-planks together so they do not fall apart when people are doing heavy work with hoes and axes, or like the small ropes used to stitch together the circles of a foot-wiping rope-mat. In terms of boundary, it is delimited by its own parts. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is like that of the hair.

Udariya (undigested food) is the food that has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, which is in the stomach. In color, it has the color of the swallowed food. In shape, it is like rice loosely tied in a water-filter cloth. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated in the stomach. The stomach (udara) is a membrane like a swelling that has arisen in the middle of a wet cloth being squeezed from both sides. It is smooth on the outside, but on the inside, it is like a dirty cloak-flower wrapping rotten meat, or it can be said to be like the inside of a rotten jackfruit skin. In that stomach, thirty-two families of worms, such as takkoṭaka, gaṇḍuppādaka, tālahīraka, sūcimukhaka, and paṭatantasuttaka, live in a confused state, moving in swarms. When there is no food or drink, they leap up, crying out, and strike the flesh of the heart. When food and drink are swallowed, they turn their mouths upward and very quickly snatch and swallow the first two or three mouthfuls of rice. That stomach is the birth-house, the latrine, the hospital, and the cemetery for those worms.

In that stomach, for example, like a cesspool near the gate of a Caṇḍāla village, when heavy rain falls in the summer, various foul things such as urine, feces, skin, bones, pieces of flesh, saliva, snot, and blood are washed down by the water and fall into it...
231:
...and remain there, stirred by the muddy water, where after two or three days a swarm of maggots arises, boiling with the heat of the sun's intensity, releasing bubbles of foam on top, having a very dark blue color, and being extremely foul-smelling and loathsome, such that it is not fit to be approached or looked at, let alone smelled or tasted.

In the same way, various foods and drinks are crushed into fine pieces by the pestle of the teeth, turned over by the hand of the tongue, and smeared with saliva and phlegm. Instantly losing their perfection of color, smell, and taste, they become like weaver's paste or dog vomit and fall (into the stomach). There, wrapped in bile, phlegm, and wind, they boil with the heat of the digestive fire (udara-aggi), swarming with families of worms, releasing bubbles of foam on top, and reaching a state of extreme foulness and loathsomeness. Just hearing about this undigested food causes a lack of delight in food and drink; how much more so if one looks at it with the eye of wisdom? The food and drink that fall into that stomach are divided into five parts: the worms eat one part, the digestive fire burns one part, one part becomes urine, one part becomes feces, and one part becomes the nutritive essence (rasa) which nourishes the blood, flesh, and so on. In terms of boundary, it is delimited by the lining of the stomach and by its own parts. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is like that of the hair.

Karīsa is feces. In color, it is generally the same color as the swallowed food. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is in the lower direction. In terms of location, it is situated in the Pakkāsaya (receptacle for digested food). The Pakkāsaya is between the navel and the base of the spine below, at the end of the large intestine, about eight inches in height, and like a bamboo tube. For example, just as rainwater falling on the upper ground flows down and fills the lower ground, so whatever food and drink fall into the stomach, being boiled by the digestive fire and producing foam, reach a soft state like something ground with a stone, and flow down through the cavity of the large intestine, accumulating like fine clay packed into a bamboo joint. In terms of boundary, it is delimited by the lining of the Pakkāsaya and by its own parts. This is its similar boundary. Its dissimilar boundary is like that of the hair.

Matthaluṅga is the mass of marrow situated inside the skull. In color, it is white, like the color of a cluster of mushrooms; it can also be said to be like the color of spoiled milk that has not yet become curd. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction.
232:
In terms of location, it exists joined together like four lumps of dough placed together, relying on the four suture lines inside the skull. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the inner surface of the skull and by the portions of the brain itself. This is its similar delimitation (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its dissimilar delimitation (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

Bile (pitta) is of two kinds: bound bile (baddha-pitta) and unbound bile (abaddha-pitta). Of these two, bound bile, in terms of color, has the color of thick madhuka oil. Unbound bile has the color of a withered and jumbled flower. In terms of shape, both have the shape of their location. In terms of direction, bound bile is produced in the upper direction. The other, unbound bile, is produced in both directions (upper and lower). In terms of location, unbound bile spreads throughout the whole body like a drop of oil on water, except for the hair, body hair, teeth, nails, areas free of flesh, and hard dry skin. When this unbound bile is disturbed, the eyes become yellow and rotate, and the body trembles and itches. Bound bile is situated in the bile-sac (gallbladder), which resembles the fruit of a large kosātakī, relying on the liver between the heart and the lungs. When this bound bile is disturbed, beings go mad; their minds become deranged, and casting off shame and fear, they do what should not be done, say what should not be said, and think what should not be thought. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of the bile itself. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair.

Phlegm (semha) exists inside the body in the measure of a bowlful. In terms of color, it is white, having the color of the juice of nāgabala leaves. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated on the stomach lining (udarapaṭala). When food and drink are swallowed, just as moss and water-weeds in water split apart when a stick or a pot-shard falls on them and then close over again, so too, when food and drink fall, it splits apart and then closes over again. When this phlegm becomes deficient, the stomach becomes extremely disgusting, having the smell of a rotting carcass, like a ripened boil or a rotten hen's egg. Because of the odor rising from that stomach, the belch and the mouth also have a foul odor like a putrid carcass. Such a person deserves to be told, "Go away, you are spreading a foul smell." When it increases and becomes thick, it stays inside the stomach lining, blocking the smell of the carcass like a wooden lid over a cesspool. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of the phlegm itself. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just like that of the hair.
233:
Pus (pubba) refers to the pus produced by the corruption of blood. In terms of color, it has the color of a pale yellow dry leaf. In a corpse, however, it has the color of thick, putrid rice-scum. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in both directions. In terms of location, there is no fixed place for pus where it always remains like blood. However, it stays in whatever part of the body where blood stagnates and festers due to being struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, or flames, or where boils and abscesses arise. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just as described for the hair.

Blood (lohita) is of two kinds: accumulated blood (sannicita-lohita) and circulating blood (saṃsaraṇa-lohita). Of these, accumulated blood, in terms of color, has the color of thick, cooked lac-dye. Circulating blood has the color of clear lac-dye. In terms of shape, both have the shape of their location. In terms of direction, accumulated blood is produced in the upper direction. The other, circulating blood, is produced in both directions. In terms of location, circulating blood spreads throughout the whole organic body, following the network of veins, except for the hair, body hair, teeth, nails, areas free of flesh, and thick dry skin. Accumulated blood fills the area below the liver to the measure of about a bowlful, and trickling slightly from above the heart, kidneys, and lungs, it remains moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. If this blood does not moisten the kidneys, heart, etc., beings become thirsty. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just as described for the hair.

Sweat (seda) is the water element (āpodhātu) that trickles from the pores and so on. In terms of color, it has the color of very clear sesame oil. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in both directions. In terms of location, there is no fixed place for sweat where it always remains like blood. However, when the body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, or seasonal changes, it trickles from all the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair, like a bundle of unevenly cut lotus stalks and fibers just pulled out of the water. Therefore, its shape should be understood only by way of the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair. A practitioner who grasps the sweat by way of knowledge should direct his mind to the sweat only as it remains filling the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion. This is its similar delimitation. Its dissimilar delimitation is just as described for the hair.
234:
Fat (medo) is the solidified grease. In color, it is the color of split turmeric. In shape, in a stout person, it has the shape of a turmeric-colored piece of fine cloth placed between the skin and the flesh. In a lean person, it has the shape of a turmeric-colored piece of fine cloth placed in two or three layers, depending on the flesh of the calves, the thighs, the back flesh near the spine, and the belly. In direction, it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. In location, it spreads throughout the whole body of a stout person; in a lean person, it is situated depending on the flesh of the calves and so on. Although it reaches the category of grease, because it is extremely loathsome, people do not take it for the purpose of hair oil for the head or for the purpose of nasal oil and so on. In terms of boundary, it is bounded below by the flesh, above by the skin, and transversely by its own portion of fat. This is its boundary of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Its boundary of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is like that of the hair.

Tears (assu) are the water element (āpodhātu) trickling from the eyes. In color, they have the color of particularly clear sesame oil. In shape, they have the shape of their location. In direction, they occur in the upper direction. In location, they are situated in the eye sockets. These tears do not always remain accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the gallbladder. But when beings are joyful and laugh loudly, or are sorrowful and weep and lament, or partake of such incompatible food, or when their eyes are struck by smoke, dust, grit, and so on, then, being produced by that joy, sorrow, incompatible food, or climate (utu), they remain filling the eye sockets or they trickle out. A meditator (yogī) who grasps the tears should grasp them only as they remain filling the eye sockets. In terms of boundary, they are bounded by their own portion of tears. This is their boundary of the similar. Their boundary of the dissimilar is like that of the hair.

Grease (vasā) is melted oil. In color, it has the color of coconut oil; it may also be said to have the color of oil poured on rice-washing water. In shape, it has the shape of a drop of oil spreading and circling on the surface of clear water at the time of bathing. In direction, it occurs in both the upper and lower directions. In location, it is mostly situated on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the points of the shoulders. This grease does not always remain melted in those places. But when those parts become heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, an incompatible climate, or incompatible elements (dhātu), then it moves here and there like a drop of oil spreading on the surface of clear water at the time of bathing. In terms of boundary, [it is bounded] by its own portion of grease...
235:
...is bounded. This is its boundary of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Its boundary of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

Saliva (kheḷo) is the water element (āpodhātu) mixed with foam inside the mouth. In color, it is white, the color of foam. In shape, it has the shape of its location; it may also be said to have the shape of foam. It occurs in the upper direction. In location, it descends from both sides of the cheeks and stays on the tongue. This saliva does not always remain accumulated in the mouth. Rather, when beings see or remember such food, or place any of the hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour tastes in the mouth, or when their heart is weary, or when disgust arises for some object, then saliva is produced and, descending from both sides of the cheeks, stays on the tongue. This saliva is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue. It is able to moisten parched rice, husked rice, or any other eatable placed in the mouth without being exhausted, like the water in a small well dug in a river sandbank. In terms of boundary, it is bounded by its own portion of saliva. This is its boundary of the similar. Its boundary of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

Nasal mucus (siṅghāṇikā) is the impure liquid trickling from the brain. In color, it has the color of the kernel of a young palmyra nut. In shape, it has the shape of its location. It occurs in the upper direction. In location, it remains filling the nostrils. This nasal mucus does not always remain accumulated in the nostrils. Rather, just as if a man were to wrap curd in a lotus leaf and pierce it from below with a thorn, then the whey of the curd would trickle through that hole and fall outside; even so, when beings weep, or when there is a disturbance of the elements produced by the power of incompatible food or climate, then the brain inside the head, having reached the state of putrid phlegm, trickles down, descends through the opening in the roof of the palate, and remains filling the nostrils or trickles out. A meditator (yogī) who grasps the nasal mucus should grasp it only as it remains filling the nostrils. In terms of boundary, it is bounded by its own portion of nasal mucus. This is its boundary of the similar. Its boundary of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

Synovial fluid (lasikā) is the viscous, putrid liquid inside the joints of the body. In color, it has the color of kaṇikāra resin. In shape, it has the shape of its location. It occurs in both directions. In location, it stays inside the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints. For one in whom this synovial fluid is scanty, that person...
236:
When standing up, sitting down, moving forward, returning, bending, or stretching, the bones (of a person with little lubricant) make a 'katakata' sound. They move as if making the sound of snapping fingers. Even when traveling a distance of one or two leagues (yojana), the air element (vāyodhātu) becomes disturbed, and the limbs ache. If that lubricant is abundant, the bones do not make the 'katakata' sound during standing, sitting, etc. Even when traveling a long distance, the air element is not disturbed, and the limbs do not ache. By delimitation, it is bounded by the portion of lubricant itself. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāgapariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāgapariccheda) is like that of the hair.

Urine (mutta) is the color of bean-broth. In shape, it is like the water inside a water pot placed upside down. In direction, it is in the lower direction. In location, it stays inside the bladder (vatthi). The bladder-sac is called the bladder (vatthi). For example, just as when a mouthless porous pot is placed in a cesspool, the liquid from the cesspool enters it but its path of entry is not apparent, so too, urine enters the bladder from the body but its path of entry is not apparent. Its path of exit, however, is clear. When the bladder is full of urine, the urge 'I will pass urine' arises in beings. By delimitation, it is bounded by the interior of the bladder and the portion of urine. This is its sabhāgapariccheda. Its visabhāgapariccheda is like that of the hair.

Thus, having defined the parts such as hair by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and by the method of not too fast and not too slow, and by way of the fivefold aspects of color, shape, smell, origin (āsaya), and location, for one who reflects 'repulsive, repulsive' (paṭikkūla), by way of transcending the concept (paññatti), just as a man with good sight looking at a garland of flowers of thirty-two colors tied with a single thread sees all the flowers clearly without before or after, so too, for one who contemplates this body as 'There are in this body hairs...', all those things appear clearly without before or after. Therefore, it is said in the 'Skill in Attention' (Manasikārakosallakathā): 'For a beginner reflecting on "hairs", the attention proceeds and stops only upon reaching the final part "urine".' If one also directs the attention externally, then when all parts have become clear to that yogi, beings such as humans and animals who are wandering about lose the appearance of a 'being' and appear only as a heap of parts. The food and drink consumed by those beings also appear as if being thrown into a heap of parts. Then to that yogi...
237:
By way of letting go in order (of the parts that are not clear) and reflecting repeatedly as 'repulsive, repulsive', the absorption (appanā) gradually arises for him.

Therein, the appearance of parts such as hair by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign (uggahanimitta). The appearance as repulsive in every aspect is the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). For one who repeatedly considers and reflects on that counterpart sign, striking it again and again with applied thought (vitakka), the four mental aggregates have the repulsive object, and absorption occurs by way of the first jhāna. The preliminary (parikamma) and access (upacāra) consciousnesses occurring before the first jhāna are accompanied by vitakka, vicāra, pīti, and somanassa, and have the repulsive sign as their object. The absorption jhāna is also accompanied by vitakka, vicāra, pīti, and somanassa. However, by way of plane, they are sublime (mahaggata) and of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). Even in this repulsive object, joy (somanassa) arises because of seeing the benefits, or it arises simply by the power of the single-pointed object. The second jhāna and so on do not arise here. Why? Because the object is gross. This object is gross. In this meditation, one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) arises only by the power of vitakka, not by transcending vitakka. This is the talk on meditation by way of serenity (samatha).

In general, without distinction, it should be understood thus: One who wishes to develop this meditation, after learning it, should at the time of recitation (sajjhāya) repeatedly recite with the voice the signs of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation of hair and so on, and for each part, recitation should be done in three ways as 'This part is similar to this thing'. How? First, in the skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka), as mentioned before, one should recite for half a month (fifteen days): five days in forward order (anuloma), five days in reverse order (paṭiloma), and five days in both forward and reverse order. Then, having gone to the teacher and learned the kidney-pentad (vakka-pañcaka), one should recite for fifteen days in the same way. Then, combining those ten parts, for fifteen days. Again, learning each of the lung-pentad (papphāsa-pañcaka) etc., for fifteen days. Then, those fifteen parts for fifteen days. The brain-pentad (matthaluṅga-pañcaka) for fifteen days. Then, the twenty-three parts for fifteen days. The fat-hexad (meda-chakka) for fifteen days. Then, combining those twenty-six parts for fifteen days. The urine-hexad (mutta-chakka) for fifteen days. Then, combining all thirty-two parts for fifteen days. Thus, recitation should be performed for six months.

Therein, for a wise monk endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), the parts appear even while learning the meditation; for some, they do not appear. Even if they do not appear, one should not give up effort. One should take as many parts as appear and perform the recitation.
238:
