Effort should not be abandoned. To the extent that the parts (koṭṭhāsa) appear, one should take up those parts and perform recitation (sajjhāya). When a teacher explains the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in this way, they should not explain it according to the capacity of one with great wisdom nor one with dull wisdom, but only according to the capacity of one with medium wisdom (majjhimapañña). This is because the teachers of old established the sequence of the texts by defining a period of six months for those of medium wisdom.

(The method of recitation during those six months is as follows: First, in the Taca-pañcaka, one should recite for fifteen days—five days in forward order (anuloma), five days in reverse order (paṭiloma), and five days in both forward and reverse order. Then, going to the teacher and learning the Vakka-pañcaka, one should recite in the same manner. Then, combining those ten parts, one should recite for fifteen days. Again, learning each group such as the Papphāsa-pañcaka and reciting for fifteen days each, then reciting the fifteen parts together for fifteen days, the Matthaluṅga-pañcaka for fifteen days, then the twenty-three parts together for fifteen days, the Meda-chakka for fifteen days, then the twenty-six parts together for fifteen days, the Mutta-chakka for fifteen days, and finally, combining all thirty-two parts together, one should recite for fifteen days. In this way, one recites for six months.)

If the parts do not become clear even within these six months, one must continue to recite beyond that period. However, one should not do so without a defined limit; it should be done by defining periods of six months each. One who performs the recitation should not contemplate the color (vaṇṇa), nor should they attend to the characteristic (lakkhaṇa); the recitation should be done only by way of the parts. The teacher also should not explain by stipulating, 'Perform the recitation by way of color.' If it is explained by stipulating, what is the fault? It is the falling into the wrong perception that something is defective even when it is perfect. For if the teacher says, 'Recite by way of color,' and while that bhikkhu is doing so, the meditation subject does not appear to him by way of color but appears by way of loathsomeness (paṭikūla) or by way of elements (dhātu), then that bhikkhu will perceive, 'This meditation subject is not of the correct characteristic,' and will try to grasp only what the teacher explained by mere conjecture. Even if told, 'Recite by way of loathsomeness,' if it does not appear to him as loathsome but appears by way of color or elements, then he will perceive, 'This meditation subject is not of the correct characteristic,' and will try to grasp only what the teacher explained by mere conjecture. Even if told, 'Recite by way of elements,' if it does not appear to him as elements but appears by way of color or loathsomeness, then he will perceive, 'This meditation subject is not of the correct characteristic,' and will try to grasp only what the teacher explained by mere conjecture. This is the fault in the teacher explaining by stipulating.

Then how should it be said? It should be said, 'Perform the recitation by way of the parts.' How? It should be said, 'Perform the recitation as the group of hair, the group of body hair, and so on.' If, while reciting by way of the parts in this way, it appears to him by way of color, then that bhikkhu should report to the instructing teacher (ovādācariya), 'Venerable Sir, I am reciting the thirty-two aspects by way of the parts, but it appears to me by way of color.' The teacher should not misguide him by saying, 'This is a false meditation subject; it is not the correct characteristic.' He should say, 'Excellent, virtuous one! In the past, you must have performed preliminary work (parikamma) on a color kasiṇa. This meditation subject that appears by way of color is indeed suitable for you.'
239:
It should be said, 'Perform the recitation only by way of color (vaṇṇa).' That bhikkhu also should perform the recitation only by way of color. One who does so obtains the four color kasiṇas within his own continuity: the blue kasiṇa, the yellow kasiṇa, the red kasiṇa, and the white kasiṇa. How? When he attends to the color in the hair, body hair, and bile, as well as the black portion of the eyes, as 'blue, blue,' the fourth and fifth jhanas arise. Making that jhana the basis and developing insight (vipassanā), he reaches the fruit of Arahatship. When he attends to the color in the fat and the yellow portion of the eyes as 'yellow, yellow,' the fourth and fifth jhanas arise. Making that jhana the basis and developing insight, he reaches the fruit of Arahatship. When he attends to the color in the flesh and blood, as well as the red portion of the eyes, as 'red, red,' the fourth and fifth jhanas arise. Making that jhana the basis and developing insight, he reaches the fruit of Arahatship. When he attends to the color in the nails, teeth, skin, and bones, as well as the white portion of the eyes, as 'white, white,' the fourth and fifth jhanas arise. Making that jhana the basis and developing insight, he reaches the fruit of Arahatship. This is the culmination (nigamana) up to Arahatship for a bhikkhu who is intent on the way of color.

To another bhikkhu, while performing the recitation by way of the parts (koṭṭhāsa), it appears by way of loathsomeness (paṭikūla). Then that bhikkhu should report to the instructing teacher. The teacher should not cause him to have a wrong view by saying, 'This is a false meditation subject, not a real one; it does not accord with the characteristic.' He should say, 'Excellent, virtuous one! In the past, you must have practiced the meditation on loathsomeness (paṭikūla-manasikāra). This meditation subject is indeed suitable for you. Perform the recitation only by way of loathsomeness.' That bhikkhu also should perform the recitation by way of loathsomeness. While he is reciting by way of loathsomeness thus: 'Hair is indeed unworthy among people, it has a foul smell, it is loathsome, it is repulsive,' the first jhana arises in the object of loathsomeness. Making that jhana the basis and developing insight, he reaches the fruit of Arahatship. This is the culmination up to Arahatship for a bhikkhu who is intent on the way of loathsomeness.

To another bhikkhu, while performing the recitation by way of the parts, it appears by way of elements (dhātu). When it appears by way of elements, how does it appear? First, the hair appears like blunt grass growing on top of an anthill. The body hair appears like dabba grass growing in an old village site. The nails appear like the shells of the seeds of the Madhuka fruit placed on small sticks. The teeth appear like gourd seeds inserted into a lump of fine clay. The skin appears like wet leather stretched over the body of a lute; the flesh appears like [clay on] a wall...
240:
Flesh appears like clay repeatedly plastered on a wall. Sinews appear like creepers binding a wooden structure. Bones appear like a wooden or bamboo wall structure set upright. Bone marrow appears like rattan shoots placed in a large bamboo and boiled. These six parts—the diaphragm, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, and lungs—appear like a kitchen where food is cooked. The large intestine, thirty-two cubits long, appears like a water snake coiled in a blood trough. The small intestine appears like a small string sewn into a foot-wiping cord. New food appears like rice placed in a filter cloth. Old food appears like yellow clay placed in a bamboo joint. The brain appears like four lumps of rice flour pressed down. The twelve types of water element appear like water filled in twelve water cups arranged in order.

When it appears thus, that meditating monk should report it to his meditation teacher. The teacher should not reject it, saying, 'This is not a meditation subject; its characteristics are different.' Instead, he should say, 'Excellent, good man! You must have practiced the reflection on elements in the past. This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Perform the recitation by way of the elements alone.' That monk should also perform the recitation by way of the elements.

The method of recitation through the reflection on elements is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk reflects: 'Hairs of the head grow on the skin that covers the head. Those hairs do not know, "We grow on the skin that covers the head." The skin that covers the head also does not know, "Hairs grow on me." These hairs are non-sentient, they are indeterminate, they are empty, they are stiff, and they are the earth element.' He reflects: 'Body hairs grow on the skin that covers the body. They do not know, "We grow on the skin that covers the body." The skin that covers the body also does not know, "Body hairs grow on me." These body hairs are also non-sentient. Nails grow on the tips of the fingers and toes. They do not know, "We grow on the tips of the fingers and toes." The tips of the fingers and toes also do not know, "Nails grow on us." These nails are also non-sentient. Teeth grow in the jawbone. They do not know, "We grow in the jawbone." The jawbone also does not know, "Teeth grow in me." These teeth are also non-sentient. The skin does not know, "I cover the body." The body also does not know, "I am covered by skin." This skin is also non-sentient. The flesh does not know, "I plaster the body." The body also does not know, "I am plastered with flesh." This flesh is also non-sentient. The sinews do not know, "I stand binding the skeleton together..."
241:
"(The sinews) do not know, 'I stand binding the skeleton together.' The skeleton also does not know, 'I am bound by a net of sinews.' These (sinews and bones) are also non-sentient.

The skull does not know, 'I rest on the neck bone.' The neck bone also does not know, 'The skull rests on me.' The neck bone does not know, 'I rest on the backbone.' The backbone, as well as the hip bone, thigh bone, shin bone, and ankle bone, do not know, 'I rest on the heel bone.' The heel bone also does not know, 'I stand supporting the ankle bone.' ... The neck bone also does not know, 'I stand supporting the skull.'

The bones stand joined end to end in order,
Protected by many joints, not joined by anyone;
Bound only by sinews, driven by old age toward death,
Non-sentient, they are just like a log or a stump.

'This (bone) is also non-sentient. Bone marrow, diaphragm ... brain are non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, stiff, and are the earth element,' he reflects. 'Bile, phlegm ... urine are non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, liquid, and are the water element,' he reflects.

For one who grasps these two great elements, the fire element becomes manifest as heat in the stomach, and the air element becomes manifest as breath in the nose. For one who grasps these four great elements, derived matter becomes manifest. What is called a great element is delimited by derived matter, and derived matter by the great elements. Just as sunlight is delimited by shadow and shadow by sunlight, even so, the great elements are delimited by derived matter and derived matter by the great elements. Then, while grasping the aggregate of form as 'The four great elements and twenty-three kinds of derived matter are the aggregate of form,' the mental aggregates become manifest to him by way of the bases and doors. Thus, the grasping of mentality and materiality constitutes the five aggregates; the five aggregates are the twelve bases; the twelve bases are the eighteen elements. Thus, by way of the aggregates, bases, and elements, he defines mentality and materiality by dividing them into two parts, like splitting a twin palmyra nut.

He investigates: 'This mentality and materiality did not arise without a cause or without conditions; it arose only with causes and conditions. What is its cause? What is its condition?' As he investigates, he discerns the causes of that mentality and materiality as being due to causes such as ignorance, craving, karma, and nutriment. He overcomes doubt regarding the three periods of time, realizing that in the past, future, and present, there are causes and there are effects produced by causes, and that beyond these causes and effects, there is no such thing as a 'being' or a 'person,' but only a mass of purely mental and material formations. This insight is called 'full understanding of the known' (ñātapariññā), which marks the notation of formations. For a monk who has thus well-noted formations, he is said to have gained a footing in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is said to have found a support, and is called a 'Lesser Stream-enterer' (cūḷasotāpanna) whose destiny is certain."
242:
"Due to the cause of ignorance, due to the cause of craving, due to the cause of kamma, and due to the cause of nutriment [mind-and-matter arises]," thus defining the causes of mind-and-matter, one overcomes doubt regarding the three periods of time, thinking: "In the past, there were causes and there were effects produced by causes. In the future and in the present, there are causes and there are effects produced by causes. Beyond these causes and effects, there is no being or person; there is only a mere heap of formations (saṅkhāra)." This marking of formations is called 'ñātapariññā' (full understanding of the known).

A monk who stands having well-marked formations in this way is said to have taken root in the Dispensation of the Buddha, to have gained a foothold, and is called a 'cūḷasotāpanna' (lesser stream-enterer) with a certain destiny. Such a monk, having obtained suitable climate, suitable persons, suitable food, and suitable hearing of the Dhamma, sitting in a single seat in the noble cross-legged posture, applying the three characteristics and contemplating formations according to the sequence of insight (vipassanā), can attain the fruit of Arahantship. This is the conclusion up to Arahantship for a monk who applies himself by way of the elements (dhātu).

If the meditation does not appear to a person by way of color, or by way of repulsiveness, or by way of voidness (suññata), he should not sit idly, abandoning the meditation subject while thinking, "It does not appear to me." Rather, he should apply effort only in the attention to the parts (koṭṭhāsa). The ancient elders said, "Attention to the parts alone is the standard (the essential)." Therefore, when that person practices recitation by way of the parts repeatedly, the parts become proficient (paguṇa). When are they said to be proficient? When, upon merely reflecting "hair of the head" (kesā), the attention goes and stays at the final part, "brain" (matthaluṅga); and upon merely reflecting "brain," the attention comes and stays at the first part, "hair of the head" (kesā).

Then, just as a man with vision looking at a garland of thirty-two kinds of colored flowers strung on a single thread, or looking back at thirty-two fence posts that have been planted, sees the thirty-two kinds of flowers or the fence posts clearly in sequence, even so the thirty-two parts appear. Moving animals and humans no longer appear as "beings" but appear only as "parts" (koṭṭhāsa). Consuming food and snacks becomes like putting them into the midst of the parts.

From the time the parts are proficient, one will be liberated through one of the three doors (color, repulsiveness, or voidness). The meditation subject [appears] by way of color, or by way of repulsiveness, or by way of voidness...
243:
...appears. For example, just as a woman wishing to bake cakes chooses and bakes whatever she desires from the kneaded flour, or just as water comes out from whichever side one tilts a pot full of water placed on level ground, even so, from the time the parts are proficient, one will be liberated through one of the three doors. The meditation subject will surely appear by way of color if desired, by way of repulsiveness if desired, or by way of voidness (suññata) if desired. This extent is called 'uggahasandhi' (the link of learning). The monks who, standing in this uggahasandhi, reached the fruit of Arahantship are beyond counting.

If the meditation subject does not appear to someone in the uggahasandhi, he should learn the meditation subject, and if the monastery where the teacher resides is suitable, staying there is good. If not, he should stay in a suitable place. The resident should avoid the eighteen faults of a monastery and stay in a lodging (senāsana) endowed with five factors; he himself must also be endowed with five factors. Thereafter, having returned from the alms round after the meal, he should enter his night quarters or day quarters and attend to the meditation subject.

How should he attend to it? First, he should attend to it in sequence as mentioned below, not skipping any. For one who attends in sequence is like a man who climbs a palace by stepping on a thirty-two-step ladder in order and enjoys the benefits of the palace; by attending to the meditation subject in sequence as 'hair of the head, body hair,' etc., he does not fall away from the meditation subject and enjoys the nine supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) which are like the benefits of the palace. In attending in sequence, he should attend neither too fast nor too slow. For one who attends too fast, although the meditation subject is memorized, it does not become clear. The simile for this has been mentioned below.

For one who attends too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach the end and falters in the middle. For example, a man sets out on a journey of three leagues in the evening, having tucked up his loincloth. From the place he started, if he sees cool shade, he rests; if he sees a pleasant sandy stretch, he lies down; if he sees a forest pond, he drinks and bathes; if he sees a mountain, he climbs it and looks at the beauty of the mountain. While he is traveling thus slowly, in the middle of the road, lions, tigers, or leopards kill him, or robbers...
244:
Furthermore, just as [robbers] plunder, destroy, and kill, so too for one who attends [to the meditation object] too slowly, the meditation does not reach its conclusion but sinks away in the middle.

Therefore, one should attend to it thirty times a day, neither too fast nor too slow. One should recite ten times in the morning, ten times at midday, and ten times in the evening; it is not proper to neglect it. For example, just as it is not proper to wake up early in the morning and not wash one's face, or not to eat food, [so it is here]. While it might be acceptable to neglect washing the face and such, it is absolutely not proper to neglect this attention to meditation. One who practices and strives remains having attained great benefit.

For example, a man has three fields: one yields eight *kumbhas*, one sixteen, and one thirty-two. If he cannot tend all three fields, he should abandon two and tend only the one that yields thirty-two *kumbhas*. In that field alone, he should perform plowing, sowing, weeding, and so on. Just as that field alone will provide the profit that would have come from the other two fields, so too, even if one must abandon other tasks like washing the face, one should strive only in this work of meditation; it is not proper to neglect it. By saying, 'One who practices and strives remains having attained great benefit,' the Middle Way (*majjhimā paṭipadā*) has been taught.

One who practices in this way should also prevent distraction (*vikkhepa*). If, having abandoned the meditation object, the mind wanders externally, one falls away from the meditation and cannot transcend the danger of the round of rebirths (*vaṭṭa*). For example, a man who has gained profit from a capital of a thousand [pieces of gold] is traveling; in the middle of his journey, he climbs onto a narrow wooden bridge the width of a single footstep, stretched over a deep mountain ravine inhabited by crocodiles, sea monsters (*makara*), and predatory *rakkhasas*. If, while crossing, he fails to pay attention to where he steps and looks here and there, he falls and becomes food for the crocodiles and so on. In the same way, if this person abandons the meditation object and his mind wanders externally, he falls away from the meditation and cannot transcend the danger of the round of rebirths.

The connection with the analogy is as follows: The time when this monk learns the meditation from his teacher should be understood as the time when the man gained profit from his capital of a thousand. *Saṃsāra* should be understood as the deep mountain ravine in between. The great sufferings rooted in the round of rebirths should be understood as the time when the crocodiles bite. This monk's sequence of recitation should be understood as the narrow wooden bridge the width of a single footstep. That man's...
245:
...climbing the narrow wooden bridge and, having abandoned the footstep, looking here and there, falling and becoming food for the crocodiles and so on—this should be understood as the state of this monk who, having abandoned the meditation object, has a mind distracted externally, falls away from the meditation, and is unable to transcend the danger of the round of rebirths.

Therefore, the hair of the head (*kesā*) should be attended to. Having attended to the hair of the head and prevented the distraction of the mind's arising to the external, one should attend with a pure mind only: 'body hair, nails, teeth, skin' (*lomā nakhā dantā taco*). One who attends in this way does not fall away from the meditation and transcends the danger of the round of rebirths. Here, the same analogy should be understood in reverse. Just as a skilled man who has completed his capital of a thousand and gained profit, having climbed the wooden bridge, arranged his inner and outer garments, and made his body firm, reaches the other shore safely; so too, a skilled monk who attends to the hair of the head, prevents distraction, and attends with a pure mind, 'body hair, nails, teeth, skin,' should be understood as not falling away from the meditation and transcending the danger of the round of rebirths.

A monk who thus prevents external distraction should also attend by way of transcending the concept (*paññatti*) according to the method mentioned below. Having abandoned the name-concept 'hair of the head, body hair,' mindfulness should be established as 'repulsive, repulsive' (*paṭikūla*). At first, however, it does not appear as repulsive. As long as it does not so appear, the name-concept should not be abandoned. When it does appear, then one should abandon the name-concept and attend to it as 'repulsive.' In doing so, one should attend to the repulsiveness by way of the five aspects according to the method mentioned below. In the 'skin-pentad' (*tacapañcaka*), the fivefold repulsiveness is obtained by way of color (*vaṇṇa*), shape (*saṇṭhāna*), smell (*gandha*), habitat (*āsaya*), and location (*okāsa*). In the remaining groups also, attention should be maintained by way of whatever [aspects] are obtained.

Among those thirty-two parts, the five groups beginning with hair of the head are known as beautiful signs (*subhanimitta*), grounds for lust (*rāga*), and desirable objects (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*). All beings who are prone to attachment are attached to these five groups. But this monk, in these groups which are the ground for the attachment of the multitude, reaches absorption (*appanā*) [by attending to them] as 'repulsive.' From the attainment of absorption therein onwards, he reaches absorption further without difficulty.

In this regard, there is this analogy: Just as a skilled archer, having pleased the king and received an excellent village yielding a hundred thousand, goes there armed with the five kinds of weapons...
246:
If one sees thirty-two thieves on a journey and kills five of the chief thieves among them, from the time those chief thieves are killed, no two of the remaining thieves will travel together on the same path. This analogy should be understood as follows: The time when this monk learns the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from his teacher and remains established in it is like the time when an archer pleases the king and receives the reward of a noble village. The thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) are like the thirty-two thieves. The five parts beginning with hair (kesā) are like the five chief thieves. The time when this monk reaches absorption (appanā) regarding the 'loathsomeness' of the skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka)—which is the object of attachment for all beings—is like the time when the chief thieves are killed. The attainment of absorption in the remaining parts without fatigue is like the time when the remaining thieves flee at the mere snapping of fingers.

A monk who thus transcends the conceptual designation (paññatti) should develop his attention (manasikāra) by letting go in successive order. While attending to the hair of the head (kesā), he should direct his mindfulness toward the hair of the body (lomā) while still maintaining regard for the hair of the head. As long as the hair of the body does not appear, he should continue to attend, 'Hair of the head, hair of the head.' When the hair of the body appears, he should let go of the hair of the head and establish mindfulness on the hair of the body. In the same way, attention should be developed for the nails (nakhā) and so forth.

In this matter, there is this simile: Just as a leech (jalūka) (or a caterpillar), while moving, does not let go of the place held by its tail until it finds a footing in front, but when it finds a footing in front, it lifts its tail and places it where it is holding with its mouth; even so, while attending to the hair of the head, the monk should direct his mindfulness toward the hair of the body while still maintaining regard for the hair of the head. As long as the hair of the body does not appear, he should continue to attend, 'Hair of the head, hair of the head.' When the hair of the body appears, he should let go of the hair of the head and establish mindfulness on the hair of the body. In the same way, attention should be developed for the nails and so forth.

A monk who proceeds in this way should perfect his skill in attention, which is said to lead to absorption. How? For one who attends to this meditation subject that leads to absorption, absorption is reached. At first, it does not appear. Indeed, the mind that has been cultivated among various objects in the beginningless cycle of Saṃsāra, upon merely reflecting 'hair of the head,' follows the flow of recitation (sajjhāya-sota) and settles on the brain (matthaluṅga). Upon merely reflecting 'brain,' it follows the flow of recitation and settles on the hair of the head. However, for one who attends repeatedly, each respective part appears.
247:
Mindfulness exists together with concentration (samādhi). For the monk who attends repeatedly in this way, each respective part (koṭṭhāsa) appears. Therefore, whichever part appears most clearly, he should apply double effort to that part and reach absorption (appanā). From the time he reaches absorption in this way, he can reach absorption in the remaining parts without fatigue. In reaching this, the simile of the monkey in the palm grove is applicable.

Furthermore, the meaning should be understood by applying it in this way: A monkey lives in a palm grove of thirty-two trees. A hunter, wishing to catch that monkey, stands at the base of a palm tree at the edge of the grove and shouts to frighten it. The proud monkey leaps from tree to tree and stands on the palm tree at the far end. The hunter also goes to that far end and shouts again. The monkey then returns to the original palm tree as before. Being chased back and forth, the monkey becomes tired. When the hunter stands at the base of each tree and shouts, the monkey gets up and moves on, becoming extremely exhausted. Finally, it firmly grasps the spike of a young palm leaf (makuḷa-paṇṇa-sūci) of one palm tree and, even when pierced by the tip of a bow (dhanu-koṭi), it no longer flees.

In this simile, the thirty-two palm trees are like the thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa). The monkey is like the mind. The hunter is like the meditator (yogāvacara). The monkey's flight to the far end when the hunter shouts at the base of the tree is like the mind—which has been expanded among various objects in the beginningless cycle of Saṃsāra—going according to the flow of recitation (sajjhāya) and settling on the brain upon merely reflecting 'hair of the head.' The return to this end when the hunter shouts at the far end is like the mind going according to the flow of recitation and settling on the hair of the head upon merely reflecting 'brain.' The monkey's moving from where the hunter shouts when it is tired from being chased back and forth is like the mindfulness being established and proceeding as each part appears through repeated attention. The monkey's not fleeing even when pierced by the tip of a bow is like reaching absorption by applying double attention to whichever part appears most clearly. (Thus should the simile and the thing signified be compared.)

From the time absorption is reached in the part that appears most clearly, one will be able to reach absorption in the remaining parts without fatigue. Therefore, one should reflect and attend repeatedly, 'Loathsome, loathsome.' One should strike it with investigation (takka) and strike it with initial thought (vitakka). For one who does so, the four [mental] aggregates (khandha) have the loathsome object, and he reaches absorption. The preliminary (parikamma) and access (upacāra) consciousnesses are accompanied by initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra); all this is exactly as stated below. However, for a yogi who attends to a single part, a single first jhāna occurs. For a yogi who attends to the parts individually, thirty-two first jhānas occur. In the hand...
248:
In the mental continuum of a yogi monk who attends to a single part (koṭṭhāsa), a single first jhāna arises. In the mental continuum of a yogi monk who attends to the various parts individually, thirty-two first jhānas arise. The matter of the question held in hand is just as it naturally is. "So taṃ nimittaṃ" means that monk [attends to] the sign which is the object of that meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Āsevati" means he pursues or associates with it. "Bhāveti" means he develops or increases it. "Bahulīkaroti" means he does it repeatedly. "Svāvatthitaṃ vavatthāpeti" means he makes it thoroughly well-defined. "Bahiddhā kāye cittaṃ upasaṃharati" means having done so, he applies, places, or directs his mind to the external body of another. "Atthissa kāye" means they exist in that other person's body. "Ajjhattabahiddhākāye cittaṃ upasaṃharati" means at the appropriate time he directs the mind to his own body, and at the appropriate time to the bodies of others. Why is the phrase "Atthi kāye" (There are in the body) said? It is said because it is not intended to refer exclusively to one's own body, nor exclusively to the body of another. In this context, for one who performs the preliminary work (parikamma) on one's own living body as "repulsive" (paṭikūla), both absorption (appanā) and access concentration (upacāra) can arise. For one who attends to another's living body as "repulsive," neither absorption nor access concentration arises. If asked, "Do both not arise in the ten foulness (asubha) meditations?" Yes, they do. Indeed, those ten foulnesses belong to the category of non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) matter. Therefore, both absorption and access concentration can arise there. But this body of another belongs to the category of clung-to (upādinnaka) matter. That is why both do not arise in this case. However, it should be understood that insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā) known as the contemplation of foulness (asubhānupassanā) can occur. What is taught in this section? Both calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are taught.

Now, in these parts such as hair, etc., the mixed analysis connected with all modes of attention should be understood in the following way: The determination of hair, etc., should be understood by way of sign (nimitta), characteristic (lakkhaṇa), element (dhātu), and furthermore by way of emptiness (suññata), and aggregates (khandha), etc. Therein, "nimittato" means there are 160 signs in the 32 parts. By means of these 160 signs, the practitioner (yogāvacara) grasps the 32 parts by way of their portions. For example, in hair, there are five signs: the sign of color, the sign of shape, the sign of direction, the sign of location, and the sign of delimitation. The same method applies to body hair, etc. "Lakkhaṇato" means there are 128 characteristics in the 32 parts. By means of these 128 characteristics, the practitioner attends to the 32 parts by way of their characteristics.
249:
For example, in hair, there are four characteristics: the characteristic of hardness, the characteristic of cohesion, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of support. The same method applies to body hair and other parts.

'By way of element' (dhātuto) means among the elements mentioned in the phrase "Monk, this person consists of four elements," there are 128 elements in the 32 parts. The practitioner monk distinguishes the 32 parts by way of elements through these. For example, in hair, the quality of hardness is the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the quality of cohesion is the water element (āpo-dhātu), the quality of heat is the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and the quality of support is the air element (vāyo-dhātu). Thus there are four elements. The same applies to body hair, etc.

'By way of emptiness' (suññato) means there are 96 kinds of emptiness in the 32 parts. The practitioner views the 32 parts as empty through these. For example, hair is empty of a self (atta), of what belongs to a self (attaniya), of permanence (nicca), of stability (dhuva), of eternity (sassata), or of the nature of non-changeability (avipariṇāmadhamma). In hair, there are three kinds of emptiness: emptiness of self, emptiness of what belongs to self, and emptiness of the nature of permanence. The same applies to body hair, etc.

'By way of aggregates, etc.' (khandhādito) means when grasping hair, etc., by way of aggregates and so on, the determination should be known by the method: "How many aggregates are hair? How many bases (āyatana)? How many elements (dhātu)? How many truths (sacca)? How many foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)?"

Having shown the contemplation of the body in detail in three ways by the division of internal, etc., the text now begins with "anupassī," etc., to analyze the terms such as "kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno." Therein, to show that contemplation by which one is called a "contemplator of the body," it is said: "Therein, what is contemplation? It is the wisdom, the act of knowing," and so on. The same method applies to "ātāpī" (ardent), etc.

Therein, the terms "paññā" (wisdom), "pajānanā" (knowing), etc., should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the section on the arising of consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) below. All terms like "upeto" are synonyms of one another. Specifically, "upeto" means endowed by way of cultivation (āsevana), and "samupeto" means well-endowed by way of development (bhāvanā). This is how the connection of meaning in these terms like "upeto" should be understood. The same method applies to terms like "endowed with this effort."

In the term "viharati," the question "What is dwelling?" is not asked; instead, because of the desire to teach by way of a person-based discourse (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna), "iriyati" (he moves/behaves), etc., is stated. The meaning is: he lives because he is endowed with one of the four postures (iriyāpatha); he exists (moves about) by making the cart of the body proceed by means of those four postures.
250:
*Samupeto* means well-attained or endowed with. In the two dyads *upāgato*, *samupāgato* and *upapanno*, *sampanno*, the same method should be understood. However, in this context, the meaning should be construed as being endowed with (*samannāgato*) by way of frequent practice (*bahulīkāra*). The same method applies to phrases such as 'endowed with this heat of effort' (*iminā ātapena upeto*).

Regarding the word '*viharati*' (dwells), without asking 'what is that dwelling?', the Buddha taught in terms of a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), saying '*iriyati*' (he moves/lives). The meaning is: he lives because he is possessed of one of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). He proceeds by moving the cart of the body through those four postures. He protects the body by preventing the suffering of one posture with another, thus maintaining it for a long time. He sustains life by the occurrence of all postures without stopping in just one. He maintains the body in various ways through various postures. He moves because he causes it to proceed for a long time. He dwells (*viharati*) because he carries on life by interrupting one posture with another.

'That very body is the world' means: in whichever body one dwells contemplating the body, that very body is the 'world' in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating (*lujjana-palujjana*). Since the greed and distress (*abhijjhā-domanassa*) abandoned in the body are also abandoned in feelings and so forth, the five aggregates of clinging are called the 'world'.

In the words beginning with '*santā*', they are 'peaceful' (*santā*) because they are peaceful by way of cessation. They are 'calmed' (*samitā*) because they are calmed by development (*bhāvanā*). They are 'tranquilized' (*vūpasantā*) by way of the tranquility of non-occurrence through the full understanding of the basis. They are 'gone to the goal' (*atthaṅgatā*) because they have reached the goal called cessation. They are 'completely gone to the goal' (*abbhatthaṅgatā*) because they have reached cessation exceedingly by preventing repeated rebirth. '*Appitā*' means destroyed, or placed in non-occurrence. '*Byappitā*' means well-destroyed, or placed exceedingly in non-occurrence. They are 'dried' (*sositā*) because they are dried up so that they do not flow again. They are 'thoroughly dried' (*visositā*) because they are well-dried. They are 'ended' (*byantīkatā*) because they are made to have no end. Here, by 'contemplation' and 'dwelling in the meditation subject,' the maintenance of the body of the meditator is meant. By 'heat' (*ātapa*), Right Effort (*sammappadhāna*) is meant. By 'mindfulness and clear comprehension,' the means of maintaining the meditation subject is meant. Or, by mindfulness, the serenity (*samatha*) obtained through body-contemplation; by clear comprehension, insight (*vipassanā*); and by the removal of greed and distress, the fruit of development is meant.

## The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Body is finished.
251:
## Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of Feelings

In the section on contemplation of feelings, the collection of words similar to those mentioned below in the section on contemplation of the body should be understood in the same way. In the phrase '*suakhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno*' (feeling a pleasant feeling), it means when feeling a pleasant feeling, whether bodily or mental, one understands clearly, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' In this regard, even infants lying on their backs understand 'we feel a pleasant feeling' when they are suckling and so forth. However, this teaching is not intended for that kind of understanding. Because such understanding cannot abandon the view of a being (*sattūpaladdhi*), cannot uproot the perception of a being (*sattasaññā*), and is neither a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) nor the development of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā*).

But the understanding of this meditating monk abandons the view of a being, uproots the perception of a being, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. It is taught with reference to feeling with clear comprehension: 'Who feels this feeling? Whose is the feeling? For what reason does the feeling arise?'

Among those questions, 'Who feels?' means no being or person feels. 'Whose is the feeling?' means it is not the feeling of any being or person. 'For what reason does the feeling arise?' means this feeling arises because of a base (*vatthu*) and an object (*ārammaṇa*). Therefore, this meditator understands: 'Taking that particular base and object of pleasant feeling etc., only the phenomenon of feeling feels; based on the occurrence of that feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say "I feel".' One who notes that 'taking the base as object, only feeling feels' should be known as 'one who understands "I feel a pleasant feeling",' like a certain elder on Cittalapabbata.

That elder, when ill, was groaning and rolling back and forth due to intense pain. Then a young monk asked, 'Venerable sir, where does it hurt?' 'Friend, there is no specific place that hurts; taking the base as object, only feeling feels,' he replied. 'Venerable sir, from the time of knowing this, is it not proper to endure?' the young monk asked. 'Friend, I will endure,' he said. 'Venerable sir, endurance is indeed noble,' the young monk said, and the elder endured. The wind [ailment] split [his body] up to the heart. His intestines were piled up on the couch. The elder showed the young monk, 'Friend, is this much endurance proper?' The young monk remained silent. The elder, balancing energy and concentration, attained Arahantship along with the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and, becoming a *samasīsī* (one who attains Arahantship and Parinibbāna simultaneously), attained final passing away.
252:
Just as when experiencing a pleasant feeling, so too when experiencing a painful feeling... (elision) ... when experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands clearly, 'I experience an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.' In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), and wishing to teach the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), taught it by way of feeling (vedanā). Indeed, meditation subjects are of two kinds: the meditation subject of materiality and the meditation subject of immateriality. These are also called the 'grasping of materiality' (rūpa-pariggaha) and the 'grasping of immateriality' (arūpa-pariggaha).

Among these two, when the Blessed One taught the meditation subject of materiality, He taught the defining of the four elements (catu-dhātu-vavatthāna) by way of either brief attention or detailed attention. Both of these methods have already been shown in all their aspects in the Visuddhimagga. However, when teaching the meditation subject of immateriality, He mostly taught it by way of feeling. Truly, there are three ways of entering into the meditation subject of immateriality: by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of consciousness (citta). How? For a certain person, when the meditation subject of materiality has been grasped either briefly or in detail, contact (phassa) becomes prominent, arising as the first encounter of the mind and mental factors upon that object, touching that object. For another person, feeling (vedanā) becomes prominent, arising as the experience of that object. For another person, consciousness (viññāṇa) becomes prominent, arising as the act of cognizing that object.

Among those three, the person for whom contact is prominent also grasps the group of five beginning with contact (phassa-pañcamaka), reflecting: 'Not only contact arises; together with that contact, feeling that experiences that same object also arises, perception (saññā) that perceives it also arises, volition (cetanā) that urges it also arises, and consciousness (viññāṇa) that cognizes it also arises.' The person for whom feeling is prominent also grasps only the group of five beginning with contact, reflecting: 'Not only feeling arises; together with that feeling, contact that touches that same object also arises, perception also arises, volition also arises, and consciousness also arises.' The person for whom consciousness is prominent also grasps only the group of five beginning with contact, reflecting: 'Not only consciousness arises; together with that consciousness, contact that touches that same object also arises, feeling also arises, perception also arises, and volition also arises.'

That yogi, investigating 'On what do these five factors beginning with contact depend?', understands that 'They depend on the base (vatthu).' The 'base' refers to the physical body (karaja-kāya), with reference to which the Blessed One said: 'And this consciousness of mine is supported here, is bound up here' (Dī. Ni. 1.235). That physical body, in its ultimate sense...
253:
...consists of the Great Essentials (bhūta) and derived materiality (upādā-rūpa). Thus, among these mental and material phenomena, he sees only mentality-materiality (nāma-rūpa), identifying the base (vatthu) as materiality and the group of five beginning with contact as mentality. In this mentality-materiality, materiality is called the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), and mentality is called the four immaterial aggregates; thus, there are only the five aggregates. Indeed, there are no five aggregates apart from mentality-materiality, nor is there mentality-materiality apart from the five aggregates.

When that yogi investigates, 'What is the cause of these five aggregates?', he sees that 'They have causes such as ignorance (avijjā), etc.' Then, he wanders about contemplating with the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), applying the three marks of existence—'impermanence, suffering, non-self'—by way of the sequence of insight (vipassanā), seeing that 'This is only the cause and the effect produced by the cause; there is no other being or person, it is merely a heap of pure formations (saṅkhāra).' That yogi, desiring the penetrative knowledge, thinking 'I shall realize it this very day, this very day,' obtains the suitability of climate (utu-sappāya), suitability of person (puggala-sappāya), suitability of food (bhojana-sappāya), or suitability of hearing the Dhamma (dhamma-savana-sappāya) on such a day. Then, sitting in a single session, he brings insight to its culmination and becomes established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). Thus, the meditation subject is taught for these three types of persons up to the attainment of Arahantship.

In this (Vibhaṅga Pāḷi), however, the Blessed One, wishing to teach the immaterial meditation subject, taught it by way of feeling. If it were taught by way of contact or by way of consciousness, it would not be clear and would appear as if in darkness. But by way of feeling, it is prominent. Why? Because the arising of feelings is prominent. Indeed, the arising of pleasant feeling and painful feeling is prominent. When pleasant feeling arises, it moves, massages, pervades, and overflows the entire body, arising as if one were being made to eat butter washed a hundred times, or as if being anointed with oil cooked a hundred times, or as if the heat were being quenched by a thousand jars of water, causing one to utter, 'Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!'

When painful feeling arises, it moves, massages, pervades, and overflows the entire body, arising as if a red-hot plowshare were being inserted, or as if one were being poured over with molten copper, or as if a bundle of wooden torches were being thrown into a forest of dry grass and trees, causing one to lament, 'Oh, what pain! Oh, what pain!' Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is prominent.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, however, is difficult to point out; it is like darkness and is not clear. That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling becomes prominent to one who grasps it by the method of inference as a neutral state by way of rejecting both the pleasant and the unpleasant when pleasant and painful feelings are absent. For example, just as a hunter following the tracks of a deer that has fled up onto a stone slab, seeing the tracks on this side and that side of the stone slab but not seeing them in the middle, knows by way of inference: 'It climbed up from here, it descended from here, and in the middle, on the stone slab, it must have gone through this spot.'
254:
Even if the footprints are not seen, just as one knows by way of inference, "He ascended from here, descended from here, and must have walked across this part of the flat rock in the middle," so too, the arising of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of ascent, and the arising of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of descent. To one who grasps it by way of inference—just as one grasps, "He ascended from here, descended from here, and went thus in the middle"—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā), which has the characteristic of neutrality by way of rejecting both the agreeable and the disagreeable when pleasure and pain are absent, becomes evident.

In this way, the Blessed One, having first taught the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and later the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), showed it by distinguishing it by way of feeling. Not only in this Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga does He show it thus, but also in the Mahānidāna Sutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, and Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya; in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and Āneñjasappāya Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya; and in the Cūḷanidāna Sutta, Rukkūpama Sutta, Parivīmaṃsana Sutta, and the entire Vedanā Saṃyutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya. In these many suttas, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and later showed the meditation subject of immateriality by distinguishing it by way of feeling. Just as He showed in those various suttas, so too in this Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and later showed the meditation subject of immateriality by distinguishing it by way of feeling.

Regarding the words beginning with "pleasant feeling" (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), this is another method of understanding: The statement "He understands: 'I feel a pleasant feeling'" means that because painful feeling is absent at the moment of pleasant feeling, while experiencing a pleasant feeling, he understands it with discrimination as "I feel a pleasant feeling." Because of such understanding, he is one who possesses clear comprehension (sampajāna) regarding that feeling, thinking: "This feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change, because the painful feeling that previously existed is now absent, and this pleasant feeling did not exist before this moment." This point has also been taught by the Blessed One:

"Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a painful feeling, nor does one feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one feels only a pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a painful feeling... [pe]... a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a pleasant feeling, nor does one feel a painful feeling; at that time one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling also, indeed..."
255:
"Aggivessana, feeling is impermanent, conditioned (saṅkhata), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna), subject to destruction (khayadhamma), subject to vanishing (vayadhamma), subject to fading away (virāgadhamma), and subject to cessation (nirodhadhamma). Painful feeling also... [pe]... Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling also, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned... [pe]... subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted (nibbindati) with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, and becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate (virajjati). Through dispassion, he is liberated (vimuccati). When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'" (M. Ni. 2.205).

In the phrases beginning with "sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ" (worldly pleasant feeling), worldly pleasant feelings refer to the six types of joy related to the household life (gehassita-somanassa) based on the five cords of sensual pleasure. Unworldly pleasant feelings (nirāmisa sukha) refer to the six types of joy related to renunciation (nekkhammasita-somanassa). Worldly painful feelings (sāmisa dukkha) refer to the six types of grief related to the household life (gehassita-domanassa). Unworldly painful feelings (nirāmisa dukkha) refer to the six types of grief related to renunciation (nekkhammasita-domanassa). Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings (sāmisa adukkhamasukha) refer to the six types of equanimity related to the household life (gehassita-upekkhā). Unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings (nirāmisa adukkhamasukha) refer to the six types of equanimity related to renunciation (nekkhammasita-upekkhā). The classification of these feelings should be understood as it appears in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali. "So taṃ nimittaṃ" means that sign of feeling. "Bahiddhā vedanāsu" means in the feelings of another person. "Sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ" refers to another person experiencing a pleasant feeling. "Ajjhattabahiddhā" means applying the mind sometimes to one's own feelings and sometimes to the feelings of others. In this section, since neither self nor other is specifically restricted, the teaching "Herein, a bhikkhu [feels] a pleasant feeling..." and so forth is stated merely to show the knowledge that discriminates feeling. The remaining meanings are clear. In this section, only pure insight (suddha-vipassanā) is taught.

## The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of Feeling is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Mind

In the section on the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), it should also be understood according to the method mentioned below. In the phrases beginning with "sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ" (mind with lust), "sarāga" refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (lobha-sahagata). "Vītarāga" (mind without lust) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate (avyākata) consciousness. Since this statement shows the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa)...
256:
This statement is not an all-inclusive summary; therefore, in this contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), the supramundane (lokuttara) is not obtained even in a single term. Because they exist and are abandoned simultaneously with lust and so forth in the sense of abandoning in one place, they are not obtained in the primary sense in those two terms and thus are not included. The remaining four types of unwholesome consciousness belong neither to the preceding term (sarāga) nor to the succeeding term (vītarāga). 'Sadosa' refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa). 'Vītadosa' refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate (abyākata) consciousness. The remaining ten types of unwholesome consciousness belong neither to the preceding term (sadosa) nor to the succeeding term (vītadosa). 'Samoha' refers to the two types of consciousness: that accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and that accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca). However, since delusion (moha) arises in all unwholesome consciousness, the remaining unwholesome types are also appropriate here. Indeed, in this dyad of samoha-vītamoha, all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are fully exhausted. 'Vītamoha' refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. 'Saṅkhitta' (contracted) refers to consciousness affected by sloth and torpor (thina-middha); this is called a shrunken mind. 'Vikkhitta' (distracted) refers to consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca); this is called a scattered mind.

'Mahaggata' (exalted) refers to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) consciousness. 'Amahaggata' refers to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness. 'Sauttara' (surpassable) refers to the sense-sphere consciousness. 'Anuttara' (unsurpassable) refers to the fine-material and immaterial sphere consciousness. Between those two, the fine-material sphere is surpassable (sauttara), and only the immaterial sphere is unsurpassable (anuttara). 'Samāhita' (concentrated) refers to a mind that has either attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). 'Asamāhita' refers to a mind devoid of both types of concentration. 'Vimutta' (liberated) refers to a mind liberated through temporary liberation (tadaṅga-vimutti) or liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti). 'Avimutta' refers to a mind not yet liberated from both types of liberation. As for liberation by destruction (samuccheda), liberation by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa), there is no occasion for them in this contemplation of the mind. 'Sarāgamassa cittaṃ' means (he knows) the mind of that person which is with lust. The remaining terms have clear meanings according to the method already stated below. In this section as well, only pure insight (suddha-vipassanā) is taught.

## The Explanation of the Contemplation of the Mind is finished.
## The Explanation of the Contemplation of Phenomena
## The Section on Hindrances

By this sequence of words, only the discernment of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) in the contemplation of the body, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) in the contemplation of feeling, and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) in the contemplation of the mind have been taught. Therefore, now, in order to teach the discernment of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) by taking the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) as the head, the Buddha said 'Kathañca bhikkhu' and so forth, showing the contemplation of phenomena. In that passage, 'santa' (present) refers to that (sensual desire) which is present due to frequent occurrence. 'Asanta' (absent) refers to...
257:
...that which is not present, either because of non-occurrence or because of being abandoned (by the Path of Non-returning). 'Yathā ca' means the reason by which the arising of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) occurs. 'Tañca pajānāti' means he knows that reason. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

Among those (causes for arising and abandoning), the arising of sensual desire occurs due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) toward the sign of beauty (subhanimitta). What is called the sign of beauty is either the previous sensual desire that is perceived as beautiful or the beautiful object itself. What is called unwise attention is attention that is not a means (for welfare), attention that is off the track, or attention to the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, or the foul as beautiful. For one who frequently applies that unwise attention to that sign of beauty, sensual desire arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Monks, there is the sign of beauty. Frequent unwise attention therein—this is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.'

On the other hand, the abandoning of that sensual desire occurs due to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) toward the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta). What is called the sign of foulness is either the meditative absorption (jhāna) having a foul object or the foul object itself. What is called wise attention is attention that is a means (for welfare), attention that is on the right track, or attention to the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, or the foul as foul. For one who frequently applies that wise attention to that sign of foulness, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Monks, there is the sign of foulness. Frequent wise attention therein—this is not the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.'

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: learning the sign of foulness, application to the meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, noble friendship, and suitable talk. Indeed, for one who learns the ten types of the sign of foulness or for one who develops them, sensual desire is abandoned. In the sense faculties...
258:
Sensual desire is abandoned by being one who has the doors of the sense faculties guarded, and by being one who knows moderation in eating—who, when four or five mouthfuls are still desired, stops eating and drinks water to sustain themselves. Regarding this, it was said: 'A monk who has dispelled the defilements should leave four or five mouthfuls uneaten and drink water; this is sufficient for living in comfort' (Theragāthā 983). Sensual desire is also abandoned by associating with good friends who delight in the meditation on foulness, such as the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of foulness, and by engaging in suitable talk concerning the ten types of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it was said: 'Six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire.' It should be understood that sensual desire abandoned by these six things is completely eradicated by the Path of Arahantship so that it does not arise again in the future.

Ill will (byāpāda) arises through unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the sign of irritation (paṭighanimitta). Here, 'sign of irritation' refers to both the nature of irritation and the object of irritation. Unwise attention has the same characteristic in all hindrances. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that sign, ill will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is the sign of irritation. Frequent unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the growth and increase of arisen ill will' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Its abandonment occurs through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettācetovimutti). Here, when 'loving-kindness' (mettā) is mentioned, both access concentration and absorption are included, but 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti) refers only to absorption. The characteristic of wise attention is as previously described. For one who frequently applies wise attention to that loving-kindness, ill will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. Frequent wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill will, or for the abandonment of arisen ill will' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of ill will: learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the cultivation of loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma...
259:
...repeated reflection, having good friends, and suitable talk. For one who learns the meditation on loving-kindness by any of the methods—whether specified, unspecified, or by pervading the directions—ill will is abandoned. It is also abandoned for one who cultivates loving-kindness by way of specified, unspecified, or directional pervading.

'What can you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Have you not come to this life because of your own kamma and will you not depart according to your own kamma? Being angry with another is like wanting to strike another after picking up a glowing coal without flame, a red-hot iron rod, or excrement. And what can this person do by being angry with you? Can he destroy your virtue and so on? He has also come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma. Like a gift that is not accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will only fall back upon his own head.' Thus, ill will is abandoned for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma of oneself and others, for one who stands firm in such reflection after considering the kamma-ownership of both, and for one who associates with good friends who delight in the cultivation of loving-kindness, such as the Elder Assagutta. It is also abandoned by suitable talk related to loving-kindness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it was said: 'Six things lead to the abandonment of ill will.' It is known that ill will abandoned by these six things is eradicated by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) so that it does not arise again.

Sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) arise through unwise attention to discontent (arati) and so on. 'Arati' means discontent (boredom). 'Tandī' means laziness of the body. 'Vijambhikā' means stretching the body (yawning). 'Bhattasammada' means the confusion or feverishness caused by food (food-stupor). 'Līnattā' of the mind means the sluggish state of the mind. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to these things like discontent, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Bhikkhus, there are discontent, laziness, stretching, food-stupor, and sluggishness of mind. Frequent unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the growth and increase of arisen sloth and torpor.'

The abandonment of that sloth and torpor occurs through wise attention to the element of arousal (ārambhadhātu) and so on. 'Element of arousal' means the initial effort of energy. 'Element of endeavor' (nikkamadhātu) means...
260:
Because it has emerged from laziness, the energy that is stronger than the element of arousal (ārambhadhātu) is called the element of exertion (nikkamadhātu). Because it reaches higher and higher states, the energy that is even stronger than the element of exertion is called the element of striving (parakkamadhātu). For one who frequently applies wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to these three types of energy, sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) are abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are the element of arousal, the element of exertion, and the element of striving. Frequent wise attention therein is not the cause for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, nor for the increase and expansion of arisen sloth and torpor."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor: perceiving the danger in overeating, changing postures, attending to the perception of light, living in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk. Indeed, for one who practices the Dhamma of a recluse while sitting in his night-quarters or day-quarters after eating in the manners known as āharahatthaka, bhuttavamitaka, tatravattaka, alaṃsāṭaka, or kākamāsaka, sloth and torpor come over him like a great elephant. However, for a monk who is moderate in eating, leaving space for four or five morsels and drinking water instead, that sloth and torpor does not occur. Thus, for one who perceives the danger in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned for one who changes from the posture in which sloth and torpor arose to another posture; for one who attends to the light of the sun by day, or the light of the moon, lamps, or torches by night; for one who lives in the open air; and for one who associates with good friends who have abandoned sloth and torpor, such as the Elder Mahākassapa. It is also abandoned by suitable talk related to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it was said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor." He understands that sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahatship.

Restlessness (uddhacca) and remorse (kukkucca) arise due to unwise attention to the unpeacefulness of the mind. Unpeacefulness (avūpasama) means the state of being unpeaceful; in essence, it is restlessness and remorse itself. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that unpeacefulness, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is unpeacefulness of mind. Frequent unwise attention therein is the cause for the arising of unarisen..."
261:
"...restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and expansion of arisen restlessness and remorse."

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the peacefulness of mind known as concentration (samādhi). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is peacefulness of mind. Frequent wise attention therein is not the cause (āhāra) for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, nor for the increase and expansion of arisen restlessness and remorse."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse: great learning (bahussutatā), inquiry (paripucchakatā), understanding the nature of the Vinaya (vinaye pakataññutā), associating with elders (vuḍḍhasevitā), good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), and suitable talk (sappāyakathā). Indeed, through great learning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned for one who learns one, two, three, four, or all five Nikāyas in terms of both the text (Pāḷi) and the meaning. They are also abandoned for one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is not (kappiyākappiya); for one who understands the nature of the Vinaya due to mastery in the Vinaya rules; for one who approaches senior elders; and for one who associates with good friends who are masters of the Vinaya, such as the Elder Upāli. Restlessness and remorse are also abandoned by suitable talk related to what is allowable and what is not while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it was said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse." He understands that when restlessness and remorse are abandoned by these six things, restlessness will not arise again through the Path of Arahatship, and remorse will not arise again through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga).

Doubt (vicikicchā) arises due to unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are simply previous instances of doubt, as they are the cause for repeated doubt. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to those grounds for doubt, doubt arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are things that are grounds for doubt. Frequent unwise attention therein is the cause (āhāra) for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt."
262:
The abandoning of that doubt (vicikicchā) occurs through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) toward phenomena such as the wholesome. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy and blameless phenomena, inferior and superior phenomena, and phenomena that are counterparts of dark and bright. Frequent wise attention therein is the non-nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the growth and expansion of arisen doubt."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt: great learning, inquiry, mastery of the Vinaya, abundance of decision (faith), good friendship, and suitable talk. For, through great learning, doubt is abandoned in one who learns even one Nikāya or all five Nikāyas, both in terms of the text (Pali) and the meaning. Doubt is also abandoned in one who is frequent in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels, in one who has achieved mastery in the Vinaya, in one who is abundant in decision—known as faith that descends into the Three Jewels—and in one who associates with good friends like the Elder Vakkali who was foremost in faith. Doubt is also abandoned by suitable talk based on the qualities of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt." He understands that doubt abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future by means of the Path of Stream-entry.

## Commentary on the Section on Hindrances
## Commentary on the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment

In the section on the Factors of Enlightenment, "santā" means existing by way of attainment. "Asantā" means not existing by way of non-attainment. Regarding the passages such as "And how [does he understand] the unarisen...", first, concerning the Mindfulness Factor of Enlightenment (sati-sambojjhaṅga):

"Bhikkhus, there are phenomena that are the basis for the Mindfulness Factor of Enlightenment. Frequent wise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen Mindfulness Factor of Enlightenment, or for the [growth] of the arisen..."
263: ...increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen mindfulness factor of enlightenment." Thus its arising occurs. Therein, among those things that are bases for the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, prior mindfulness itself is the thing that is the base for the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is of the characteristic already mentioned. For one who frequently applies that wise attention to those bases of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment arises. Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that mindfulness factor of enlightenment. For, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as moving forward and so forth; by avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness who are like crows with eyes fixed on food; by associating with persons of established mindfulness like Elder Tissadatta and Elder Abhaya; and by the state of having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the establishment of mindfulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. He understands that for the mindfulness factor of enlightenment arisen through these four causes, its fulfillment through development occurs by way of the Path of Arahatship. Regarding the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states... states that are counterparts of dark and bright. Therein, making much of wise attention is the cause for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment." Thus its arising occurs. Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment: frequent inquiry, cleansing the physical bases, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reviewing the range of profound knowledge, and inclination towards that investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment. Therein, "frequent inquiry" (paripucchakatā) means the abundance of inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, jhānas, serenity, and insight. "Cleansing the physical bases" (vatthu-visadakiriya) means making the internal and external bases clean. For when one's hair, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is full of humors (phlegm, bile, wind) and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal base is unclean and impure.
264:
When the robes are old, dirty, and foul-smelling, or when the lodging is cluttered with rubbish, the external object is unclarified and impure. Therefore, the internal object should be made clear by cutting the hair and so on, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives, and by massaging and bathing. The external object should be made clear by sewing, washing, dyeing, and smoothing the ground, etc. Indeed, when these internal and external objects are unclarified, the knowledge (ñāṇa) in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also unclarified and impure, like the light of a lamp flame produced depending on an impure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. But when the internal and external objects are clarified, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also clarified and pure, like the light of a lamp flame produced depending on a pure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. For this reason, it is said: "The cleansing of objects leads to the arising of the Dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga (Enlightenment Factor of Investigation of States)."

What is called "balancing the faculties" (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā) is the making equal of the faculties such as faith and so on. If, for that practitioner, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is strong and the remaining faculties are weak, then the faculty of effort (vīriyindriya) cannot perform the function of uplifting, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) cannot perform the function of establishing on the object, the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) cannot perform the function of seeing. Therefore, that faith should be weakened either by reflecting on the nature of the Dhamma or by not attending to it in the way that it became strong. The story of Vakkali Thera is an illustration here. If the faculty of effort is strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform the function of decision (adhimokkha), and the remaining faculties likewise cannot perform their respective functions. Therefore, that effort should be weakened by developing tranquility (passaddhi) and so on. In that case, the story of Soṇa Thera should be shown. Thus, it should be understood that when any one of the remaining faculties is strong, the others are unable to perform their own functions.

Particularly here, the balance of faith with wisdom, and concentration with effort, is praised. For a person with strong faith and weak wisdom is one who is blindly confident and becomes devoted to objects that are not worthy of devotion. A person with strong wisdom and weak faith falls into the side of craftiness; like a disease caused by medicine, he is difficult to cure. Thinking excessively that "merit occurs merely by the arising of a thought," he does not perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and may be reborn in hell. However, through the balance of both faith and wisdom, one becomes devoted only to objects worthy of devotion. For a person with strong concentration and weak wisdom, because concentration is on the side of laziness (kosajja), laziness overcomes him. For a person with strong effort and weak concentration, because effort is on the side of restlessness (uddhacca), restlessness overcomes him. But concentration coupled with effort cannot fall into laziness. Effort coupled with concentration cannot fall into restlessness. Therefore, both should be made equal. Indeed, through the balance of both, absorption (appanā)...
265:
