...occurs. Furthermore, for a practitioner whose work is concentration, strong faith is also suitable. Thus, believing and reposing confidence, he will reach absorption.

Among concentration and wisdom, for one whose work is concentration, the strength of one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is suitable. Only when there is strength of one-pointedness does that person reach absorption. For one whose work is insight (vipassanā), the strength of wisdom is suitable. Only when there is strength of wisdom does that person reach the penetration of characteristics (lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha). However, it is only through the balance of both [concentration and wisdom] that absorption occurs. But mindfulness (sati) is suitable to be strong in all matters. Mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness through the power of faith, effort, and wisdom which are on the side of restlessness, and from falling into laziness along with concentration which is on the side of laziness. Therefore, that mindfulness is desired in all matters, just as salt and seasoning are desired in all dishes, and just as a minister skilled in all affairs is desired in all the king's business. Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One: "Mindfulness is said to be desired in all matters. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there can be no uplifting or restraining of the mind."

Avoiding unwise persons means keeping far away from foolish people who do not have wisdom that penetrates into the categories of the aggregates (khandha) and so on. Associating with wise persons means associating with those endowed with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) which grasps the fifty characteristics precisely. Reflecting on the conduct of deep knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions of deep wisdom occurring in the deep aggregates and so on. Inclination towards that state means having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the arising of the Dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga while standing, sitting, and so on. He knows that for one who has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā) by the Path of Arahantship.

## The Arising of Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga -

"Monks, there is the element of inception (ārambha-dhātu), the element of exertion (nikkama-dhātu), and the element of striving (parakkama-dhātu). Making much of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) therein—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga (Enlightenment Factor of Effort), or for the increase, expansion, and fulfillment of development of the arisen Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga." Thus does the arising occur.

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga. They are: reflecting on the fear of woeful states, seeing the benefits [of effort], reflecting on the path of travel,
266:
Honoring the alms-food in return, reflecting on the greatness of being an heir, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one's birth, reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and being committed to that energy.

Among these, it is not possible to arouse the Enlightenment Factor of Energy (Vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) when experiencing great suffering in hells, starting from being tortured with the fivefold binding; nor when being caught in nets, traps, and the like in the animal realm; nor when being a beast of burden pulling a cart while being beaten and prodded with goads and spikes; nor when being afflicted by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years, even for the interval between two Buddhas, in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas); nor when experiencing the suffering of wind and heat with a body sixty or eighty cubits high, consisting only of skin and bone, in the realm of Kālakañjika Asuras. The Enlightenment Factor of Energy arises in one who reflects on the danger of the lower realms (apāya-bhaya) thus: "O monk, this is the only time for you to exert energy."

It also arises in one who sees the benefits of energy, thinking: "A lazy person cannot attain the nine supramundane states (nava lokuttara-dhamma); only one with exerted energy can; this is the benefit of energy." It also arises in one who reflects on the path to be traveled, thinking: "You must travel the path taken by all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples, and that path cannot be traveled by a lazy person." It also arises in one who reflects on honoring the alms-food, thinking: "These people who serve you with alms-food and other requisites are not your relatives, nor are they your servants or workers. They do not give these excellent alms-food thinking they will live depending on you; rather, they give desiring the great fruit of their own meritorious deeds. Even the Teacher did not permit these requisites for you by seeing that 'this monk, by using these requisites, will live happily with a strong body.' Rather, he permitted them by seeing that 'this monk, while using these requisites, will practice the Dhamma of a recluse and be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha).' If you now live lazily, you will not be honoring that alms-food. Only the state of one with exerted energy is called honoring the alms-food." This is how it arose in Mahāmitta Thera.

It is heard that Mahāmitta Thera resided in a cave named Kassakalena. In his alms-resort village, a great female lay devotee looked after the Elder, treating him like her own son. One day, as she was about to go to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Dear daughter, there is old rice in such a place, milk in such a place, ghee in such a place, and molasses in such a place. When your brother, the Venerable Mitta, arrives, cook the rice and offer it together with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should eat as well." The daughter asked, "Mother, what will you eat?" "As for me, yesterday..."
267:
"Offer it, and you eat as well," (the mother instructed). "Mother, what will you eat?" (the daughter asked). "I have already eaten stale rice from yesterday with fermented scum (kanji)," (the mother said). "What will you eat during the day, mother?" (the daughter asked again). "Put some leaves in and cook a sour gruel with broken rice, dear daughter," (the mother replied).

Mahāmitta Thera, while putting on his robe and taking his bowl out of its bag, heard those words and admonished himself: "This great lay devotee is said to have eaten stale rice with fermented scum, and during the day she will eat sour gruel cooked with broken rice and leaves. For your sake, however, she speaks of preparing old rice and so on. This lay devotee does not desire fields, property, food, or clothing because of you; she gives desiring only the three types of attainment (sampatti). Will you be able to give those attainments to this lay devotee, or will you not? This alms-food cannot be eaten by you while you are possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion." Having admonished himself, he put the bowl back into the bag, unfastened the robe-button, turned back, and went only to Kassakalena. He placed the bowl under the bed and the robe on the robe-rack and sat down, resolving his energy: "I will not go out until I have attained Arahantship."

That monk, who had lived heedfully for a long night, developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship even before the mealtime. Becoming a great Arahant like a blooming lotus, he sat with a smiling face. Then, the deity residing in the tree near the cave door uttered this inspired exclamation:

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man!
You whose taints (āsavas) are exhausted, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable one."

After uttering this exclamation, the deity said: "Venerable sir, by giving alms to Arahants like you who have entered for alms, this old woman will be liberated from suffering."

The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking at the time, realized, "It is still early." He took his bowl and robe and entered the village. The young girl, having prepared the food, sat looking out and opening the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now my brother will come." When the Elder reached the house door, she took the bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The Elder said, "May you be happy," and after giving the blessing, he departed. The girl also stood watching the Elder as he went away.
268:
At that time, the Elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, and his faculties were especially clear; his face shone brilliantly like a ripe palm fruit released from its stalk. The great female lay follower, returning from the forest, asked, "Dear daughter, has your brother arrived?" The girl related all that had happened. Realizing, "Today my son's task of monkhood has reached its summit," the laywoman said, "Dear daughter, your brother takes great delight in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied."

The seven noble wealths are the great inheritance of the Teacher, the Buddha. That great inheritance cannot be obtained by a lazy person. Just as parents might cast out a wayward son, saying, "This is not our son," making him an outsider so that he does not receive the inheritance upon their passing, so too a lazy person does not receive this inheritance of noble wealth; only one who has aroused energy receives it. Thus, the enlightenment factor of energy arises through reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance. "My Teacher is truly great. When the Teacher took conception in his mother's womb, when he renounced the world, when he attained enlightenment, when he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, when he performed the Twin Miracle, when he descended from the deva realm, when he relinquished the life-force, and at the time of his Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it proper for you to remain lazy after ordaining in the Dispensation of such a Teacher?" Thus, the enlightenment factor of energy arises through reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher.

"By birth, you are no longer of low birth; you are born in the Okkāka royal dynasty, descended from the unbroken lineage of King Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Prince Rāhula. Being such a son of the Conqueror (Jina), it is not proper for you to live lazily." Thus, the enlightenment factor of energy arises through reflecting on the greatness of birth. "Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Moggallāna, and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners, or will you not?" Thus, the enlightenment factor of energy arises through reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners.

The enlightenment factor of energy also arises by avoiding lazy persons who are like pythons lying full of food and who lack physical and mental energy; by associating with persons who have aroused energy and are resolute; and by having a mind that is inclined, prone, and directed toward arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. He understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of energy reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.

"Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy... (in detail) ... the arising occurs." Thus, the enlightenment factor of joy arises. Among those things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy, prior joy itself is called the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. The attention that produces that joy is called wise attention. Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and deities; recollection of peace; avoiding rough persons; associating with refined persons; reflecting on inspiring discourses...
269:
## Pīti-sambojjhaṅga

"Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. Making much of wise attention to those things is conducive to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of joy," so it is stated (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

Thus, the enlightenment factor of joy arises. In that text, prior joy itself is called the things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. The attention that produces that joy is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy. They are: the repeated recollection of the Buddha's qualities, the repeated recollection of the Dhamma's qualities, the repeated recollection of the Saṅgha's qualities, the repeated recollection of one's own virtue, the repeated recollection of one's own generosity, the repeated recollection of one's own qualities using deities as witnesses, the repeated recollection of the peace of Nibbāna, avoiding rough persons, associating with refined and gentle persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being firmly inclined toward the arising of that joy.

For one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body up to the level of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). It also arises for one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for a monk who reflects on the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) which he has kept unbroken for a long time; and for a layperson who reflects on the ten precepts or the five precepts. The enlightenment factor of joy arises for one who, having given excellent food to fellow practitioners during times of famine and the like, reflects on their own generosity, thinking, "We have given such a gift"; and for a layperson who reflects on the gifts given to virtuous ones at such times. It arises for one who reflects on the existence within themselves of such qualities by which deities attained their divine state; and for one who reflects that the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment have not arisen for sixty or seventy years. It arises for one who avoids rough persons—those who show their roughness by acting disrespectfully when visiting a shrine, a Bodhi tree, or a senior Elder, and who, lacking the sap of faith in the Buddha and so on, are like dust on a donkey's back; for one who associates with refined persons who have much faith in the Buddha and so on and have gentle minds; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that illustrate the qualities of the Triple Gem; and for one who has a mind inclined toward producing joy in postures such as standing and sitting. He understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of joy reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.
270: Regarding the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquillity (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga): "Monks, there is physical tranquillity (kāya-passaddhi) and mental tranquillity (citta-passaddhi). Therein, frequently applying wise attention is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquillity, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquillity." Thus it arises as spoken. Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquillity: resorting to fine food, resorting to a comfortable climate, resorting to a comfortable posture, maintaining a balanced effort, avoiding people with restless bodies, associating with people with tranquil bodies, and being inclined towards that tranquillity. Indeed, tranquillity arises for one who eats fine, oily, and suitable food; and for one who resorts to a suitable climate among cold and hot climates, and to suitable postures such as standing, etc. However, this is not said with reference to a person of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisajātika) who can endure all climates and postures. For a person who has suitability (sabhāga) and unsuitability (visabhāga), tranquillity arises only when they avoid unsuitable climates and postures and resort to suitable ones. Balanced effort (majjhatta-payoga) refers to the reflection on the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā) of oneself and others; tranquillity arises through this balanced effort. It also arises for one who avoids a person with a restless body who wanders about harassing others with clods, sticks, etc.; for one who associates with a person with a tranquil body whose hands and feet are restrained; and for one whose mind is inclined, sloped, and directed towards the arising of tranquillity in postures such as standing, sitting, etc. It should be understood that for the tranquillity enlightenment factor that has arisen in this way, the fulfillment of its development is reached through the path of Arahatship. Regarding the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga): "Monks, there is the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) and the sign of non-distraction (avyagga-nimitta). Therein, frequently applying wise attention is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration." Thus it arises as spoken. In that text, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, and it is called the sign of non-distraction in the sense of being unwavering.
271:
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga). They are: cleansing the bases (vatthu), balancing the faculties (indriya), skill in the sign (nimitta), uplifting the mind on the proper occasion, restraining the mind on the proper occasion, gladdening the mind on the proper occasion, looking on the mind with equanimity on the proper occasion, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, reflecting on the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha), and being resolute upon that concentration (tadadhimuttatā). Among these eleven, cleansing the bases and balancing the faculties should be understood in the manner previously described.

Skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā) means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign. Uplifting the mind on the proper occasion means that on occasions when the mind is sluggish due to overly lax energy and so forth, one uplifts it by bringing into being the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (vīriya), and joy (pīti). Restraining the mind on the proper occasion means that on occasions when the mind is restless due to overly exerted energy and so forth, one restrains it by bringing into being the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā). Gladdening the mind on the proper occasion means that on occasions when the mind is without relish (bored) due to weak application of wisdom or the non-attainment of the bliss of peace, one strikes it with urgency by reflecting on the eight bases of urgency (saṃvegavatthu). The eight bases of urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (four); the suffering of the lower realms as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for food in the present. One also generates confidence by repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. This is called gladdening the mind on the proper occasion.

Looking on the mind with equanimity on the proper occasion means that on occasions when, through practicing the right path, the mind is not sluggish, not restless, not without relish, but proceeds evenly on the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), the yogi does not then apply effort toward uplifting, restraining, or gladdening, just as a charioteer does not interfere with horses that are running evenly. This is called looking on the mind with equanimity on the proper occasion. Avoiding unconcentrated persons means keeping far away from persons who have not attained either access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā) and whose minds are distracted. Associating with concentrated persons means associating with, following, and attending upon persons whose minds are concentrated through access or absorption concentration. Being resolute upon that concentration means having a mind that is inclined, leaned, and sloped toward the arising of concentration while standing, sitting, and so forth. For one who practices in this way, this enlightenment factor of concentration arises. He knows that for the enlightenment factor of concentration thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.

## For the Enlightenment Factor of Equanimity (Upekkhāsambojjhaṅga):

"Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen..."
272:
"...for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the further growth, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity" (as stated in Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232)—it occurs in this way. Among those states, equanimity itself is known as the state that is the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Furthermore, five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: equanimity towards beings (satta-majjhattatā), equanimity towards formations (saṅkhāra-majjhattatā), avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who have equanimity towards beings and formations, and being inclined towards that enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Among those five things, one develops equanimity towards beings through two reasons: by reflecting on the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) thus, "You have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma; this person also has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma. Whom are you cherishing?" and by reflecting on the absence of a being (nissatta-paccavekkhaṇa) thus, "In the ultimate sense, there is no being at all. Such being the case, whom are you cherishing?"

One develops equanimity towards formations through two reasons as well: by reflecting on the ownerless nature (assāmika-bhāva-paccavekkhaṇa) thus, "This robe will gradually reach a state of discoloration and wear, and having become a foot-wiping cloth, it will be fit to be discarded with the tip of a stick. If it had an owner, he would not allow it to perish in this way," and by reflecting on its temporary nature (tāvakālika-bhāva-paccavekkhaṇa) thus, "This robe is not lasting; it is only temporary." Just as with the robe, the same application should be made for the alms-bowl and other requisites.

Regarding the avoidance of persons who are attached to beings and formations: whether a layperson who cherishes his own sons and daughters, etc., or a monk who cherishes his own resident pupils and fellow preceptors, etc., as "mine," and performs tasks such as hair-cutting, sewing, washing and dyeing robes, and firing alms-bowls for them with his own hands. If he does not see them for even a moment, he looks around here and there like a frightened deer, asking, "Where is that novice? Where is that young monk?" Even when requested by another for the sake of hair-cutting and so forth, "Please send him for a moment," he refuses, saying, "Even we do not dare to make him do our own work; if you take him, you will make him tired." Such a person is called one who cherishes beings (satta-kelāyana).
273:
A person who cherishes robes, alms-bowls, cups, walking sticks, and so forth as "mine," and does not allow even the touch of another's hand, and when asked for them as a temporary loan, says, "Even we, cherishing these items, do not dare to use them; how could we give them to you?"—such a person is called one who cherishes formations (saṅkhāra-kelāyana). A person who is neutral and indifferent towards both those objects, namely beings and formations, is called one who has equanimity towards beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta). Thus, this enlightenment factor of equanimity arises in one who avoids from afar such persons who cherish beings and formations, in one who associates with persons who have equanimity towards beings and formations, and in one whose mind is inclined, leaned, and sloped towards the arising of that enlightenment factor of equanimity during standing, sitting, and so forth. He understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship. The meaning of all the remaining terms is clear in every respect.

## Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

In these two sections—the section on the hindrances and the section on the enlightenment factors—pure insight (suddha-vipassanā) alone has been taught. Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage of the Path. Indeed, one grasps the body with one consciousness, feeling with another, the mind with another, and mental objects with another. However, at the moment of the supramundane Path, they are obtained in a single consciousness. For a yogi who has come grasping the body from the beginning, the mindfulness associated with insight is called contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of the body (kāyānupassī). For one who has reached the Noble Path after exerting in insight, the mindfulness associated with the Path at the moment of the Path is called contemplation of the body. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of the body. [The same applies to] grasping feeling... grasping the mind... For a yogi who has come grasping mental objects, the mindfulness associated with insight is called contemplation of mental objects (dhammānupassanā). A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of mental objects (dhammānupassī). For one who has reached the Noble Path after exerting in insight, the mindfulness associated with the Path at the moment of the Path is called contemplation of mental objects. A person endowed with that mindfulness is called a contemplator of mental objects. Thus, first, the teaching stands on the person.

However, the mindfulness that grasps the body and abandons the perversion of "beauty" (subha) in the body is called contemplation of the body because it is accomplished by the Path. The mindfulness that grasps feeling and abandons the perversion of "pleasure" (sukha) in feeling is called contemplation of feeling because it is accomplished by the Path. The mindfulness that grasps the mind and abandons the perversion of "permanence" (nicca) in the mind is called contemplation of the mind because it is accomplished by the Path. The mindfulness that grasps mental objects and abandons the perversion of "self" (atta) in mental objects is called contemplation of mental objects because it is accomplished by the Path. Thus, the single mindfulness associated with the Path, by way of performing four functions,
274:
(Mindfulness associated with the path) receives the four names such as contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna) because it accomplishes the four functions. Therefore, I have said: "In the moment of the supramundane path, however, these four names are obtained in a single consciousness alone."

## Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājanīya.

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya

In the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, because the teaching is undertaken by way of supramundane satipaṭṭhāna, the sequence of the Pali text is not established as it was in the mundane satipaṭṭhānas having the body, etc., as objects. Instead, all satipaṭṭhānas such as contemplation of the body are shown by merely indicating the opening of the method of teaching analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali.

In that method of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, the variety of methods should be understood. How? First, in the contemplation of the body, in the section on the application of jhāna (jhānābhinivesa) of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), there are ten methods by way of the two methods—the fourfold and fivefold—in each of these five instances: pure practice (suddhika-paṭipadā), pure emptiness (suddhika-suññata), emptiness practice (suññata-paṭipadā), pure desireless (suddhika-appaṇihita), and desireless practice (appaṇihita-paṭipadā). Similarly, in the remaining applications, there are two hundred methods in the twenty applications. When these methods are multiplied by four by way of the four predominant factors (adhipati), there are eight hundred methods. Thus, the two hundred pure methods (suddhika) not combined with predominant factors and the eight hundred methods combined with predominant factors together make one thousand methods in all. Likewise, in the contemplation of feeling, etc., and in the pure satipaṭṭhāna, there are five thousand methods in the Path of Stream-entry. Just as there are five thousand methods in the Path of Stream-entry, so too in the remaining three paths; thus there are twenty thousand methods in the wholesome (kusala). In the paths distinguished by emptiness, desireless, and signless, etc., when those twenty thousand methods are multiplied by three, there are sixty thousand methods in the resultant (vipāka). Thus, by way of the description (niddesa) of the wholesome satipaṭṭhānas that accomplish their own functions and the resultant satipaṭṭhānas whose functions are already accomplished, there are two types. By way of contemplation of the body, etc., and by way of the pure (suddhika), there are five sections of description in the wholesome and five in the resultant; thus, by way of the ten sections of description, the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya description is distinguished into ten parts and adorned with eighty thousand methods.

## 3. Commentary on the Pañhāpucchaka

In the Pañhāpucchaka, the state of satipaṭṭhānas as wholesome, etc., should be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text. In the triads of objects (ārammaṇa-ttika), however, all these supramundane satipaṭṭhānas have the immeasurable as their object because they occur by taking Nibbāna, which is immeasurable, as their object. They do not have the path as their object (maggārammaṇa). Nevertheless, they are "having the path as cause" (magga-hetuka) by way of the conascent cause. When the path is developed by making energy (vīriya) or investigation (vīmaṃsā) the predominant factor, they are "having the path as predominant" (maggādhipati). When the path is developed by making desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) the predominant factor, they should not be called "having the path as predominant." Also, at the time of the fruit consciousness (phala-citta), they should not be called "having the path as predominant." They should also not be described as having a single object among the past objects, etc.

Because Nibbāna is an external (bahiddha) phenomenon, they are said to have an external object. In this Pañhāpucchaka, only the supramundane satipaṭṭhānas that have arisen are taught. Indeed, the Blessed One taught the satipaṭṭhānas mixed with mundane and supramundane only in the Suttanta-bhājanīya. In the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya and the Pañhāpucchaka, however, He taught only the supramundane satipaṭṭhānas. Thus, this Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga has also been brought out and analyzed by the method of the three rounds (parivaṭṭa).

The explanation of the Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga in the Vibhaṅga Commentary named Sammohavinodanī is finished.
275:
Because they occur by taking Nibbāna as their object, (these supramundane satipaṭṭhānas) have only the immeasurable as their object; they do not have the path as their object. By way of the conascent cause, however, they are "having the path as cause" (magga-hetuka). When the path is developed by making energy (vīriya) or investigation (vīmaṃsā) the predominant factor, they are "having the path as predominant" (maggādhipati). In the development of the path where desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) are the predominant factors, they should not be called "having the path as predominant." 276:
## 8. Sammappadhānavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
Now, in the Sammappadhānavibhaṅga, which immediately follows the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga, the word 'cattāro' (four) is a numerical delimitation. By this word, it is shown that the limit of the right exertions is four; there are none below or above that number. Sammappadhāna means exertion as a proper cause, exertion as a means, and exertion through wise consideration. In this context, 'a monk' refers to a monk who is practicing meditation in this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Unrisen' refers to states that have not yet arisen. 'Evil' refers to base states. 'Unwholesome states' refers to states born of lack of skill (delusion). 'For the non-arising' means for the purpose of not producing them. 'Generates desire' means he generates or produces wholesome desire, which is characterized by the wish to act (kattukamyatā), in order to prevent unrisen unwholesome states from arising. 'Strives' means he makes an effort or endeavor. 'Arouses energy' means he exerts bodily and mental energy. 'Upholds the mind' means he lifts up the mind by that very co-nascent energy. 'Exerts' means he performs the exertion of effort. In sequence, all these four terms should be associated with repeated practice, development, frequent cultivation, and continuous action.

'Arisen evil states' refers to unwholesome states that have reached a condition where they cannot be called 'unrisen'. 'For the abandoning' means for the purpose of giving them up. 'Unrisen wholesome states' refers to states born of skill (wisdom) that have not yet arisen. 'For the arising' means for the purpose of producing them. 'Arisen' refers to wholesome states that have already been produced. 'For the maintenance' means for the purpose of stability. 'For non-disappearance' means for the purpose of not being lost. 'For increase' means for the purpose of repeated occurrence. 'For abundance' means for the purpose of reaching a state of fullness. 'For development' means for the purpose of growth. 'For fulfillment' means for the purpose of completion. This is first the extraction of the meaning of each term according to the brief exposition (uddesavāra) of the four right exertions.

Now, in order to show those terms by analyzing them in detail in sequence, the exposition section (niddesavāra) is begun with the method starting with 'How does a monk... unrisen...'. In that exposition, whatever is similar to what appeared below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary of that Dhammasaṅgaṇī. As for what did not appear in that text, first in the exposition of desire (chanda), 'the desire which' refers to the desire that occurs by way of the wish to act. 'The state of having desire' (chandikatā) means the state of being one who has desire, or the manner of making desire. 'The wish to act' (kattukamyatā) means the state of wanting to act. 'Skillful' (kusalo) means clever. 'Desire for the Dhamma' (dhammacchanda) means desire for the natural state (sabhāva). Indeed, this so-called desire is of many kinds and various types, such as desire as craving (taṇhāchanda), desire as wrong view (diṭṭhichanda), desire as energy (vīriyachanda), and desire for the Dhamma (dhammacchanda).
277:
Among those many types of desire, in this context of the exposition of desire, 'dhammacchanda' is intended as the wholesome desire for the ultimate reality, which is the state of wishing to act. 'Generates desire' (chandaṃ janeti) means that one who is making desire is said to generate desire. 'Fully generates' (sañjaneti) is the word 'janeti' expanded by the prefix 'saṃ'. 'Arouses' (uṭṭhapeti) means that one who is making desire is said to arouse that desire. 'Fully arouses' (samuṭṭhapeti) is the word 'uṭṭhapeti' expanded by the prefix 'saṃ'. 'Produces' (nibbatteti) means that one who is making desire is said to produce that desire. 'Fully produces' (abhinibbatteti) is the word 'nibbatteti' expanded by the prefix 'abhi'. Alternatively, one who makes desire is said to generate desire. One who makes that same desire constantly is said to fully generate (sañjaneti) it. One who again lifts up a desire that has fallen due to some obstacle is said to arouse (uṭṭhapeti) it. One who brings it to a state of continuous stability is said to fully arouse (samuṭṭhapeti) it. One who makes that desire manifest is said to produce (nibbatteti) it. One who produces it by facing it directly with a non-retreating and non-shrinking occurrence is said to fully produce (abhinibbatteti) it.

In the exposition of energy, one who makes energy is said to arouse energy (ārabhati). The second term 'samārabhati' is an expansion by a prefix. One who makes energy is also said to cultivate (āsevati) and develop (bhāveti) it. One who does it again and again is said to make much of it (bahulīkaroti). Alternatively, one who does it from the beginning is said to arouse (ārabhati) it. One who does it again and again is said to fully arouse (samārabhati) it. One who associates with it by way of meditation is said to cultivate (āsevati) it. One who increases it is said to develop (bhāveti) it. One who makes that same energy frequent in all tasks should be known as 'making much of it' (bahulīkaroti).

In the exposition of upholding the mind, it means he upholds (paggaṇhāti) or lifts up the mind, associating it with the upholding of energy. One who upholds it again and again is said to fully uphold (sampaggaṇhāti) it. One who supports the mind thus fully upheld with the support of energy so that it does not fall is said to support (upatthambheti) it. One who supports it again and again for the sake of the stability of the mind already supported is said to continually support (paccupatthambheti) it.

In the exposition of the term 'for maintenance' (ṭhitiyā), in order to show that all terms such as non-disappearance (asammosa) are synonyms of maintenance (ṭhiti), it was said: "That which is maintenance is non-disappearance," and so on. Here, it is also appropriate to say that each preceding term is the meaning of each succeeding term, and each succeeding term is the meaning of each preceding term. All the rest has an obvious meaning. This is the commentary on the Pali text (Pāḷivaṇṇanā).

This is the analytical discussion (vinicchayakathā) herein: This discussion on right exertion is of two kinds—mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Among those two, mundane right exertion occurs in the entire preliminary stage of the paths.
278:
This mundane discourse should be understood at the moment of the mundane path according to the method of the Kassapa Saṃyutta. Indeed, in that Kassapa Saṃyutta, it was said thus:

"Friends, there are these four right efforts (sammappadhāna). What are the four? Here, friends, a monk makes an effort, thinking, 'If my unarisen evil unwholesome states were to arise, they would lead to my harm'; he makes an effort, thinking, 'If my arisen evil unwholesome states are not abandoned, they would lead to my harm'; he makes an effort, thinking, 'If my unarisen wholesome states do not arise, it would lead to my harm'; and he makes an effort, thinking, 'If my arisen wholesome states were to cease, it would lead to my harm.'"

In this Pali text, 'unarisen wholesome states' refers to serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the path (magga). 'Arisen wholesome states' refers only to serenity and insight. As for the path, although it arises only once and then ceases, there is no such thing as a path that leads to harm upon ceasing. This is because that path ceases only after giving its causal condition to the fruition (phala). Alternatively, it was stated in the old commentary that in the previous passage, only serenity and insight should be taken. However, that statement is not appropriate.

In that context, this story is presented to clarify the meaning of the phrase "arisen serenity and insight lead to harm when they cease": It is said that an Arahant Great Elder, intending to worship the Mahācetiya and the Great Bodhi Tree, came from the countryside to the Mahāvihāra together with a novice (sāmaṇera) who had attained the eight meditative attainments and who carried his bowl and robes. He entered the monastery precinct. In the evening, while a large community of monks was worshipping the stupa, he did not go out to worship. Why? Because Arahants have great reverence for the Triple Gem. Therefore, when the community of monks had finished worshipping and departed, at the time when people were having their evening meal, he went out alone to worship the stupa without even informing the novice. The novice thought, "Why is the Great Elder going out alone at an improper time? I shall find out," and he followed closely in his preceptor's footsteps. The Great Elder, not noticing him, ascended the platform of the Mahācetiya through the southern gate. The novice also ascended, following right behind him.
279:
The Great Elder looked up at the Great Stupa, and having aroused rapture (pīti) with the Buddha as the object, he focused his mind entirely and worshipped the Great Stupa with great joy. When the novice saw the manner of the Elder's worship, he thought, "My preceptor is worshipping with an extremely devout heart; if I could get some flowers, it would be good to make an offering." While the Elder, having finished his worship, stood looking up at the Great Stupa with his hands joined at his forehead, the novice cleared his throat to let his arrival be known. The Elder turned and looked, asking, "When did you arrive?" "Venerable Sir, I arrived while you were worshipping the stupa. You worshipped the stupa with great devotion. If you could get some flowers, would you like to make an offering?" he asked. "Yes, novice. There is no other stupa with such a vast enshrinement of relics as in this stupa. Who would not worship such an incomparable Great Stupa if they had flowers?" the Elder replied. "In that case, Venerable Sir, please wait a moment; I shall bring some flowers," the novice said. Immediately entering into a meditative absorption (jhāna), he went to the Himalayas by psychic power, gathered flowers endowed with color and fragrance, and filled his water-strainer (parissāvana). He returned before the Great Elder had even moved from the southern face to the western face, and placing the water-strainer full of flowers in the Elder's hand, he said, "Venerable Sir, please make the offering."

The Elder said, "Novice, are these flowers not too few for us?" "Venerable Sir, please proceed; contemplate the qualities of the Blessed One and make the offering," the novice replied.

The Elder ascended by the stairway at the western gate and began to offer the flowers at the middle terrace (kucchi-vedikā) of the stupa. That terrace became full, and the flowers overflowed, filling the second level to the height of the knees. Descending from there, he offered them at the base level, which also became full. Realizing it was full, he proceeded while scattering them on the lower courtyard, and the entire stupa courtyard became full. When it was thus filled, he said, "Novice, the flowers are not exhausted!" "Venerable Sir, turn the water-strainer upside down," the novice replied. Only when he turned it upside down and shook it did the flowers run out. The Elder gave the water-strainer back to the novice, circumambulated the stupa three times clockwise along with the elephant-wall, worshipped at the four sides, and while returning to the monastery, he thought: "How great is the psychic power of this novice! Will he be able to protect this power?" Seeing that he would not be able to protect it, he said to the novice, "Novice, you are now of great psychic power. However, by destroying such power..."
280:
“In the future, you will drink sour gruel kneaded by the hand of a blind weaver woman,” he said. This was the fault of youth: though he was startled by his preceptor's words, he did not ask, “Venerable sir, please teach me a meditation subject.” Instead, as if not hearing what his preceptor said, thinking, “What is our preceptor saying?” he went away.

The Elder, after paying homage to the Mahācetiya and the Mahābodhi tree, had the novice take his bowl and robes and gradually went to Kuṭeḷitissa Mahāvihāra. The novice did not follow his preceptor's footsteps for alms-round. Having asked, “Venerable sir, which village will you enter?” and knowing, “Now my preceptor must have reached the village gate,” he would take both his and his preceptor's bowl and robes, come through the air, give the bowl and robes to the Elder, and then enter for alms. The Elder constantly admonished him: “Novice, do not do this. The psychic power of worldlings is unstable and not permanent. When encountering unsuitable objects like sights and so on, it breaks even by a slight cause. Those who have fallen away from peaceful attainments are unable to remain firm in the holy life.” The novice, not wishing to listen, thinking, “What is my preceptor saying?” continued to do the same. The Elder, while paying homage to shrines in succession, arrived at Kammupenda Vihāra. Even while staying at that monastery, the novice did the same.

Then one day, a very beautiful weaver's daughter in her first youth came out from Kammupenda village, went down to the Paduma lotus pond, and plucked flowers while singing. At that time, the novice was flying over the Paduma lotus pond. While going, he became ensnared by the sound of her song, like a blind fly caught in sticky syrup. At that very moment, his psychic power disappeared, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. However, by the power of his peaceful attainments, he did not fall directly onto the water but descended like silk-cotton down and gradually stood on the bank of the Paduma pond. He went quickly, gave the bowl and robes to his preceptor, and returned. The Great Elder, thinking, “I saw this beforehand; even if forbidden, he will not turn back,” said nothing and entered for alms.

The novice went and stood on the bank of the Paduma pond, waiting for her to come out of the water. That woman, seeing the novice flying through the air and then returning to stand there...
281:
Realizing, “Surely this novice has become dissatisfied because of me,” she said, “Step aside, novice.” He stepped aside. She came out of the water, dressed in her garment, approached him, and asked, “What is it, venerable sir?” He told her the matter. Although she admonished him by showing the danger in household life and the benefits in the life of purity through many reasons, she was unable to dispel his dissatisfaction. Thinking, “This novice has fallen away from such psychic power because of me; it is not proper to abandon him now,” she said, “Stay here for a moment,” went home, and told the news to her parents. They also came and gave various advice, but when the novice would not listen to their words, they said, “Do not consider us as being of high birth. We are but weavers. Will you be able to do the work of a weaver?” The novice said, “Lay devotee, one who has become a layman must do either the work of a weaver or the work of a reed-worker. What is there to ask about this? Do not be greedy even for a small cloth.” The weaver gave him the cloth tied around his own waist, took him home, and gave him his daughter.

He learned the craft of weaving and worked in the weaving hall together with other weavers. The wives of the others prepared and brought food early in the morning. His wife had not yet arrived. While the others stopped work and were eating, he sat winding the shuttle. She arrived late. Then he rebuked her, saying, “You have come very late!” A woman, even if it be a universal monarch, once she knows his heart is bound to her, regards him like a slave. Therefore, she said, “In other people's houses, wood, vegetables, salt, and so on are stored; there are also weaver husbands who bring them from outside. But I am alone. You also do not know ‘this is in my house, this is not.’ If you want to eat, eat; if you do not want to eat, do not eat.” He became angry, thinking, “Not only do you bring food late in the day, but you also wound me with words.” Seeing no other weapon to strike with, he pulled that very shuttle-pin from the shuttle and threw it. Seeing it coming, she turned slightly. The tip of the shuttle-pin was very sharp. As she turned, it entered and stuck in the corner of her eye. She quickly covered her eye with both hands. Blood flowed from the ruptured spot.
282:
At that time, he remembered the words of his preceptor: "In the future, you will drink sour gruel (kanji) pressed by the hands of a blind weaver. This is what my preceptor meant when he spoke to me. This situation must have been seen by the Elder. Oh, how far-sighted my master was!" Thinking thus, he began to cry loudly. Others said to him, "Friend, enough, do not cry. Once the eyes are destroyed, they cannot be restored to their original state just by crying." He replied, "I am not crying because of the loss of my eyes. Indeed, I am crying with this reason in mind," and he related the whole sequence of events. Thus, when samatha and vipassanā that have arisen cease, they lead to misfortune.

Another story: About thirty monks, after worshipping at the Kalyāṇī Mahācetiya, were descending from a forest path to the main road. On the way, they saw a man returning from working in a burnt field. His body was smeared with soot, and he wore only a single soot-stained dyed cloth (robe) tucked at his waist. Looking at him, he appeared like a burnt stump. Having worked during the day, he was carrying a bundle of half-burnt wood on his back, with his hair disheveled, coming from an off-road path and standing before the monks. Seeing him, the novices looked at one another and jokingly said, "Friend, is he your father, your grandfather, or your uncle?" and laughing, they went and asked his name, "Lay devotee (upāsaka), what is your name?" When asked his name, he became remorseful, dropped the bundle of wood, adjusted his cloth neatly, and after paying homage to the Great Elders, said, "Venerable sirs, please wait a moment." The Great Elders stopped.

The young monks and novices came and mocked him even in the presence of the Great Elders. The lay devotee said, "Venerable sirs, you look at me and mock me. Do you think that just by this much (wearing the robe) you have reached the pinnacle? I too was once a monk like you. But in you, there is not even a trace of one-pointedness of mind. I was once a person of great psychic power and majesty in this Dispensation. I could take the sky and make it earth, and take the earth and make it sky. I could make the far near, and the near far. I could pierce through a thousand world-systems in an instant. Look at my hands; now they are like the hands of a monkey. With these very hands, while sitting in this spot, I once touched the moon and the sun. With these very feet, I once sat using the moon and the sun as a footstool. Such power has vanished due to negligence. Venerable sirs, do not be negligent. For through negligence..."
283:
"...through negligence, one meets with such ruin. Those who live without negligence can make an end of birth, aging, and death. Therefore, venerable sirs, taking even me as an object of reflection, do not be negligent." Thus he warned and gave them advice. While he was speaking, those monks were struck with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), practiced insight (vipassanā), and all thirty of them attained Arahantship right there. Thus, it should be understood that when samatha and vipassanā that have arisen cease, they lead to misfortune. This is the conclusion of the discussion on mundane Right Effort (lokiya sammappadhāna).

## In the moment of the supramundane path, however, this Right Effort is a single energy (viriya), but it receives four names because it accomplishes four functions.

In that Pali text, 'anuppannānaṃ' refers to states that have not yet arisen either because they have not been practiced in this life or because they have not yet been experienced as objects. This is because in the beginningless saṃsāra, there are no base unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) that have never occurred. When unrisen unwholesome states arise, they are only those that have occurred before in this saṃsāra. When they are abandoned, they are only those that have occurred before in this saṃsāra.

Among those that have not yet arisen, for some individuals, defilements do not arise by the power of their duties (vatta). For others, defilements do not arise by the power of one of the following: scriptures (gantha), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), concentration (samādhi), insight (vipassanā), or new construction work (navakamma). How? Some person is accomplished in duties. While he is performing the eighty-two minor duties (khuddakavatta), the fourteen major duties (mahāvatta), the duties of the shrine terrace, the Bodhi tree terrace, the water-stand, the Uposatha hall, the duties for guests, and the duties for those departing, defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, when he abandons his duties and wanders about with broken duties, defilements arise depending on improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the lapse of mindfulness. In this way, unrisen defilements are said to arise.

Some person is devoted to the study of scriptures. He learns one Nikāya, or two, three, four, or five. While he is learning, reciting, reflecting upon, teaching, preaching, and explaining the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) known as the Tipiṭaka—by way of meaning, by way of Pali, by way of sequence, and by way of context—defilements find no opportunity. Later, however, when he abandons his scriptural work and wanders about lazily, defilements arise depending on improper attention and the lapse of mindfulness. In this way too, unrisen defilements are said to arise.

Some person is a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). He undertakes and practices the thirteen dhutaṅga qualities. While he is maintaining these dhutaṅga qualities, defilements find no opportunity.
284:
In another way, when that person gives up the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) and wanders about revolving in the abundance of the four requisites, defilements arise based on unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and the lapse of mindfulness (sativossagga). Thus, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of non-occurrence (asamudācāra).

A certain person has mastery (vasī) practiced in the eight attainments (samāpattis). While he dwells by way of mastery in advertence (āvajjanavasī) and so on in the first jhāna and others, the defilements do not get an opportunity. In another way, when he has fallen away from jhāna or has set aside jhāna, and dwells devoted to talk (bhassa) and so on, defilements arise based on unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness. Thus, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of non-occurrence.

A certain person is a practitioner of insight (vipassaka). He dwells applying himself to the seven types of insight or the eighteen types of great insight. While he dwells thus, the defilements do not get an opportunity. In another way, when he gives up the work of insight and dwells emphasizing bodily vigor (kāyadaḷhī), defilements arise based on unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness. Thus, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of non-occurrence.

A certain person is a builder (navakammika); he builds Uposatha halls, refectories, and so on. While he is thinking about the materials for those buildings, the defilements do not get an opportunity. In another way, when the new construction work is finished or set aside, defilements arise based on unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness. Thus, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of non-occurrence.

A certain person is a pure being come from the Brahma world (brahmaloka). Because of his lack of habituation (anāsevanā) [to defilements], the defilements do not get an opportunity. In another way, when he has gained habituation, defilements arise based on unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness. Thus, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of non-occurrence. Thus should the state of not having arisen by way of non-occurrence be understood.

How is it by way of an unexperienced object (ananubhūtārammaṇa)? Here, a certain person obtains an object, such as a pleasant one, that he has not experienced before. In him, defilements such as greed (rāga) arise based on unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness regarding that object. Thus...
285:
...defilements that have not yet arisen are said to arise by way of an unexperienced object. However, at the moment of the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga), energy (vīriya) is only one (yet it receives four names by way of accomplishing four functions).

Those defilements that have not yet arisen might arise; [the path] accomplishes the task of preventing their arising so that they do not arise at all, and the task of abandoning those unwholesome states that have already arisen. Therefore, in the phrase "uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ" (of the evil states that have arisen), "arisen" (uppanna) is of four kinds: presently arisen (vattamānuppanna), arisen by having been and gone (bhutvāvigatuppanna), arisen by making an opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and arisen by obtaining a ground (bhūmiladdhuppanna).

Among those four, those defilements which are manifest and possessed of the moments of arising and so on—this is called "presently arisen." When kamma has run its course (javita), experienced the taste of the object, and ceased, the resultant (vipāka) is called "having been and gone." Kamma also, having arisen and ceased, is called "having been and gone." Both that resultant and kamma come under the designation "arisen by having been and gone." Wholesome or unwholesome kamma obstructs the result of another kamma and makes an opportunity for its own result. When an opportunity has been thus made, the resultant, as it arises, is said to be "arisen" from the time the opportunity was made. This "arisen" is called "arisen by making an opportunity."

The five aggregates (pañcakkhandha) are the ground (bhūmi) of insight. Those aggregates are divided into past and so on. The defilements latent (anusayita) in those aggregates should not be called past, future, or present. For the defilements latent in past aggregates are indeed unabandoned. The defilements latent in future aggregates and present aggregates are also indeed unabandoned. This "arisen" is called "arisen by obtaining a ground." Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "The defilements not yet eradicated by the path in those various grounds of the five aggregates come under the designation ground-obtained arisen."

Another four kinds of "arisen" are: arisen by occurrence (samudācāruppanna), arisen by seizing an object (ārammaṇādhigahituppanna), arisen by not being suppressed (avikkhambhituppanna), and arisen by not being eradicated (asamugghātituppanna).

Among those four, that which is currently occurring is called "arisen by occurrence." It cannot be said that defilements will not arise in the moments of repeated recollection after one has once opened the eyes and taken a sign (nimitta) in an object. Why? Because the object has been seized. Like what? Just as it cannot be said that sap will not come out from every place struck by an axe on a milk-tree, so it is here. This "arisen" is called "arisen by seizing an object."

It cannot be said that defilements not yet suppressed by an attainment (samāpatti) will not arise in such and such a place. Why? Because they have not been suppressed. For example, if they were to strike a milk-tree with an axe, "in such and such a place the sap will not..."
286:
Just as it cannot be said that milk will not flow in such a place, so too (because they have not been removed by meditative attainment), it cannot be said that defilements will not arise in such a place. This is called 'arisen through non-suppression' (avikkhambhituppanna). Furthermore, defilements not yet uprooted by the Path will not arise even in the continuum of a person reborn in the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), which is the peak of becoming; this should be expanded in detail according to the previous method. This is called 'arisen through non-uprooting' (asamugghātituppanna).

Among these 'arisen' states, the four types—presently arisen (vattamānuppanna), arisen and gone (bhutvāvigatuppanna), arisen by opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and arisen by habitual practice (samudācāruppanna)—are not to be abandoned (eradicated) by the Path. Only the four types—arisen by gaining ground (bhūmiladdhuppanna), arisen by seizing an object (ārammaṇādhighitituppanna), arisen through non-suppression, and arisen through non-uprooting—are to be abandoned by the Path. Indeed, when the Path arises, it abandons these defilements (such as those arisen by gaining ground). Those defilements which the Path abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present. This matter has been stated (by the Marshal of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta) as follows:

"If it abandons past defilements, then it would be exhausting what is already exhausted, causing what has ceased to cease, causing what has gone to go, causing what has disappeared to disappear. It would be abandoning past defilements that do not exist. If it abandons future defilements, then it would be abandoning what is not yet born, what has not been produced, what has not arisen, what has not manifested. It would be abandoning future defilements that do not exist. If it abandons present defilements, then the one who is lustful would be abandoning lust, the one who is hateful would be abandoning hatred, the one who is deluded would be abandoning delusion, the one who is bound would be abandoning conceit, the one who has misapprehended would be abandoning wrong view, the one who is distracted would be abandoning restlessness, the one who is undecided would be abandoning doubt, and the one who has reached strength would be abandoning underlying tendencies. (If that were so) dark unwholesome states and bright wholesome states would occur simultaneously in conjunction. The development of the Path would be defiled... therefore there would be no development of the Path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of defilements, and no penetration of the Dhamma. (But in reality) there is development of the Path... there is penetration of the Dhamma. How is it so? It is just like a young tree... those that have not appeared simply do not appear" (Paṭisambhidāmagga).

Thus, although the analogy of a tree without fruit appears in the Pali text, it should be explained by means of a tree with fruit. It is like a young mango tree with fruit. People might consume its fruits and shake down the rest to fill baskets. Afterwards, another man might cut that tree with an axe. By doing so, he does not destroy the past fruits, nor does he destroy the future or present fruits. For the past fruits have been consumed by people, and the future fruits, not having been produced, cannot be destroyed...
287:
...cannot be destroyed. However, at the time the tree is cut, there are no fruits at all, so even the present fruits are not (individually) destroyed (rather, they are destroyed by the act of cutting the tree). If the tree had not been cut, those fruits that would have been produced depending on the essence of the earth and the essence of water are said to be destroyed. They, being unborn, do not take birth; being unproduced, they are not produced; being unmanifested, they do not manifest. In the same way, the Path neither abandons defilements categorized as past and so on, nor does it not abandon them. For as long as the aggregates are not fully understood by the Path, the arising of those defilements would occur; because the aggregates are fully understood by the arising of the Path, those defilements, being unborn, do not take birth; being unproduced, they are not produced; being unmanifested, they do not manifest. This meaning should be illustrated by a woman with a young child taking medicine to prevent further childbirth, or by the sick taking medicine to appease a disease. Thus, those defilements which the Path abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present. Yet, it is not that the Path does not abandon defilements. It is with reference to those defilements which the Path abandons that it was said, "Of evil (unwholesome states) that have arisen," and so forth.

The Path does not only abandon defilements; it also abandons the acquired aggregates (upādinnakkhandha) that would have arisen because the defilements had not been abandoned. This has also been stated in detail: "By the cessation of the consciousness of formations (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) through the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, those names and forms that would have arisen in the beginningless Saṃsāra, except for seven births, cease here (in this Path knowledge)." Thus, the Path emerges from both the acquired and the unacquired. In terms of existence (bhava), the Path of Stream-entry emerges from the plane of misery (apāya). The Path of Once-returning emerges from a portion of the happy plane of existence; the Path of Non-returning emerges from the happy sense-sphere plane; the Path of Arahantship emerges from the fine-material and immaterial planes; some say it emerges from all planes of existence.

Then, at the moment of the Path, how is there development (bhāvanā) for the unarisen (wholesome) states to arise? Or how is there development for the arisen states to persist? It is by the very occurrence (pavattī) of the Path. For when the Path occurs, it is called 'unarisen' (anuppanna) because it has never arisen before. Just as there are people who, having reached a place never reached before or having experienced an object never experienced before, say, "We have reached a place never reached before, we experience an object never experienced before." The very occurrence of that Path is called 'persistence' (ṭhiti); therefore, it is proper to say it develops for the sake of persistence. Thus, this effort (vīriya) of that monk at the moment of the supramundane Path is "for the sake of [preventing] unarisen evil unwholesome states..."
288:
It receives the four names beginning with "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states." This is the discourse on Right Exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya) at the moment of the supramundane path. Thus, in this Suttanta Analysis (Suttanta-bhājanīya), the Right Efforts which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane are explained.

## Commentary on the Suttanta Analysis

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis

In the Abhidhamma Analysis (Abhidhamma-bhājanīya), all Right Efforts are indicated by showing only the mere opening of the method of teaching as analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. In that Abhidhamma Analysis, the distinction of methods should be understood. How? Firstly, in the first Right Effort, in the application of jhāna (jhānābhinivesa) within the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), there are ten methods by way of the two—the fourfold and fivefold methods—in each of these five instances: the pure mode of progress (suddhika-paṭipadā), the pure void (suddhika-suññata), the void mode of progress (suññata-paṭipadā), the pure undirected (suddhika-appaṇihita), and the undirected mode of progress (appaṇihita-paṭipadā). Likewise, in the remaining Right Efforts, there are also such methods; thus, in the twenty applications of jhāna, there are two hundred methods. When those two hundred methods are multiplied by four by way of the four predominant factors (adhipati), there are eight hundred methods. Thus, there are one thousand methods in total: two hundred pure methods without predominant factors and eight hundred methods together with the four predominant factors. Similarly, in the second Right Effort and so on, and in the pure Right Effort, there are thus five thousand methods in the Path of Stream-entry. As in the Path of Stream-entry, so also in the remaining paths; thus, by way of the wholesome (kusala) alone, there are twenty thousand methods. However, in the section on resultants (vipākavāra), the section on resultants is not taken because there is no task to be performed by the Right Efforts. In this Abhidhamma Analysis, it should be understood that the Right Efforts are only the supramundane ones extracted separately from the mundane.

## Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis

## 3. Commentary on the Questionnaire

In the Questionnaire (Pañhāpucchaka), the nature of the Right Efforts as wholesome and so on should be understood only in accordance with the Pali text. Regarding the Triad of Objects (ārammaṇa-ttika), all these Right Efforts have the infinite (appamāṇa) as their object because they occur by taking Nibbāna, which is infinite, as their object; they do not have the path as their object. By way of the conascent cause, they have the path as their cause. Having made wisdom (vīmaṃsā) the chief...
289:
At the time of developing the path, there are path-predominant (maggādhipati) factors. When developing the path by making desire (chanda) the chief or by making consciousness (citta) the chief, those Right Efforts should not be called 'path-predominants.' However, at the time of developing the path by making energy (vīriya) the chief, because there is no energy other than the energy named Right Effort, they should not be called 'path-predominants' nor 'not path-predominants.' In the objects of the past and so on, they should not be spoken of as having a single object. Because Nibbāna is an external state (bahiddhā-dhamma), they are called 'having external objects' (bahiddhārammaṇa).

Thus, in this Questionnaire method, only the supramundane Right Efforts are spoken of. Indeed, the Blessed One spoke of the Right Efforts as a mixture of mundane and supramundane only in the Suttanta Analysis; but in the Abhidhamma Analysis and the Questionnaire, only the supramundane Right Efforts were spoken of. Thus, this Analysis of Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) is also shown by being analyzed and extracted by way of the threefold round (te-parivaṭṭa).

## 9. Analysis of the Bases of Power
## 1. Commentary on the Suttanta Analysis

Now, in the Analysis of the Bases of Power (Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga) taught immediately after that, the word "four" (cattāro) is a delimitation of number. In this term "iddhipāda," it is called "iddhi" because it succeeds; it means accomplishment or manifestation. Alternatively, by this state, beings are successful, prosperous, and have reached excellence; therefore, it is also called "iddhi."

According to the first meaning, since the accomplished fruit itself is the constituent part, it is called "iddhipāda" (the constituent part of success). According to the second meaning, it is called "iddhipāda" (the base of success) because it is the base of success. "Pāda" means the foundation or the means of attainment. For, because one reaches or attains the success (iddhi) known as the higher and higher distinctions, it is called "pāda" (foot/base). Thus, the meaning of the phrase "four bases of power" should first be understood.

Now, to show them by way of analysis, the passage beginning with "Here, a monk" is commenced. Therein, "Here, a monk" means a monk in this Dispensation. In the phrase "endowed with concentration of intention and the effort of formation" (chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgata), the concentration that has intention as its cause or has intention as its predominant factor is "concentration of intention" (chanda-samādhi). This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) the predominant factor. The formations that are principal are "striving-formations" (padhāna-saṅkhāra). This is a designation for the Right Exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya) that accomplishes the four tasks. "Endowed with" means being possessed of both the concentration of intention and the striving-formations.

"Base of power" (iddhipāda) refers to the remaining group of consciousness and mental factors which serve as the foundation for the intention, concentration, and striving-formations associated with the wholesome consciousness of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) and so on, which have reached the designation of "iddhi" either by way of accomplishment or by way of being the cause for beings to become successful, prosperous, and excellent. This is because the statement made later, "The base of power is the aggregate of feeling... the aggregate of consciousness of one who is such," is consistent with this meaning. In this same way, the meaning should be understood in the remaining bases of power as well. Just as the concentration obtained by making intention the predominant factor is called "concentration of intention," so also for energy... consciousness. The concentration obtained by making investigation (vīmaṃsā) the predominant factor is called "concentration of investigation" (vīmaṃsā-samādhi).

Now, to show the analysis of the terms "concentration of intention" and so on, the passage beginning with "How, monk" is commenced. Therein, "If a monk, making intention the predominant factor" means if a monk obtains and produces concentration by making intention the predominant, the chief, the leader, and the precursor, the concentration thus produced is called "concentration of intention."
291:
The same method applies to the words beginning with "viriya" (energy) as well. By this sequence of the Pali text, "These states are called volitional efforts (padhāna-saṅkhāra)," He [the Buddha] spoke of the energy that accomplishes the four functions known as volitional efforts of a monk who develops the base of power consisting of desire (chandiddhipāda). "Having combined them all together" means making all that concentration and energy into a single mass. "Enters into the count" means it should be understood that it enters into the designation "volitional effort of concentration of desire" (chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra).

Now, in order to analyze and show the states such as desire in this group of words "chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra," the passage beginning with "Therein, what is desire?" is undertaken. That group of words has an obvious meaning.

"Upeto hoti" means he is endowed with the collection of states called the bases of power (iddhipāda). "Of those states" refers to those associated states such as desire. All the words such as iddhi (power), samiddhi (success), and so on, are merely synonyms for accomplishment. Even so, it is called iddhi because of the sense of accomplishing. Complete iddhi is called samiddhi; or the word is intensified by a prefix. The mode of accomplishing is called ijjanā. Samijjanā means the word is intensified by a prefix. Obtaining due to manifestation within one's own continuity is called lābha (gain). Regaining states that were lost through the exertion of energy is called paṭilābha (attainment); or the word is intensified by a prefix. Patti means attainment (adhigama). Attaining well without decline is called sampatti (achievement). Phusanā is the touching that is attainment. Sacchikiriyā is the realization that is attainment. Upasampadā should be understood as the fulfillment that is attainment.

"Tathābhūtassa" means for one who has become thus, that is, for the person who remains having obtained those states such as desire. By the words beginning with "aggregate of feeling" (vedanākkhandha), all four mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha) are spoken of, including desire and so on. "Those states" refers to those four mental aggregates; or it is also said to refer to the three states such as desire. The words beginning with "āsevati" (he frequents) have the meanings already mentioned. In the remaining descriptions of the bases of power, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

What is taught by this sequence of the Pali text? The meditation subject that has reached the summit for four types of monks is taught. For one monk relies on desire; when there is the accomplishment of the goal through the wholesome desire for action (kattukamyatā-kusala-dhamma-chanda), he brings about the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma), making desire the chief, making desire the dominant factor, and making desire the precursor, thinking: "I will bring about the supramundane state; there is no burden for me in bringing this state about." One monk relies on energy. One relies on consciousness (citta), and one relies on wisdom (paññā). When there is the accomplishment of the goal through wisdom, [thinking:] "I [will bring about] the supramundane state...
292:
"...'I will bring it about; there is no burden for me in bringing this state about,' he brings about the supramundane state, making wisdom the chief, making wisdom the dominant factor, and making wisdom the precursor."

How? For example, while four sons of ministers were wandering about desiring a position, one relied on service (upaṭṭhāna), one on bravery (sūrabāva), one on birth (jāti), and one on counsel (manta). How? Among them, the first son of ministers thought: "If there is accomplishment of the goal through diligence in service, I will obtain this position which is obtainable." Thus he relied on service. The second son of ministers thought: "Even if one is diligent in service, some cannot stand firm when a battle arises. The King's border region will certainly rebel. When it rebels, I will serve at the head of the chariot, please the King, and receive this position." Thus he relied on bravery. The third son of ministers thought: "Even if there is bravery, some are of low birth. When they give positions after investigating birth, they will give it to me." Thus he relied on birth. The fourth son of ministers thought: "Even if one has [noble] birth, some are not fit for counsel. When a matter to be done through counsel arises, I will receive this position." Thus he relied on counsel. All of them reached their respective positions by the power of what they relied upon.

Among them, like the one who reached the position by being diligent in service, one who brings about the supramundane state by relying on desire—when there is accomplishment of the goal through the wholesome desire for action—making desire the chief, making desire the dominant factor, and making desire the precursor, thinking: "I will bring about the supramundane state; there is no burden for me in bringing this about," should be understood like the Elder Raṭṭhapāla. For that venerable one brought about the supramundane state by making desire the dominant factor. Like the one who reached the position by pleasing the King through bravery, one who brings about the supramundane state by making energy the chief, making energy the dominant factor, and making energy the precursor, should be understood like the Elder Soṇa. For that venerable one brought about the supramundane state by making energy the dominant factor.
